claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides in general kill target cells by disrupting the cell membranes.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref [6]); not demonstrated de novo for ocellatin-PTs in this study.

claim_text: Ocellatin-PT peptides interact electrostatically with the cell membranes of microorganisms.
limitations: Stated as a general property of cationic AMPs in the abstract; not directly measured for ocellatin-PTs in this study.

claim_text: Ocellatin-PT peptides are unstructured (random coil) in aqueous solution but adopt alpha-helical secondary structure upon contact with lipid membranes.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism in TFE gradients and in presence of LUVs
limitations: Helicity was measured in TFE (membrane-mimicking solvent) and LUVs, not in intact cell membranes; estimated helicity varied widely across peptides (17–38%).

claim_text: Ocellatin-PT1 and PT8 develop alpha-helical character preferentially in the presence of bacterial membrane-mimicking lipids (POPE:POPG) and to a lesser extent leishmania-mimicking lipids (POPC:POPE), suggesting membrane-composition-dependent structural activation.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism with LUVs
limitations: Only two of eight peptides were tested in LUV-CD experiments; results with DMPC were inconsistent between PT1 and PT8.

claim_text: Ocellatin-PT1 and PT8 show higher binding affinity for bacteria-mimicking (POPE:POPG) and leishmania-mimicking (POPC:POPE) lipid membranes than for mammalian-mimicking (DMPC) membranes, indicating selective targeting of microbial membranes.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance
limitations: Only two of eight peptides tested; synthetic lipid bilayer models used, not native cell membranes; saturation could not be reached at tested concentrations so Kd values are from kinetic two-state model fits.

claim_text: At sub-lethal concentrations (16 µg/mL, below IC50), ocellatin-PT1 and PT8 cause formation of blister-like vesicular protrusions and membrane thinning on L. infantum promastigote surfaces.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy
limitations: Only two representative peptides studied morphologically; SEM requires fixation/dehydration that may introduce artefacts; BSE dark patches interpreted as thinning but not confirmed biochemically.

claim_text: At lethal concentrations (64 µg/mL, above IC50), ocellatin-PT1 and PT8 cause deep holes penetrating into the cell body of L. infantum promastigotes, consistent with cell lysis.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Lysis is inferred from morphological appearance; direct measurement of membrane integrity (e.g., dye leakage) was not performed.

claim_text: The blister-like protrusions and membrane holes observed by microscopy are most likely the result of vesicalization and/or micellization of membrane lipids by the peptides.
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation of SEM/AFM morphology; no direct lipid extraction or membrane composition analysis performed.

claim_text: Ocellatin-PT peptides increase the surface roughness of L. infantum promastigote membranes, indicating disruption of membrane texture.
direct_assay_types: atomic force microscopy (RMS roughness measurement)
limitations: Roughness increase (2.78 nm control vs 4.22/5.08 nm treated) did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05) due to high biological variability; only two peptides tested.

claim_text: The selectivity of ocellatin-PTs for microbial over mammalian membranes is related to differences in lipid composition, specifically the higher content of anionic lipids (PE, PG) in microbial membranes versus low anionic lipid content in mammalian membranes.
limitations: Inferred from SPR affinity data combined with known lipid composition differences; not tested by varying lipid composition systematically.

claim_text: The mechanism of action of ocellatin-PT peptides on L. infantum is distinct from that of the AMP DRS-01, based on qualitatively different morphological effects (localized blistering and holes vs. global rounding, shortening, and flagellar changes).
limitations: Comparison is indirect, based on contrasting microscopy results across two separate studies using the same parasite model.

claim_text: SAAP-145 and SAAP-276 kill S. aureus by rapidly permeabilizing the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in bacterial death within minutes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (propidium iodide influx flow cytometry on live S. aureus), fluorescent dye leakage (ANTS/DPX from POPG liposomes), time-kill assay
limitations: All membrane permeabilization assays performed in PBS; activity reduced in 50% human plasma, suggesting physiological conditions may affect potency

claim_text: SAAP-145 resides preferentially at the membrane interface, inducing chain-interdigitation in the gel phase and membrane thinning in the fluid phase of the bacterial membrane mimic.
direct_assay_types: differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on DPPG liposomes
limitations: DPPG liposomes are a simplified membrane mimic; thermotropic behavior in artificial bilayers may not fully recapitulate interaction with intact bacterial membranes

claim_text: SAAP-276 penetrates deeper into the bilayer core than SAAP-145, strongly perturbing hydrocarbon chain packing, consistent with its larger hydrophobic region.
direct_assay_types: differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on DPPG liposomes, helical wheel projection (hydrophobicity analysis)
limitations: Depth of membrane penetration inferred from thermotropic phase behavior changes and hydrophobicity calculations, not directly measured (e.g., by neutron scattering or fluorescence depth quenching)

claim_text: The cationic and amphipathic nature of SAAP-145 and SAAP-276 drives electrostatic binding to the anionic bacterial cell surface and insertion into the cytoplasmic membrane, resulting in membrane perturbation.
limitations: Attributed by the authors as a general AMP class mechanism applicable to these LL-37-derived peptides; electrostatic binding to live bacterial surface not directly measured for SAAP-145/276 specifically

claim_text: Membrane permeabilization/disruption by SAAP-145 and SAAP-276, acting without a specific intracellular target, implies efficacy against both dividing and metabolically inactive non-dividing bacteria residing in biofilms.
limitations: Authors state this as an implication of the membrane MOA; direct killing of non-dividing or biofilm-embedded bacteria by the membrane mechanism was not experimentally demonstrated in this study (anti-biofilm assays used a medium that prevented killing)

claim_text: Because SAAP-145 and SAAP-276 attack the bacterial membrane rather than a specific molecular target, resistance development is unlikely, consistent with the absence of resistance induction observed over 22 serial passages.
limitations: Authors note that resistance to AMPs via efflux pumps, surface charge modification, proteolytic degradation, and biofilm matrix can occur; the mechanistic link between membrane targeting and low resistance is a long-standing hypothesis, not proven causally here

claim_text: Melittin binds to lipid bilayers and causes membrane permeabilization through the formation of transmembrane pores or lesions.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (ONPG/β-galactosidase inner membrane assay, nitrocefin/β-lactamase outer membrane assay, DAPI membrane integrity assay), electrophysiology (transmembrane current across planar lipid bilayers), MIC assay
limitations: Pore geometry and exact molecular architecture not directly resolved in this study; E. coli inner membrane permeabilization was incomplete relative to detergent control, attributed to the peptide first needing to traverse the outer membrane.

claim_text: Membrane permeabilization by melittin is a concentration-dependent phenomenon requiring four to six melittin peptides to homooligomerize into a lesion-competent structure, most likely forming a stable barrel-stave model pore.
limitations: Qualifier 'most likely' used by the authors; oligomeric state and pore geometry not directly measured in this study; claim is drawn from prior literature (ref 35).

claim_text: More recent data suggest the melittin pore may be more transient rather than a stable barrel-stave structure.
limitations: Presented as an alternative model based on prior literature (ref 36); not directly tested or resolved in this study.

claim_text: Melittin disrupts both the outer and inner membranes of Escherichia coli in a concentration-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane permeabilization via nitrocefin/β-lactamase enzymatic assay, inner membrane permeabilization via ONPG/β-galactosidase enzymatic assay
limitations: Inner membrane permeabilization did not reach the level of the detergent (CTAB) control, attributed to the requirement for the peptide to first bind and traverse the outer membrane before accessing the inner membrane.

claim_text: Melittin disrupts the membrane of Staphylococcus aureus in a concentration-dependent manner, allowing normally membrane-impermeant molecules to enter the cell and access bacterial DNA.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeability assay using DAPI fluorescent DNA-binding reporter

claim_text: Melittin adopts an alpha-helical secondary structure upon binding to phospholipid bilayers, representing the membrane-active conformation of the peptide.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: CD indicates bulk secondary structure and cannot resolve local conformational heterogeneity or transmembrane vs. surface-adsorbed populations.

claim_text: Upon membrane binding, melittin inserts into the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer, positioning the tryptophan residue in close proximity to the acyl chain region.
direct_assay_types: fluorescence quenching with membrane-embedded quencher 10-doxyl nonadecane (10-DN), dual quencher analysis (DQA) comparing aqueous acrylamide vs. membrane-embedded 10-DN quenching
limitations: Exact fluorescence lifetime values for AzAla at various bilayer depths have not been determined, so DQA results are interpreted as relative; slight changes in pore-forming conformation could alter quencher accessibility and influence the quenching ratio.

claim_text: Melittin creates functional ion-conducting transmembrane channels (pores) in model lipid bilayer membranes, as evidenced by measurable conductance increases.
direct_assay_types: electrophysiology (patch-clamp-style transmembrane current recording across planar DPhyPC bilayers)
limitations: Measurements performed in a cell-free model membrane system (DPhyPC planar bilayers); single-channel vs. multi-channel conductance events not fully resolved at all conditions; local peptide concentration at membrane surface subject to uncertainty from tip position and applied pressure.

claim_text: Melittin's interaction with lipid bilayers is relatively non-specific, with lipid headgroup composition modulating the degree of permeabilization rather than preventing pore formation.
limitations: Stated as an established property from prior literature (refs 33, 34); not directly re-tested with a pore-formation readout across varied lipid compositions in this study, though differential quenching constants across PC vs. PC:PG vesicles are consistent with this claim.

claim_text: Melittin inhibits various ion channels through calmodulin-mediated pathways.
limitations: Cited as a known secondary activity from prior literature (ref 39); not investigated or tested in this study.

claim_text: Seminalplasmin specifically interferes with RNA synthesis in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: inhibition of RNA synthesis in E. coli
limitations: Mechanism of RNA synthesis inhibition is not elucidated; assay used as a proxy for biological activity throughout, not to characterize mechanism per se

claim_text: Seminalplasmin very likely must penetrate cells to be effective.
limitations: Explicitly flagged as unpublished data (Scheit et al., unpublished); no experimental details provided in this paper

claim_text: Treatment of seminalplasmin with trypsin, chymotrypsin, thermolysin, aminopeptidase M, or carboxypeptidase Y completely eliminated biological activity.
direct_assay_types: inhibition of RNA synthesis in E. coli
limitations: Activity loss is consistent with structure-dependence but does not distinguish between loss of cell penetration, RNA-binding, or other mechanistic steps

claim_text: Removal of only residues 41–48 from the C-terminus (by carboxypeptidase Y, which stopped at Lys-40) was sufficient to abolish biological activity entirely.
direct_assay_types: inhibition of RNA synthesis in E. coli
limitations: Implies the C-terminal region (residues 40–48, predicted α-helix) is required for activity, but the paper makes no mechanistic inference beyond noting the result is 'interesting'

claim_text: Cecropins attack the cell membrane and efficiently lyse a wide variety of bacteria.
limitations: This is a background statement citing prior literature (Dunn 1986; Boman and Hultmark 1987), not a new result from this paper; no membrane assay performed here.

claim_text: Andropin has moderate antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria but little or no activity against Gram-negative bacteria under standard (unbuffered) assay conditions.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay, MIC assay
limitations: Activity measured with synthetic peptide assuming signal peptide cleavage after residue 23 is the only post-translational modification; assay conditions (unbuffered LB) may not reflect physiological ionic strength.

claim_text: Andropin becomes a potent bactericidal agent against Escherichia coli at high phosphate buffer concentrations, indicating its activity is strongly dependent on ionic strength.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay (buffer concentration series)
limitations: Mechanism by which ionic strength potentiates activity is not determined; 0.2 M NaCl gave similar effect to 0.05 M phosphate, suggesting ionic strength rather than phosphate-specific effect, but no membrane or molecular assay was done to explain this.

claim_text: Andropin is predicted to form two amphipathic alpha-helices with a strong hydrophobic moment, suggesting a membrane-disrupting mechanism of action similar to the cecropins.
limitations: Based solely on computational secondary structure prediction (Chou-Fasman rules); authors explicitly note 'the predictive value of the methods used is limited'; no biophysical or membrane assay performed on andropin.

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of andropin likely reflects its physiological function in protecting the seminal fluid and male reproductive tract against microbial infection.
limitations: Inference based on co-migration of synthetic peptide with one natural antibacterial band on acidic PAGE and tissue-specific expression in ejaculatory duct; no in vivo infection model tested.

claim_text: Hyalophora cecropins are strongly amphipathic peptides that efficiently kill and lyse bacteria by attacking the cell membrane.
limitations: This claim is attributed to Steiner et al. (1988) and concerns Hyalophora cecropins, not Drosophila cecropins; the paper cites it as background context only.

claim_text: Drosophila cecropin A accumulates in the hemolymph of immunized flies at a concentration of 25–50 µM, sufficient to kill all tested bacteria except Serratia marcescens.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay, native acidic polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis with bacterial overlay, MIC assay
limitations: Concentration is a crude estimate by comparison with synthetic cecropin dilution series; hemolymph volume assumptions not stated; activity inferred from in vitro killing, not in vivo clearance.

claim_text: Drosophila cecropins A and B kill both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria across a wide spectrum, with cecropin A at least as potent as Hyalophora cecropin A against Gram-negative bacteria but less active against Gram-positives.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay, MIC assay
limitations: Cecropin B results may be confounded by gel-forming behavior in aqueous solution under ionic assay conditions, potentially underestimating its potency.

claim_text: Serratia marcescens is highly resistant to Drosophila cecropins A and B, with MIC values that could not be calculated from inhibition zone assays due to very small and diffuse zones.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay, MIC assay
limitations: Resistance mechanism is not determined; the non-pathogenic Serratia mutant Db140, known to be sensitive to immune hemolymph, was also resistant to purified cecropins, suggesting other hemolymph components contribute to killing of this strain in vivo.

claim_text: Ubonodin inhibits RNA polymerase (RNAP) in vitro, as demonstrated by abortive transcription initiation assays with E. coli RNAP.
direct_assay_types: abortive transcription initiation assay (in vitro RNAP inhibition)
limitations: Assay used E. coli RNAP, not Burkholderia RNAP; ubonodin's potency in this assay was lower than MccJ25, which authors attribute to E. coli not being the natural target.

claim_text: RNAP inhibition is the putative antimicrobial mode of action of ubonodin, inferred from its structural similarity to known RNAP-inhibiting lasso peptides (MccJ25 and citrocin) and confirmed in vitro RNAP inhibition.
direct_assay_types: abortive transcription initiation assay
limitations: No direct demonstration that RNAP inhibition causes growth arrest in Burkholderia; uptake into susceptible cells has not been characterized and is explicitly noted as a future study.

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity and spectrum of ubonodin is hypothesized to be dictated by its uptake into susceptible bacteria rather than intrinsic differences in RNAP binding potency.
limitations: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis for future study; no transport or uptake experiments were performed; no Burkholderia homolog of the MccJ25 transporter FhuA (>40% identity) was identified.

claim_text: The Tyr/Tyr/Gly motif (Tyr at position 9, Tyr at penultimate position, and C-terminal Gly) is proposed as a structural predictor of RNAP-inhibiting lasso peptides, supported by the MccJ25-RNAP crystal structure showing contacts between these residues and the β and β' subunits of RNAP.
limitations: Predictive motif inferred by comparative sequence analysis and analogy to MccJ25 crystal structure data; not experimentally validated for ubonodin by mutagenesis of these specific residues or co-crystallography.

claim_text: Cec4 sterilizes A. baumannii through disruption of cell membrane integrity, as evidenced by SEM showing progressive hole formation, cell surface roughening, pore enlargement, cell shrinkage, and contents extrusion over 2–6 hours at 1× MIC.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SEM morphology), intracellular content leakage (260 nm absorbing material)
limitations: Single bacterial strain (4367992 isolate); SEM performed at only one concentration (1× MIC); mechanism inferred from morphological and leakage data, not from receptor/target identification

claim_text: Cec4 causes dose- and time-dependent leakage of intracellular material across the A. baumannii outer membrane, indicating membrane disruption as its primary antibacterial mechanism.
direct_assay_types: intracellular content leakage (260 nm absorbing material assay)
limitations: 260 nm absorbance detects nucleic acids and aromatic amino acids but does not distinguish specific intracellular components; leakage could reflect outer membrane disruption without specifying inner membrane involvement

claim_text: Cec4 kills A. baumannii in a rapid and concentration-dependent manner, eliminating bacteria within 24 h at both 1× MIC and 2× MIC.
direct_assay_types: time-kill assay (OD600 growth curve)
limitations: Growth inhibition measured by turbidity, not CFU counts; does not distinguish bactericidal from bacteriostatic activity definitively

claim_text: Cec4 targets the A. baumannii outer membrane, causing intracellular material to leak outward, as indicated by increased absorbance at 260 nm in a dose-dependent fashion.
direct_assay_types: intracellular content leakage (260 nm absorbing material assay)
limitations: The paper infers outer membrane targeting from leakage data; no inner membrane integrity assay (e.g., propidium iodide, ONPG) was performed to distinguish outer vs. inner membrane effects

claim_text: Attacins are bactericidal against growing Escherichia coli cells, producing a dramatic reduction in colony-forming units after 6 hours of incubation in rich medium.
direct_assay_types: colony-forming unit survival counting on agar plates
limitations: Demonstrated only for attacin E against E. coli D31; bactericidal vs. bacteriostatic distinction not resolved for agar inhibition zone experiments used for other strains

claim_text: Attacins require actively growing bacterial cells for killing activity; cells suspended in phosphate buffer (non-growing) are completely resistant.
direct_assay_types: colony-forming unit survival counting comparing LEG medium vs. phosphate buffer suspensions
limitations: Tested only with attacin E and E. coli D31; mechanism by which growth-dependence confers resistance is not determined

claim_text: Attacins cause treated E. coli to form chains typically containing 4–6 cell-sized units, indicating interference with cell division.
direct_assay_types: phase contrast microscopy
limitations: Morphological observation only; causal link to the lethal mechanism not established

claim_text: Attacin treatment causes partial lysis of E. coli, as evidenced by decreased phase contrast and the formation of spherical blebs attached to bacterial chains.
direct_assay_types: phase contrast microscopy
limitations: Lysis was partial and appeared secondary to chain formation; not quantified; may reflect a secondary consequence rather than primary MOA

claim_text: The primary target(s) of attacins is likely in the bacterial cell division cycle, supported by the markedly greater sensitivity of the chain-forming envA (division-defective) mutant D22 relative to its parental strain D21.
direct_assay_types: inhibition zone assay comparing D21 vs. D22 lethal concentrations
limitations: Authors present this explicitly as a hypothesis; D22 is also outer-membrane-barrier defective, providing an alternative explanation unrelated to cell division

claim_text: Alternatively, the heightened attacin sensitivity of strain D22 may reflect increased outer membrane permeability rather than a cell-division-cycle target, since D22 is barrier defective.
limitations: Explicitly flagged by the authors as an alternative explanation; outer membrane permeability to attacins was not directly measured

claim_text: Attacins do not act by destroying bacterial membranes, in contrast to the cecropins, whose mechanism involves membrane destruction.
limitations: Inferred indirectly from the growth-dependence of attacin activity and the chain-formation phenotype; no direct membrane integrity assay (e.g., dye leakage, electron microscopy of membranes) was performed on attacin-treated cells; cecropin membrane-disruption claim is cited from Steiner et al. 1981, not shown here

claim_text: Antibacterial activity of attacins may depend on an unidentified cofactor that is lost during purification, potentially contributing to the observed activity losses.
limitations: Speculative; authors were unable to reconstitute activity by recombining separated fractions; normal UV absorption spectra of attacins provided no evidence of a chromophore cofactor

claim_text: Positive charges are required for antibacterial and haemolytic activity, as the truncated synthetic peptide A, which lacks the C-terminal Lys-Lys-Ile-amide residues and therefore the positive charges, was devoid of both antibacterial and lytic activity.
limitations: Peptide A differs from peptide B in both charge and length; the lack of activity cannot be unambiguously attributed to charge alone versus the missing residues; no systematic charge-modification experiments were performed; mechanistic interpretation relies on a cited external reference (Cruciani et al., 1988) rather than direct assay in this study.

claim_text: Bombinins H cannot form an amphipathic helix, indicating they act by a mechanism distinct from the amphipathic helix-mediated membrane disruption employed by most other amphibian antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: Based solely on sequence/structural analysis; no biophysical or membrane experiments were performed to confirm the absence of helix formation or to characterise the actual mechanism; the alternative mechanism is not proposed or tested.

claim_text: The D-alloisoleucine residue at position 2 of bombinins H3–H5 confers resistance to aminopeptidase degradation, which may contribute to their biological persistence and sustained antimicrobial efficacy.
direct_assay_types: aminopeptidase M digestion
limitations: Proteolytic resistance is a stability property, not a bactericidal mechanism per se; in vivo relevance is not demonstrated; the contribution of this stability to observed MIC values is not quantified.

claim_text: The D-alloisoleucine stereochemistry at position 2 is not essential for the antibacterial or haemolytic mechanism, as the L-isoleucine-containing isomers (H1, H2) and the D-alloisoleucine-containing isomers (H3, H4) display similar potency.
limitations: Comparison is between peptide variants that also differ at positions 1 and 8 (Ile/Leu and Met/Leu), confounding attribution of similar potency to position-2 stereochemistry alone; only an inhibition zone assay was used, which measures growth inhibition but not mechanism.

claim_text: Kalata B1 does not require chiral recognition by a protein receptor to be active, as its all-D enantiomer retains anti-HIV and hemolytic activity.
direct_assay_types: anti-HIV cytopathic inhibition assay (HIV-1 RF on human lymphoblastoid cells), hemolysis assay (human RBCs)
limitations: D-enantiomer was less potent (EC50 0.9→2.5 µM anti-HIV; IC50 26→77 µM hemolysis), so the membrane environment still modulates activity quantitatively even without chiral receptor involvement

claim_text: Kalata B1 activity is mediated primarily by interaction with phospholipid membranes rather than by a receptor-dependent mechanism, as lower membrane affinity of the D-enantiomer directly correlates with its lower biological activity.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) on POPC/POPE model bilayers, hemolysis assay
limitations: Correlation shown between model bilayer affinity and RBC hemolysis; model membranes (POPC/POPE 4:1) are a simplification of native cell membranes

claim_text: Kalata B1 selectively binds membranes containing phosphoethanolamine (PE) headgroups; this PE selectivity governs membrane affinity and thereby modulates biological activity.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) comparing POPC vs. POPC/POPE bilayers
limitations: Tested only on two model lipid compositions; PE content in the SPR model (20%) approximates but may not perfectly represent target cell membranes

claim_text: The reduced potency of D-kalata B1 relative to native L-kalata B1 is explained by a slower membrane association rate, not by differences in membrane dissociation rate, indicating association kinetics limit local peptide concentration at the membrane surface.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) kinetics (initial binding rate and kd measurement on POPC/POPE bilayers)
limitations: Kinetics measured on model bilayers only; dissociation rates for pure L and pure D were comparable (0.0166 vs. 0.0184 s−1), supporting the conclusion but not ruling out subtle differences at higher concentrations

claim_text: Kalata B1 hemolytic activity operates via a concentration-threshold mechanism at the membrane surface, as evidenced by time-dependent and dose-dependent hemolysis curves.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay (1 h vs. 14 h incubation at multiple concentrations)
limitations: Threshold concentration not directly quantified; inferred from shift in IC50 with incubation time (IC50 drops from 26 to 5 µM for native peptide at 1 h vs. 14 h)

claim_text: Kalata B1 self-associates (oligomerizes) at the membrane surface, and this self-association is required for membrane disruption and biological activity.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay with L/D enantiomer mixtures, SPR binding and dissociation kinetics of L/D mixtures
limitations: Oligomerization is inferred from non-additive hemolytic and SPR behavior of L/D mixtures, not directly observed; oligomeric state or stoichiometry in the membrane was not characterized structurally

claim_text: Oligomerization of kalata B1 requires monomers of identical chirality; mixing L and D enantiomers disrupts productive self-assembly, reduces membrane insertion depth, and lowers hemolytic efficacy.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay (L/D ratio series), SPR dissociation kinetics of L/D mixtures
limitations: Inferred from the disproportionately low hemolysis and faster membrane dissociation of the 25:75 L/D mixture; no direct structural characterization of mixed vs. homomeric oligomers

claim_text: Kalata B1 disrupts membranes through a four-step pore-formation mechanism: (1) binding to the membrane surface via PE headgroup interactions and hydrophobic forces; (2) oligomerization of membrane-bound monomers; (3) insertion into the hydrophobic lipid core facilitated by self-association; (4) pore formation as embedded peptides span the bilayer.
limitations: Proposed model integrating SPR, hemolysis, and L/D mixture data from this paper with previously published electron microscopy (ref 5) and electrophysiology data (ref 19); individual mechanistic steps were not all directly demonstrated here; pore structure and spanning geometry not resolved

claim_text: Kalata B1 disrupts the membrane of midgut cells in lepidopteran larvae, supporting a receptor-independent, membrane-disruption mechanism for its insecticidal activity.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy of larval midgut cells (cited from prior work, ref 5; not performed in this study)
limitations: Evidence is from a previously published study, not generated here; mechanism in larval gut may differ from mammalian cell contexts tested in this paper

claim_text: Kalata B1 induces membrane leakage in model membranes through pore formation, as an initial silent period followed by stepwise current increases until membrane rupture was observed in electrophysiological recordings.
direct_assay_types: electrophysiological recordings on model membranes (cited from prior work, ref 19; not performed in this study)
limitations: Evidence is from a previously published study; the paper cites it as corroborating evidence for the self-association/pore-formation model

claim_text: The lipid moiety of fusaricidin analogs helps target them to the bacterial membrane, inferred from the inactivity of nonlipidated analogs and by analogy with other lipopeptide antibiotics.
limitations: Explicitly framed as an assumption ('we can assume'); no direct membrane-targeting or binding assay performed; relies on analogy with structurally distinct lipopeptides.

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of analogs with a guanidylated lipid tail may be explained by the guanidinium group binding the anionic phosphate of the bacterial phospholipid membrane via H-bonding and charge-charge interactions.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('could possibly be explained by'); no direct membrane-binding, phospholipid interaction, or biophysical assay performed.

claim_text: Only analogs bearing a guanidino-functionalized lipid tail show antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria, indicating the positively charged guanidino group and the lipid tail are required for antimicrobial activity.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay (broth microdilution)
limitations: Structural requirement established by SAR; the killing mechanism itself was not directly investigated; MIC reflects growth inhibition outcome, not mechanism.

claim_text: A positive charge at the end of the lipid tail together with overall hydrophobicity and amphiphilicity are crucial determinants of antibacterial activity in fusaricidin A/LI-F04a analogs.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay (broth microdilution)
limitations: Conclusion drawn from SAR correlations across 18 analogs; no mechanistic or target-identification assay performed.

claim_text: Increased hydrophobicity of depsipeptide analogs correlates with enhanced hemolytic activity against human erythrocytes, suggesting hydrophobicity drives disruption of human cell membranes.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Correlation only; no direct membrane-disruption or permeabilization assay; DMSO co-solvent and potential aggregation at high concentrations are confounders acknowledged by the authors.

claim_text: Ester bond hydrolysis and consequent ring-opening of the depsipeptide macrocycle is not the cause of hemolytic activity, because the ring-opened linear analog 18 is not hemolytic.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Indirect argument relying on a single linear control; does not exclude other ring-opening-independent mechanisms.

claim_text: Lower overall hydrophobicity and amphiphilicity of amide analogs compared to depsipeptide analogs may explain the dissociation of antibacterial activity from human cell cytotoxicity observed for the amide series.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay, cell viability assay (WRL 68 and HepG2 lines)
limitations: Stated as a possible explanation ('may explain'); hydrophobicity is proxied by HPLC retention time, not a direct biophysical membrane-partitioning measurement; mechanistic basis not tested directly.

claim_text: The antimicrobial mechanism of XLAsp-P1 is destruction of the bacterial cell membrane, as investigated by transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: membrane disruption (transmission electron microscopy)
limitations: Only TEM imaging is cited; no quantitative membrane permeabilization assay (e.g., dye leakage, propidium iodide uptake) or controls described in the abstract; full methods not available in this excerpt.

claim_text: Lipidated antimicrobial peptides act by targeting the bacterial plasma membrane.
limitations: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis based on literature analogy; no direct membrane assay performed in this study.

claim_text: Electrostatic interactions between the positively charged residues of antimicrobial peptides and negatively charged lipopolysaccharide (Gram-negative bacteria) or teichoic acids (Gram-positive bacteria) are responsible for the initial interaction of peptides with bacterial cells.
limitations: Presented as a general mechanistic principle; no direct binding assay conducted in this paper to test it for the new analogues.

claim_text: Hydrophobic residues of antimicrobial peptides penetrate the bacterial membrane to interact with lipids.
limitations: General principle stated in the Discussion; not directly tested for the new analogues in this study.

claim_text: Side chains of Pro3, Ala6, Asn7, Leu12, and Leu13 of TB_KKG6A penetrate LPS micelles, mediating membrane interaction.
direct_assay_types: NMR paramagnetic relaxation enhancement, saturation transfer difference (STD) NMR
limitations: Data from prior cited studies (refs [7a, 8]), not generated in this paper; performed on LPS micelles and E. coli cells, not intact membrane bilayers.

claim_text: TB_KKG6A adopts an α-helical conformation in the presence of E. coli LPS and E. coli cells, which is associated with its antimicrobial mechanism.
direct_assay_types: NMR, circular dichroism
limitations: Structural data from prior cited studies (refs [7a, 8]); helical structure is correlated with but not proven to be causally required for activity.

claim_text: Binding of TB_KKG6A to E. coli cells causes aggregation and death of bacterial cells.
limitations: Cited from a prior study (ref [12]); the mechanism of aggregation-induced death is not elaborated or directly tested here.

claim_text: Introduction of a positively charged lysine at position 6 in TB_KKG6K increases antimicrobial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria likely because favorable electrostatic interactions with negatively charged outer membranes are enhanced.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination, killing kinetics
limitations: Mechanism inferred from structure-activity relationship data; word 'likely' used by authors; no direct binding assay performed.

claim_text: The 4-carbon acyl side chain of lysine in TB_KKG6K is likely able to destabilize the bacterial membrane without promoting peptide self-aggregation.
direct_assay_types: critical aggregation concentration (fluorescence), MIC determination
limitations: Authors use 'likely'; membrane destabilization is inferred from activity data and non-aggregating behavior; no direct membrane permeabilization assay performed.

claim_text: Acetylation of Lys6 in TB_KKG6K(Ac) reduces antimicrobial activity by suppressing the positive charge on the residue and slightly increasing the acyl chain length.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination
limitations: Dual effect (charge loss + chain extension) cannot be experimentally deconvolved from MIC data alone; no direct charge-interaction assay performed.

claim_text: Increasing acyl chain length beyond the lysine side chain (i.e., via DAVA, Ahx, or Aund modifications) is detrimental to antimicrobial activity against E. coli and S. epidermidis, likely due to excess hydrophobicity impairing membrane interaction.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination
limitations: Mechanism inferred from SAR trend; no direct membrane or hydrophobicity assay performed; relationship does not hold clearly for P. aeruginosa.

claim_text: TB_KKG6K folds into a partial α-helical secondary structure upon interaction with E. coli cells, and this folding upon membrane contact is associated with antimicrobial activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism
limitations: Association between folding and activity is correlative; authors note this is consistent with other peptides (temporin L, cecropin A, magainin 2) from cited literature, not proven mechanistically here.

claim_text: The palmitoylated analogue TB_KKG6K(Pal) self-assembles into aggregates in solution, and its reduced antimicrobial activity is likely due to disaggregation upon contact with bacterial cells yielding a conformationally disrupted peptide.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism, critical aggregation concentration (fluorescence)
limitations: Authors use 'likely'; the mechanistic link between aggregate disaggregation and loss of bactericidal potency is inferred from CD spectral changes and low MIC activity, not directly demonstrated.

claim_text: Pep-7 caused pore formation at the poles of the cytoplasmic membranes of P. gingivalis.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
limitations: TEM images alone cannot distinguish transient from stable pores, nor confirm ion-channel vs detergent-like pore mechanism; full methods/controls not visible in preview text

claim_text: Pep-7 showed selective activity against Porphyromonas sp. by altering the permeability barriers of P. gingivalis.
limitations: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from TEM pore-formation images and MBC selectivity data; no direct permeability assay (e.g., SYTOX uptake, membrane depolarization, liposome leakage) is reported in the available text

claim_text: Trilenodin's antimicrobial activity is unlikely to result solely from lipid II recruitment, because lipid II is unique to Gram-positive bacteria while trilenodin is active against both Gram-positive B. subtilis and Gram-negative K. pneumoniae.
direct_assay_types: disk diffusion, broth microdilution
limitations: No direct lipid II binding or competitive inhibition assay was performed; exclusion of lipid II as the sole target is inferred from broad-spectrum activity data, not from mechanistic experiments.

claim_text: Trilenodin may interact with bacterial lipid membranes due to the high hydrophobicity of its tail region (including the tri-isoleucine motif) and a net positive charge arising from three basic residues (Lys6, Arg14, Lys18) with no free acidic residues.
limitations: No membrane interaction assays (e.g., membrane permeabilization, liposome leakage, dye release) were performed; hypothesis is based solely on primary sequence composition.

claim_text: The positively charged basic residues of trilenodin (Lys6, Arg14, Lys18) may enable initial electrostatic association with the negatively charged bacterial membrane, after which the hydrophobic tail inserts into the membrane core to form pores.
limitations: No pore formation, membrane depolarization, or ion flux assays were conducted; the two-step model is entirely speculative and drawn by structural analogy to other cationic membrane-active peptides.

claim_text: The presence of a nisin-homologous ABC transporter immunity system (PatsFEG, homologous to NisFEG) in the pats BGC suggests that trilenodin may employ a membrane-targeting mechanism of action analogous to nisin.
limitations: BGC-level homology does not establish mechanistic equivalence; the transporter system was not functionally characterized; the paper simultaneously argues that full nisin-like lipid II recruitment is unlikely given Gram-negative activity.

claim_text: Trilenodin exerts bactericidal (cell-death-inducing) activity against B. subtilis, as supported by progressive culture transparency in the heterologous expression strain 168_pats that lacked the immunity transporter genes patsE and patsG.
direct_assay_types: disk diffusion, broth microdilution
limitations: Culture transparency is a population-level correlate; whether killing is bactericidal versus bacteriostatic, and whether lysis is the mode, was not directly tested; the transparency phenotype could also reflect growth inhibition rather than cell lysis.

claim_text: Esculentin(1-21) kills P. aeruginosa by a membrane-disrupting mechanism rather than by inhibiting intracellular processes such as DNA, protein, or cell wall synthesis, as bactericidal activity (99.9% killing) is achieved within 15 minutes at 1 µM.
direct_assay_types: time-killing assay
limitations: Rapid killing is used to reason away intracellular targets; no direct assay of DNA/protein/cell-wall synthesis inhibition was performed to confirm exclusion.

claim_text: Esculentin(1-21) permeabilizes the cytoplasmic membrane of planktonic P. aeruginosa cells in a dose- and time-dependent manner, with membrane perturbation detectable within the first 15 minutes of peptide addition.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (Sytox Green fluorescent dye influx assay)
limitations: Detection required a higher cell density (1×10^7 CFU/ml) than used for MIC/killing assays (1×10^6 CFU/ml); Sytox Green reports pore size ≥ ~900 Da but does not identify the molecular mechanism of pore formation.

claim_text: Esculentin(1-21) causes extensive disruption of the cytoplasmic membrane of planktonic P. aeruginosa cells, as evidenced by extracellular leakage of the large intracellular enzyme β-galactosidase (~50–60% release at concentrations causing complete microbial death).
direct_assay_types: cytoplasmic enzyme leakage (β-galactosidase/ONPG colorimetric assay)
limitations: β-galactosidase release did not reach 100% even at fully bactericidal concentrations (8–32 µM), indicating incomplete or heterogeneous membrane rupture; assay was conducted on a recombinant strain constitutively expressing β-galactosidase.

claim_text: Esculentin(1-21) induces gross morphological changes in planktonic P. aeruginosa cells, including bleb (pustule) formation and release of cell debris, consistent with membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: SEM documents morphological outcomes but does not resolve the molecular mechanism (e.g., pore formation vs. membrane solubilization); images were captured at a single time point after 30 min treatment.

claim_text: Membrane perturbation is proposed as the plausible mechanism underlying the anti-biofilm activity of esculentin(1-21) against sessile P. aeruginosa, supported by Sytox Green uptake and β-galactosidase leakage from biofilm cells after peptide treatment.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (Sytox Green assay), cytoplasmic enzyme leakage (β-galactosidase/ONPG assay)
limitations: The paper explicitly describes this as a 'plausible mechanism'; β-galactosidase leakage from biofilm cells was weaker than from planktonic cells at equivalent killing concentrations, suggesting the biofilm matrix attenuates peptide access or membrane damage; causality between membrane perturbation and biofilm killing is not directly proven.

claim_text: Esculentin(1-21) causes dose-dependent morphological changes in P. aeruginosa biofilm cells—including surface protrusions and shrinkage of cell bodies—and disintegrates the extracellular polymeric matrix, as visualized by scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological changes were absent at a sublethal concentration (0.75 µM) and pronounced only at near-complete-eradication concentrations (3–24 µM); SEM does not distinguish primary membrane action from secondary structural collapse following cell death.

claim_text: Penaeidin antifungal activity against filamentous fungi is associated with inhibition of spore germination.
direct_assay_types: spore germination assay, MIC assay
limitations: Inactive against yeasts (S. cerevisiae, C. albicans); tested on specific fungal strains only.

claim_text: At sub-inhibitory concentrations, penaeidins cause growth inhibition of fungal hyphae accompanied by morphological abnormalities.
direct_assay_types: fungal growth inhibition assay, morphological observation
limitations: Specific strains and concentrations not fully detailed in this review.

claim_text: Penaeidins display a strain-specific rapid bactericidal or bacteriostatic mode against Gram-positive bacteria, suggesting they act through multiple modes of action.
direct_assay_types: killing kinetics assay, MIC assay, time-kill assay (24-h incubation)
limitations: Mechanism underlying the killing vs. stasis dichotomy is not directly characterized; 'multiple modes' is inferred from differential kinetics.

claim_text: Loss of COOH-terminal amidation in penaeidins reduces antibacterial activity approximately twofold, likely due to loss of a positive charge at the C-terminus and consequently less efficient interaction with bacterial membranes.
direct_assay_types: antibacterial activity assay comparing native vs. non-amidated recombinant penaeidins
limitations: Membrane interaction is not directly demonstrated for penaeidins; mechanistic explanation is drawn by analogy with insect cecropins.

claim_text: The penaeidin NH2-terminal proline-rich domain is not directly responsible for antimicrobial activity but is proposed to mediate target cell interaction through electrostatic binding to membranes.
direct_assay_types: antimicrobial activity assay of synthetic NH2-terminal peptide (residues 1–20)
limitations: Membrane-binding role is speculative and inferred by analogy with bovine bactenecin-7, which binds artificial membranes electrostatically; not directly demonstrated for penaeidins.

claim_text: The penaeidin COOH-terminal cysteine-rich domain is proposed to mediate penaeidin antimicrobial properties, based on analogy with defensins and the inactivity of the isolated NH2-terminal domain.
limitations: COOH-terminal domain has not been tested in isolation; 3D structure and cysteine connectivity remain undetermined.

claim_text: Penaeidins bind chitin via their COOH-terminal domain, and this chitin-binding activity is believed to mediate their antifungal activity.
direct_assay_types: chitin-binding assay (intact penaeidins vs. synthetic NH2-terminal domain)
limitations: Chitin binding is demonstrated but the causal link to antifungal killing is inferred; the downstream mechanism after chitin binding is not characterized.

claim_text: Penaeidins may exert intracellular antimicrobial activity during phagocytic and post-phagocytic events by degranulation of granule contents into the microbe-containing phagosome, analogous to vertebrate defensins.
limitations: Purely speculative analogy with mammalian neutrophil defensins (HNP1–4); no direct experimental evidence in penaeidins or shrimp hemocytes.

claim_text: Moricin-like AMPs affect the structural integrity of the bacterial plasma membrane.
limitations: Stated as established fact for the moricin class citing Hara & Yamakawa 1995 (ref 9); no direct membrane-integrity assay performed on M. sexta moricin in this paper.

claim_text: The amino-terminal amphipathic α-helical segment (residues 5–22) is important for bactericidal activity.
limitations: Inferred by structural analogy with B. mori and S. litura moricins (refs 11, 12); no truncation or mutagenesis assay performed on M. sexta moricin.

claim_text: The carboxyl-terminal cluster of positively charged residues accounts for the broad-spectrum activity of moricins against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
limitations: Inferred from charge distribution in the solved NMR structure and from analogy with other moricins; no C-terminal deletion experiment performed in this paper.

claim_text: Moricin permeabilizes the lipid bilayer, as shown by the ability of B. mori moricin residues 1–29 to permeabilize liposomal membrane.
direct_assay_types: liposomal membrane permeabilization
limitations: The liposome permeabilization assay was performed by Hara & Yamakawa (ref 9) on B. mori moricin, not on M. sexta moricin; extrapolated by the authors to the M. sexta homolog.

claim_text: M. sexta moricin likely adopts a predominantly α-helical conformation when interacting with the bacterial membrane.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: CD was performed in membrane-mimicking solvents (TFE/water, SDS micelles, methanol), not in native bacterial membrane; α-helical induction in these solvents is used as a proxy for membrane interaction.

claim_text: The positively charged regions (G1KI3, K6–R20, K38KKKH42) are initially attracted to the anionic bacterial surface through electrostatic interactions.
limitations: Inferred from the NMR-derived surface electrostatic potential map; no binding or surface-interaction assay performed.

claim_text: Through electrostatic interactions with negatively charged lipopolysaccharides, teichoic acids, and peptidoglycans, moricin traverses the capsular polysaccharide layer and attaches to phospholipids of the cytoplasmic membrane.
limitations: Entirely speculative model based on structural charge properties; no LPS/teichoic acid binding assay or membrane-attachment assay was performed.

claim_text: The clustered basic residues at the carboxyl-terminus of moricin contribute to tighter binding to Gram-positive bacteria such as S. aureus, whose reduced surface negative charge (via dlt-operon-mediated D-alanylation of teichoic acids) is partially compensated by the extra cationic tail.
limitations: Inferred from structural data and the known S. aureus surface-charge biology; the authors state they plan to test this with C-terminal deletion mutants but have not yet done so.

claim_text: After electrostatic attachment to the bacterial plasma membrane, the Pro4/Pro37-flanked central α-helix of moricin may be partially embedded in the lipid bilayer.
limitations: Speculative; based on the amphipathic character of the solved NMR structure; no membrane-insertion or depth-of-penetration assay performed.

claim_text: The five positively charged and twelve hydrophobic residues in the amphipathic amino-terminal segment (V5–I22) stabilize peptide–phospholipid complexes in the membrane.
limitations: Inferred from helical-wheel analysis of the NMR structure; no direct measurement of peptide–lipid complex formation.

claim_text: The carboxyl-terminal helical segment of moricin (residues 23–36) is less hydrophobic than the corresponding region of cecropin and is therefore less likely to span the lipid bilayer, potentially limiting or altering the mode of membrane disruption relative to cecropin.
limitations: Inferred by comparative hydrophobicity calculation between M. sexta moricin and H. cecropia cecropin; no experimental validation of membrane-spanning behavior.

claim_text: When moricin concentration exceeds a threshold, moricin molecules cause membrane bending followed by pore formation consistent with the toroidal model.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('could cause'); no ion-flux, pore-size, or conductance assay was performed in this paper; authors suggest future experiments to test ion selectivity.

claim_text: The amino-terminal α-helical segment of moricin is hypothesized to form ion channels with selectivity for Cl− or other negatively charged ions.
limitations: Explicitly labeled as a hypothesis by the authors; based solely on the positive surface charge of the helix interior; no electrophysiology or ion-flux assay performed.

claim_text: LPS dose-dependently suppressed Mdc antibacterial potency, indicating that LPS is the initial binding site of Mdc in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: LPS competition/inhibition assay
limitations: Dose-dependent suppression is consistent with LPS binding but does not formally prove LPS is the exclusive or primary initial target; competition assays can reflect non-specific sequestration.

claim_text: Mdc causes membrane permeabilization of MDR E. coli, as revealed by propidium iodide uptake measured by flow cytometry.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (propidium iodide-based flow cytometry)
limitations: PI uptake reports loss of membrane integrity but does not distinguish pore-forming from detergent-like membrane disruption mechanisms.

claim_text: Mdc induces remarkable damage to the outer and inner membranes of E. coli and causes leakage of cytoplasmic contents, as shown by transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: membrane disruption (transmission electron microscopy)
limitations: TEM provides morphological evidence of membrane damage but cannot reveal the molecular mechanism of disruption; sample preparation artifacts cannot be fully excluded.

claim_text: DNA is one possible intracellular target of Mdc, as implied by DNA binding experiments.
direct_assay_types: DNA binding
limitations: Paper uses the word 'implies' and 'possible', indicating this is a supporting rather than conclusive finding; the physiological relevance of in vitro DNA binding to the bactericidal mechanism is not established.

claim_text: Mdc kills MDR E. coli rapidly at its MIC, as demonstrated by bactericidal kinetics assays.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal kinetics (time-kill assay)
limitations: Kinetics are described at MIC only; mechanism underlying rapid killing is inferred from other assays rather than directly demonstrated by this experiment.

claim_text: CSA-13 permeabilized the outer membrane of Pseudomonas aeruginosa with a half-maximal concentration of 4.4 mg/L.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane permeabilization assay
limitations: Half-maximal concentration is substantially lower than concentrations required for bactericidal effect in biofilms (avg 88 mg/L), suggesting outer membrane disruption alone is insufficient for killing in biofilm context

claim_text: At concentrations higher than 20 mg/L, CSA-13 also permeabilized the plasma membrane of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), indicating cytotoxic activity at supratherapeutic concentrations.
direct_assay_types: plasma membrane permeabilization assay (HUVEC)
limitations: Assay performed on a single eukaryotic cell line (HUVEC); clinical relevance of this concentration threshold is uncertain

claim_text: CSA-13, as a cationic steroid antibiotic (ceragenin) derived from cholic acid, is inferred to act by disrupting bacterial membranes through electrostatic interaction with anionic membrane components, analogous to cationic antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: Mechanistic analogy drawn from class-level literature (ceragenins/cationic peptides); not directly demonstrated for CSA-13 in this study beyond outer membrane permeabilization data

claim_text: The combination of CSA-13 with tobramycin was synergistic in five of eight strains in young (24 h) biofilms, consistent with CSA-13 outer membrane disruption facilitating tobramycin uptake.
direct_assay_types: combination susceptibility testing (biofilm)
limitations: Synergy is inferred from checkerboard or killing-curve data; the mechanistic explanation (enhanced aminoglycoside uptake via outer membrane disruption) is not directly tested in this study

claim_text: CSA-13 retained bactericidal activity against P. aeruginosa in mature (12-day) biofilms, though the effect was delayed, with some strains requiring 9 days of exposure before a bactericidal effect was observed.
direct_assay_types: time-kill assay in mature biofilm model
limitations: Slow kinetics suggest reduced penetration or activity in mature biofilm matrix; mechanism of delayed killing not elucidated

claim_text: CSA-13 was resistant to inactivation by DNA or F-actin (cited from Bucki et al. 2007), suggesting it retains membrane-disrupting activity in the viscous cystic fibrosis sputum environment.
limitations: This finding is cited from a prior publication, not demonstrated in the present study; activity in actual CF sputum under the current experimental conditions was not directly tested

claim_text: The hybrid peptides were designed based on the amphipathic and cationic properties of antimicrobial peptides, implying a membrane-targeting mechanism of action.
limitations: Only the abstract is visible; no direct mechanistic experiments are reported in the accessible text. This claim derives from the stated design rationale (structure–activity relationship of amphipathic/cationic AMPs), not from experiments performed on the hybrids themselves.

claim_text: LH28 did not cause obvious hemolysis of rabbit erythrocytes at 3.13 μM while retaining antimicrobial activity, indicating selective disruption of bacterial over mammalian membranes.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Hemolysis absence is consistent with membrane selectivity but does not directly measure bacterial membrane disruption or confirm the precise mechanism; full experimental details are behind a paywall and not visible.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides of this class possess rapid bactericidal activity and a low propensity for resistance development.
limitations: Stated as a general class property in the abstract introduction, not demonstrated experimentally for the novel hybrids in the visible text; no time-kill or resistance-induction data are reported in the accessible portion.

claim_text: Brevinin-1Ma (FLPILAGLAANLVPKLICSITKKC) inhibits growth of the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) in culture assays.
direct_assay_types: growth inhibition assay (amphibian skin cultures)
limitations: Full assay conditions, MIC/MFC values, and the molecular mechanism of fungal inhibition (e.g., membrane disruption vs. other targets) are not reported in the available text; only the abstract is accessible.

claim_text: Brevinin-1Ma inhibits growth of the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal) in culture assays.
direct_assay_types: growth inhibition assay (amphibian skin cultures)
limitations: Full assay conditions, MIC/MFC values, and molecular mechanism of inhibition are not reported in the available text.

claim_text: Brevinin-1Ma enhances (facilitates) the growth of antifungal probiotic bacteria including Janthinobacterium lividum, Chryseobacterium ureilyticum, Serratia grimesii, and Pseudomonas sp. in culture assays.
direct_assay_types: bacterial growth assay (amphibian skin cultures)
limitations: The molecular mechanism by which brevinin-1Ma promotes bacterial growth is not characterized; the assay may not reflect in vivo skin conditions.

claim_text: Brevinin-1Ma is downregulated on frog skin following probiotic bacterial treatment, indicating it participates in host immune modulation of the skin microbiome.
limitations: Downregulation is correlative (skin peptide sampling); no causal experiment demonstrates that reduced brevinin-1Ma directly mediates microbiome changes; direction of causality is inferred.

claim_text: Brevinin-1Ma's differential activity—inhibiting fungal pathogens while facilitating probiotic bacterial growth—suggests it functions as an immune effector that selectively regulates skin microbial community composition.
limitations: This mechanistic interpretation is derived by combining growth-assay results with field observations of peptide downregulation; no mechanistic experiments (e.g., receptor binding, membrane assays, selective toxicity mechanism) were reported to explain the differential specificity.

claim_text: ATCUN motifs (GGH, VIH) bound to Cu2+ generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) through Cu II/Cu III cycling via Fenton-type reactions with H2O2 or O2, with GGH and VIH being the most potent ROS producers among the 13 sequences screened.
direct_assay_types: ascorbic acid consumption assay (ROS turnover rate measurement with and without H2O2)
limitations: Ascorbic acid consumption is an indirect proxy for ROS; no direct identification of specific ROS species; cell-free conditions only

claim_text: ATCUN-anoplin derivatives exhibit increased pore-forming/membrane-permeabilizing activity compared to parent anoplin, with DAH-anoplin showing the greatest enhancement in lytic activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (β-galactosidase leakage assay in E. coli)
limitations: GGH-anoplin and VIH-anoplin did not show significant membrane-permeabilizing enhancement despite lower MICs; membrane permeabilization does not fully correlate with MIC values for this series

claim_text: The increased antibacterial activity of Cu-ATCUN-anoplin derivatives is primarily caused by ROS-mediated nonenzymatic oxidative damage of membrane phospholipids (lipid peroxidation), initiated by hydroxyl radicals abstracting hydrogen from unsaturated fatty acid CH2 groups adjacent to double bonds.
direct_assay_types: lipid peroxidation assay (thiobarbituric acid/malonyldialdehyde quantification on DOPE/DOPG small unilamellar vesicles)
limitations: Lipid peroxidation measured on model SUVs mimicking E. coli outer membrane, not live bacteria; mechanistic link to MIC is correlational; radical chain mechanism (reactions 1–3) is proposed by inference from known chemistry, not directly measured

claim_text: Anoplin and VIH-anoplin localize at the bacterial outer membrane of E. coli, indicating that the addition of the ATCUN motif does not substantially alter the membrane-targeting localization of the parent AMP.
direct_assay_types: laser confocal fluorescence microscopy (5(6)-carboxyfluorescein-labeled peptides in live E. coli)
limitations: Fluorescently labeled derivatives used; appended fluorophore and lysine residue may alter peptide properties; live-cell imaging does not resolve molecular-level membrane interaction

claim_text: ATCUN-PAP derivatives (GGH-PAP, VIH-PAP) act primarily by disrupting the prokaryotic cell membrane, with GGH and VIH motifs doubling membrane-permeabilizing activity relative to parent PAP.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (β-galactosidase leakage assay in E. coli), laser confocal fluorescence microscopy
limitations: Close correlation between membrane permeabilization and MIC is correlational evidence, not a causal proof; DAH-PAP showed no increased lytic activity despite improved MIC

claim_text: The increased membrane-permeabilizing activity of GGH-PAP and VIH-PAP relative to DAH-PAP and parent PAP is attributable to greater amphipathicity of their helical structures, as the Asp residue in DAH-PAP is detrimental to amphipathicity by appearing surrounded by hydrophobic residues.
limitations: Amphipathicity inferred from helical wheel diagrams using Eisenberg consensus hydrophobicity scale; no direct structural measurement (e.g., CD spectroscopy or NMR) confirming helical conformation or amphipathicity in solution

claim_text: sh-Buforin and VIH-sh-buforin penetrate into E. coli cells, localize in the cytoplasmic space, and bind to bacterial DNA without causing cell lysis as their primary mode of action.
direct_assay_types: laser confocal fluorescence microscopy (cytoplasmic localization and fluorescence quenching at nucleoid by adenine and guanine via photoinduced electron transfer)
limitations: DNA binding inferred from fluorescence quenching of carboxyfluorescein by nucleobases—an indirect indicator; fluorescently labeled and lysine-appended derivative may not perfectly replicate unlabeled peptide behavior

claim_text: Cu-ATCUN-sh-buforin complexes generate intracellular ROS within E. coli, with VIH- and GGH-sh-buforin producing the largest amounts of intracellular ROS.
direct_assay_types: intracellular ROS detection (DCFDA/2',7'-dichlorofluorescein diacetate fluorescence assay in live E. coli)
limitations: DCFDA reports generalized oxidative stress, not specific ROS species; assay performed at MIC/4 concentration; intracellular ROS does not linearly correlate with MIC across all derivatives

claim_text: Cu-ATCUN-sh-buforin complexes cleave DNA in a time-dependent manner, converting supercoiled plasmid to nicked and linearized forms, and DNA damage—not total ROS production—is the major contributor to the antibacterial activity of ATCUN-sh-buforin peptides.
direct_assay_types: DNA cleavage assay (agarose gel electrophoresis of pUC19 plasmid), intracellular ROS assay (DCFDA)
limitations: DNA cleavage demonstrated in vitro with purified plasmid only; intracellular DNA damage is inferred; DAH-sh-buforin has similar MIC to GGH-sh-buforin despite less intracellular ROS, suggesting the correlation is between DNA cleavage activity and MIC rather than total ROS and MIC

claim_text: Metal chelation (copper ion starvation) is not the mechanism of action of the ATCUN-AMPs, as supplementing growth media with 32 μM Cu2+ does not reduce antibacterial activity against B. subtilis or E. coli.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay with supplemental Cu2+ ions in growth medium
limitations: Tested only against two of four bacterial strains (B. subtilis, E. coli); does not rule out partial contribution of metal chelation at sub-MIC concentrations

claim_text: The antimicrobial action of histatins is related to their ability to generate ROS after binding copper and iron ions, and this property derives from the ATCUN motif present in histatin-3 and histatin-5.
limitations: Based entirely on prior cited literature; no new experimental data generated in this paper for histatins

claim_text: Indolicidin kills bacteria in part by generating superoxide radicals, with NADH from the tricarboxylic acid cycle serving as an important electron donor for superoxide production.
limitations: Based on prior cited literature; no new experimental data generated in this paper for indolicidin

claim_text: APP induced membrane permeabilization in a kinetic manner, causing membrane lesions that allowed O-nitrophenyl-β-d-galactoside (ONPG) uptake into bacterial cells.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (ONPG uptake assay)
limitations: Kinetic data shown only for S. typhimurium and S. pyogenes; generalizability to other strains not established.

claim_text: APP caused potassium release from treated bacterial cells, consistent with membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (potassium release assay)
limitations: Potassium leakage is a proxy for membrane disruption; does not distinguish pore-forming from detergent-like mechanisms.

claim_text: APP induced bacterial live-cell membrane damage as demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis.
direct_assay_types: membrane integrity (flow cytometry)
limitations: Flow cytometry reports membrane integrity loss but cannot resolve the molecular mechanism of membrane disruption.

claim_text: APP exhibited high membrane selectivity for bacterial (EYPC/EYPG) over mammalian-mimetic (EYPC/cholesterol) lipid vesicles, as shown by calcein leakage assays.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from liposomes)
limitations: Liposome models are simplified surrogates; actual bacterial and mammalian membrane compositions are more complex.

claim_text: After penetrating the cell membrane, APP interacted with and intercalated into bacterial DNA base pairs, as confirmed by circular dichroism, fluorescence spectra, and gel retardation analysis.
direct_assay_types: DNA binding (circular dichroism, fluorescence spectroscopy, gel retardation assay)
limitations: Intercalation was inferred from spectroscopic signatures and gel shift; structural resolution (e.g., crystallography) was not performed. Experiments likely conducted with purified/naked DNA, not necessarily in the full intracellular context.

claim_text: APP affected DNA synthesis in bacterial cells, as demonstrated by cell cycle assay.
direct_assay_types: cell cycle analysis (flow cytometry-based cell cycle assay)
limitations: Perturbation of DNA synthesis could be a downstream consequence of membrane damage or DNA binding; the specific molecular step disrupted is not resolved.

claim_text: APP exerts its antibacterial activity through a dual mechanism: damaging bacterial cell membranes and binding to bacterial DNA to inhibit cellular functions, ultimately leading to cell death.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (ONPG uptake, K+ release, flow cytometry, calcein liposome leakage), DNA binding (CD, fluorescence spectra, gel retardation), cell cycle assay
limitations: The dual-mechanism conclusion integrates results from multiple independent assays; whether both mechanisms are obligatorily required for killing, or whether one is sufficient, is not directly demonstrated.

claim_text: TOP (Tosyl-Octyl-Peptoid) demonstrates broad-spectrum bactericidal action, killing bacteria rather than merely inhibiting growth.
direct_assay_types: minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC)
limitations: Full methods and MBC data tables are paywalled and not present in the provided text; 'bactericidal' is asserted in the abstract without mechanistic explanation of how killing occurs.

claim_text: TOP kills bacteria under non-dividing conditions, indicating its mechanism of action does not require active bacterial cell division.
direct_assay_types: non-dividing bacteria killing assay
limitations: The molecular target responsible for killing non-dividing cells is not specified in the available text; inference about mechanism is the authors' own, not independently validated here.

claim_text: TOP exhibits intracellular bacterial killing activity, implying it can penetrate mammalian cell membranes to reach and kill bacteria residing inside host cells.
direct_assay_types: intracellular bacterial killing assay
limitations: The mechanism of host-cell penetration and intracellular killing is not described in the provided abstract text; figure data supporting this claim is paywalled.

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of TOP is associated with amphiphilic character conferred by the octyl (eight-carbon) side chains, as shorter butyl and hexyl peptoid analogues failed to show significant activity, establishing a structure-activity relationship linking alkyl chain length to antimicrobial potency.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination across 13 peptoid analogues with varying chain lengths
limitations: SAR correlation is observational; the biophysical mechanism (e.g., membrane insertion depth, self-assembly) underlying the chain-length dependence is not directly measured in the available text.

claim_text: TOP's bactericidal mechanism has selectivity for bacterial over mammalian membranes, as evidenced by a selectivity ratio of 100 (10% haemolysis dose divided by median MIC), substantially exceeding the ~20 reported for comparator peptidomimetics.
direct_assay_types: haemolysis assay, MIC determination
limitations: Haemolysis is used as a proxy for mammalian membrane disruption, not a direct mechanistic assay; the molecular basis for bacterial selectivity (e.g., differences in membrane composition) is not demonstrated experimentally in the provided text.

claim_text: DEFB126 binds directly to LPS with measurable affinity, as demonstrated by SPR kinetic analysis showing concentration-dependent binding responses ranging from 20 to 200 nM.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) binding assay
limitations: SPR measures binding to immobilized LPS on a sensor chip, which may not fully recapitulate solution-phase or membrane-embedded LPS interactions.

claim_text: DEFB126 undergoes conformational changes upon interaction with LPS in a concentration-dependent manner, suggesting the peptide's secondary structure is modulated by LPS binding.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy
limitations: CD spectra reflect bulk secondary structure changes; the specific structural transition type and whether it is required for anti-inflammatory activity is not established from this data alone.

claim_text: DEFB126 is internalized by RAW264.7 macrophage cells, accumulating intracellularly over 40 minutes, suggesting cellular uptake as part of its mechanism.
direct_assay_types: live-cell spinning disc confocal fluorescence microscopy (DyLight 488-labeled DEFB126)
limitations: Internalization was observed with a fluorescently labeled construct; whether the label alters uptake kinetics or trafficking is not addressed. Functional consequence of internalization is not demonstrated in this supporting data.

claim_text: DEFB126 inhibits LPS-mediated inflammation, implying its mechanism involves neutralization or sequestration of LPS signaling.
limitations: This claim derives from the paper title; the supporting information alone does not contain functional inflammation assay data to substantiate the mechanism downstream of LPS binding.

claim_text: NZ17074 exerts candidacidal activity in an energy-dependent manner, indicating that cellular energy (ATP) is required for its killing mechanism.
limitations: Energy-dependence is inferred from experimental conditions (e.g., metabolic inhibitors or energy-depleted cells) rather than direct ATP measurement; full experimental details not visible from abstract alone.

claim_text: NZ17074 exerts candidacidal activity in a salt-sensitive manner, suggesting that electrostatic interactions are important for its activity.
limitations: Salt sensitivity is a common indirect indicator of electrostatic membrane interaction; mechanistic interpretation is inferred.

claim_text: NZ17074 perturbs the plasma membrane of C. albicans, as demonstrated by propidium iodide uptake in flow cytometric analysis.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (propidium iodide flow cytometry)
limitations: PI uptake indicates loss of membrane integrity but does not distinguish between membrane disruption as a primary event versus secondary consequence of cell death.

claim_text: NZ17074 arrests C. albicans cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle, as shown by flow cytometric analysis.
direct_assay_types: cell cycle analysis (flow cytometry, propidium iodide)
limitations: Whether G2/M arrest is a direct effect of the peptide or a downstream consequence of membrane damage or ROS is not established.

claim_text: NZ17074 induces increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in C. albicans, as demonstrated by dihydrorhodamine-123 (DHR-123) staining.
direct_assay_types: ROS detection (DHR-123 fluorescent staining)
limitations: ROS increase could be a cause or consequence of cell death; causal direction not definitively established.

claim_text: NZ17074 causes mitochondrial degradation in C. albicans, as revealed by rhodamine 123 (RH123) staining and transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: mitochondrial membrane potential (rhodamine 123 staining), ultrastructural imaging (TEM)
limitations: Mitochondrial damage may be secondary to ROS accumulation or membrane disruption rather than a primary peptide target.

claim_text: NZ17074 causes nuclear fragmentation and chromatin condensation in C. albicans, indicative of apoptosis, as shown by DAPI staining and TEM.
direct_assay_types: nuclear morphology (DAPI staining, TEM)
limitations: Nuclear fragmentation and chromatin condensation are morphological markers of apoptosis but do not confirm activation of a specific apoptotic pathway; caspase or metacaspase activity not reported.

claim_text: NZ17074 causes nuclear membrane disruption in C. albicans, as revealed by transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: ultrastructural imaging (TEM)
limitations: Could be a late-stage secondary event rather than a primary mechanism.

claim_text: At low concentrations (4–8 μg/ml), NZ17074 localizes to the cell membrane of C. albicans, while at high concentrations (16–32 μg/ml) it penetrates into the cytoplasm, suggesting a concentration-dependent dual mechanism.
direct_assay_types: intracellular localization (confocal fluorescence microscopy)
limitations: Localization studies typically require fluorescent labeling of the peptide, which may alter its native behavior; intracellular targets at high concentration are not identified.

claim_text: NZ17074 exerts its candidacidal effects by disrupting the cell membrane, inducing apoptosis, and interrupting the cell cycle.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (PI flow cytometry), ROS detection (DHR-123), mitochondrial staining (RH123), nuclear staining (DAPI), TEM, cell cycle analysis, intracellular localization (confocal microscopy)
limitations: This is an integrative conclusion synthesizing multiple assays; the relative contribution of each mechanism to cell killing is not quantified, and causal ordering of events is not established.

claim_text: Teixobactin binds to bacterial lipid II and lipid III, disrupting cell wall biosynthesis.
limitations: Cited from the original teixobactin discovery paper (ref [4]); no direct binding assay performed in this study.

claim_text: Teixobactin synergistically blocks the biosyntheses of peptidoglycan and teichoic acid, resulting in a weakened cell wall and autolysin-mediated cell lysis.
limitations: Cited from references [4] and [11]; no new mechanistic assays performed in this paper to confirm this pathway.

claim_text: Teixobactin binds to the pyrophosphate and N-acetylmuramic acid amino sugar moieties of lipid II, with its macrocyclic ring acting as the principal site of molecular recognition.
limitations: Described with qualifying language ('appears to bind', 'believed to act'); cited from reference [4] without independent confirmation in this study.

claim_text: The cationic L-allo-enduracididine at position 10 of teixobactin is crucial for electrostatic interaction with the negatively charged pyrophosphate moiety of lipid II.
limitations: Inferred from SAR data and structural analogy to lipid II; no direct binding assay performed to confirm this specific electrostatic contact.

claim_text: A non-polar (hydrophobic) residue at position 11 is required for antimicrobial activity via hydrophobic interactions with the target; replacement with a polar residue abolishes activity.
limitations: Inferred from IC50/MIC data for analogues 57–60 and supported by cited references [27,31]; the identity of the hydrophobic contact site on the target is not directly demonstrated.
