claim_text: A minimum alkyl chain length of four carbons at position 11 is necessary for optimal hydrophobic interactions with the molecular target, as progressive chain shortening (Nle→Nva→Abu→Ala) causes stepwise loss of activity to complete abolition.
limitations: Inferred solely from comparative MIC and IC50 data; no structural or biophysical binding data identify the precise hydrophobic contact.

claim_text: NG-monomethylation of the arginine guanidino group at position 10 increases binding affinity to the target through increased hydrophobicity rather than increased basicity, accounting for the 2- to 4-fold potency gain of [Arg(Me)10,Nle11]teixobactin 63.
limitations: Hydrophobicity vs. basicity distinction is inferred by combining IC50/MIC data with pKa data from an external study (Evich et al., ref [69]); no direct binding assay to lipid II was performed.

claim_text: Symmetric or asymmetric NG-dimethylation of arginine at position 10 reduces antimicrobial potency, likely by disrupting hydrogen bonds with the target or introducing steric hindrance.
limitations: Explicitly framed as 'possibly due to disruption of potential hydrogen bond(s) or significant steric hindrance'; mechanistic interpretation rests solely on IC50/MIC activity data without structural evidence.

claim_text: The electronegativity of fluorine atoms in (Arg10,Tfn11)teixobactin 61 detrimentally affects interaction with the molecular targets, or alternatively the steric bulk of the CF3 group reduces binding efficacy.
limitations: Two competing mechanistic explanations are offered for the same MIC/IC50 data; neither is confirmed by direct structural or binding experiments.

claim_text: Conformational restriction of the macrocyclic ring by introduction of Z-dehydrobutyrine at position 9 has an unfavourable effect on target binding, reducing potency 2- to 4-fold relative to the flexible Abu-containing analogue.
limitations: Inferred from comparative MIC/IC50 data for analogues 67 and 68; no structural data confirm the nature of the conformational change or its effect at the lipid II interface.

claim_text: Teixobactin analogues are not sequestered by the thicker peptidoglycan layers of vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus (VISA) strains, unlike vancomycin, explaining their retained activity against VISA.
limitations: Inferred from consistent MIC values across MSSA, MRSA, and VISA strains; the mechanism of vancomycin trapping is cited from refs [8,9] and the corresponding teixobactin behaviour is extrapolated from ref [11], not directly demonstrated here.

claim_text: The steep sigmoidal dose-response curves of active teixobactin analogues, mirroring vancomycin behaviour, are consistent with a mechanism of action as lipid II and/or lipid III binders.
limitations: Pharmacodynamic curve shape is treated as a phenotypic fingerprint of lipid II/III binding; no direct binding assay was performed to confirm this inference.

claim_text: The outer membrane of P. aeruginosa acts as a permeability barrier preventing teixobactin analogues from accessing their lipid II/III targets, and sub-MIC colistin restores activity by disrupting this outer membrane.
direct_assay_types: MIC combination assay (teixobactin analogue + colistin against P. aeruginosa PAO1)
limitations: Synergistic killing is demonstrated functionally but outer membrane penetration and lipid II/III engagement in P. aeruginosa are not directly confirmed; colistin's outer membrane disruption is the assumed (not measured) intermediate mechanism.

claim_text: [Arg(Me)10,Nle11]teixobactin 63 is bactericidal against S. aureus USA300 JE2, reducing viable counts by more than 3 log10 CFU/mL within one hour at 10x MIC.
direct_assay_types: time-kill assay
limitations: Bactericidal effect is concentration-dependent: regrowth was observed at 4x MIC; tested against a single S. aureus strain (USA300 JE2) in one growth condition.

claim_text: rMP1102 exerted stronger activity against S. aureus than NZ2114 via a different mechanism, suggesting MP1102 and its parental peptide NZ2114 do not share the same killing mechanism.
limitations: Only the abstract is available; the mechanistic inference is drawn solely from comparative MIC and pharmacodynamic (time-kill) differences between MP1102 and NZ2114, not from direct mechanistic assays reported in the available text.

claim_text: The higher sensitivity of MRSA to MP1102 than to its parental peptide NZ2114, as indicated by pharmacodynamic analysis, suggests a possible difference in the killing mechanism of these two molecules.
limitations: Explicitly qualified by the authors as 'suggests a possible difference'; no direct mechanistic assay (e.g., membrane permeabilization, cell wall target binding) is described in the available text; conclusion is based entirely on comparative MIC data against MRSA isolates.

claim_text: rMP1102 is bactericidal, killing over 99.9% of S. aureus cells within 6 hours at one, two, and four times its MIC.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics
limitations: Demonstrates bactericidal rate but does not identify the molecular target or killing mechanism; full methodology and controls are behind the paywall.

claim_text: APP caused slight depolarization (12.32 ± 0.87%) of the membrane potential of intact C. albicans cells during its anti-candidal activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential depolarization assay
limitations: Depolarization was described as 'slight', suggesting membrane disruption is not the primary killing mechanism

claim_text: APP caused only 21.52 ± 0.48% C. albicans cell membrane damage.
direct_assay_types: membrane integrity/permeabilization assay
limitations: Low level of membrane damage indicates membrane lysis is not the primary mechanism of action

claim_text: APP interacted with the cell wall membrane and caused potassium efflux and nucleotide leakage.
direct_assay_types: potassium efflux assay, nucleotide leakage assay
limitations: Partial membrane interaction does not fully account for killing activity given low overall membrane damage

claim_text: FITC-labeled APP penetrated C. albicans cell membranes with 52.31 ± 1.88% cell-penetrating efficiency and accumulated in the cytoplasm.
direct_assay_types: confocal fluorescence microscopy, flow cytometry
limitations: FITC labeling may alter peptide behavior; efficiency measured on population level, not all cells are penetrated

claim_text: APP interacted with C. albicans genomic DNA and completely suppressed DNA migration at peptide/DNA weight ratios at or above 2.
direct_assay_types: DNA binding/gel retardation assay
limitations: Gel retardation assay is performed in vitro and may not fully replicate intracellular conditions

claim_text: APP significantly arrested the C. albicans cell cycle during S-phase, with S-phase cell population of 27.09 ± 0.73% (p < 0.05) after penetrating the cell membrane.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry cell cycle analysis
limitations: Causal link between intracellular DNA binding and S-phase arrest is inferred rather than mechanistically proven

claim_text: APP kills C. albicans through a combination of efficient cell-penetrating ability, strong intracellular DNA-binding affinity, and induction of S-phase cell cycle arrest.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential assay, membrane damage assay, potassium efflux assay, nucleotide leakage assay, confocal fluorescence microscopy, flow cytometry, DNA gel retardation assay, cell cycle flow cytometry
limitations: The relative contribution of each mechanism to killing has not been quantitatively dissected; intracellular DNA binding causing S-phase arrest is mechanistically plausible but not directly demonstrated via rescue experiments or genetic approaches

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 causes intracellular ROS generation in E. coli, with elevated ROS observed in ΔdinF mutants compared to wild type.
direct_assay_types: intracellular ROS measurement (H2DCFDA fluorescent indicator)
limitations: Supplementary figures only; full quantitative data and dose-response context require the main paper; ΔdinF comparison suggests but does not prove ROS is mechanistically central

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 induces membrane integrity disruption in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: membrane integrity assay (propidium iodide, PI)
limitations: Described only in the context of NAC control validation; full mechanistic dose-response data not presented in this supplementary text

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 causes membrane depolarization in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization assay (DiBAC4(3))
limitations: Mentioned only as a measured endpoint in the NAC control figure; magnitude and dose-dependence not detailed here

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 causes lipid peroxidation in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: lipid peroxidation (TBARS assay)
limitations: Reported only in the context of NAC pretreatment controls; primary dose-response data in main paper

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 induces DNA oxidation (8-OHdG formation) in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: DNA oxidation quantitation (8-OHdG)
limitations: Listed as a measured endpoint in supplementary control data; extent of damage not quantified in this text

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 causes DNA strand breaks in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: DNA strand break assay (TUNEL)
limitations: Mentioned only in NAC control figure legend; primary data in main paper

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 activates caspase-like activity in E. coli, consistent with apoptosis-like death.
direct_assay_types: caspase activation (FITC-VAD-FMK)
limitations: E. coli lacks true caspases; FITC-VAD-FMK detects caspase-like proteases; interpretation as apoptosis-like is an analogy, not direct evidence of canonical apoptosis

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 induces phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization in E. coli, a hallmark of apoptosis-like death, and this effect is modulated by SOS-response genes recA and dinF.
direct_assay_types: PS externalization (Annexin V/PI double staining)
limitations: PS externalization is used as an apoptosis marker by analogy; causality of recA/dinF involvement is inferred from mutant MIC shifts and PS data, not direct biochemical pathway mapping

claim_text: Periplanetasin-2 increases intracellular Ca2+ levels in E. coli, and this increase persists even when ROS is scavenged by NAC pretreatment.
direct_assay_types: intracellular calcium measurement (Fura-2 AM)
limitations: Ca2+ signaling role in bacteria is less well-characterized than in eukaryotes; mechanistic link between Ca2+ elevation and cell death pathway is inferred, not directly demonstrated

claim_text: SOS-response genes recA and dinF contribute to E. coli resistance to periplanetasin-2, as deletion mutants show altered (dinF lower, recA higher) MIC values.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination against defined gene-deletion mutants (KEIO collection)
limitations: MIC changes indicate involvement but do not establish the mechanistic role of RecA or DinF in the apoptosis-like pathway; direction of effect differs between mutants, complicating a unified mechanistic interpretation

claim_text: P2 increases plasma membrane permeability in multidrug-resistant S. aureus (both clinical isolate E48 and ATCC43300) in a time- and dose-dependent manner, as demonstrated by propidium iodide (PI) uptake reaching up to 20–26.6% PI-positive cells at 4×MIC after 2 h.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (FACS/flow cytometry with propidium iodide staining)
limitations: PI staining indicates loss of membrane integrity but does not distinguish primary membrane disruption from secondary membrane damage downstream of another primary target; only two strains tested; data are from supplementary tables/figures with no statistical analysis reported in the provided text; the percentage of PI-positive cells even at 4×MIC after 2 h remains relatively low (~20–27%), leaving the dominant killing mechanism ambiguous

claim_text: Ranalexin acts as a membrane-active peptide against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, consistent with its structural relatedness to the bacterial antibiotic polymyxin.
limitations: Mechanism is inferred from structural analogy to polymyxin (Clark et al. 1994) and by categorization of ranalexin among 'membrane-active peptides' in cited literature (Giacometti et al. 1998); no direct membrane-disruption assay (e.g., liposome leakage, membrane potential) is reported in the available text. Full methods/results section is behind paywall and not provided.

claim_text: Recombinant ranalexin is cytotoxic to HeLa and COS7 human cancer cells with IC50 values of 13–15 μg/ml, implying a cell-killing action against mammalian cancer cells.
direct_assay_types: cytotoxicity assay (IC50 determination, likely MTT based on Mosmann 1983 citation)
limitations: IC50 measurement confirms cytotoxic potency but does not identify the molecular mechanism (membrane lysis, apoptosis induction, etc.); no selectivity data versus non-cancerous cells is reported in the abstract; mechanism is not discussed in available text.

claim_text: Disulfide bond formation is not essential for the antimicrobial activity of H4 against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, because recombinant H4 expressed in E. coli (which fails to form proper disulfide bonds) exhibited bactericidal activity statistically equivalent to that of chemically synthesized H4 (IC50 2.85 vs 3.67 µg/mL, P=0.655).
direct_assay_types: bactericidal colony count assay (CFU enumeration on LB agar after 2-hour peptide treatment)
limitations: Disulfide bond status of rH4 was not directly confirmed by redox analysis, alkylation, or disulfide-mapping mass spectrometry; the inference rests solely on activity equivalence between two peptide preparations rather than structural characterization; tested against a single MDR clinical isolate and one reference strain; may not generalise to other bacterial species or to activity against host membranes.

claim_text: H4 exerts direct bactericidal (lethal) effects against multidrug-resistant A. baumannii MDR-ZJ06, killing bacteria within 2 hours rather than merely inhibiting growth.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal colony count assay (modified microdilution, CFU enumeration on LB agar)
limitations: Assay performed in PBS at 1000 CFU/well, which may not reflect physiological salt or protein conditions; the specific killing mechanism (membrane disruption, intracellular targeting, etc.) was not investigated; MBC/MIC ratio not reported; a single clinical strain used.

claim_text: H4 kills Acinetobacter baumannii adhered to the surface of human type II alveolar lung cells (A549), demonstrating bactericidal activity in an in vitro cell infection context with an IC50 of approximately 3.17 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: cell infection bactericidal assay (A549 lung epithelial infection model, CFU enumeration after peptide treatment)
limitations: Only surface-adhered bacteria assessed; intracellular bacteria not evaluated; peptide stability and effective concentration at the cell surface not measured; cytotoxicity of H4 toward A549 cells not reported; ATCC19606 reference strain (not the MDR isolate) used for this model.

claim_text: Lin-Lf4NH2 and Lin-Lf5NH2 penetrate the bacterial membrane more rapidly than their parent peptides Lf4NH2 and Lf5NH2, as measured by membrane penetration percentages at 5 minutes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (quantitative penetration assay), laser scanning confocal microscopy
limitations: Assay type (likely dye-uptake flow cytometry) not fully named in available text; mechanism of penetration (pore formation vs. membrane thinning vs. carpet model) not distinguished

claim_text: Lin-Lf4NH2 and Lin-Lf5NH2 disrupt S. hyicus cell membranes and cause leakage of intracellular contents.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy (SEM/TEM morphological observation)
limitations: Electron microscopy shows structural damage but does not identify the molecular mechanism of disruption; downstream consequences of leakage (e.g., loss of specific ions, ATP, or nucleic acids) not quantified

claim_text: Lin-Lf4NH2 and Lin-Lf5NH2 reduce the levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β and chemokine MCP-1 in S. hyicus skin lesions.
direct_assay_types: cytokine/chemokine quantification in vivo (mouse skin lesion model)
limitations: In vivo cytokine reduction may be secondary to bacterial load reduction rather than a direct immunomodulatory mechanism of the peptides; the two effects are not decoupled in the available text

claim_text: Membrane permeabilization is the cause of SD-8 antimicrobial activity, as demonstrated by transmission electron microscopy studies.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization, transmission electron microscopy
limitations: TEM is a structural/morphological readout; it shows membrane disruption but does not rule out additional intracellular mechanisms.

claim_text: SD-8 kills methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) within 120 minutes and MRSA within 90 minutes, as shown by kinetics (time-kill) assays.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics assay
limitations: Killing kinetics are consistent with membrane-active mechanisms but do not by themselves confirm mechanism.

claim_text: SD-8 inhibits COX-2 with a K_D of 2.36×10⁻⁹ M and K_i of 4.8×10⁻⁸ M, demonstrating anti-inflammatory activity via COX-2 inhibition.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (binding affinity), enzyme inhibition assay (K_i)
limitations: COX-2 inhibition is a distinct mechanism from antibacterial activity; in vivo anti-inflammatory relevance is supported only by histopathology, not a dedicated inflammation assay.

claim_text: NZX exhibited intracellular antibacterial activity against S. hyicus in HaCaT cells.
direct_assay_types: intracellular killing assay in HaCaT keratinocytes
limitations: Single cell line used; assay details (MOI, timepoint, CFU recovery method) not visible in abstract; mechanism of intracellular accumulation/action not characterized

claim_text: NZX is bactericidal against S. hyicus NCTC10350, killing the organism completely at 2× and 4× MIC within 24 hours.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics
limitations: Single strain tested; killing rate and concentration-dependence details not reported in abstract

claim_text: NZX inhibited bacterial translocation in a mouse infection model.
limitations: In vivo endpoint; mechanistic basis of translocation inhibition (direct bactericidal, barrier-protective, or immunological) is not distinguished in the available text

claim_text: NZX downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, and upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 in a mouse infection model.
limitations: Whether immunomodulation is a direct peptide effect or secondary to bacterial load reduction is not resolved in the abstract; cytokine assay details not provided

claim_text: NZX, as a plectasin-derived peptide, is implicitly associated with the plectasin mechanism of targeting the bacterial cell wall precursor lipid II, as established for the parent molecule.
limitations: The paper cites Schneider et al. 2010 for lipid II targeting by plectasin, but no direct assay (e.g., lipid II binding, cell wall biosynthesis inhibition) demonstrating this mechanism for NZX itself is reported in the available abstract text; attribution is by lineage, not direct evidence

claim_text: P2 induced membrane damage of S. dysgalactiae, causing leakage of cellular content and eventually cell death.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), flow cytometry
limitations: Full paper paywalled; specific membrane assay details (e.g., propidium iodide, SYTOX) not described in available abstract text

claim_text: P2 achieved rapid bactericidal action with a 3.0 log unit reduction in viable S. dysgalactiae within 2–4 hours.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics
limitations: Mechanism driving the killing rate is not distinguished from membrane damage data

claim_text: P2 inhibited early biofilm formation of S. dysgalactiae.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM)
limitations: Molecular basis of biofilm inhibition (e.g., interference with adhesion, signaling) is not specified in the available text

claim_text: P2 eradicated mature S. dysgalactiae biofilms, reducing biofilm thickness from 18.82 to 7.94 μm.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM)
limitations: Mechanism of mature biofilm disruption is not elaborated; physical vs. bactericidal action not distinguished

claim_text: P2 killed 99.9% of S. dysgalactiae persister cells that were resistant to 100× MIC vancomycin.
direct_assay_types: persister cell viability assay
limitations: Mechanism by which P2 overcomes vancomycin-resistant persister tolerance is not mechanistically explained; persister identity not independently confirmed

claim_text: P2 decreased the number of mammary bacteria and alleviated breast inflammation by regulating cytokines and inhibiting bacterial proliferation in a mouse mastitis model.
direct_assay_types: in vivo mouse mastitis model, bacterial colony counts, cytokine quantification
limitations: In vivo cytokine regulation may be an indirect consequence of bacterial clearance rather than a direct immunomodulatory MOA; specific cytokines not named in available text

claim_text: No resistant mutants of S. dysgalactiae emerged after 30-day serial passage in the presence of P2, suggesting a mechanism that is difficult to develop resistance against.
direct_assay_types: serial passage resistance frequency assay
limitations: Absence of resistance is consistent with membrane-targeting mechanisms but does not by itself confirm any specific MOA; 30-day passage may not capture all resistance routes

claim_text: The p53-derived peptides exert cytotoxicity on breast cancer cells by disrupting the p53–MDM2 protein–protein interaction, thereby releasing p53 from its negative regulator MDM2.
limitations: Mechanism is inferred from the design rationale (MDM2-binding affinity) and IC50 measurements; no direct intracellular p53 activation, MDM2-displacement, or apoptosis assays are described in the abstract or accessible text.

claim_text: Targeting the p53–MDM2 protein–protein interaction is proposed as the mechanistic basis for the anticancer activity of the designed peptides.
limitations: This is a design hypothesis supported only by computational binding affinity predictions and cytotoxicity (IC50) data; no cell-based confirmation of MDM2 displacement or p53 pathway activation is reported in the available text.

claim_text: Globomycin inhibits signal-peptidase II (LspA), thereby preventing cleavage of the prespiralin leader peptide in Spiroplasma melliferum.
direct_assay_types: SDS-PAGE protein analysis, immunolabeling (Western blotting), crossed immunoelectrophoresis
limitations: Demonstrated only in S. melliferum; mechanism assigned by analogy to known globomycin biochemistry in other organisms.

claim_text: Prespiralin blocked by globomycin accumulates in the membrane fraction and does not accumulate in the cytoplasm or culture medium, indicating membrane retention of the unprocessed precursor.
direct_assay_types: cell fractionation
limitations: Fractionation purity and completeness not assessable from the abstract alone.

claim_text: Globomycin at concentrations up to 30 μM does not alter the electrical transmembrane potential of S. melliferum, indicating it does not act via membrane depolarization.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential-sensitive fluorescent dye (diS-C3-[5])
limitations: Only tested up to 30 μM, which exceeds the MIC (6.25–12.5 μM) but may not cover all pharmacologically relevant concentrations; single dye readout.

claim_text: The toxicity of globomycin for spiroplasma cells is mainly if not exclusively due to inhibition of spiralin processing rather than membrane disruption.
limitations: Inferred by elimination (no transmembrane potential effect observed); other non-membrane mechanisms not directly tested; 'mainly if not exclusively' qualifier acknowledges residual uncertainty.

claim_text: Melittin (bee-venom) disrupts the electrical transmembrane potential of S. melliferum, consistent with a membrane-depolarization mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential-sensitive fluorescent dye (diS-C3-[5])
limitations: Melittin is cited only as a positive-control comparator; no dose-response or mechanistic detail for melittin is reported in this paper.

claim_text: Spiralin and probably other mollicute lipoproteins are acylated and membrane-targeted through a pathway involving type II signal peptidase (LspA)-dependent processing of a prelipoprotein precursor.
limitations: Authors use 'suggest' and 'probably'; based on combining present results with previously published data; direct acylation and full trafficking pathway not demonstrated in this paper.

claim_text: Proline-rich antimicrobial peptides' reduced efficacy against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus could be related to inadequate uptake mechanisms.
limitations: Stated as a possible explanation ('could be related to'), no uptake assay data presented in the text provided; full paper body not available to confirm experimental support.

claim_text: Proline-rich antimicrobial peptides act intracellularly by targeting the bacterial 70S ribosome or the chaperone DnaK.
limitations: Presented as established background knowledge attributed to prior cited work (Krizsan et al. 2014; Knappe et al. 2011b; Roy et al. 2015; Seefeldt et al. 2015); no direct assay data for this mechanism is reported within the text of this paper as provided.

claim_text: Reduced antibacterial activity of proline-rich antimicrobial peptides against certain pathogens could be related to structural differences in the intracellular target proteins (70S ribosome or DnaK) compared to susceptible species.
limitations: Framed as a speculative explanation ('could be related to') alongside the uptake hypothesis; no comparative structural or binding data presented in the available text to distinguish this from the uptake hypothesis.

claim_text: CM11 is a short cationic peptide with high antimicrobial activity against bacterial pathogens, consistent with membrane-active mechanisms described for cationic antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: The paper cites prior work (Moghaddam et al. 2012, 2014) and a general reference (Shai 2002) for mechanism; no direct mechanistic assay is performed in this study itself.

claim_text: CM11 acts as a membrane-active antimicrobial peptide, consistent with its cationic nature enabling interaction with bacterial membranes.
limitations: Inferred solely from the peptide's cationic character and citation of Shai (2002) on membrane-active AMPs; no membrane disruption, dye-leakage, or electron microscopy assay is reported in this paper.

claim_text: Silver ions exert antibacterial effects, implicated in disruption of bacterial cellular functions.
limitations: Mechanism attributed entirely to a cited external study (Feng et al. 2000) on silver ions against E. coli and S. aureus; not demonstrated for the AgBG formulation or against the clinical isolates studied here.

claim_text: SMAP-29 kills microorganisms by disrupting and perturbing the lipid bilayer of bacterial cell membranes.
direct_assay_types: dye leakage from bacterial membrane-mimicking liposomes (LUVs), NPN uptake, ONPG hydrolysis
limitations: Assays use membrane-mimicking liposomes and outer-membrane permeabilization proxies, not live bacterial membranes; exact molecular mechanism (carpet vs. toroidal pore) not resolved in this paper.

claim_text: SMAP-18-W kills bacteria by forming pores or ion channels on bacterial cell membranes, similar in mechanism to SMAP-29 but acting at a distinct structural level.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3-5 probe, >80% depolarization of S. aureus at 2×MIC)
limitations: Pore/ion-channel assignment is proposed based on depolarization data alone; SMAP-18-W showed only weak dye leakage, NPN uptake, and ONPG hydrolysis, making a pure membrane-disruption model inconsistent; no single-channel electrophysiology or structural pore evidence presented.

claim_text: SMAP-18 kills bacteria via an intracellular-targeting mechanism rather than membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy (membrane translocation without disruption); absence of membrane depolarization at up to 4×MIC (DiSC3-5); weak dye leakage, NPN uptake, and ONPG hydrolysis
limitations: Intracellular target(s) are not identified; translocation observed by confocal microscopy does not directly demonstrate killing at an intracellular site; mechanistic conclusion is inferential from the combination of negative membrane-disruption results and positive translocation observation.

claim_text: SMAP-18 translocates across the bacterial membrane in a non-membrane-disruptive manner.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy
limitations: Confocal imaging resolution and fluorescent labeling may not fully distinguish membrane insertion from true translocation; experiments performed at specific peptide concentrations and bacterial strains that may not generalize.

claim_text: SMAP-18-W causes significant membrane depolarization (>80%) of Staphylococcus aureus at 2×MIC.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization assay (DiSC3-5 fluorescent probe)
limitations: Single bacterial species tested; depolarization magnitude may vary with membrane composition and growth conditions.

claim_text: SMAP-18 does not cause membrane depolarization of Staphylococcus aureus even at 4×MIC.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization assay (DiSC3-5 fluorescent probe)
limitations: Negative result confined to S. aureus at tested concentrations; does not rule out partial or species-specific depolarization.

claim_text: SMAP-18 and SMAP-18-W have relatively weak ability to permeabilize the outer bacterial membrane compared to SMAP-29, as measured by NPN uptake and ONPG hydrolysis.
direct_assay_types: NPN uptake (outer membrane integrity), ONPG hydrolysis (inner membrane permeabilization)
limitations: Assays probe membrane permeabilization proxies and may underreport subtle perturbations; species and strain specificity not fully characterized.

claim_text: SMAP-29 and SMAP-18-W are unable to translocate the bacterial membrane, unlike SMAP-18.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy
limitations: Same microscopy resolution and labeling caveats as for SMAP-18 translocation; limited to conditions tested.

claim_text: Cationic peptides studied are membrane-active, functioning through membrane perturbation as their primary mode of antibacterial action.
direct_assay_types: haemolytic activity assay, antibacterial activity assay (MIC)
limitations: Only abstract and reference list are available; full experimental data and mechanistic assays are behind paywall; membrane activity is inferred from the 'membrane-active' descriptor and haemolysis results, not from direct mechanistic experiments described in the accessible text.

claim_text: Buforin 2 translocates through lipid bilayers, with proline acting as a translocation-promoting factor, allowing it to enter cells rather than lyse membranes.
limitations: This claim is attributed to a cited reference (Kobayashi et al. 2000), not to original experiments in this paper; the paper uses Buforin as a comparative example but the mechanistic evidence is external.

claim_text: CM15, a hybrid cecropin A-melittin peptide, acts by membrane insertion and bilayer perturbation.
limitations: Mechanistic claim is supported by a cited reference (Pistolesi et al. 2007), not by original experiments performed in this paper.

claim_text: Melittin induces leakage of internal markers from erythrocytes and lipid vesicles, consistent with a membrane-disrupting mechanism.
limitations: Referenced from Portlock et al. 1990 and Habermann 1972; not an original finding of this paper.

claim_text: Penetratin exerts antibacterial activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae at concentrations (MIC < 1.2 μM) more than 250-fold below its haemolytic concentration (HC50), suggesting a bacterium-selective membrane-active mechanism.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination, haemolysis assay (HC50)
limitations: Selectivity index is reported but the precise molecular mechanism is not directly characterized in experiments described in the accessible text; membrane activity is inferred from peptide class designation.

claim_text: Transportan exhibits antibacterial activity against both Streptococcus pneumoniae (MIC < 1.2 μM) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis, acting as a membrane-active cationic peptide.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination
limitations: Mechanism inferred from class ('membrane-active'); no direct mechanistic assay described in accessible text.

claim_text: The molecular targets of the majority of basic antimicrobial peptides are thought to be acidic phospholipids in biomembranes.
limitations: Attributed to field consensus ('it is thought'); no supporting assay in this paper; applies to AMPs generally, not specifically to PDFLs.

claim_text: For at least some AMPs, biomembranes may function merely as a barrier hindering access to a primary intracellular target rather than being the target themselves.
limitations: Presented as a possibility ('may just be a barrier'); no supporting assay in this paper; scope ('some AMPs') is unspecified.

claim_text: Plant defensins originally called γ-thionins inhibit α-amylase activity.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref 28); not tested in this paper; restricted to a specific defensin sub-class.

claim_text: Plant defensins originally called γ-thionins inhibit protein synthesis.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref 29); not tested in this paper; restricted to a specific defensin sub-class.

claim_text: Arabidopsis PDF1.1 protects the plant against Pectobacterium carotovorum via iron capture (metal-withholding defence).
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref 35); not tested or reproduced in this paper.

claim_text: Arabidopsis PDF2.5 and PDF2.6 chelate cadmium, suggesting a metal-binding mechanism of action.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (refs 36, 37); not tested in this paper; cadmium chelation may reflect abiotic stress tolerance rather than antimicrobial MOA.

claim_text: PDFL1.1 and PDFL2.1 induce hyperbranching and swollen hyphal tips in Fusarium graminearum at higher concentrations, indicative of antimicrobial activity affecting hyphal morphology.
direct_assay_types: fungal hyphal morphology microscopy
limitations: Observed only in F. graminearum, not in F. oxysporum or B. cinerea; described as 'indicative' of activity but specific underlying mechanism (e.g. cell wall disruption, membrane permeabilisation) is not determined; paper explicitly states the mechanism of action for these two PDFLs is unknown.

claim_text: Plant defensins are known to target intracellular targets including interaction with nucleic acids and inhibition of ion channels as antifungal mechanisms.
limitations: Cited from a review (ref 88); not tested in this paper; presented as general knowledge about plant defensins, not demonstrated for PDFLs.

claim_text: The Medicago truncatula defensin MtDef4 damages the outer membrane of Pseudomonas species as its antibacterial mechanism.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref 89) for a different species' defensin; not tested in this paper; not extrapolated by authors to PDFLs.

claim_text: The Medicago truncatula defensin MtDef5 inhibits translation in Pseudomonas species as its antibacterial mechanism.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref 89) for a different species' defensin ('seemed to inhibit translation' — authors' own qualifier); not tested in this paper; not extrapolated to PDFLs.

claim_text: The higher antimicrobial activity of PDFL1.1 compared to PDFL2.1 could be due to its higher isoelectric point (pI 8.62 vs 7.63), implying an electrostatic/charge-based interaction with microbial membranes or surfaces.
limitations: Authors use 'could be due to'; no mechanistic assay performed; pI difference is the sole basis for the inference; structural differences (one vs. two β-sheets) are acknowledged as a confounding variable.

claim_text: Alyteserin-2a is classified as a cell-penetrating peptide, implying its cytotoxic mechanism involves direct membrane penetration or translocation into target cells.
limitations: Classification stated in abstract and keywords; no cell-penetration assay (e.g., confocal internalization, flow cytometry) is described in the available text; full paper is paywalled so supporting data cannot be confirmed.

claim_text: The cytotoxic activity of alyteserin-2a analogs against tumor cells is mediated by a membrane-disrupting mechanism consistent with their amphipathic α-helical, cationic structure, as evidenced by parallel increases in hemolytic activity when hydrophobic-face substitutions are made.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay, cell viability/cytotoxicity assay (LC50 against A549, HepG2, MDA-MB-231, HT-29)
limitations: No direct membrane-permeabilization assay (e.g., dye leakage, FITC-dextran uptake) described in the abstract; membrane disruption is inferred from the co-variation of hemolytic and cytotoxic activities with structural changes rather than directly demonstrated.

claim_text: Increasing cationicity (e.g., N15K substitution) preferentially enhances electrostatic attraction to negatively charged tumor cell membranes over neutral erythrocyte membranes, underpinning improved tumor-cell selectivity.
limitations: Inferred from SAR data (improved therapeutic index with added Lys); no direct membrane-binding or zeta-potential assay described; the paper does not measure membrane surface charge of the cell lines used.

claim_text: Reducing α-helicity while increasing cationicity (incorporation of d-Lys11) lowers activity against non-neoplastic erythrocytes while retaining potency against tumor cells, suggesting helicity modulates non-selective membrane insertion.
limitations: Inferred from comparative LC50 and therapeutic index values; helicity change is presumed from d-amino acid substitution but not confirmed by CD spectroscopy in the abstract; mechanism of helicity-dependent selectivity not directly assayed.

claim_text: [G11k, N15K] alyteserin-2a inhibits the release of the immunosuppressive cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β from both unstimulated and concanavalin A-stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells at concentrations as low as 1 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: cytokine release assay (PBMC stimulation with concanavalin A, measurement of IL-10 and TGF-β)
limitations: Whether cytokine inhibition results from direct membrane disruption of PBMCs, intracellular signaling interference, or cytotoxicity to the PBMC subset is not specified in the abstract; downstream mechanism is uncharacterized.

claim_text: K11 localizes exclusively in the bacterial membrane, leading to cell death.
direct_assay_types: membrane localization by confocal microscopy
limitations: Reported as prior work by the same group, not re-demonstrated in this study; causal link from localization to cell death is asserted, not mechanistically dissected.

claim_text: K11 exerts its antimicrobial action by destabilizing the bacterial membrane, as evidenced by blisters and bubbles formed on the surface of Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923 exposed to K11 at MIC.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (surface morphology)
limitations: SEM captures surface morphology changes only; paper uses hedged language ('suggesting'); no direct membrane permeability or leakage assay (e.g., dye release, ion conductance) is reported in this study.

claim_text: The polyproline II (PPII) secondary structure of K11 is stabilized by interaction with negatively charged phospholipids in the bacterial membrane.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy with DMPG-LUV and bacterial membrane lipid extract-LUV
limitations: Experiments used model lipid vesicles (LUV), not intact bacterial membranes; PPII enhancement in the presence of DMPG-LUV is a structural correlation—the causal relationship between PPII stabilization and membrane disruption is not directly demonstrated.

claim_text: The PPII secondary structure of K11 is not the sole determinant of its antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Conclusion is drawn by comparing MIC values of proline/alanine analogs with their CD-measured PPII propensity; no mechanistic experiment isolates PPII contribution independently; alternative determinants are not identified.

claim_text: Lysostaphin kills staphylococcal bacteria by cleaving the pentaglycine bridges in the cell wall.
limitations: Mechanism cited from prior literature (refs 3, 31), not directly demonstrated in this study; this paper only measures viable counts.

claim_text: Most of the antimicrobial peptides used in this study act against bacteria by affecting the integrity and functioning of the cell membrane.
limitations: Attributed to cited literature (refs 25, 32–37), not demonstrated by any assay in this study.

claim_text: Synergistic bactericidal activity of lysostaphin with antimicrobial peptides could result from the peptides having greater access to the cell membrane thanks to the cell wall-degrading abilities of lysostaphin.
limitations: Explicitly framed as a proposed mechanism ('could result from'); no mechanistic assay performed to test this in the study.

claim_text: Resistance to antimicrobial peptides is reported only rarely because these compounds typically disrupt the bacterial cell membrane.
limitations: General claim attributed to cited literature (refs 24–27); not tested in this study.

claim_text: dUSCLs 2 and 6 potentiate chloramphenicol against wild-type P. aeruginosa PAO1 (FIC ≤0.281) but show only additive effects against efflux-deficient strains lacking MexAB-OprM (PAO200) or five efflux pumps plus OpmH (PAO750), indicating the dUSCLs act at least in part by interfering with efflux, particularly the MexAB-OprM pump.
limitations: Additive (not antagonistic) effects in efflux-null strains mean efflux inhibition is not the sole mechanism; the paper does not measure direct pump inhibition or binding to pump components; strain differences in outer membrane composition could confound the comparison.

claim_text: dUSCL 2 synergises with structurally/functionally diverse antibiotics including rifampicin (256-fold potentiation), trimethoprim, minocycline, fosfomycin, piperacillin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, linezolid, and vancomycin against P. aeruginosa PAO1, consistent with outer membrane permeabilisation that increases intracellular accumulation of multiple antibiotic classes.
limitations: Synergy in checkerboard assays is phenotypic and does not directly demonstrate outer membrane disruption; no permeabilisation assay (e.g. NPN uptake, ONPG hydrolysis) is reported in this supplementary document; alternative mechanisms (efflux inhibition, membrane depolarisation) are not excluded.

claim_text: Simple cationic amphiphiles (benzethonium chloride, benzalkonium chloride, cetrimonium bromide) produce only additive—not synergistic—effects with chloramphenicol against P. aeruginosa, A. baumannii, and E. coli, implying that the adjuvant mechanism of dUSCLs is not merely attributable to generic cationic membrane disruption.
limitations: Comparison is between chemically distinct compound classes; differences in potency, amphiphilicity, or physicochemical properties (not mechanism per se) could explain the divergent outcomes; no direct mechanistic assay was performed on the comparators.

claim_text: All nine synthesized peptides had hydrophobic content ranging from 30 to 70% and were predicted to form alpha-helices, structural properties associated with membrane-active antimicrobial mechanisms.
limitations: Alpha-helix formation and hydrophobicity are predicted in silico; no direct membrane disruption assay reported in the available text. Structural prediction does not confirm actual MOA.

claim_text: Three of the synthesized peptides possess sequence similarities with piscidins, antimicrobial peptides known to act via membrane disruption, implying a similar membrane-targeting mechanism.
limitations: Similarity to piscidins is sequence-based; no direct mechanistic assay performed on these peptides to confirm membrane disruption. MOA is inferred by analogy to the piscidin family.

claim_text: One synthesized peptide possesses sequence similarity with BMAP-27, a cathelicidin that disrupts bacterial membranes, suggesting a membrane-lytic mechanism of action.
limitations: Similarity is sequence-based only; no direct mechanistic assay performed on this peptide.

claim_text: Peptides VA 20 and FK 19 were hemolytic, indicating they possess membrane-disrupting activity.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Hemolysis demonstrates membrane interaction with eukaryotic red blood cells, but does not directly characterize the antibacterial mechanism against prokaryotic membranes.

claim_text: GR 21 induced less than 10% hemolysis on human blood cells at 200 µM, suggesting it has low membrane-disrupting activity toward eukaryotic cells while retaining antibacterial efficacy.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Low hemolysis supports membrane selectivity but does not directly characterize the mechanism of bacterial killing; no bacterial membrane permeabilization assay reported in available text.

claim_text: The mechanism of SB056 is attributed to disruption of bacterial membranes.
limitations: Stated as prior attribution from earlier work (ref 21), not re-demonstrated in this study; no direct membrane disruption assay (e.g., dye leakage) performed here.

claim_text: AMPs generally act by physically destroying or permeabilizing the microbial plasma membrane through unspecific interactions with the lipids, rather than engaging specific intracellular targets.
limitations: General statement about AMP class, not specific to SB056; backed only by citations [7,8], not by data in this paper.

claim_text: SB056 is membrane-active by folding into an amphiphilic β-type conformation in lipidic environments.
direct_assay_types: biophysical characterization, membrane affinity assays (prior work, ref 21)
limitations: Data are from a prior publication (ref 21), not reproduced in this study; structural details of vesicle-bound state described as 'still lacking' in the current paper.

claim_text: Enhanced amphipathic profile of the analog (lin-SB056-1) leads to formation of more ordered and stable β-strands when the monomeric linear peptide binds to model membranes, correlating with increased antimicrobial performance.
direct_assay_types: model membrane binding, structural characterization (prior work, ref 22)
limitations: Data from prior publication (ref 22); structural characterization not repeated here.

claim_text: Electrostatics plays a fundamental role in the first step of peptide action—membrane binding—as demonstrated by reduced peptide-lipid affinity upon addition of physiological salt concentrations.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy (membrane binding titration with LUVs in presence/absence of 150 mM NaCl)
limitations: Blue-shift data are qualitative; quantitative binding constants were not calculated due to lack of structural information about the vesicle-bound state.

claim_text: Membrane affinity of all SB056 peptides increases with increasing content of negatively charged lipid (PG), consistent with electrostatic attraction between cationic peptides and anionic bacterial membranes.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy with LUVs at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% PG
limitations: Only model membranes (PC/PG LUVs) used; no native bacterial membrane experiments performed.

claim_text: lin-SB056-1 displayed the highest overall membrane affinity including for zwitterionic PC bilayers, indicating that beyond electrostatics, the distribution of charged/polar and hydrophobic residues along the sequence has a significant role in driving peptide-lipid interaction.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy with LUVs
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation is inferred from fluorescence affinity data; specific hydrophobic insertion depth or orientation not determined; quantitative binding constants not calculated.

claim_text: The dendrimeric scaffold retains membrane affinity at physiological ionic strength to a greater extent than the linear form, suggesting that the higher local charge density per mole of dendrimer partially offsets electrostatic screening by salt.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy with LUVs in PBS (150 mM NaCl)
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation is inferred; den-SB056-1 retains more salt-resistant affinity than den-SB056 despite identical net charge, which the authors note is unexplained by electrostatics alone.

claim_text: Dendrimeric peptides act bactericidally with a much faster killing rate (complete kill within 5 min) than linear peptides (30–90 min), consistent with a membrane-disruption mechanism.
direct_assay_types: killing kinetics assay (CFU enumeration over time against E. coli and S. aureus)
limitations: Rapid killing is consistent with but does not directly prove membrane disruption; no complementary membrane integrity assay (e.g., propidium iodide uptake) was performed in this study.

claim_text: The higher hemolytic activity of dendrimeric peptides compared to their linear counterparts is likely due to the higher local concentration of bioactive units presented by the dendrimeric scaffold.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Mechanistic explanation ('higher local concentration') is speculative; no direct structural or biophysical evidence for this interpretation is provided in the paper.

claim_text: The peptide tryptophan residue inserts into the hydrophobic core of the lipid bilayer upon membrane binding, as evidenced by a blue shift in tryptophan fluorescence emission.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan fluorescence spectroscopy (blue-shift assay with LUVs)
limitations: Exact insertion depth and peptide orientation not determined; fluorescence intensity changes were not used quantitatively due to multiple confounding factors (self-quenching, lysine-tryptophan quenching, PG head-group quenching).

claim_text: PMAP-23 adopts a dynamic helix–hinge–helix structure, initially attaching to membrane surfaces through the N-helix and subsequently inserting the C-helix into the lipid bilayer.
limitations: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis from earlier studies; structural model underpinning the design rationale, not directly demonstrated in this paper.

claim_text: PMAP-NC largely disrupted membrane integrity, and the efficiency and kinetics of bacterial killing are associated with membrane permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (fluorescence studies)
limitations: Specific fluorescence assay details (e.g., dye leakage, propidium iodide uptake) are not described in the abstract/visible text; full methods are behind paywall.

claim_text: The structural arrangement of an amphipathic helix–hinge–hydrophobic helix plays a critical role in rapid and efficient membrane permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (fluorescence studies)
limitations: Causal role of the specific structural arrangement is inferred from comparing PMAP-NC to PMAP-23; direct structural proof (e.g., NMR, MD simulation) is not reported in the visible text.

claim_text: PMAP-NC exhibited much better anticancer activity against tumor cells than PMAP-23, consistent with membrane disruption as the mechanism.
limitations: Anticancer mechanism is implied by analogy to antibacterial membrane permeabilization; no direct mechanistic assay for cancer cell killing is described in the visible text.

claim_text: Increased amphipathicity in the N-helix and increased hydrophobicity in the C-helix of PMAP-NC underlie its improved bactericidal activity relative to parental PMAP-23.
limitations: Conclusion is based on rational design logic and activity comparisons; individual contributions of N- vs C-helix modifications are not separately dissected by assay in the visible text.

claim_text: L1A and its analogs kill bacteria by disrupting lipid packing of the bacterial membrane through a lytic mechanism, without requiring membrane receptors.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (carboxyfluorescein dye leakage from LUVs)
limitations: Lytic mechanism demonstrated only in model membrane liposomes (LUVs), not directly in intact bacterial cells; the paper explicitly notes that correlation between liposome lytic activity and antibacterial activity could not be established for the N-terminus-modified analogs.

claim_text: The initial step of Gram-negative antibacterial activity is electrostatic interaction between the cationic peptide and the anionic lipopolysaccharides of the Gram-negative outer membrane, mediating selectivity toward Gram-negative over Gram-positive bacteria.
limitations: Inferred solely from the observation that reducing net charge (+3 to +2) impaired Gram-negative MIC; no direct LPS-binding or outer-membrane-disruption assay was performed.

claim_text: Formation of an amphipathic helical structure upon contact with the lipid bilayer interface is required for the lytic and antibacterial activity of L1A, because it enables productive membrane interaction.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (carboxyfluorescein dye leakage), circular dichroism in SUVs
limitations: Causality is correlational: higher helical fraction in anionic vesicles accompanies higher lytic efficiency, but the paper cannot exclude that charge or other structural factors are primary drivers; bacterial cells are more complex than model vesicles.

claim_text: Elimination of the positive N-terminal amino group charge reduces repulsive interactions with the membrane dipole, allowing deeper penetration of the peptide into the bilayer and more efficient disturbance of lipid packing, thereby enhancing lytic activity in anionic vesicles.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (carboxyfluorescein dye leakage from POPC/POPG LUVs), electrophoretic mobility (zeta potential) titration
limitations: Deeper penetration is inferred from MD simulations performed in TFE/water solvent mixture, not in a lipid bilayer environment; the enhanced lytic efficiency in anionic vesicles did not translate to improved antibacterial activity, limiting mechanistic interpretation in bacteria.

claim_text: Hemolytic activity of the peptides is mechanistically correlated with lytic activity in zwitterionic POPC vesicles, indicating that the same membrane-disruption mechanism underlies both hemolysis and cytotoxicity toward red blood cells.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (dye leakage in POPC LUVs), hemolysis assay (absorbance at 540 nm)
limitations: Correlation only; the Abz analog showed unexpectedly elevated hemolysis (~10-fold versus L1A) without proportionally greater POPC vesicle lytic efficiency, indicating the correlation is not universal across all modifications and the mechanism for the Abz hemolysis increase is unexplained.

claim_text: Blocking the N-terminus (by acetylation or Abz conjugation) prevents proteolytic digestion of the peptide, which is an alternative resistance mechanism used by some bacterial strains against antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: Not experimentally tested in this paper; the claim is made by citing prior literature (Andreu and Rivas 1998; Strömstedt et al. 2009) and presented as rationale for the modifications rather than as a result demonstrated here.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides have mechanisms of action that differ from those of current antifungals, making the acquisition of resistant mutants less likely.
limitations: General class-level assertion; no mechanistic experiments are performed in this paper to demonstrate the specific mechanism(s) or resistance frequency for any peptide tested.

claim_text: hLF(1–11), and perhaps dhvar5 as well, stimulates the antimicrobial activities of host cells, such as human mononuclear phagocytes.
limitations: Attributed entirely to a single conference abstract (ref 15, van der Does et al. 2007); no primary data from this study support the claim; the extension to dhvar5 is explicitly speculative ('perhaps').

claim_text: In vivo antifungal efficacy of hLF(1–11) at doses lower than required in vitro may be explained by synergistic or additive interactions with host-derived antifungal factors, including endogenous antimicrobial proteins/peptides and reactive oxygen intermediates.
limitations: Explicitly framed as a 'possible explanation'; no experiments in this paper test synergy with host factors or ROS; based on reasoning from prior in vivo/in vitro dose discrepancy data (ref 6).

claim_text: hLF(1–11) and dhvar5 act synergistically in vitro with current antifungal agents (amphotericin B, fluconazole) against Candida species.
limitations: Data are from prior publications on Candida (refs 9, 16), not from experiments in this paper; extrapolation to A. fumigatus is speculative ('it may be expected that such combinations are also highly effective').

claim_text: rMBD3-treated S. aureus and C. albicans cells showed delamination and perforation of the peripheral cell walls.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy (morphological/structural analysis)
limitations: Electron microscopy shows structural outcomes but does not identify the molecular mechanism causing wall disruption; causality inferred from treated vs. untreated comparison.

claim_text: rMBD3-treated cells showed porosity and inanition (loss) of cytoplasmic contents.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy (morphological/structural analysis)
limitations: Cytoplasmic leakage is a downstream consequence; the paper does not use biochemical assays (e.g., membrane permeabilization dyes, ATP release) to confirm or quantify the leakage independently.

claim_text: rMBD3 in combination with ampicillin acts synergistically against methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA).
direct_assay_types: checkerboard synergy assay (FICI determination)
limitations: Synergy against MRSA but not against S. aureus ATCC 25923, indicating strain-dependent effect; mechanism underlying differential synergy is not explained.

claim_text: Combinations of rMBD3 with itraconazole, amphotericin B, or 5-fluorocytosine are synergistic against C. albicans.
direct_assay_types: checkerboard synergy assay (FICI determination)
limitations: Mechanistic basis for synergy (e.g., whether cell wall disruption by rMBD3 enhances uptake of antifungals) is not investigated; purely phenotypic measurement.

claim_text: Mammalian β-defensins mediate innate immune defenses against microbial infection through their cationic, small-peptide nature.
limitations: This is a class-level background claim attributed to cited literature, not directly demonstrated in this study for MBD3 specifically.

claim_text: rCmDef exerts its antibacterial effect through membrane depolarization as the initial step in a multimodal mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization
limitations: Sequential ordering (depolarization 'followed by' permeabilization) is asserted in the abstract but full kinetic/dose-response data are behind a paywall; only the abstract was available for review.

claim_text: rCmDef causes membrane permeabilization of bacterial cells following membrane depolarization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization
limitations: Methodological details (dye/probe used, concentration range, strains tested) are paywalled; cannot confirm whether permeabilization was measured independently of depolarization.

claim_text: rCmDef induces reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in bacteria as a component of its antibacterial mechanism.
direct_assay_types: ROS production
limitations: Whether ROS is a direct consequence of peptide action or secondary to membrane damage is not resolvable from the abstract alone; full assay details are paywalled.

claim_text: rCmDef exhibits anti-cancer activity, predicted computationally (in silico), without causing hemolysis.
limitations: Anti-cancer activity is based solely on in silico prediction tools (referenced tools include AntiCP 2.0, ACPred); no cell-based cytotoxicity or mechanistic assay for anti-cancer action is reported. Hemolysis prediction also appears to be computational (HemoPred cited in references).

claim_text: LyeTx I permeabilizes L-α-phosphatidylcholine (POPC) liposomes, causing immediate, dose-dependent release of entrapped calcein.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from POPC liposomes)
limitations: Liposome model lacks the compositional complexity of biological membranes (no proteins, limited lipid diversity); results may not fully translate to intact microbial cells.

claim_text: LyeTx I-induced membrane permeabilization exhibits dose-dependent, cooperative kinetics.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization kinetics (calcein leakage from POPC liposomes)
limitations: Cooperative behavior characterized only in the POPC liposome model, not in intact microbial membranes.

claim_text: The presence of cholesterol (7:3 molar ratio) in POPC liposomes reduces LyeTx I-induced membrane permeabilization approximately five-fold, indicating that cholesterol decreases LyeTx I-lipid interaction.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from POPC/cholesterol liposomes)
limitations: Tested only in a simple binary lipid model; cholesterol content, distribution, and interplay with other lipids in actual eukaryotic cell membranes is more complex.

claim_text: The presence of ergosterol (7:3 molar ratio) in POPC liposomes does not significantly alter LyeTx I-induced membrane permeabilization compared to pure POPC liposomes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from POPC/ergosterol liposomes)
limitations: Binary liposome model does not reflect the full lipid composition of fungal membranes; moderate antifungal MIC values suggest additional factors limit activity against intact fungal cells.

claim_text: Antimicrobial (microbial) membranes, rather than vertebrate membranes, appear to be the preferential targets of LyeTx I, based on its low hemolytic activity relative to its antibacterial concentrations and on differential liposome permeabilization data.
limitations: Inference combines data from a simplified liposome model and an in vitro hemolytic assay (rabbit erythrocytes); biological membranes contain proteins and specific lipids not captured by the POPC model; the paper explicitly notes these other components cannot be excluded as contributors.

claim_text: LyeTx I adopts an α-helical secondary structure in membrane-mimicking environments (TFE, DPC micelles, POPC and POPC:POPG SUVs), and this propensity for α-helix formation is compatible with the conditions required to initiate its antimicrobial action.
limitations: CD and NMR characterization performed in membrane mimics (DPC micelles, liposomes), not in actual bacterial or fungal membranes; α-helix formation is a structural correlate of activity, not direct proof of the membrane disruption mechanism.

claim_text: Cholesterol in POPC SUVs reduces the degree of α-helix formation of LyeTx I at the membrane interface, indicating decreased peptide-lipid interaction in cholesterol-containing membranes.
limitations: Based on CD spectroscopy in liposome model; does not directly measure the functional impact on antimicrobial activity in cholesterol-containing intact cells.

claim_text: The tryptophan residue located at the N-terminus of LyeTx I may anchor the peptide at the phospholipid membrane interface, facilitating membrane insertion.
limitations: Inference based solely on the known general preference of tryptophan residues for membrane interfaces (cited from Ulmschneider and Sansom 2001); not directly tested for LyeTx I.

claim_text: The secondary structure of LyeTx I—a small random-coil region at the N-terminus followed by an α-helix extending to the amidated C-terminus—might favor peptide-membrane interaction.
limitations: Structural inference from NMR data in DPC micelles; the functional consequence of the N-terminal disorder for membrane interaction has not been directly tested in LyeTx I.

claim_text: The less amphipathic profile of the C-terminal portion of LyeTx I (compared to related peptides) may affect the detailed mechanism of its interaction with membrane bilayers.
limitations: Speculative interpretation of the NMR-derived structure; no direct experimental test of how the reduced C-terminal amphipathicity alters the mechanism of bilayer interaction for LyeTx I.

claim_text: Membrane components other than phospholipids, such as membrane proteins and specific lipids not present in the liposome model, cannot be excluded as contributors to LyeTx I's preferential action against the tested microorganisms.
limitations: Explicitly acknowledged as a caveat by the authors; no experimental data presented to test the role of non-lipid membrane components in LyeTx I activity.

claim_text: ABP-CM4 causes the morphology of Aspergillus niger conidia to become more irregular and swollen at its MIC of 8 μM.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological change is an endpoint observation; it does not establish whether membrane disruption or another mechanism is the initiating event.

claim_text: The plasma membrane, not the cell wall, is the prime target of ABP-CM4 action against A. niger.
direct_assay_types: cell wall regeneration assay (protoplast model)
limitations: Cell wall regeneration assay identifies the target by exclusion; it does not directly visualize or quantify membrane damage, and protoplast preparation itself may alter peptide behavior.

claim_text: ABP-CM4 at 8 μM destroys the cytoskeleton of A. niger.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy
limitations: Cytoskeletal disruption could be a secondary consequence of membrane permeabilization rather than a direct drug-target interaction; causality not established.

claim_text: ABP-CM4 disrupts the membranes and cellular organelles of A. niger and induces vacuole formation within fungal cells.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy
limitations: TEM provides static ultrastructural snapshots; organelle disruption and vacuolization may reflect downstream cell death rather than primary mechanism.

claim_text: ABP-CM4 binds the DNA of A. niger.
direct_assay_types: gel-retardation assay
limitations: Gel retardation demonstrates binding affinity in vitro but does not prove intracellular DNA binding is mechanistically responsible for killing, nor does it rule out binding artefacts from the assay conditions.

claim_text: ABP-CM4 exerts its antifungal activity through a multi-target mechanism involving disruption of the cell membrane and cytoskeleton, interaction with organelles including mitochondria, and DNA binding, culminating in cell death.
limitations: This is an author-synthesized model integrating all individual observations; no single experiment demonstrates that all mechanisms operate simultaneously or that any one is necessary and sufficient for killing. The contribution of each target to overall lethality is unquantified.

claim_text: The specific binding of antimicrobial peptides to gold nanoclusters improves the interaction of these nanostructured systems with the biological target.
limitations: No mechanistic assay is described; 'biological target' is unspecified; conclusion is drawn from comparative MIC50 data showing conjugates outperform free peptides, not from a direct interaction study.

claim_text: Both cationic peptides (NBC2253 and NBC2254) are designed based on principles whereby cationic charge governs antimicrobial activity and microbial specificity.
limitations: This is a design rationale drawn from cited literature (Tam et al. 2008), not directly tested for these specific peptides in the paper.

claim_text: The antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLs) from Bacillus subtilis fmbj exerted a direct inactivation effect on cell-free virus stocks of PRV, PPV, NDV, and IBDV.
direct_assay_types: cell-free virus inactivation assay
limitations: Only abstract/preview text available; full methodology and dose-response data are behind paywall; mechanism of inactivation (e.g., envelope disruption, protein denaturation) is not specified

claim_text: The AMLs effectively inhibited infection and replication of NDV and IBDV in vitro.
direct_assay_types: cell-based infection/replication inhibition assay
limitations: The specific step(s) of the replication cycle targeted (entry, uncoating, replication, assembly, egress) are not described in the available text; full data behind paywall

claim_text: The AMLs failed to inhibit infection and replication of PRV and PPV despite direct inactivating activity on cell-free stocks.
direct_assay_types: cell-based infection/replication inhibition assay
limitations: No mechanistic explanation for the differential activity is provided; may reflect cytotoxicity constraints (lower selectivity index for PK-15 cells hosting PRV/PPV) rather than a mechanistic distinction

claim_text: The mode of bacterial killing of indolicidin and its glycosylated analogue [βGlc-T9,K7]indolicidin seemed unaffected upon glycosylation, indicating the glycosylated peptide retains the parental mechanism of bacterial killing.
limitations: Abstract states the mode is retained but does not specify what the mode is; full experimental details inaccessible (paywalled); 'seemed unaffected' hedges the conclusion

claim_text: Indolicidin and [βGlc-T9,K7]indolicidin bind lipopolysaccharide (LPS), and this LPS-binding activity was unaffected upon glycosylation.
direct_assay_types: LPS binding assay
limitations: Specific assay format not described in visible abstract; full paper behind paywall; LBP listed in abbreviations suggests a competition/displacement assay but cannot be confirmed

claim_text: The cytokine inhibitory potential of indolicidin and [βGlc-T9,K7]indolicidin (IL-6 and TNF-α inhibition) was unaffected upon glycosylation.
direct_assay_types: cytokine inhibition assay (IL-6, TNF-α)
limitations: Whether inhibition acts via LPS neutralization, direct cell-signaling interference, or another route is not stated in the visible abstract; assay conditions not described

claim_text: The absence of significant structural changes upon glycosylation accounts for the retained functions and mode of action of [βGlc-T9,K7]indolicidin.
limitations: Causal link between structural conservation and retained mechanism is inferred from correlation, not directly demonstrated; NMR structure used as proxy; 'possibly retained' language in abstract acknowledges uncertainty

claim_text: LfcinB causes depolarization of the cytoplasmic membrane in susceptible bacteria.
limitations: Stated as established background from prior work (Ulvatne et al. 2001); the present paper's mechanism-of-action experiments are described as still needing elucidation.

claim_text: When bacteria were treated with LfcinB at the MIC for 1 hour, blebs formed and holes of various sizes appeared on the cell surface while the cell still maintained its overall integrity, indicating a major membrane permeability effect on the cytoplasmic membrane of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
direct_assay_types: atomic force microscopy (AFM), morphological imaging of peptide-treated bacteria
limitations: AFM provides surface/morphological data only; cannot directly confirm which membrane leaflet is disrupted, the precise mechanism of pore formation, or events below the cell surface. Integrity being maintained limits conclusions about lethality mechanism.

claim_text: Because cell integrity was maintained despite membrane disruption at the MIC, LfcinB may act on an intracellular target in addition to its membrane-permeabilizing effect.
limitations: Explicitly framed as a possibility ('may be a possible intracellular target'); no direct intracellular-targeting assay (e.g., DNA/RNA/protein binding) was reported in the visible text; inferred solely from AFM morphology.

claim_text: The combination of LfcinB with aureomycin produced synergistic bactericidal activity against E. coli, S. aureus, and P. aeruginosa, consistent with LfcinB enhancing antibiotic access through membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: synergy testing (killing kinetics / MIC-based combination assay)
limitations: Synergy data are consistent with but do not prove a membrane-permeabilization-mediated uptake mechanism; neomycin did not show the same synergy, indicating the effect is antibiotic-class-dependent and the precise basis is not established.

claim_text: The combination of cecropin A and LfcinB had synergistic antimicrobial effects against E. coli, suggesting the two peptides act through complementary or cooperative membrane-targeting mechanisms.
direct_assay_types: synergy testing
limitations: The mechanistic basis of the synergy is not determined; no assay distinguishing additive membrane disruption from independent killing pathways was reported.

claim_text: Lycosin-II kills tumor cells through cell membrane disruption, as demonstrated by lactate dehydrogenase leakage assay and scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH leakage assay), scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Assays performed on HCT 116 colorectal cancer cell line only; SEM provides morphological evidence but does not resolve molecular mechanism of membrane disruption

claim_text: Lycosin-II activates the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, evidenced by increased Bax proapoptotic protein expression and elevated caspase-3 activity after treatment.
direct_assay_types: Bax protein expression assay, caspase-3 activity assay
limitations: Upstream triggers of Bax activation not identified; mitochondrial membrane potential or cytochrome c release not measured to fully confirm intrinsic pathway

claim_text: Lycosin-II possesses cytotoxic activity against HCT 116 human colorectal cancer cells with an IC50 of 70.79 µg/ml, killing cells within 30 minutes of treatment.
direct_assay_types: MTT assay
limitations: Single cell line tested; rapid 30-min kill time is consistent with membrane disruption but MTT alone cannot distinguish membrane lysis from other rapid cytotoxic mechanisms

claim_text: Lycosin-II's antitumor activity is structurally enabled by its cationicity, α-helical conformation, and amphipathicity, which are properties appropriate for membrane-active peptides.
limitations: Based solely on computational (PEP-FOLD) structural prediction; no direct experimental validation of secondary structure (e.g., CD spectroscopy) reported in this paper

claim_text: Lycosin-II exerts moderate hemolytic activity, indicating some degree of non-selective membrane disruption toward normal erythrocytes.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Degree of selectivity between cancer and normal cells not fully characterized; hemolytic activity described as 'moderate' without quantitative comparison to therapeutic doses

claim_text: RP9 affects bacterial cell surfaces directly, as observed by scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of bacterial surfaces
limitations: SEM shows surface morphological changes but does not distinguish pore formation, membrane disruption, or other surface-level mechanisms; only tested against V. cholerae and B. pumilus.

claim_text: KT2 and RT2 induce apoptotic cell death in HeLa human cervical cancer cells.
direct_assay_types: human apoptosis array assay
limitations: Apoptosis array detects protein-level markers of apoptosis but does not resolve the upstream trigger (membrane disruption, receptor signaling, etc.); tested only in HeLa cells, not in CaSki or normal cells; specific apoptotic pathway (intrinsic vs. extrinsic) is not delineated in the available text.

claim_text: Smp76 prevents HCV infection by inactivating extra-cellular infectious particles.
direct_assay_types: cell culture infectivity assay (Huh7it-1 cells, HCV JFH1 genotype 2a)
limitations: Only genotype 2a tested; full-text methods not accessible from this abstract/reference-list excerpt, so precise assay details unverifiable

claim_text: Smp76 suppresses secondary HCV infection without affecting viral replication.
direct_assay_types: cell culture infectivity assay distinguishing entry/replication steps
limitations: Mechanistic distinction between entry inhibition and replication suppression relies on experimental design details not fully described in the available text

claim_text: Smp76 exerts antiviral activity against dengue virus (DENV type 2) in cell culture.
direct_assay_types: cell culture infectivity assay (Vero/SLAM cells, DENV Trinidad 1751 type 2)
limitations: Only DENV serotype 2 tested; mechanism of anti-DENV action not characterised beyond virocidal/entry inhibition inference

claim_text: Smp76 inactivates extracellular (virion-level) infectious particles rather than acting intracellularly on viral replication machinery.
direct_assay_types: virocidal/extracellular inactivation assay in cell culture
limitations: Exact protocol for distinguishing extracellular inactivation from intracellular effects not detailed in the accessible text; mechanism of virion inactivation (e.g., envelope disruption, receptor blocking) not determined

claim_text: Smp76 is neither cytotoxic nor hemolytic at concentrations 1000-fold above the antiviral IC50, implying its antiviral mechanism does not involve non-specific membrane lysis of host cells.
direct_assay_types: cytotoxicity assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Absence of toxicity constrains but does not define the mechanism; selective virion targeting mechanism remains uncharacterised

claim_text: d-Leucine modified CM11 peptide disrupts bacterial cell morphology and structural integrity, as visualized by scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of bacterial cell morphology
limitations: SEM documents gross morphological changes but cannot distinguish the specific mechanistic basis (e.g., membrane lysis, cell wall degradation, intracellular target disruption); full methods and results sections are paywalled, so the extent of SEM characterization is unknown from the available text.

claim_text: OM19R penetrates rapidly into E. coli cells without causing membrane damage, consistent with a non-lytic intracellular mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: confocal laser scanning microscopy (cell penetration and membrane integrity assessment)
limitations: Demonstrated only in E. coli; the specific intracellular target is not identified in the text provided; microscopy does not exclude transient or sub-lethal membrane perturbation below detection threshold.

claim_text: OM19R activity against E. coli is dependent on the inner membrane transporter protein SbmA, which is required for peptide uptake into the cell.
direct_assay_types: sbmA gene-knockout strain susceptibility assay
limitations: Knockout experiments establish necessity of SbmA but do not resolve the downstream intracellular mechanism; SbmA dependence is inferred from loss-of-activity phenotype, not from direct transport measurement.

claim_text: Proline-rich antimicrobial peptides (PR-AMPs) including OM19R do not kill bacteria by lytic (membrane-disrupting) mechanisms.
