limitations: This is partly a class-level attribution from the PR-AMP literature applied to OM19R by design rationale; the paper's own direct evidence (confocal microscopy showing no membrane damage) supports but does not fully prove the claim for OM19R across all target organisms.

claim_text: Inhibited activity of OM19R against Klebsiella pneumoniae implies that SbmA or an equivalent uptake route is absent or non-functional in that organism, blocking intracellular access.
limitations: The paper does not directly test SbmA expression or function in K. pneumoniae; the mechanistic inference is based solely on the MIC result and analogy to known SbmA biology in E. coli.

claim_text: Temporin-1RNa and temporin-1RNb adopt an aperiodic structure in water but transition to an organised α-helical conformation in membrane-mimicking environments (SDS micelles and TFE), consistent with a membrane-active mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy in SDS and TFE
limitations: SDS and TFE are membrane mimics, not actual lipid bilayers; no direct membrane permeabilization, leakage, or disruption assay is reported in the available text.

claim_text: The conformational transition of temporin-1RNa and temporin-1RNb induced by TFE or SDS reflects their potential ability to interact with anionic membranes.
limitations: Authors explicitly qualify this as 'potential ability'; the inference is based solely on secondary-structure data in membrane-mimicking solvents with no direct binding or permeabilization assay reported.

claim_text: Serum (10% v/v) inhibited the antibacterial effect of LK3, consistent with serum protein binding reducing peptide bioavailability.
limitations: Mechanism of inhibition (e.g., albumin binding vs. protease degradation vs. charge neutralization) was not directly determined; inferred from activity loss in serum conditions.

claim_text: The cationic character of LK3 and LK4 is proposed as the physicochemical basis for their antimicrobial activity through electrostatic attraction to negatively charged bacterial membranes.
limitations: No direct membrane interaction or permeabilization assays are reported in the available text; cationicity is a design rationale inferred from AMP field conventions, not demonstrated experimentally for these peptides.

claim_text: LK3 exhibited antibiofilm activity (44.45% reduction) against P. aeruginosa at 4× MIC, implying the peptide disrupts or prevents biofilm formation.
direct_assay_types: antibiofilm assay
limitations: The assay measures biofilm mass reduction but does not identify whether the mechanism is bactericidal killing of sessile cells, inhibition of biofilm matrix synthesis, or dispersal; no mechanistic dissection is reported.

claim_text: Hydrophobicity is crucial for the interaction between amphipathic antimicrobial peptides and microbial pathogens.
limitations: Stated as background rationale in the abstract, not demonstrated by a specific assay in the available text; full methods/results section is paywalled.

claim_text: Higher hydrophobicity in mastoparans correlates with higher helical content, which is associated with greater antimicrobial and hemolytic activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism (helical content), MIC assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Correlation across only three peptides; causal direction (hydrophobicity → helix → activity) is inferred from structural comparison, not mechanistically dissected; full data not visible in available text.

claim_text: Self-assembly of the peptides reduces their biological potency, as mastoparan L (least hydrophobic) shows the least self-assembly yet the weakest antimicrobial activity, while mastoparan C (most hydrophobic) shows greater self-assembly alongside higher activity.
direct_assay_types: reversed-phase chromatography temperature profiling (self-assembly), MIC assay
limitations: Self-assembly is treated as a modulating factor, not a primary mechanism; the relationship is correlative across three peptides only.

claim_text: Optimal hydrophobicity, rather than the highest possible hydrophobicity, enhances antimicrobial efficacy while minimizing hemolytic activity, suggesting a hydrophobicity threshold for selective membrane targeting.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Mechanistic basis for selectivity (e.g., differential membrane composition between bacteria and erythrocytes) is implied but not directly demonstrated in the available abstract text; only three peptides compared.

claim_text: Brevilaterin B inhibits proliferation of epidermal cancer cell A431 in a dose-dependent manner while having no effect on normal control cells at 2.0 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: CCK-8 proliferation assay, LDH membrane permeability assay
limitations: Only A431 and its paired normal cells tested for selectivity; dose range and normal cell identity not fully described in abstract

claim_text: Brevilaterin B induces apoptosis in A431 epidermal cancer cells, with an apoptotic ratio of 71.0% observed at 2.0–3.0 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry, morphological apoptosis assessment
limitations: Apoptotic pathway (caspase-dependent vs. independent) not characterized; mechanism upstream of apoptosis not fully resolved

claim_text: Brevilaterin B increases intracellular ROS levels in A431 cells by 21.3%, implicating oxidative stress in its anticancer mechanism.
direct_assay_types: DCFH-DA fluorescent probe ROS detection
limitations: Causal relationship between ROS increase and cell death not experimentally established; whether ROS is upstream or downstream of mitochondrial damage is not determined

claim_text: Brevilaterin B reduces mitochondrial membrane potential in A431 cells by 48.8%, indicating mitochondrial dysfunction as a key component of its anticancer action.
direct_assay_types: JC-1 fluorescent probe mitochondrial membrane potential assay
limitations: Whether mitochondrial membrane potential collapse is the initiating event or a downstream consequence is not resolved

claim_text: Brevilaterin B's anticancer action is mainly focused on the mitochondria of cancer cells, based on concurrent ROS elevation and mitochondrial membrane potential reduction.
direct_assay_types: DCFH-DA ROS detection, JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential assay
limitations: Inference drawn from two indirect readouts; direct demonstration of mitochondrial targeting (e.g., mitochondrial localization, cytochrome c release, caspase activation) is not reported in the abstract

claim_text: Brevilaterin B increases membrane permeability of cancer cells, consistent with a membrane-disrupting component of its mechanism.
direct_assay_types: LDH release assay
limitations: LDH release may reflect late-stage apoptotic/necrotic membrane breakdown rather than primary membrane disruption; not distinguished from secondary permeabilization due to apoptosis

claim_text: KABT-AMP exerts putative membranolytic (membrane-disrupting) activity against target microbial cells, as substantiated by electron microscopic analysis.
direct_assay_types: electron microscopy (SEM morphological analysis of membrane damage)
limitations: Authors use the qualifier 'putative'; evidence is morphological (EM imaging) only — no functional membrane permeabilization assay (e.g., propidium iodide uptake, membrane potential measurement) is reported in the visible text; mechanism is inferred from structural observations of cell damage rather than direct measurement of membrane disruption kinetics or pore formation.

claim_text: Mobilisin destroys the cell membrane integrity of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as confirmed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) in vitro.
direct_assay_types: membrane disruption (SEM imaging)
limitations: SEM shows morphological damage but does not distinguish between primary membrane disruption and secondary cell death consequences; full-text methods not visible to confirm quantitative details

claim_text: Plantaricin KL-1Y exhibited bactericidal activity against Bacillus cereus JCM 2152T, indicating it kills rather than merely inhibits this organism.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal vs. bacteriostatic determination (mode-of-killing assay)
limitations: Only one indicator strain tested for bactericidal mode; whether killing mechanism generalises to other susceptible organisms (including Gram-negatives) is not established in the available text.

claim_text: The peptide Tβ4 9-19 (EIEKFDKSKLK) possesses a central hydrophobic core flanked by peripheral charged residues, suggesting a possible mechanism of interaction with bacterial and eukaryotic membrane models.
limitations: Derived solely from 1 µs MD simulation in water; no experimental membrane-interaction assay performed; reviewer explicitly noted no direct confirmation of mode of action

claim_text: The anti-biofilm activity of the peptide at sub-inhibitory concentrations could be due to its MD-derived conformations interacting with the bacterial membrane.
limitations: Authors use hedged language ('could be due to'); based entirely on computational simulation; reviewer noted biofilm inhibition may simply reflect antimicrobial (growth-inhibitory) nature of peptide; no mechanistic experiment performed

claim_text: Near the surface of both POPC and POPC:POPG membrane models, the peptide engages the bilayer through electrostatic and van der Waals interactions, adopting open/random conformations rather than a fixed structure.
limitations: MD simulation only (200 ns production run with a single peptide molecule); peptide oligomerization not modeled; no experimental membrane-binding assay; cluster analysis shows no preferred conformation, limiting mechanistic interpretation

claim_text: In the bacterial membrane model (POPC:POPG 2:1), the peptide shows a preference for associating with the leaflet containing fewer POPG lipids, suggesting charge-dependent membrane leaflet selectivity.
limitations: Single MD trajectory observation; reviewer flagged lack of statistical significance and requested replicate simulations; no experimental validation of leaflet preference

claim_text: Bac-GM17 displays a bactericidal mode of action against Agrobacterium tumefaciens C58.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal mode determination (killing vs. inhibition assay)
limitations: Full methodology not available in the provided text (abstract/preview only); the specific assay used to distinguish bactericidal from bacteriostatic activity is not described.

claim_text: Bac-GM17 displays a fungistatic mode of action against Candida tropicalis R2 CIP203.
direct_assay_types: fungistatic mode determination (growth inhibition vs. killing assay)
limitations: Full methodology not available in the provided text (abstract/preview only); the specific assay used to distinguish fungistatic from fungicidal activity is not described.

claim_text: MAD1 forms pore-like supramolecular assemblies within the plasma membranes of cancer cells to potentiate lytic cell death.
direct_assay_types: microscopy, spectrophotometry, flow cytometry
limitations: Full methods and data are behind a paywall; only abstract-level summary is available; pore 'like' language implies structural inference rather than atomic-resolution confirmation.

claim_text: MAD1 forms pore-like supramolecular assemblies within the nuclear membranes of cancer cells, contributing to cell death.
direct_assay_types: microscopy
limitations: Nuclear membrane targeting is reported but mechanistic detail (e.g., how MAD1 reaches the nucleus) is not visible in the available text; full data are paywalled.

claim_text: MAD1 kills cancer cells through apoptotic mechanisms in addition to lytic membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry
limitations: Specific apoptotic markers or pathway (intrinsic vs. extrinsic) are not described in the available abstract text.

claim_text: The anticancer activity of MAD1 is driven by electrostatic targeting of the electronegative (anionic) cancer cell surface, analogous to AMP targeting of anionic bacterial membranes.
limitations: Stated as a mechanistic rationale and design principle in the introduction; direct binding or zeta-potential measurements are not described in the visible text.

claim_text: Spatial sequestration of amphiphilic regions in the peptide sequence increases anticancer peptide potency.
direct_assay_types: cellular viability assays (implied by SAR investigation)
limitations: Structure-activity relationship conclusion drawn from de novo peptide design panel; specific assay types confirming the structural basis are not detailed in the abstract.

claim_text: Increasing amphiphilicity via spatial sequestration reduces cancer-cell specificity (selectivity over normal cells), representing a potency-specificity trade-off.
direct_assay_types: cellular assays (implied)
limitations: Only stated as an SAR trend in the abstract; quantitative selectivity data are paywalled.

claim_text: Cbf-K16 selectively kills MRSA cells whose cell wall integrity has been compromised by beta-lactam antibiotics, suggesting its bactericidal activity depends on cell wall non-integrity as the entry point.
limitations: Mechanism inferred from synergy pattern (checkerboard FIC ≤0.5 + killing kinetics); the paper does not isolate which downstream step (membrane access, cytoplasmic target) is rate-limiting; only MRSA tested for this synergy hypothesis.

claim_text: Combination treatment of Cbf-K16 with beta-lactam antibiotics causes complete physical rupture of MRSA cells with leakage of cellular contents.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization/rupture (flow cytometry), ultrastructural cell disruption (transmission electron microscopy)
limitations: Rupture is demonstrated for the combination condition; whether Cbf-K16 alone at sub-MIC causes any partial membrane disruption is not distinguished in the available abstract text; full quantitative flow cytometry data not extractable from the abstract alone.

claim_text: Cbf-K16 acts through cytoplasmic membrane penetration followed by intracellular DNA binding, as established in prior work cited by the paper (Hao et al. 2013).
limitations: This mechanism is cited from a separate prior study on E. coli (NDM-1-carrying), not directly demonstrated against MRSA in this paper; applicability to the MRSA context is assumed by the authors but not re-tested here.

claim_text: Enterocin LD3 causes dissipation of membrane potential in the indicator strain Micrococcus luteus.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential dissipation assay
limitations: Demonstrated only in a single indicator strain (M. luteus); full experimental details (dye, concentration, time course) are in the paywalled full text and not available in the provided excerpt.

claim_text: Enterocin LD3 causes loss of internal ATP in Micrococcus luteus.
direct_assay_types: intracellular ATP measurement
limitations: Demonstrated only in M. luteus; loss of ATP is consistent with membrane disruption but the paper does not explicitly attribute it to a specific pore-forming mechanism in the available text.

claim_text: Enterocin LD3 is bactericidal against Micrococcus luteus.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal activity assay (viability/kill measurement)
limitations: Reported for one indicator strain only; broader bactericidal vs. bacteriostatic distinction across the full spectrum of inhibited organisms is not stated.

claim_text: Carbohydrate and lipid moieties play no role in the antimicrobial activity of enterocin LD3, as activity was unaffected by amylase and lipase treatment.
limitations: Enzyme insensitivity is indirect evidence; absence of activity loss rules out essential carbohydrate/lipid components but does not fully characterize the functional pharmacophore.

claim_text: Lactocin 160 targets the cytoplasmic membrane of Gardnerella vaginalis as its primary molecular site of action.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (inferred from ATP efflux and proton motive force dissipation assays)
limitations: Full experimental methods and figures are behind paywall; claim is supported by the two downstream readouts (ATP efflux, PMF dissipation) rather than a direct membrane-binding or structural assay visible in this text.

claim_text: Lactocin 160 causes efflux of ATP molecules from G. vaginalis cells.
direct_assay_types: ATP efflux measurement
limitations: Quantitative data and assay details are not available in the abstract-only preview; no time-course or dose-response data are visible.

claim_text: Lactocin 160 dissipates the proton motive force of G. vaginalis.
direct_assay_types: proton motive force dissipation (membrane potential and/or pH gradient measurement)
limitations: Specific sub-components measured (ΔΨ vs. ΔpH) and assay methodology are not described in the visible text; full data are paywalled.

claim_text: Lactocin 160 selectively inhibits BV-associated vaginal pathogens (G. vaginalis and Prevotella bivia) without inhibiting healthy vaginal lactobacilli.
limitations: This selectivity claim is presented as background/prior knowledge rather than a result of the current mechanistic study; underlying growth-inhibition data are cited from earlier work (Dover et al. 2007; Li et al. 2005) and not re-demonstrated here.

claim_text: Increasing the net positive charge of antimicrobial peptides increases their antimicrobial activity, as demonstrated by Cath-A (+17 net charge) showing the highest activity against MRSA compared to Cath-BF and Cath-B.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (32–128 µg/ml against MRSA strains)
limitations: MIC data show correlation between charge and activity but do not directly probe the molecular mechanism; full-text methods not accessible to confirm assay details

claim_text: Cath-A exerts bactericidal (not merely bacteriostatic) activity, neutralizing a clinical MRSA isolate within 60 minutes at 1× MIC concentration.
direct_assay_types: bacterial time-kill kinetic assay
limitations: Only one MRSA isolate tested at 1× MIC in the kinetic experiment; mechanism underlying rapid killing is not directly characterized in this study

claim_text: The parent compound BF-30, structurally related to Cath-A and Cath-B, kills bacteria through cytoplasmic membrane permeabilization and DNA binding, implying a similar dual mechanism for the derivatives studied here.
limitations: This mechanism was established for BF-30 in cited prior studies (Wang et al. 2013; Zhou et al. 2011), not directly demonstrated for Cath-A or Cath-B in the present paper; extrapolation across peptide variants may not hold

claim_text: The cationic, amphipathic helical structure of Cath-BF-derived peptides enables interaction with negatively charged bacterial membranes, underpinning their broad antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Stated as design rationale based on general cathelicidin/AMP literature; no membrane interaction assays (e.g., dye leakage, depolarization) are reported in this paper for Cath-A or Cath-B

claim_text: High concentrations of subtilosin are virucidal against HSV-1.
direct_assay_types: virucidal assay
limitations: Concentration threshold not defined in the available abstract text; full dose-response data not visible.

claim_text: At non-virucidal concentrations, subtilosin inhibits wild-type HSV-1 and aciclovir-resistant HSV-1 mutants in a dose-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: antiviral inhibition assay
limitations: Inhibitory mechanism is not resolved; the paper explicitly states the antiviral mechanism is not fully understood.

claim_text: Subtilosin does not affect viral multiplication steps prior to protein synthesis.
direct_assay_types: time-of-addition assay, western blot
limitations: Conclusion is inferential from a negative finding (absence of effect on pre-synthesis steps); the paper explicitly acknowledges the exact antiviral mechanism is not fully understood; full results section not available to assess controls or quantitative thresholds.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), including EmPis-1L, possess bactericidal effects in a rapid membrane attacking mode, which is the proposed basis for their effectiveness against VBNC state bacteria.
limitations: This is stated as a rationale in the abstract ('are supposed to be effective'), not demonstrated mechanistically in the accessible text; full experimental data is behind paywall.

claim_text: EmPis-1L kills (lyses) VBNC state cells of E. coli O157, S. aureus, and V. parahaemolyticus, with 10 μmol/L achieving 100% killing within 1 h.
limitations: The term 'lysed' implies membrane disruption but no direct mechanistic assay (e.g., membrane permeabilization, dye leakage) is described in the accessible abstract text; figures are paywalled.

claim_text: The membrane-attacking mode of action of EmPis-1L circumvents the antibiotic resistance acquired by VBNC state bacteria, which resist ampicillin and kanamycin through mechanisms that do not protect against membrane disruption.
limitations: Inferred from the juxtaposition of antibiotic resistance data and AMP activity data; no direct comparative mechanistic experiment is described in the available text.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides (including C18G) selectively bind to bacterial cell surfaces through electrostatic interactions.
limitations: Stated as established background knowledge for AMPs generally; not demonstrated by a new direct assay in this paper for C18G variants.

claim_text: After binding to the bacterial cell surface, C18G inserts into the cell membrane and causes local disruptions of membrane integrity, leading to cell death.
limitations: Framed as prior/general knowledge for AMPs; membrane insertion not directly measured in this study (no patch-clamp, leakage kinetics, or electron microscopy reported in the available text).

claim_text: C18G and its non-natural amino acid variants preferentially bind anionic lipids over zwitterionic lipids.
direct_assay_types: Trp fluorescence binding assay (lipid vesicles)
limitations: Vesicle-based assay; may not fully recapitulate the heterogeneous bacterial membrane environment.

claim_text: More hydrophobic C18G variants are more deeply buried within anionic lipid bilayers compared to zwitterionic bilayers.
direct_assay_types: Trp fluorescence quenching (depth-of-insertion measurement)
limitations: Depth inferred from quenching efficiency; exact insertion geometry not structurally resolved.

claim_text: The most bactericidally effective C18G variants are those that also produce measurable disruption of bacterial membranes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization assay (type not fully specified in abstract)
limitations: Correlation between MIC and membrane disruption does not exclude additional intracellular targets; one variant with strong activity showed only low-level disruption, suggesting the relationship is not absolute.

claim_text: Amino acid substitutions with long flexible carbon chains in C18G maintain or increase antimicrobial activity relative to natural hydrophobic residues, implying these substitutions preserve the membrane-active mechanism.
limitations: Activity (MIC) data support the claim, but mechanism equivalence is inferred; no direct assay rules out alternative modes of action for the non-natural variants.

claim_text: GIBIMPY4 likely exerts its antibacterial activity through electrostatic interactions with bacterial membranes, as evidenced by its sensitivity to salt concentration in E. coli O157:H7.
limitations: Salt sensitivity is an indirect proxy for electrostatic mechanism; no direct membrane assay (e.g., permeabilization, dye leakage) is reported in the visible paper text; full paper is paywalled so additional mechanistic data may exist.

claim_text: GIBIMPY4 is designed to act on bacterial membranes via an amphipathic α-helical structure with a net cationic charge of +5, properties associated with membrane disruption in cationic AMPs.
limitations: Mechanism is inferred from structural design rationale (amphipathicity, α-helix, cationic charge); no direct membrane-disruption assay is reported in the abstract; the link to mechanism is based on class-level analogy, not peptide-specific experimentation.

claim_text: GIBIMPY4 shows selectivity for bacterial cells over eukaryotic cells, with a specificity index of 9.01 for E. coli O157:H7, suggesting differential membrane targeting.
limitations: Specificity index is derived from cytotoxicity vs. antibacterial activity comparison (in vitro); it implies but does not directly demonstrate a membrane-selectivity mechanism; no mechanistic assay (e.g., bacterial vs. mammalian membrane binding) is described.

claim_text: GIBIMPY4 exerts a bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal effect against E. coli O157:H7, indicating growth inhibition rather than direct cell killing as the primary mode of action for that organism.
limitations: Bacteriostatic classification is inferred from optical density measurements by broth microdilution; the specific molecular mechanism underlying growth inhibition is not determined; full paper may contain time-kill data.

claim_text: rCf-ALF2 disrupts the bacterial cell membrane of E. coli, as evidenced by membrane blebbing, disruption, and cell content leakage observed by scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: membrane disruption (SEM: blebbing, cell content leakage)
limitations: SEM observation is morphological only; does not distinguish primary membrane disruption from secondary damage; tested on E. coli only, not S. aureus or other strains

claim_text: The cationic net charge (+9) and hydrophobic ratio (34%) of Cf-ALF2 are proposed to underlie its membrane-targeting antimicrobial activity, consistent with characteristic AMP properties.
limitations: Inferred from physicochemical properties alone; no direct charge-ablation or hydrophobicity-ablation experiments performed; correlation does not establish causation

claim_text: Bomidin penetrated the bacterial membrane and induced the release of cytoplasmic contents, as demonstrated by PNP and ONPG assays measuring membrane permeability.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (PNP assay, ONPG assay)
limitations: Assays performed on V. parahaemolyticus only; membrane disruption inferred from release of cytoplasmic markers rather than direct imaging of pore formation

claim_text: Bomidin interacted with DNA to form a bomidin–DNA complex that inhibits bacterial survival.
direct_assay_types: DNA binding
limitations: Only the abstract is available; the specific assay used to demonstrate DNA binding (e.g., gel retardation, fluorescence displacement) is not described in the available text; functional consequence (inhibition of survival) is inferred rather than mechanistically resolved

claim_text: Bomidin caused damage and dysfunction to the bacterial cell wall and membrane, as revealed by transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological damage observed but does not distinguish between primary mechanism and downstream structural consequence; limited to V. parahaemolyticus

claim_text: Bacteriocin PFS-3 exerts bactericidal effects on MDR E. coli B2 by disrupting cardiolipin in the outer membrane of the cells.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane disruption (cardiolipin targeting)
limitations: Only the abstract is available; full experimental details (assay methods, controls, dose-response) are behind a paywall and cannot be verified from this text alone.

claim_text: So-Crustin disrupts bacterial membranes, as demonstrated by scanning electron microscopy revealing bacterial lysis and structural damage.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
limitations: SEM shows morphological outcome but does not distinguish between primary membrane disruption and secondary lysis from other mechanisms

claim_text: So-Crustin dissipates bacterial membrane potential (membrane depolarization) as a mode of antibacterial action.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential assay (membrane depolarization)
limitations: Full article text not available; assay methodology details and bacterial strains tested cannot be verified beyond abstract

claim_text: So-Crustin induces reactive oxygen species (ROS) in bacteria as a mode of antibacterial action.
direct_assay_types: ROS induction assay
limitations: Full article text not available; whether ROS induction is a primary mechanism or a downstream consequence of membrane damage cannot be determined from the abstract alone

claim_text: The cationic (+6.25) and amphipathic (34% hydrophobicity) properties of So-Crustin contribute to its antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
limitations: Physicochemical characterization is correlative; causal role of charge and hydrophobicity in membrane interaction is inferred from peptide properties and MIC data, not from direct biophysical membrane-interaction assays described in the abstract

claim_text: K4 exerts a bactericidal (rather than bacteriostatic) effect on Aeromonas salmonicida and Vibrio splendidus LGP32 at concentrations below 45 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: automated optical density growth monitoring (OD meter)
limitations: Only two aquatic bacterial species tested; MIC/MBC ratio not explicitly reported; full-text results tables not visible in the provided preview.

claim_text: K4's cationic N-terminal moiety and amphipathic α-helical structure are presented as the structural basis underlying its antibacterial activity.
limitations: The paper states the structural features but does not perform new mechanistic assays to link them to a specific killing mechanism; mechanistic characterization is attributed to a prior study (Legrand et al. 2011) cited in the references.

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of Mu-17 likely occurs through membrane interaction.
limitations: Authors use 'likely' — no membrane assay data (permeabilization, leakage, depolarization, etc.) is reported in the available text; inference appears to rest on the amphipathic alpha-helical structure and analogy to other scorpion AMPs rather than direct experimental evidence.

claim_text: Mu-17 forms an amphipathic alpha-helix structure, which is the structural basis proposed for its membrane-targeting activity.
limitations: Amphipathic helix is a structural prediction/design feature (leucine zipper-like motif); the text does not report CD spectroscopy or NMR confirming the helix in solution or at a membrane interface.

claim_text: Iturin V disrupts the membrane of Pseudomonas aeruginosa cells, as evidenced by morphological alterations observed in electron micrographs of treated versus untreated cells.
direct_assay_types: membrane morphology imaging (SEM, TEM)
limitations: Demonstrated only against P. aeruginosa MTCC 1934 at 1x MIC; electron microscopy shows gross morphological changes but does not resolve molecular mechanism (e.g., pore formation vs. membrane solubilization vs. lipid extraction); no quantitative membrane integrity metric (e.g., dye leakage) reported in this excerpt.

claim_text: FengycinA-M3 binds to penicillin-binding protein 2B (PBP2B) on the cell membrane of Listeria monocytogenes, which is identified as its primary molecular target.
direct_assay_types: molecular docking
limitations: Full methods are paywalled; the abstract and title assert PBP2B binding but the specific binding assay(s) used (e.g., molecular docking, SPR, pulldown) cannot be confirmed from available text. Molecular docking is computational and does not confirm in-cell binding.

claim_text: FengycinA-M3 disrupts the permeability of the L. monocytogenes cell membrane.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization
limitations: Specific assay type (e.g., fluorescent dye leakage, SYTOX, ONPG) not confirmable from abstract alone; full methods paywalled.

claim_text: FengycinA-M3 causes physical rupture of the L. monocytogenes cell membrane.
direct_assay_types: cell structure/morphology analysis
limitations: Imaging modality (e.g., SEM, TEM) not specified in available abstract text; inference drawn from 'cell structure disruption' framing in title and abstract.

claim_text: FengycinA-M3 acts synergistically with Cefalexin (a beta-lactam PBP inhibitor) against L. monocytogenes, supporting a PBP-related mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: checkerboard MIC assay
limitations: Synergy with a PBP-targeting antibiotic is consistent with PBP2B binding but does not prove it; could reflect additive membrane stress rather than shared target engagement.

claim_text: Transcriptomic and proteomic profiling identified 20 differentially expressed genes/proteins in L. monocytogenes upon FengycinA-M3 treatment, providing molecular evidence of its antibacterial mechanism.
direct_assay_types: RNA-seq transcriptomics, TMT proteomics
limitations: The identities and pathways of the 20 DEGs are not reported in the available abstract text, preventing assessment of which specific cellular processes are implicated; multi-omics data alone do not establish causality.

claim_text: TnCRT2 and TnCRT3 increased the positive charge on the cell surface of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as measured by zeta potential analysis.
direct_assay_types: zeta potential measurement
limitations: Zeta potential shift indicates peptide-membrane surface interaction but does not directly demonstrate membrane permeabilization, pore formation, or cell death mechanism; full mechanistic pathway not established from this assay alone; only abstract text available, not full results/discussion sections

claim_text: Omw1 and omw2 exhibit membranolytic activity, evidenced by propidium iodide uptake (red fluorescence) in peptide-treated cells compared to untreated controls, indicating disruption of membrane integrity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (propidium iodide fluorescence staining)
limitations: PI assay confirms membrane compromise but does not distinguish primary pore formation from secondary membrane collapse; only abstract-level detail available, full dose–response data behind paywall.

claim_text: Omw1 acts by causing complete lysis of E. coli ATCC 25922 at 1× MIC within 40 min and of S. aureus ATCC 25923 at 2× MIC within 60 min, demonstrating rapid bactericidal kinetics consistent with a membrane-targeting mechanism.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics
limitations: Time-kill confirms bactericidal activity but does not by itself establish the molecular target; lysis is inferred from killing curve shape, not directly visualised in this excerpt.

claim_text: Omw1 and omw2 cause notable morphological damage to microbial cells, as shown by scanning electron microscopy, consistent with cell-surface or membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
limitations: SEM reveals surface/structural changes but cannot resolve whether membrane disruption is the primary lethal event or a downstream consequence; only described qualitatively ('notable') in the abstract.

claim_text: Omw1 and omw2 inhibit biofilm formation and disperse mature biofilms of C. albicans at sub-MIC concentrations (1/2× MIC), indicating an anti-biofilm mechanism distinct from bulk bactericidal/fungicidal killing.
direct_assay_types: biofilm inhibition assay, biofilm dispersal assay
limitations: Mechanism of biofilm disruption (e.g., matrix degradation, interference with adhesion signalling, or membrane damage within biofilm) is not characterised; tested against C. albicans only in this context.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF kills bacteria via membrane permeabilisation, as demonstrated by SYTOX green uptake and DAPI/PI fluorescence staining showing compromised membrane integrity in S. aureus, E. coli, and C. albicans.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green uptake assay, DAPI/PI fluorescence staining)
limitations: Permeabilization at 1×MIC was only clearly shown for S. aureus; E. coli and C. albicans required 4×MIC for ~100% permeabilization, suggesting weaker primary membrane action against these organisms.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF adopts a random coil structure in aqueous solution but transitions to an α-helical conformation in membrane-mimic environments, consistent with membrane-targeting activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: CD was performed in TFE/SDS membrane-mimic solutions, not intact bacterial membranes; α-helical structure in mimic does not directly prove the same conformation occurs in vivo.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF is less effective against Gram-negative P. aeruginosa because its helical structure has higher affinity for LPS in the outer membrane, which may prevent translocation to the inner cell membrane.
limitations: Mechanistic explanation for P. aeruginosa reduced activity is inferred from published literature on AMP-LPS interactions; no direct LPS-binding or translocation assay was performed in this study.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF eradicates MRSA biofilms by a detergent-like action that disintegrates the biofilm matrix and kills all sessile bacteria within.
direct_assay_types: biofilm eradication/disruption assay (crystal violet staining for MBEC; colony count CFU assay after biofilm disruption)
limitations: The 'detergent-like' characterization is an interpretive label; no direct structural analysis of biofilm matrix disruption (e.g., confocal imaging, EPS quantification) was performed.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF does not induce resistance in MRSA because its membrane-disruption mechanism targets the bacterial cell membrane, which does not differ significantly between susceptible and resistant strains and is not affected by resistance genes for conventional antibiotics.
direct_assay_types: resistance induction assay (15-cycle sub-MIC passage, followed by MIC re-determination)
limitations: Absence of resistance after 15 cycles is consistent with the hypothesis but does not mechanistically prove the membrane target explanation; the claim about resistance genes not affecting AMP activity is cited from published literature rather than tested directly.

claim_text: Japonicin-2LF passed through the hydrophilic peptidoglycan layer of S. aureus to disrupt the underlying intact cytoplasmic membrane, which is why it is more potent against Gram-positive than Gram-negative bacteria.
limitations: Peptidoglycan passage is inferred from differential MIC/membrane permeability data and the known cell wall architecture; no direct imaging or biochemical assay of peptidoglycan penetration was performed.

claim_text: Biofilm inhibition by japonicin-2LF at concentrations equal to its MIC/MBC is likely related to growth inhibition of planktonic bacteria and prevention of surface colonisation during initial biofilm formation, rather than a distinct anti-biofilm mechanism.
limitations: Authors explicitly state this is an assumption ('We assumed'); no direct experiments distinguishing anti-biofilm from anti-planktonic mechanisms were conducted.

claim_text: The reduced antimicrobial activity of japonicin-2LF in the presence of P. aeruginosa supernatant is likely due to non-specific binding of the peptide to hydrophobic/amphipathic compounds (e.g., quorum-sensing molecules) in the supernatant, reducing the concentration of free active peptide rather than direct proteolytic cleavage.
limitations: Authors explicitly characterize this as a suggestion; no cleaved peptide fragments were detected by MS, supporting the non-cleavage hypothesis, but the specific binding partners were not identified. The 8-fold MIC increase and rapid peptide disappearance at 0 min are the only supporting data.

claim_text: BaCf3 inhibits growth of food-borne pathogens and food spoilage bacteria.
limitations: Only the abstract is visible; no MIC values, killing kinetics, or mode-of-action assays are described in the available text. 'Inhibitory potential' leaves the mechanism unspecified.

claim_text: BaCf3 reduces biofilm formation by strong biofilm-producing strains from food samples by up to 80%.
direct_assay_types: microtiter plate biofilm reduction assay
limitations: The assay measures biomass reduction (outcome), not the mechanism by which biofilm is disrupted (e.g., interference with adhesion, matrix degradation, quorum sensing). Full results section is paywalled.

claim_text: The disulphide linkage between C6 and C13 is structurally important for BaCf3 activity, as the peptide is sensitive to the reducing agent DTT and the oxidizing agent DMSO.
limitations: Sensitivity to DTT/DMSO is reported but activity loss is not explicitly linked to disulphide disruption in the abstract text; the mechanistic inference is implicit. Full experimental data not visible.

claim_text: Peptides m2163 and m2386 greatly enhance cell membrane permeability in SW480 human colorectal cancer cells.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (flow cytometry with FITC-labeled peptides)
limitations: Assay measures permeability change but does not resolve whether membrane disruption is the primary lethal event or a secondary consequence of intracellular signaling.

claim_text: Peptides m2163 and m2386 localize on the cell membrane for a substantial length of time before penetrating into the cell cytoplasm to induce apoptosis.
direct_assay_types: confocal microscopy (FITC-labeled peptides), subcellular fractionation + flow cytometry
limitations: Confocal imaging and fractionation were explicitly demonstrated for m2163; m2386 localization is stated in the abstract as confirmed by confocal microscopy but details are limited in the available text.

claim_text: FITC-m2163 accumulates predominantly in the cytoplasm rather than in the mitochondria of treated SW480 cells.
direct_assay_types: subcellular fractionation + flow cytometry fluorescence intensity measurement
limitations: Only tested for m2163; relies on FITC label not altering peptide localization; fractionation purity is not described.

claim_text: Peptide m2163 induces upregulation of the extrinsic apoptosis death receptors Fas and TRAILR1 on the cell surface of SW480 cells.
direct_assay_types: qRT-PCR, Western blot
limitations: mRNA and protein upregulation is shown but functional receptor activation (ligand-independent clustering, caspase-8 cleavage) is not directly demonstrated.

claim_text: Peptide m2386 induces upregulation of the extrinsic apoptosis death receptors Fas, TNFR1, and TRAILR1 on the cell surface of SW480 cells.
direct_assay_types: qRT-PCR, Western blot
limitations: mRNA and protein upregulation is shown but functional receptor activation is not directly demonstrated; m2386 activates a broader receptor set than m2163 but the mechanistic basis for this difference is not explained.

claim_text: Both peptides m2163 and m2386 induce expression of the mitochondrial apoptosis protein Smac, indicating activation of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway.
direct_assay_types: qRT-PCR, Western blot
limitations: Only Smac is cited as representative of the intrinsic pathway; upstream events (cytochrome c release, Bcl-2 family changes, mitochondrial membrane potential) are not directly measured; Smac upregulation is used as a surrogate for pathway activation.

claim_text: Peptides m2163 and m2386 trigger both the extrinsic (death receptor) and intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis pathways in SW480 cells.
limitations: This is a synthesized conclusion drawn from death-receptor upregulation and Smac induction data; cross-talk between the two pathways (e.g., caspase-8-mediated BID cleavage) is not directly measured; upstream caspase activation is not reported in the available text.

claim_text: pBD-5 causes modest membrane permeabilization of model bacterial membranes, achieving on average 15.45% leakage at 100 µM and 14.55% at 200 µM after 24 h of co-incubation.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage assay with DOPC/DOPG liposomes)
limitations: Model membrane (liposomes), not intact bacteria; leakage is modest (~15% at 200 µM); DOPC/DOPG proxy may not fully replicate Gram-positive vs Gram-negative membrane compositions; in vitro only

claim_text: pBD-5 significantly reduces E. coli metabolic activity in a dose-dependent manner, with reductions of 58–77% at concentrations of 25–200 µM.
direct_assay_types: metabolic activity (resazurin fluorometric reduction assay)
limitations: Effect is significant for E. coli but not for S. epidermidis; resazurin reduction measures overall metabolic activity and does not identify which specific metabolic pathway(s) are impaired; in vitro only

claim_text: pBD-5 causes bacterial cell membrane damage leading to cell death in E. coli, as evidenced by dose-dependent increases in propidium iodide uptake.
direct_assay_types: membrane integrity (confocal fluorescence microscopy with LIVE/DEAD BacLight SYTO-9/propidium iodide staining)
limitations: Images represent selected fields of view; PI uptake confirms loss of membrane integrity but does not distinguish primary vs secondary membrane damage; qualitative/semi-quantitative; in vitro only

claim_text: pBD-5 induces apparent aggregation of E. coli cells at higher concentrations (25–200 µM), possibly through interactions with extracellular bacterial components or direct interference with cell division.
direct_assay_types: confocal fluorescence microscopy
limitations: Authors explicitly caution that aggregation-like appearance is from selected fields of view and should be interpreted as qualitative only; mechanistic basis (extracellular interaction vs. cell division interference) is not experimentally determined

claim_text: pBD-5 exerts a partially bacteriostatic effect on E. coli in addition to its bactericidal effect, as metabolic activity is reduced at concentrations (25 µM) where CFU counts are also significantly decreased.
direct_assay_types: metabolic activity (resazurin), colony-forming unit counts
limitations: Bacteriostatic vs bactericidal distinction is inferred by combining two separate assays (resazurin and CFU), not demonstrated by a direct static/cidal endpoint assay such as time-kill kinetics; in vitro only

claim_text: The primary antimicrobial mechanism of pBD-5 against S. epidermidis is distinct from metabolic inhibition, since CFU counts are significantly reduced while metabolic activity remains statistically unchanged.
direct_assay_types: metabolic activity (resazurin), colony-forming unit counts
limitations: Mechanism is inferred by exclusion; the actual mechanism operative against S. epidermidis is not identified; discrepancy could also reflect technical limitations of resazurin assay with S. epidermidis (e.g., low metabolic baseline or dye interference)

claim_text: pBD-5's bactericidal activity is not solely dependent on membrane disruption but likely involves additional mechanisms such as metabolic inhibition or intracellular target interactions, given that membrane leakage is modest (~15%) at concentrations that produce significant bacterial killing.
limitations: Entirely inferential; no direct intracellular assay (e.g., DNA/RNA binding, enzyme inhibition) was performed; the argument rests on the gap between low membrane leakage and observed bactericidal effect, which could also reflect assay model limitations (liposomes vs. intact bacterial membranes)

claim_text: Pc-CATH1 and its homologues adopt α-helical conformation in negatively charged membrane-mimicking environments (SDS micelles) due to electrostatic interaction, and this structural transition is associated with their antimicrobial activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy in SDS micelles
limitations: CD performed in SDS micelles, not actual bacterial membranes; helical structure shown to form but not directly demonstrated to be the mechanistically active conformation against bacteria; multiple structural parameters co-vary across peptide series

claim_text: Tryptophan residues in the RL-series homologues reside in the hydrophobic core of the peptides and engage in hydrophobic interactions with acyl chains of membrane phospholipids, contributing to antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Mechanism directly cited from literature on other AMPs (melittin, IsCT, papiliocin, mastoparan B, refs 7–10) and applied by structural analogy (helix-wheel analysis) to Pc-CATH1 homologues; no direct membrane interaction assay performed on these peptides

claim_text: Tryptophan residues exhibit restricted motion upon insertion into the bacterial membrane, implying membrane embedding as part of the antimicrobial mechanism of RL-series peptides.
limitations: Directly cited from literature on other AMPs (refs 7–10), not experimentally demonstrated for Pc-CATH1 or any homologue in this study

claim_text: The absence of tryptophan and low degree of amphipathicity in RL6 may explain its markedly reduced antimicrobial activity relative to RL5.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay
limitations: Removal of Trp simultaneously reduces hydrophobicity and amphipathicity; the two variables cannot be independently attributed; helix-wheel analysis and hydrophobicity calculations are computational, not experimental

claim_text: Tryptophan anchoring into the red blood cell membrane contributes to hemolytic activity, and the positional flexibility of tryptophan (N-terminal position 1 vs. position 2) modulates the strength of this anchoring.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Anchoring is inferred from differential hemolysis between RL4 and RL5 and positional reasoning about Trp flexibility; no direct membrane insertion or fluorescence measurement performed

claim_text: Phenylalanine residues can anchor into the red blood cell membrane, and their deletion reduces hemolytic activity.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Inferred from hemolytic activity difference upon single-residue deletion (RL4 vs. RL5); Phe and Trp are removed together in this comparison, making individual attribution uncertain; no direct membrane binding assay performed

claim_text: Amphipathicity is required for antimicrobial activity; loss of amphipathicity at the C-terminus, coinciding with decreased net positive charge, contributes to reduced antimicrobial and hemolytic activities in LR4–6.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Amphipathicity loss co-occurs with net charge reduction and sequence truncation; effects cannot be attributed to a single structural variable; amphipathicity assessed computationally via helix-wheel, not by experiment

claim_text: Hydrophobicity is positively correlated with antimicrobial potency within the LR1–LR3 sub-series of Pc-CATH1 homologues.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay
limitations: Correlation observed in only three peptides (LR1–3) with co-varying sequence length and charge; not a controlled single-variable experiment; hydrophobicity calculated computationally

claim_text: A sufficient degree of α-helical structure in membrane-like conditions is associated with stronger antimicrobial and hemolytic activities; peptides with low α-helical content (LR11–16, RL14) show weak or absent activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy, MIC assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Helical content measured in SDS micelles, not in the presence of target organisms or erythrocytes; multiple structural properties change simultaneously across the truncation series

claim_text: K17 adopts α-helical conformation in membrane-mimicking environments (50% TFE or 1% SDS), transitioning from random coil in aqueous solution, consistent with the membrane-interaction mechanism typical of cationic α-helical AMPs.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: TFE and SDS are membrane mimics, not actual bacterial membranes; CD confirms structural transition but does not directly demonstrate membrane insertion or permeabilization in bacteria.

claim_text: K17 exerts bactericidal activity against Gram-negative S. typhimurium and Gram-positive S. aureus through a mechanism that requires cationic charge, as the charge-neutralized analogue A17 (lysines replaced by alanines) lacks antimicrobial activity despite retaining α-helical structure.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal CFU assay, circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: The charge-dependence inference is based on a single analogue comparison; alternative explanations (e.g., altered amphipathicity or hydrophobicity from the substitutions) are not ruled out; direct membrane interaction was not measured.

claim_text: Most AMPs, including the class to which K17 belongs, share a common mechanism of action involving membrane permeabilization of the pathogen cell membrane.
limitations: This is a general statement from the literature (cited to Brogden 2005) applied by the authors to contextualize K17; no direct membrane permeabilization assay was performed on K17 in this study.

claim_text: K17 is selectively toxic to bacteria and not to mammalian cells, suggesting its membrane-disrupting mechanism preferentially targets bacterial membranes over mammalian cell membranes or erythrocytes.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal CFU assay, XTT cytotoxicity assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Selectivity is demonstrated by differential activity assays, not by a direct mechanistic comparison of membrane interactions with bacterial vs. mammalian membranes; the basis for selectivity is inferred, not mechanistically explained.

claim_text: Use of the defensin-sensitive phoP strain of S. typhimurium, which lacks the PhoP-mediated antimicrobial resistance system, supports that K17 acts via a mechanism targeted by defensin-type peptides.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal CFU assay (phoP-strain vs. wild-type comparison)
limitations: Enhanced sensitivity of the phoP strain is consistent with a defensin-like mechanism but does not specify the exact molecular target; the PhoP system modulates multiple resistance pathways.

claim_text: Cc-LTP1 permeabilized the plasma membranes of S. cerevisiae, C. albicans, and C. tropicalis, as shown by SYTOX green fluorescence uptake in all treated yeast cells observed by fluorescence microscopy.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green dye uptake, fluorescence microscopy)
limitations: Assay performed at a single high concentration (400 µg/ml) after 36 h incubation; does not distinguish primary membrane disruption from secondary permeabilization due to cell death

claim_text: Cc-LTP1 interfered with yeast H+-ATPase-dependent acidification of the medium in a dose-dependent manner, enhancing glucose-stimulated acidification by 89–390% across S. cerevisiae, C. albicans, and C. tropicalis.
direct_assay_types: glucose-stimulated medium acidification (pH measurement)
limitations: pH change is an indirect proxy for H+-ATPase activity; the observed enhancement (not inhibition) of acidification is opposite to other antimicrobial peptides tested and its link to cell killing is not explained; H+-ATPase activity was not measured directly

claim_text: Cc-LTP1 caused structural compromise of the C. albicans plasma membrane, evidenced by cellular agglomeration and apparent extracellular release of cytoplasmic material observed by scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: The extracellular agglutinated material is presumed by the authors to be cytoplasmic content but is not biochemically confirmed; SEM is morphological and cannot establish mechanism

claim_text: Cc-LTP1 induced a yeast-to-pseudohyphae dimorphic transition in C. tropicalis, possibly as a consequence of pH alterations in the growth medium caused by the peptide's effect on the plasma membrane.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: The causal link between LTP-induced membrane perturbation, pH change, and pseudohyphae induction is speculative and not experimentally verified; alternative triggers for dimorphism are not excluded

claim_text: Cc-LTP1 may interact with proteinaceous components of the fungal plasma membrane and cause changes in ion permeability (H+, K+, Cl−), analogously to elicitins, based on its phylogenetic proximity to that protein family.
limitations: Proposed solely by analogy to elicitins based on phylogenetic data; no ion flux measurements or membrane protein-binding assays were performed to test this hypothesis

claim_text: EcDBS1R6 permeabilizes the cytoplasmic membrane of both E. coli and S. aureus, as demonstrated by SYTOX Green fluorescence uptake showing complete permeabilization comparable to the membrane-permeabilizing positive control melittin.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green uptake assay)
limitations: Assay performed at 2x MIC only; S. aureus showed a lower maximum SG fluorescence signal than melittin, suggesting partial or kinetically different permeabilization; single representative experiment shown from three replicates.

claim_text: EcDBS1R6 rapidly depolarizes the cytoplasmic membrane potential of both E. coli and S. aureus, as indicated by an immediate increase in DiSC3(5) fluorescence reaching a threshold equal or similar to melittin.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3(5) fluorescent probe assay)
limitations: Assay performed at 2x MIC only; S. aureus depolarization reached a maximum similar but not equal to the positive control; single representative experiment shown from three replicates.

claim_text: EcDBS1R6 kills E. coli and S. aureus rapidly and completely within 15 minutes at 2x MIC, indicating a bactericidal membranolytic mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: time-kill assay (colony-forming unit counts)
limitations: Rapid killing is consistent with but does not exclusively prove a membranolytic mechanism; tested only on two reference strains; the methods section states E. coli was tested at 4x MIC, creating a minor inconsistency with the 2x MIC stated in the results.

claim_text: EcDBS1R6 causes visible membrane deformation and loss of membrane integrity in P. aeruginosa and L. ivanovii, as directly observed by FEG-SEM imaging.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (FEG-SEM)
limitations: Morphological imaging demonstrates membrane damage but cannot distinguish between pore-forming, carpet, or detergent-like disruption modes; cells were fixed with glutaraldehyde prior to imaging, which may introduce artifacts.

claim_text: The N-terminal portion of EcDBS1R6 is the active core responsible for antibacterial activity, as the first four N-terminal sliding-window fragments (10-residue each) were the most active against P. aeruginosa, while the three C-terminal fragments were completely inactive.
direct_assay_types: peptide fragment antimicrobial activity screening (SPOT cellulose synthesis, bioluminescent P. aeruginosa inhibition assay)
limitations: Fragment activity tested against a single organism (P. aeruginosa); crude peptides from cellulose SPOT synthesis may have variable concentrations and purity; overlapping 10-residue windows make precise boundary determination approximate.

claim_text: The C-terminal residues Pro17–Trp19 do not contribute to EcDBS1R6 antibacterial activity, as fragments containing only these residues were inactive (MIC >200 µg/mL) against P. aeruginosa.
direct_assay_types: peptide fragment antimicrobial activity screening (SPOT cellulose synthesis)
limitations: Inactivity of C-terminal fragments tested only against P. aeruginosa; the presence of Pro17 as an α-helix breaker is proposed to explain structural instability in this region, but no direct biophysical measurement of fragment–membrane interaction was performed.

claim_text: The α-helix at the N-terminus of EcDBS1R6 is maintained in a membrane-mimetic environment and constitutes the structural basis for membrane interaction and antibacterial activity, consistent with classical AMP membrane disruption models requiring α-helix formation.
limitations: Based on 50 independent 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations in 50% TFE/water (a membrane mimetic), not a lipid bilayer or direct experimental structural determination (e.g., NMR, CD in lipid vesicles); TFE may not fully recapitulate a true membrane environment; the link to membrane disruption models is by analogy, not direct measurement.

claim_text: The Joker-introduced amino acid changes increased the positive net charge of EcDBS1R6, which may have facilitated membrane interaction and enabled antimicrobial activity relative to the parent signal peptide.
limitations: Authors explicitly note that charge increase alone is insufficient for activity, since two other Joker variants of the same parent sequence (EcDBS1R1 and EcDBS1R7) with similar charge increases were inactive; no direct membrane-binding experiment comparing parent peptide and EcDBS1R6 was presented.

claim_text: EcDBS1R6 may act in a detergent-like manner on bacterial membranes, inferred from its derivation from a signal peptide sequence (which naturally inserts into phospholipid bilayers) and the localization of its active core to the α-helical signal peptide portion.
limitations: Explicitly speculative; no direct experimental evidence distinguishing a detergent-like (carpet/micellization) mechanism from pore-forming or toroidal pore models is presented; the authors state 'might have acted in a detergent-like manner.'

claim_text: The synthetic cationic peptides *VAYR*, *ARVA, and VVRG bind selectively and strongly to microbes with partial β-sheet secondary structure and permeabilize their cytoplasmic membranes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye uptake)
limitations: Data from prior referenced studies [15,16], not generated in this paper; all three species-level differences noted below.

claim_text: *VAYR* causes very rapid cytoplasmic membrane depolarization of E. coli within approximately 20 seconds of exposure.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization
limitations: Cited from prior referenced studies [15]; not independently replicated in this paper.

claim_text: *VAYR* causes rapid entry of the membrane-impermeant SYTOX Green DNA-binding dye into both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria within approximately 10 minutes, indicating large-scale cytoplasmic membrane permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye uptake)
limitations: Cited from prior referenced studies [15]; SYTOX Green is used as a surrogate marker for antibiotic entry, not a direct measure of antibiotic penetration.

claim_text: *ARVA does not cause membrane depolarization over the first 3 minutes of exposure but allows SYTOX Green to enter all tested bacteria by 5 minutes.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization, membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye uptake)
limitations: Cited from prior referenced studies; depolarization and permeabilization are temporally dissociated, suggesting a mechanistic detail not fully resolved.

claim_text: VVRG causes large-scale permeabilization of Staphylococcus aureus membranes to SYTOX Green but does not produce the same permeabilizing effect in E. coli membranes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye uptake)
limitations: Cited from prior referenced studies; species-specific difference in membrane permeabilization is described but not mechanistically explained.

claim_text: Melittin is a non-selective, generic membrane-permeabilizing peptide that binds to and permeabilizes bacterial, eukaryotic, and fungal membranes indiscriminately.
limitations: Cited as established prior knowledge [36]; not directly assayed in this paper beyond MIC and FIC measurements.

claim_text: AMPs act on bacterial membranes globally rather than on a specific macromolecular target, which likely explains why resistance to AMPs is uncommon and not readily selectable or inducible.
limitations: Mechanistic inference supported by literature citation [21,22]; not directly demonstrated in this study.

claim_text: Large-scale membrane disruption and permeabilization of bacterial membranes by cationic AMPs is not sufficient by itself to produce synergistic interactions with conventional chemical antibiotics, including those that act intracellularly.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green, prior studies), fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) synergy assay
limitations: Only four AMPs, four antibiotics, and three bacterial species tested; extrapolation to all AMPs or all pathogens is not warranted.

claim_text: Magainin II has a mechanism of action involving selective targeting of anionic microbial membranes, possibly similar to melittin but with greater selectivity.
limitations: Inferred from cited literature [45]; not directly assayed in this study; the comparison to melittin is speculative.

claim_text: Magainin II synergizes with β-lactam antibiotics through a unique mechanism distinct from generic membrane permeabilization, as demonstrated by its synergy with β-lactams (FIC < 1) while melittin and other membrane-permeabilizing peptides show no synergy with the same drug class.
direct_assay_types: FIC synergy assay
limitations: The specific molecular mechanism of synergy is explicitly stated to remain unknown; synergy is inferred by contrast with non-synergizing peptides rather than by direct mechanistic assay.

claim_text: AMPs could potentially synergize with antibiotics by increasing the permeability of bacterial membranes, including the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, thereby enhancing antibiotic access to intracellular targets.
limitations: Cited from prior literature [26] as a proposed mechanism; the current study's results argue against this as a general mechanism, finding no synergy across 40 peptide-drug-organism combinations.

claim_text: AMPs could enhance the activity of bacterial murein hydrolases or other enzymes that degrade the peptidoglycan layer, thereby allowing cell-wall-targeting antibiotics such as β-lactams to act more efficiently.
limitations: Cited from prior literature [27,28] as a proposed mechanism; not tested in this study.

claim_text: Cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl) inhibits biofilm formation of Staphylococcus epidermidis ATCC 35984 by up to 85% at 1.0 mg/mL without interfering with bacterial growth.
direct_assay_types: biofilm inhibition (crystal violet), bacterial growth (turbidimetric assay), scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Single strain tested (ATCC 35984); mechanism downstream of biofilm inhibition not determined; no dose-response below 0.25 mg/mL reported

claim_text: Cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl) reduces exopolysaccharide (EPS) matrix formation, as evidenced by weakly-formed EPS and fewer cell aggregates in treated samples compared to untreated controls.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: SEM is morphological/descriptive only; EPS identity inferred visually, not biochemically confirmed; single concentration (1.0 mg/mL) shown

claim_text: Diketopiperazines such as cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl) may interfere with quorum-sensing systems in gram-positive bacteria, analogous to how related dipeptides cyclo(L-Phe-L-Pro) and cyclo(L-Tyr-L-Pro) repress virulence factor TSST-1 expression in Staphylococcus aureus via the agr quorum-sensing system.
limitations: Authors cite this mechanism only for structurally related dipeptides from a different study; no agr interference assay was performed for cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl) in this paper; explicitly flagged as future work

claim_text: Diketopiperazines can mimic N-acyl homoserine lactones by interacting with LuxR proteins at or near their binding site, suggesting a possible quorum-sensing interference mechanism for cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl).
limitations: No experimental data for cis-cyclo(leucyl-tyrosyl) on LuxR or any quorum-sensing assay; based entirely on literature analogy; authors acknowledge this mechanism of action requires further exploration

claim_text: Both horine and verine-L induce membrane permeabilization of model membranes mimicking S. aureus and E. coli, with greater extent and faster kinetics against S. aureus mimetics.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (carboxyfluorescein leakage from LUVs)
limitations: Model membranes only; LUV lipid compositions approximate but do not fully replicate native bacterial membranes

claim_text: Both peptides bind model membranes mimicking S. aureus with approximately 30-fold higher affinity (KD ~0.3 µM) than E. coli mimetics (KD ~11 µM).
direct_assay_types: isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)
limitations: Model membranes only; affinity measured at 37°C in phosphate buffer, may differ in vivo

claim_text: Binding of both peptides to E. coli model membranes is driven primarily by entropy, consistent with hydrophobic forces dominating the interaction.
direct_assay_types: isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)
limitations: Thermodynamic inference from ΔH/−TΔS decomposition; model membranes only

claim_text: Binding of both peptides to S. aureus model membranes is driven by comparable enthalpic and entropic contributions, suggesting involvement of hydrophobic forces as well as electrostatics, hydrogen bonding, and/or dehydration.
direct_assay_types: isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)
limitations: Thermodynamic decomposition cannot distinguish individual non-hydrophobic contributions; model membranes only

claim_text: Both peptides induce lipid flip-flop (transverse lipid movement) in both S. aureus and E. coli model membranes.
direct_assay_types: dithionite quenching of NBD-DPPE fluorescence, pyrene-labeled lipid (Pyr-PC) excimer redistribution
limitations: Dithionite assay cannot distinguish flip-flop from pore-mediated dithionite access to inner leaflet without corroborating assay; two complementary assays were used to address this

claim_text: Horine-induced permeabilization of E. coli model membranes does not involve formation of stable membrane pores, because lipid flip-flop occurs only at peptide:lipid ratios much higher than those causing permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (CF leakage), dithionite quenching of NBD-DPPE
limitations: Absence of flip-flop at low peptide:lipid ratio is consistent with a carpet or detergent-like mechanism but does not conclusively rule out transient or small pores; model membranes only

claim_text: Verine-L permeabilization of E. coli model membranes may involve membrane pore formation, because its flip-flop activity onset correlates with its permeabilization activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (CF leakage), dithionite quenching of NBD-DPPE
limitations: Correlation of onset concentrations is suggestive but not proof of pore formation; model membranes only

claim_text: Both peptides act via a similar cooperative membranolytic mechanism against S. aureus model membranes, as evidenced by the sigmoidal permeabilization concentration-response and similar flip-flop profiles for both peptides.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (CF leakage), lipid flip-flop assays
limitations: Cooperativity inferred from sigmoidal curve shape; similar profiles for two peptides support, but do not prove, identical molecular mechanisms; model membranes only

claim_text: Horine and verine-L act via different mechanisms against E. coli model membranes, as evidenced by their differing permeabilization profiles and flip-flop concentration-dependences.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (CF leakage), lipid flip-flop assays
limitations: Mechanistic difference inferred from phenotypic differences; molecular details of the two mechanisms are not resolved; model membranes only

claim_text: Both peptides alter the molecular packing (hydration) at the membrane-water interface of both model membrane types, with greater changes observed in S. aureus mimetics.
direct_assay_types: Laurdan generalized polarization (GP340) fluorescence
limitations: GP340 reports on bulk interfacial hydration; model membranes only

claim_text: Both peptides induce lateral lipid segregation in both model membrane types, with a greater extent in S. aureus mimetics.
direct_assay_types: NBD-DPPE self-quenching fluorescence assay
limitations: Self-quenching reports on NBD-lipid clustering as a proxy for lipid domain formation; model membranes only

claim_text: Upon membrane binding, both horine and verine-L adopt conformations featuring stacked tryptophan residues, as indicated by exciton coupling bands in CD spectra.
direct_assay_types: far-UV circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy
limitations: W electronic transitions dominate far-UV CD of short Trp-rich peptides, precluding standard secondary structure analysis; conformation in model membranes may differ from live bacterial membranes

claim_text: Horine acquires a helical-like conformation upon membrane binding with stacked W residues, though the helix may be shorter or less complete in lipid bilayers than in micelles.
direct_assay_types: far-UV CD spectroscopy (this paper); NMR structure of K6 analogue in micelles (cited prior work)
limitations: Helical assignment in bilayers is inferred by analogy to the NMR-resolved micelle structure of a close analogue; CD spectral shifts may reflect W exciton coupling rather than helix length differences

claim_text: Verine-L does not acquire a highly ordered conformation upon membrane binding, but its W residues adopt a stacked arrangement at the C-terminus.
direct_assay_types: far-UV circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy
limitations: Absence of helix-like CD features is interpreted as lack of ordered secondary structure, but short peptides may adopt transient or partial structures not resolved by CD

claim_text: The antimicrobial and anti-biofilm activity of these peptides involves permeabilization of the bacterial membrane.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (CF leakage from model LUVs); antibacterial/anti-biofilm MIC/MBIC/MBEC assays (this paper); prior membrane permeabilization studies on parent peptide TetraF2W-RR cited from references 13 and 24
limitations: Direct causal link between model membrane permeabilization and antibacterial killing was not established in this paper; the claim for live bacteria rests primarily on cited prior work

claim_text: The mechanism of action of cell-death induced by AMPs putatively involves initial binding to the membrane, induction of peptide secondary structure, local aggregation of peptides at the membrane, and subsequent cell lysis caused by membrane destabilization.
limitations: Described as putative; explicitly noted that current simulations cannot access aggregation, pore formation, or carpet formation time scales.

claim_text: Electrostatic interactions between cationic sidechains of unstructured AMPs and anionic lipid headgroups drive the initial binding of AMPs to bacterial membrane interfaces.
limitations: Stated as an established principle from literature rather than directly demonstrated in this paper's simulations; causal directionality not independently tested here.

claim_text: The electrostatic differences between anionic bacterial and zwitterionic mammalian plasma membranes are responsible for the selective toxicity of cationic AMPs.
limitations: Cited as a belief from the field; the paper's simulations support the correlation but do not mechanistically prove causation.

claim_text: OVIS is more toxic than its analogues G10 and T7 because OVIS embeds more deeply into the zwitterionic (DPC) micellar interface, driven by retention of its helical structure and cooperative hydrophobic insertion.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: radial electron density profiles, peptide center-of-mass distance from micelle, radial distribution functions
limitations: Derived from micelle simulations, which are membrane mimics rather than real mammalian membranes; hemolysis data used as correlate but not a direct MOA assay; micelle does not recapitulate full bilayer geometry or lateral tension.

claim_text: Hydrophobic interactions drive the strong association of the OVIS peptide with DPC lipids, with the hydrophobic face of the amphipathic helix embedded in the micellar core.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: radial distribution functions, electron density profiles, residue insertion depth analysis
limitations: Observed in a micellar model system; may not quantitatively reflect bilayer insertion energetics.

claim_text: The point mutations in G10 (H10G) and T7 (I7T) reduce toxicity by inducing loss of helical structure in the presence of zwitterionic membranes, which lowers overall peptide amphipathicity and reduces depth of insertion into the membrane.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: backbone dihedral clustering, electron density profiles, radial distribution functions
limitations: Inferred from DPC micelle simulations correlated with hemolysis data; the paper acknowledges that both reduced helicity and reduced total hydrophobic content contribute, making it difficult to isolate the structural contribution alone.

claim_text: Both G10 and T7 retain their helical structure and bind equivalently to anionic SDS micelles (bacterial membrane mimic), consistent with their preserved antimicrobial activity.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: backbone dihedral angles, peptide center-of-mass distance from micelle
limitations: SDS head group differs significantly from natural anionic phospholipids; antimicrobial activity data used as correlate.

claim_text: Positively charged amino acid side chains of OVIS form hydrogen bonds with phosphate oxygens (DPC) or sulfate oxygens (SDS), and these interactions are stronger with the anionic SDS interface due to reduced electrostatic screening compared to zwitterionic DPC.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: radial distribution functions between charged sidechains and head-group oxygens
limitations: Observed in micelle models; screening effects from the choline group in DPC are inferred from simulation geometry rather than directly measured experimentally.

claim_text: In protegrin-1, Leu-5 plays an integral role in interactions with the anionic SDS micelle (bacterial membrane mimic) but does not interact with the zwitterionic DPC micelle (mammalian membrane mimic).
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: per-residue insertion depth analysis in SDS and DPC micelles
limitations: Residue-level functional assignment derived from a single structural model in micelles; not confirmed by mutagenesis or experimental binding assays.

claim_text: In protegrin-1, Phe-12 and Val-14 are the residues most involved in disruption of the zwitterionic DPC micelle, implicating them in mammalian cell toxicity.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: per-residue insertion depth analysis in DPC micelle
limitations: Toxicity role inferred from DPC insertion depth; direct functional consequence not verified by mutation experiment in this paper.

claim_text: For protegrins PC101 and PC104, the second strand of the β-hairpin inserts into the anionic SDS micelle, suggesting that these C-terminal residues (Phe-12, Val-14, Ile-16) play a role in the antimicrobial activity of these peptides.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: per-residue insertion depth analysis in SDS micelle
limitations: Insertion into a micellar model is used as a proxy for antimicrobial mechanism; causal link to activity not directly tested.

claim_text: Removing the C-terminal positive charge of protegrin and replacing it with a negative glutamate (PC107) causes electrostatic repulsion from the anionic SDS surface, shifting insertion toward Leu-5 on the first strand rather than C-terminal residues.
direct_assay_types: MD simulation: per-residue insertion depth in SDS micelle, charge-based analysis
limitations: Mechanistic assignment based on charge geometry in simulation; alternate explanations not ruled out.
