claim_text: Gloverin permeabilizes negatively charged phosphatidylglycerol (PG) vesicles, causing rapid release of encapsulated calcein at nanomolar concentrations.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein dye-release from unilamellar vesicles)
limitations: Tested on artificial unilamellar vesicles only, not actual viral or bacterial membranes; lipid composition is simpler than native envelopes.

claim_text: Gloverin membrane interaction is charge-dependent: it permeabilizes negatively charged PG vesicles but causes negligible (<2%) calcein release from neutral phosphatidylcholine (PC) vesicles.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein dye-release, PG vs. PC comparison)
limitations: Only two phospholipid compositions tested; the charge profile of the AcMNPV BV envelope in vivo is not fully characterized.

claim_text: Gloverin membrane permeabilization activity is rapid, with calcein release from PG vesicles largely complete within 30 seconds and near-maximum within 2 minutes of gloverin addition.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization kinetics (time-resolved calcein fluorescence)
limitations: Measured in an artificial vesicle system at 37 °C; kinetics in vivo or against intact virus may differ.

claim_text: Gloverin reduces the infectivity of AcMNPV budded virus (BV) in a concentration-dependent manner in vitro.
direct_assay_types: viral infectivity reduction (plaque assay)
limitations: In vitro only; purified gloverin showed lower activity than unpurified supernatant, suggesting partial loss of activity during purification or additional antiviral factors in supernatant.

claim_text: Gloverin inactivates AcMNPV BV by disrupting the lipid envelope surrounding the nucleocapsid, consistent with its membrane-permeabilizing activity on PG vesicles.
limitations: Inferred from correlation between PG vesicle permeabilization and BV inactivation data; no direct visualization of viral envelope disruption (e.g., electron microscopy) was performed.

claim_text: Gloverin may inhibit baculovirus infection by binding negatively charged regions of the GP64 envelope fusion protein and blocking the conformational changes GP64 requires to initiate cell entry.
limitations: No experimental data in this paper directly tests GP64 binding or conformational effects; proposed solely on the basis of charge complementarity between cationic gloverin and anionic GP64 domains.

claim_text: Gloverin may disrupt the BV envelope by accumulating on its negatively charged phospholipid surface and inducing membrane strain or pore formation.
limitations: Proposed as an alternative or complementary mechanism to GP64 inhibition; not tested directly; vesicle data are the only experimental support.

claim_text: Gloverin is likely toxic to Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli), as bacteria transformed with gloverin expression vectors failed to grow robustly under inducing conditions.
limitations: Observation is an indirect by-product of a cloning experiment, not a controlled antibacterial assay; poor growth could have alternative explanations (metabolic burden, leaky expression toxicity unrelated to the antibacterial mechanism).

claim_text: HNP1 binds to SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein with submicromolar affinity (Kd = 146 ± 18 nM), more than 20-fold stronger than its binding to serum albumin (Kd = 3.4 ± 0.3 µM).
direct_assay_types: fluorescence anisotropy (Cy5-HNP1 titrated against recombinant Spike or BSA)
limitations: Measured against recombinant Spike stabilized in prefusion conformation by K986P/V987P mutations; binding stoichiometry not determined; Kd for RC-101 not measured

claim_text: HNP1 and RC-101 inhibit SARS-CoV-2 Spike-mediated membrane fusion between Spike-expressing and ACE2-positive cells.
direct_assay_types: syncytia formation assay (fluorescence microscopy, fusion index quantification)
limitations: Inhibition was largely abrogated by 10% serum; cell-culture model only; not a viral infection assay

claim_text: HNP1 and RC-101 act on the viral particle rather than on host cell molecules such as ACE2 to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 Spike-pseudotyped infection.
direct_assay_types: pseudotyped lentivirus infection assay (NanoLuc luciferase reporter) comparing virus pre-treatment vs. cell pre-treatment
limitations: Demonstrated with HIV-based pseudotyped virus bearing SARS-CoV-2 Spike, not authentic SARS-CoV-2; host-directed effects not formally ruled out at higher concentrations

claim_text: HNP1 and RC-101 destabilize the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein, reducing its thermal stability and promoting exposure of hydrophobic residues at temperatures below its normal melting point.
direct_assay_types: differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) with Sypro Orange dye
limitations: Recombinant prefusion-stabilized Spike used; destabilization effects of RC-101 were less prominent than HNP1; native Spike on virions may be more susceptible; DSF reports bulk thermodynamic change, not atomic-resolution unfolding mechanism

claim_text: HNP1 and RC-101 induce partial aggregation and precipitation of SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein through exposure of hydrophobic surfaces upon defensin-induced unfolding.
direct_assay_types: ultracentrifugation (100,000 g) followed by SDS-PAGE of soluble and insoluble fractions
limitations: Recombinant stabilized Spike used; RC-101 effects were milder than HNP1; precipitation extent in the authentic virion context is unknown

claim_text: HNP1 and RC-101 inhibit the interaction between SARS-CoV-2 Spike and the ACE2 receptor in a concentration-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: solid-phase binding assay (biotinylated ACE2 on NeutrAvidin plate, anti-Spike S2 antibody detection)
limitations: High defensin concentrations (>5 µM) caused elevated background noise, limiting dose-response range; assay used recombinant proteins; Spike was pre-incubated with defensins before addition to ACE2, so blocking of ACE2 by defensins was not tested

claim_text: Defensins promote unfolding of conformationally plastic (thermolabile) viral proteins by preferentially binding to partially unfolded states and locking them in non-native, non-functional conformations that are prone to aggregation.
direct_assay_types: differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF)
limitations: Mechanistic model inferred from DSF data combined with prior literature on bacterial toxins and other viral proteins; direct structural evidence for defensin binding to partially unfolded Spike not provided in this paper; integration into the hydrophobic core is proposed but not directly demonstrated

claim_text: Serum proteins compete with SARS-CoV-2 Spike for HNP1 binding, reducing defensin availability and attenuating its antiviral activity.
direct_assay_types: syncytia formation assay, pseudotyped virus infection assay, authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection assay — all with serum titration; fluorescence anisotropy showing HNP1 binds BSA
limitations: Direct competition between serum proteins and Spike for HNP1 not formally demonstrated in a competition assay; BSA binding used as a proxy for all serum proteins

claim_text: Additional mechanisms beyond Spike/ACE2 interaction disruption — such as blocking protease cleavage sites or preventing conformational changes required for membrane fusion — may contribute to defensin-mediated inhibition of SARS-CoV-2.
limitations: Not directly tested in this study; proposed on the basis of the multifaceted nature of defensin biology and the mild destabilization/precipitation effects of RC-101 relative to its antiviral potency

claim_text: Defensin-mediated stabilization of non-enveloped viral capsids (reported in other viruses) may paradoxically result from prior defensin-induced unfolding of conformationally flexible capsid-protein interface regions, causing abnormal hydrophobic cross-links that resist programmed disassembly.
limitations: Not tested in this study; speculative mechanistic model proposed to reconcile published capsid-stabilization observations with the general unfolding model; no supporting experiments provided

claim_text: NYAD-1 binds to residues 169-191 of the C-terminal domain of HIV-1 capsid (C-CA), encompassing the hydrophobic cavity formed by helices 1, 2, and 4 and the critical dimerization domain.
direct_assay_types: NMR chemical shift perturbation (1H-15N HSQC titration)
limitations: Binding affinity for NYAD-1 itself could not be reliably determined by NMR due to low solubility; Kd ~1 µM estimated from soluble analog NYAD-13; NMR used a double mutant C-CA (W184A/M185A), not wild-type protein

claim_text: NYAD-1 disrupts assembly of both immature-like (Gag-derived spherical) and mature-like (CA-derived tubular) HIV-1 virus particles in a dose-dependent manner in a cell-free in vitro system.
direct_assay_types: negative-stain transmission electron microscopy, in vitro assembly assay
limitations: Cell-free assembly conditions (high NaCl, E. coli RNA) do not fully recapitulate intracellular assembly; scrambled-sequence control NYAD-17 showed no effect, supporting specificity

claim_text: NYAD-1 binding to capsid inhibits HIV-1 Gag-mediated particle production and causes dose-dependent intracellular accumulation of uncleaved Pr55 Gag, indicating impairment of both assembly and Gag processing.
direct_assay_types: metabolic radiolabeling (35S-Met/Cys), immunoprecipitation, SDS-PAGE, phosphorimager quantification
limitations: Accumulation of Pr55 Gag could reflect assembly block rather than direct effect on protease processing; n=4 replicates

claim_text: NYAD-1 penetrates cells and colocalizes with the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein during Gag trafficking to the plasma membrane, suggesting interaction with Gag prior to assembly.
direct_assay_types: laser scanning confocal microscopy, FACS
limitations: Colocalization (weighted coefficient 0.402 ± 0.051) indicates spatial overlap but does not confirm direct molecular binding to Gag in cells; FACS data noted as potentially unreliable for cell-penetrating peptides due to membrane binding

claim_text: NYAD-1 impairs proper HIV-1 particle morphology in cell-based systems, producing aberrant particle shapes in Gag-expressing cells and markedly inhibiting electron-dense core formation in Gag-Pol-expressing cells.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy of thin-sectioned cells
limitations: Morphological disruption is observed but the molecular basis distinguishing assembly block from maturation defect is not resolved at this resolution

claim_text: NYAD-1 does not inhibit HIV-1 entry into cells, indicating its antiviral mechanism operates post-entry.
direct_assay_types: GFP-Vpr-labeled virion flow cytometry entry assay, cell fusion assay
limitations: Flow cytometry measures virion association with/entry into cells but may not distinguish surface-bound from internalized virus; cell fusion assay data only cited as 'data not shown'

claim_text: NYAD-1 most likely targets HIV-1 capsid at a post-entry stage, as it retained inhibitory activity when added up to 8 h post-infection but lost activity when added at 16 h, unlike the entry inhibitor T-20 which lost activity by 4 h.
direct_assay_types: time-of-addition single-cycle infection assay (luciferase reporter)
limitations: Timing data indicate post-entry activity but cannot pinpoint the exact post-entry step (uncoating, reverse transcription, nuclear import, etc.); pre-entry contribution cannot be fully excluded

claim_text: NYAD-1 may affect the HIV-1 uncoating process by binding to capsid after viral entry.
direct_assay_types: time-of-addition assay, single-cycle infection assay
limitations: Uncoating effect is inferred from inhibition kinetics; uncoating was not directly measured (e.g., by fate-of-capsid or cyclosporine washout assay)

claim_text: NYAD-1 impairs HIV-1 assembly and/or affects the dimer interface conformation by binding directly to critical residues of C-CA spanning the dimerization domain (residues 169-189), since mutations at these residues (W184, M185, L189, L190, Y169) are known to disrupt assembly.
direct_assay_types: NMR chemical shift perturbation, in vitro assembly assay, electron microscopy
limitations: Whether NYAD-1 disrupts dimerization directly or sterically blocks Gag polymerization at another step is not mechanistically resolved; mutation evidence is drawn from literature, not new experiments in this study

claim_text: NYAD-1's antiviral activity is specific to HIV-1 and not due to non-specific cytotoxicity, as demonstrated by its failure to inhibit release of the related lentivirus EIAV.
direct_assay_types: EIAV particle release assay, metabolic radiolabeling, immunoprecipitation
limitations: EIAV specificity supports HIV-1 CA-targeting mechanism but does not rule out all potential off-target effects; CC50 > 135 µM (MT-2) and > 300 µM (PBMC) reported from parallel cytotoxicity assays

claim_text: Most antimicrobial peptides share an amphipathic structure that enables interaction with microbial membranes, commonly leading to disruption of membrane integrity through permeabilization as a major killing mechanism against bacteria, fungi, parasites, and enveloped viruses.
limitations: General background statement endorsed from prior literature (Brogden 2005); not experimentally tested in this paper.

claim_text: Proline-rich antimicrobial peptides act without membrane permeabilization by translocating across bacterial membranes and reaching an intracellular target that causes cell death, with activity predominantly against Gram-negative bacteria.
limitations: Authors explicitly describe the underlying mechanisms as 'unresolved'; based on cited prior literature; membrane permeabilization was not tested for Cg-Prp in this paper.

claim_text: PR39, a mammalian proline-rich antimicrobial peptide, kills Gram-negative bacteria by inhibiting DNA and protein synthesis.
limitations: Cited from Gennaro et al. 2002; not tested in this paper.

claim_text: The insect proline-rich antimicrobial peptides pyrrhocoricin, drosocin, and apidaecin enter bacterial cells and specifically bind to DnaK (a heat shock protein involved in chaperone-assisted protein folding), with pyrrhocoricin inhibiting DnaK's ATPase activity, resulting in accumulation of misfolded proteins and subsequent cell death.
direct_assay_types: DnaK binding assay, ATPase inhibition assay
limitations: Cited from Kragol et al. 2001; not tested in this paper; the ATPase inhibition detail was reported specifically for pyrrhocoricin and may not apply equally to drosocin or apidaecin.

claim_text: Cg-Prp, the first proline-rich antimicrobial peptide identified in a mollusk, acts primarily through synergistic antimicrobial activity with the co-expressed oyster defensin Cg-Def rather than through direct killing of microbes.
direct_assay_types: minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) determination, checkerboard fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) assay
limitations: Demonstrated in vitro only; molecular mechanism of synergy between Cg-Prp and Cg-Def is not elucidated; in vivo synergy is supported by co-localization of both peptides in the same hemocytes and tissues but not directly tested; weak direct antimicrobial activity of Cg-Prp22-36 (against M. lysodeikticus) and antifungal activity of Cg-Prp20-36/Cg-Prp22-36 are also reported but at high concentrations (100–200 µM); the paper acknowledges poor in vitro activity may underestimate in vivo activity due to absence of post-translational modifications (glycosylation, proline isomerization) on synthetic peptides.

claim_text: Loss of a single positively charged arginine residue (R12W substitution in AP2 vs. AP1) was sufficient to abolish antimicrobial activity against M. abscessus, implying that cationic charge is critical to the mechanism of action of AP1.
limitations: Paper reports only MIC values for AP1 vs AP2; no membrane-interaction, binding, or killing-kinetics assays are performed. The mechanistic inference (cationic charge drives activity) is not explicitly stated by the authors—it is deducible from the structure-activity observation but not tested. Single substitution also changes hydrophobicity and geometry, so the causal factor is not isolated.

claim_text: AP1 at 3× MIC protected Acanthamoeba castellanii from killing by intracellular M. abscessus strains (including an MDR outbreak strain), demonstrating antimycobacterial activity inside a host-cell-like environment.
direct_assay_types: intracellular killing surrogate (LDH release ratio in amoeba-MAB infection model)
limitations: LDH release measures amoeba survival, not direct bacterial killing; does not distinguish whether AP1 kills intracellular bacteria, prevents egress, or acts extracellularly on bacteria released during amoeba lysis. No CFU counts from infected amoebae reported. No mammalian cell or in vivo data.

claim_text: The bactericidal activity of VIP and ORXB is mediated by their strong positive charge binding to negatively charged bacterial cell walls, analogous to the mechanism of other cationic antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: Mechanism inferred entirely from chemical properties (net charge +3.1, cationic amino acid content, isoelectric point); no membrane binding, permeabilization, or structural assay was performed to directly test this in the study.

claim_text: The antimicrobial potency of VIP and ORXB can be predicted from their amphipathic nature and net positive cationic charge, placing them in the same functional class as LL-37, HNP-1, and HBD-1.
limitations: Stated as a hypothesis supported by chemical property comparison (Table 1) and bactericidal assay results; no structural assays (e.g., circular dichroism, membrane permeabilization assay) were performed to confirm the amphipathic mechanism.

claim_text: The bactericidal activities of VIP and ORXB against Gram-negative bacteria are attenuated at physiological NaCl concentrations (150 mM) because Na+ ions compete with cationic peptides for electrostatic interaction with the negatively charged bacterial membrane, inhibiting the initial peptide-membrane contact.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal colony-count assay across 0–300 mM NaCl gradient
limitations: NaCl-dependent attenuation of killing was directly demonstrated by assay; however, the charge-competition mechanistic explanation is attributed to prior literature (Lehrer et al., 1993) and not independently verified in this study; underlying mechanism stated as 'remains to be elucidated'.

claim_text: Differences in bacterial cell-surface charge determine the range of susceptibilities of various bacterial species to VIP and ORXB, with S. aureus resistance attributable to cell-surface electrostatic alterations that reduce net negative charge and thereby attenuate cationic peptide binding.
limitations: Mechanistic explanation is applied by analogy to prior work on S. aureus resistance to other cationic AMPs (Peschel et al., 1999); no direct assay of surface charge, peptide-binding affinity, or membrane interaction with S. aureus was performed in this study.

claim_text: VIP and ORXB exert additive (not synergistic) bactericidal effects when combined with LL-37 against Gram-negative bacteria, with FIC indices of 0.55–0.75, indicating the two agents act through complementary rather than identical pathways.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal colony-count assay, checkerboard FIC titration
limitations: FIC classification as 'additive' (0.5 < FIC ≤ 1) does not identify the molecular basis of complementarity; primary FIC assays conducted at sub-physiological NaCl; activity spectrum limited to E. coli and P. aeruginosa.

claim_text: When combined with LL-37, VIP and ORXB restore bactericidal activity against Gram-negative bacteria at physiological NaCl (150 mM), suggesting that cooperative action between cationic peptides with complementary properties overcomes salt-mediated inhibition that each peptide alone cannot resist.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal colony-count assay at 150 mM NaCl with peptide combinations
limitations: The molecular mechanism by which combination overcomes salt inhibition is not determined; results limited to E. coli and P. aeruginosa; whether the effect generalises to other physiological ionic conditions was not tested.

claim_text: The acidic cleft between domains I and II of TcOsm1 is potentially involved in catalytic activity against β-1,3 glucan, a component of the fungal cell wall, which could explain its antifungal properties.
limitations: Described as 'potentially involved' and 'could explain'; inferred from structural homology to other PR-5 proteins via 3D modeling; no enzymatic or cell-wall-degradation assay performed in this study.

claim_text: Osmotin is recognized by a membrane receptor on fungal cells, triggering a signaling pathway that results in reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, leading to cell death.
limitations: Attributed entirely to Narasimhan et al. (2001) [ref 9]; not tested in this study; authors explicitly state 'the actual mechanism(s) remains unclear'.

claim_text: The guanidinium group of arginine residues in Osm-pepA interacts with membrane phosphate groups by electrostatic and steric complementarity, favoring peptide insertion into the hydrophobic part of the membrane.
limitations: Inferred by analogy from cited literature [ref 42] on arginine-rich peptides in general; no membrane permeabilization, lipid-binding, or fluorescence assay performed for Osm-pepA specifically.

claim_text: The five N-terminal residues RRLDR of Osm-pepA significantly alter its tertiary structure compared to Osm-pepB, and this structural difference is likely important for its greater antimicrobial potency.
limitations: Based solely on computational molecular dynamics modeling; no experimental structural determination (e.g., NMR, CD) or mutagenesis performed; causal link to potency is asserted but not directly tested.

claim_text: Clusters of arginine residues in Osm-pepA increase its antimicrobial effect relative to Osm-pepB, by analogy with the finding that arginine-to-glycine substitutions in Protegrin-1 reduce antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Inferred by analogy to Protegrin-1 data from cited literature [ref 43]; not tested directly by mutagenesis or charge-neutralization experiments in this study.

claim_text: Osm-pepA alters the morphology of Moniliophthora perniciosa mycelium, causing increased hyphal density and a more compact phenotype, indicating an effect on hyphal architecture beyond simple growth-rate reduction.
direct_assay_types: mycelial morphology observation on PDA
limitations: Phenotypic observation only; underlying cellular or molecular mechanism (e.g., cell-wall, membrane, cytoskeletal) is not determined; comparison to sakuranetin effects is analogical only.

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of murepavadin is caused by its interaction with the essential outer-membrane b-barrel transporter LptD, which essentially blocks LPS assembly in the outer membrane of the bacterial cell.
limitations: This mechanistic claim is cited from prior literature (ref 1, Srinivas et al. 2010); the present paper does not perform mechanistic assays—it reports MIC values only and attributes mechanism by citation.

claim_text: Murepavadin represents one of the first members of a novel class of antimicrobial peptides targeting outer membrane bacterial proteins.
limitations: Classification claim derived from cited literature (refs 1–3); no direct target-binding or outer-membrane protein interaction assay performed in this paper.

claim_text: Murepavadin exhibits potent and specific antimicrobial activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa but not against other bacteria (S. aureus, E. coli), with MIC values ranging from 8 nM to 0.5 μM against P. aeruginosa clinical isolates and >10 μM against S. aureus and E. coli.
direct_assay_types: broth microdilution MIC assay
limitations: Narrow species panel tested (two non-target organisms as negative controls); mechanism of species selectivity is attributed to LptD targeting by citation rather than demonstrated here.

claim_text: CC-AMP1 permeabilizes the outer membrane of gram-negative E. coli ATCC 25922, with 100% NPN uptake observed from 10 to 40 µM.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane permeabilization (NPN fluorescent probe uptake assay)
limitations: Tested against a single gram-negative strain (E. coli ATCC 25922) only; outer membrane permeabilization alone does not confirm killing mechanism.

claim_text: CC-AMP1 permeabilizes the inner membrane of gram-negative E. coli ATCC 25922, as evidenced by increased absorbance at 420 nm in an ONPG assay.
direct_assay_types: inner membrane permeabilization (ONPG/β-galactosidase release assay)
limitations: Tested against a single gram-negative strain (E. coli ATCC 25922) only; assay is indirect readout of membrane breach via enzymatic reporter.

claim_text: CC-AMP1 is bactericidal rather than bacteriostatic against Acinetobacter baumannii 5075, with an MBC of 8.6 µM.
direct_assay_types: minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC, colony-forming unit recovery assay)
limitations: MBC determined for A. baumannii 5075 only; bactericidal nature against other susceptible gram-negative strains was not confirmed by MBC.

claim_text: CC-AMP1 appears to exert a bactericidal mechanism of action against gram-negative bacteria through permeabilization of both the outer and inner membranes.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane permeabilization (NPN uptake), inner membrane permeabilization (ONPG), minimum bactericidal concentration
limitations: Membrane permeabilization was demonstrated only in E. coli; bactericidal activity was confirmed only in A. baumannii; whether dual-membrane disruption is the sole or proximal lethal mechanism is not established.

claim_text: Crotalicidin (Ctn) induced cell death in T. cruzi epimastigotes through necrosis, as the remaining live epimastigotes after 24 h treatment at EC50 were mainly labelled with 7-AAD only (41.6%) or 7-AAD and annexin V (39.6%), indicating necrosis or necrosis/late apoptosis.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with 7-AAD and annexin V probes
limitations: Only epimastigote forms were used in the flow cytometry death-pathway assays; other T. cruzi developmental forms not assessed for death mechanism. Single time point (24 h).

claim_text: Ctn caused loss of membrane integrity with the presence of pores in T. cruzi epimastigotes, as observed by scanning electron microscopy after 12 h treatment at EC50.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: SEM provides morphological evidence of membrane disruption but cannot distinguish primary membrane attack from secondary membrane collapse due to upstream cell death events; single time point (12 h).

claim_text: Ctn caused cell shrinkage in T. cruzi epimastigotes, a morphological hallmark consistent with necrotic cell death, observed by scanning electron microscopy after 12 h treatment at EC50.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological interpretation; shrinkage could also accompany other death modalities; single time point.

claim_text: Ctn induced a burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in T. cruzi epimastigotes, increasing the DCFH-DA fluorescent signal approximately 3-fold compared to untreated parasites after 24 h at EC50.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with DCFH-DA (ROS probe)
limitations: DCFH-DA reports general oxidative stress and is not specific to any ROS species; causality (whether ROS drives death or is a consequence) is not established.

claim_text: Ctn caused a reduction in mitochondrial transmembrane potential (MTP) in T. cruzi epimastigotes, decreasing the rhodamine 123 fluorescent signal by approximately 50% compared to untreated parasites after 24 h at EC50.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with rhodamine 123 (mitochondrial membrane potential probe)
limitations: Whether MTP loss is a primary mechanistic event or a downstream consequence of membrane disruption is not determined.

claim_text: Ctn does not kill T. cruzi epimastigotes via autophagy, as treatment at EC50 for 24 h produced no increase in acridine orange fluorescence (a marker of acidic reservosomes).
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with acridine orange (reservosome/autophagy probe)
limitations: Negative result; acridine orange is an indirect proxy for autophagy flux in trypanosomes and may not capture all autophagic activity.

claim_text: The higher susceptibility of T. cruzi trypomastigote forms to Ctn compared to epimastigotes is inferred to result from the prevalence of negatively charged surface molecules (mucin glycoproteins, sialic acid) on trypomastigotes that facilitate electrostatic attraction of the cationic peptide.
limitations: No direct binding or surface-charge assay performed; explanation is cited from literature on host–parasite interactions, not demonstrated for Ctn specifically.

claim_text: Both large molecular size and high net positive charge are proposed to be required for Ctn's anti-T. cruzi activity against epimastigote forms, based on structure–activity comparison with Ctn fragments and batroxicidin.
limitations: Inference from comparative IC50 data across peptides differing in multiple physicochemical properties simultaneously; no mutagenesis or charge-neutralisation experiment performed.

claim_text: Ctn, as a cationic amphipathic peptide, is proposed to interact with and disrupt parasite cell membranes through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, consistent with the general mechanism attributed to venom antimicrobial peptides of its class.
limitations: Explicitly attributed to cited references on related venom AMPs (McGwire & Kulkarni 2010; Teixeira et al. 2012), not directly demonstrated for Ctn; no membrane-binding or lipid-bilayer assay reported in this study.

claim_text: The mechanism of action employed by most known AMPs involves physical disruption of target membranes via an induced or permanent amphipathic motif, which has historically prevented widespread AMP resistance by requiring major remodeling of basic membrane structure.
limitations: General class-level claim about AMPs supported only by citations to prior literature (Sato and Feix, 2006; Zhang and Gallo, 2016; Peters et al., 2010); no membrane-disruption assays performed on any peptide in this study; applies to cyclotides by inference only.

claim_text: Cancer and microbial cells enriched with anionic surface molecules can be selectively targeted by AMPs, with cell death caused by either membranolytic or intracellular mechanisms, in contrast to neutrally-charged mammalian cells.
limitations: General claim about the AMP class cited entirely from prior literature (Brogden, 2005; Guzman-Rodriguez et al., 2015; Lee and Kim, 2015; Mahlapuu et al., 2016; Rotem and Mor, 2009); no mechanistic assays were performed in this study to confirm this applies to cyO8 or any other cyclotide characterized here.

claim_text: CyO8 preferentially kills cancer cells over non-cancerous cells, showing approximately three-fold greater cytotoxicity against MDA-MB-231, PC-3, and OVCAR-3 cancer cell lines (IC50 0.80–1.15 µM) than against human dermal fibroblasts (IC50 ~3.13 µM), consistent with selective targeting of anionic cancer cell membranes.
limitations: Selectivity is demonstrated by MTT viability assay comparing cancer vs. non-cancer cell lines; the molecular basis for selectivity (e.g., membrane lipid composition, surface charge) is never experimentally investigated in this paper; the anionic-membrane explanation is implied by the introductory AMP framework but not directly tested or stated for cyO8.

claim_text: Chaxapeptin 1 inhibits invasion of human lung cancer cell line A549 through the extracellular matrix (ECM) in a concentration-dependent manner (28% inhibition at 5 µM, 56% at 50 µM).
direct_assay_types: cell invasion assay (ECM gel-coated chamber, CyQuant fluorescent staining)
limitations: Molecular mechanism of invasion inhibition is not identified; no mechanistic target specified; assay run at a single time point (36 h); effect comparable to sungsanpin but mechanistic basis of that comparison is not explored

claim_text: Chaxapeptin 1 shows a weak antibacterial effect against Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus subtilis at 30–35 µg/mL, with no activity against Gram-negative Escherichia coli up to 50 µg/mL.
direct_assay_types: agar diffusion (disk), MIC broth microdilution
limitations: Mechanism of antibacterial action is not investigated; activity is described as weak; only three strains tested; no time-kill kinetics or target identification performed

claim_text: The lack of antimicrobial self-resistance (and possibly reduced antibacterial potency) of chaxapeptin 1 may be explained by the absence of an ABC-transporter immunity gene in the cpt biosynthetic gene cluster.
limitations: Purely an inference from gene-cluster analysis; no functional deletion or complementation experiments performed; absence of the gene does not rule out alternative immunity mechanisms

claim_text: Chaxapeptin 1 inhibits A549 cell invasion without affecting cell morphology, suggesting the effect is not due to gross cytotoxicity.
direct_assay_types: cell morphology observation (qualitative)
limitations: No quantitative cytotoxicity assay (e.g., MTT, LDH) reported; morphological assessment alone is insufficient to exclude cytostatic effects or sub-lethal toxicity

claim_text: SAP1, SAP2, and SAP6 (ACE2-derived peptides) inhibit SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV Spike-mediated viral entry by disrupting the interaction between the viral Spike receptor-binding domain (RBD) and the host ACE2 receptor.
direct_assay_types: pseudovirus infection inhibition (luciferase reporter), genuine SARS-CoV-2 infection (flow cytometry/N-protein staining), affinity precipitation binding assay
limitations: Blocking of Spike-ACE2 interface is inferred from co-occurrence of RBD binding and infection inhibition; no direct competition assay (e.g., ACE2 vs. peptide displacement) was performed; IC50 values are in low millimolar range, indicating weak potency

claim_text: SAP1 and SAP6 directly bind the SARS-CoV-2 Spike RBD with apparent Kd values of 0.53 ± 0.01 mM and 1.36 ± 0.14 mM, respectively, as shown by affinity precipitation assays.
direct_assay_types: affinity precipitation (FITC-labeled peptides co-precipitated with His-tagged Spike RBD on Ni-NTA beads; fluorescence quantification by ImageJ; Kd fit to Hill equation)
limitations: In vitro binding only; millimolar Kd indicates weak affinity; SAP5, which has no detected RBD binding, confirms assay specificity but does not rule out indirect binding modes for SAP1/SAP6

claim_text: The minimal essential inhibitory motif is the six-amino-acid EDLFYQ sequence (Glu37–Gln42 of ACE2, corresponding to SAP6), which is sufficient to disrupt Spike RBD-ACE2 interaction and inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection.
direct_assay_types: comparative pseudovirus infection inhibition assay, genuine SARS-CoV-2 infection assay (flow cytometry)
limitations: Minimal motif defined by comparison of SAP1, SAP2, and SAP6 activity, not by alanine-scanning mutagenesis; shorter or rearranged sequences were not tested

claim_text: The polar residues Glu37, Asp38, Tyr41, and Gln42 of SAP6 form a hydrogen-bond network with SARS-CoV-2 Spike RBD residues Thr500, Tyr449, Asn501, and Tyr505, providing the atomic basis for Spike-ACE2 disruption.
limitations: Based entirely on structural modeling using the published cocrystal structure (PDB: 6M0J) and previously reported modeling studies; no experimental validation of specific H-bond contacts (e.g., mutagenesis of contact residues, NMR, or co-crystal structure of SAP6 with RBD) was performed in this study

claim_text: SAP1, SAP2, and SAP6 specifically inhibit ACE2-dependent coronavirus entry (SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, HCoV-NL63) but do not affect VSV-G-mediated viral entry, indicating their mechanism of action is specific to the Spike-ACE2 interaction interface.
direct_assay_types: pseudovirus infection inhibition assay with VSV-G specificity control (luciferase reporter); HCoV-NL63 plaque assay and cytopathic effect assay
limitations: VSV-G uses a structurally unrelated receptor (LDL-R); specificity for Spike-ACE2 interface is inferred from the negative VSV-G result, but alternative off-target antiviral mechanisms (e.g., post-entry effects) were not ruled out

claim_text: SAP1 and SAP6 act on virion-associated Spike protein prior to host cell attachment, since peptides were pre-incubated with virus particles before addition to cells.
direct_assay_types: pseudovirus and live SARS-CoV-2 infection inhibition assays (pre-incubation protocol)
limitations: The pre-incubation experimental design is consistent with virion-targeting but does not exclude additional activity at the cell surface during entry; no assay directly distinguished virion-bound vs. cell-surface-bound peptide activity

claim_text: Pseudodesmin A and B possess bacteriostatic but not bactericidal properties against Gram-positive bacteria at concentrations up to 25 µg/ml.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (broth microdilution)
limitations: Bactericidal endpoint (MBC) not measured; 25 µg/ml was the maximum test concentration so higher bactericidal concentrations cannot be excluded; no mechanistic basis for Gram-positive selectivity is determined.

claim_text: Transmembrane pore formation has been proposed as the most likely biological mode of action for viscosin-group cyclic lipodepsipeptides, including pseudodesmin A and B by structural analogy.
limitations: No pore-formation assay was performed on pseudodesmins; inference rests entirely on structural similarity to other viscosin-group members for which pore formation has been proposed or demonstrated in separate studies.

claim_text: WLIP, a viscosin-group member closely related to pseudodesmin A, inserts itself within model membranes.
direct_assay_types: model membrane insertion assay
limitations: Demonstrated for WLIP (Coraiola et al. 2006, ref 20), not for pseudodesmins; data are imported by analogy.

claim_text: WLIP demonstrates pore-forming capability as shown by osmotic protectant experiments on erythrocytes.
direct_assay_types: erythrocyte osmotic protectant assay
limitations: Demonstrated for WLIP (Lo Cantore et al. 2006, ref 12), not for pseudodesmins; erythrocyte model may not reflect target bacterial membranes.

claim_text: Viscosinamide, a related viscosin-group CLP, is believed to induce Ca2+-transporting pores in membranes as the basis for inhibiting fungal growth.
direct_assay_types: Ca2+ transport / pore induction assay (cited from Thrane et al. 1999, ref 13)
limitations: Applies to viscosinamide acting on fungi; pseudodesmins show no antifungal activity, limiting direct applicability to their antibacterial mechanism.

claim_text: The antibiotic mechanism of CLPs is hypothesized to involve the formation of passive-transport ion channels in cellular membranes that destabilize microbial metabolism by disturbing cytoplasmic ion concentrations.
limitations: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis in the paper; no ion transport, electrophysiology, or whole-cell ion flux assay was performed on pseudodesmins.

claim_text: The practical water-insolubility, hydrophobic side chains, and fatty acid chain of pseudodesmin A make insertion into the apolar lipid bilayer physically plausible as a first step in membrane disruption.
limitations: Physicochemical/structural inference only; no membrane partition coefficient, lipid-binding, or bilayer-insertion assay was performed.

claim_text: The amphipathic structure of pseudodesmin A suggests a pore-formation model in which molecules assemble as reverse micelles inside the membrane—hydrophilic surfaces facing inward—creating an ion-conducting channel that can span the bilayer.
limitations: Structural model only; no experimental verification of micelle assembly, bilayer spanning, or ion conductance for pseudodesmins; the reverse-micelle principle is analogized from syringomycin (ref 21) with no direct data.

claim_text: The conserved αL-helical conformation found in pseudodesmin A and across structurally characterized CLPs suggests this secondary-structure element plays an important role in the antimicrobial biological function of these peptides.
limitations: Inference based on structural conservation across multiple CLP crystal structures; no structure–activity relationship or mutagenesis data link the helix directly to antimicrobial activity.

claim_text: The conserved amphipathic arrangement of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues across viscosin-group CLPs and related compounds (amphisin, tensin) is proposed to be important for their antimicrobial function.
limitations: Based on sequence and structural conservation; no direct experimental evidence (e.g., side-chain substitution) connects amphipathicity to antimicrobial potency in pseudodesmins.

claim_text: Magainin 2 and its analogues appear to act via disruption of bacterial membrane barrier function.
limitations: Paper acknowledges 'for many membrane-active antimicrobial peptides, the relevant mechanism is unclear'; this is a general family-level attribution, not demonstrated here for Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 specifically.

claim_text: Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 belongs to the group of antimicrobial peptides that disrupt membranes by non-channel mechanisms.
limitations: Explicitly attributed by the authors as a classification ('specifically, we have determined the structure of...a polycationic host-defense peptide from the large group that appears to disrupt membranes by non-channel mechanisms'), but no mechanistic assay is performed in this paper to confirm it.

claim_text: The crystal structure of Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 reveals an antiparallel homochiral dimer with a phenylalanine zipper interface, consistent with a dimerization mode previously proposed to play a role in antibacterial activity.
limitations: Crystal structure was obtained under non-physiological conditions (35% tert-butanol, racemic mixture); the paper explicitly states 'the conditions used to crystallize Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 are not representative of the membrane environment.' Consistency with NMR-based dimer models is structural, not functional.

claim_text: The hydrophobic surface of the Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 homochiral dimer, comprising Phe and other residue side chains, may help anchor the dimer to a lipid bilayer.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('this surface may help to anchor'); no membrane-binding or lipid interaction assay is performed.

claim_text: Magainin 2 dimerizes upon binding to the surface of a lipid bilayer, contributing to antibacterial activity.
limitations: Attributed to Matsuzaki et al. (ref 28), not demonstrated in this paper; the authors note 'inconsistency among NMR studies leaves this hypothesis in question,' and prior NMR studies of magainin 2 and Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 in micelles did not reveal evidence of dimer formation.

claim_text: The L- and D-enantiomers of Ala8,13,18-magainin 2 display identical antibacterial activities, suggesting the mechanism of action does not depend on chiral recognition of a specific receptor.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (E. coli, B. subtilis, S. aureus MRSA, E. faecium VRE)
limitations: Enantioequipotency is consistent with a membrane-disruption mechanism but does not directly demonstrate it; the paper draws this conclusion by reference to prior literature on other host-defense peptides.

claim_text: The heterochiral (L+D) packing mode observed in the racemate crystal is not relevant to the biological activity of Ala8,13,18-magainin 2.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination; hemolytic activity assay
limitations: Inference is based on equipotency of racemic mixture vs. pure enantiomers; absence of a difference in activity does not fully rule out transient heterochiral interactions in solution.

claim_text: Alo-3 has no negatively charged residues and displays a cationic pole on its surface that may account for its antifungal activity against Candida species.
limitations: No direct mechanistic assay performed; inference is based solely on Poisson-Boltzmann electrostatic surface calculations and the correlation between net charge differences among Alo-1, -2, and -3 and their MIC values.

claim_text: Being cationic (net charge +6), Alo-3 most probably acts directly with the negatively charged fungal membranes, as proposed for most antimicrobial peptides.
limitations: Purely electrostatic inference by analogy to other AMPs; no membrane interaction, permeabilization, or lipid-binding experiments were conducted for Alo-3.

claim_text: The specific arrangement of cationic residues (Cys1, Lys3, His23, Lys24, Arg34, Arg35, Lys36) generating a large electropositive potential over a defined region of the molecule most probably plays a key role in antifungal activity.
limitations: Residue-level assignment of functional importance is based on structural analysis only; no mutagenesis or charge-neutralization experiments were performed to test individual contributions.

claim_text: The balance between the electropositive face and the neutral (non-charged) region of Alo-3 appears to be an important feature for its antifungal activity, as supported by the correlation between the increased cationicity of Alo-3 versus Alo-1/Alo-2 and the improved MIC against C. glabrata.
direct_assay_types: growth inhibition MIC assay (activity readout only, not mechanistic)
limitations: Correlation between charge distribution and activity is drawn from only three closely related analogues differing at multiple positions simultaneously; causality cannot be established without mutational dissection.

claim_text: Alo-3 likely acts by a mechanism different from that of amphiphilic CS-fold antifungal defensins, because its molecular surface is predominantly hydrophilic with only a small hydrophobic patch, in contrast to the marked amphiphilicity of CS-fold peptides.
limitations: Mechanistic difference is inferred entirely from comparison of hydrophobicity surface maps; no functional or biophysical assay comparing the two mechanism types was performed for Alo-3.

claim_text: DFTamP1 caused bacterial surface damage and cell leakage (blebs) in MRSA USA300, as visualized by transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy (membrane morphology/blebbing)
limitations: Single strain tested (USA300); TEM is a snapshot method and does not establish kinetics or primary vs. secondary damage

claim_text: DFTamP1 permeabilized the MRSA USA300 membrane, enabling entry of a DNA-binding dye and producing steep fluorescence buildup within 30 minutes as measured by flow cytometry.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with DNA-binding dye (membrane permeabilization)
limitations: Dye entry reflects loss of membrane integrity but does not distinguish primary membrane disruption from downstream lysis; single strain

claim_text: DFTamP1 acts on bacterial membranes, as indicated collectively by surface damage observed in TEM and membrane permeabilization detected by flow cytometry.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy, flow cytometry with DNA-binding dye
limitations: Neither assay resolves the precise molecular mechanism (e.g., pore formation vs. carpet/detergent model); no lipid-interaction or ion-flux assay performed

claim_text: The broad hydrophobic surface of DFTamP1 allows it to penetrate deeper into bacterial membranes to exert its damaging effect, according to the authors' membrane perturbation potential model.
limitations: Explicitly framed as a model/proposal by the authors; no depth-of-insertion assay (e.g., EPR, neutron diffraction) was performed in this study

claim_text: The leucine-rich hydrophobic surface of DFTamP1 is critical for membrane targeting and MRSA killing, as isoleucine and valine substitution analogs lost antimicrobial activity and were unable to kill MRSA even at 32-fold the MIC of DFTamP1.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay, bacterial killing kinetics (analog substitution experiments)
limitations: Loss of activity in analogs is attributed to reduced hydrophobicity and lower helix-forming propensity simultaneously; cannot isolate which factor is dominant; does not directly measure membrane binding

claim_text: The equal potency of the all-D-amino acid form of temporin-PTa against MRSA, E. coli, and B. subtilis substantiates that its mechanism is membrane targeting rather than binding to a chiral protein receptor.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay (D-amino acid analog)
limitations: Retention of activity in D-form rules out chiral receptor binding but does not specify the exact membrane mechanism; temporin-PTa is a different peptide from DFTamP1

claim_text: DFTamP1's low cationicity overcomes MRSA resistance because MRSA deploys positively charged moieties on its surface to repel classical cationic AMPs, and the minimized positive charge of DFTamP1 prevents this electrostatic repulsion.
limitations: The MRSA surface-charge resistance mechanism is cited from prior literature (ref 12), not directly demonstrated here; no direct measurement of peptide–surface interaction or surface charge modification was performed in this study

claim_text: Magainin 2 family peptides seem to act by disrupting bacterial membranes, among other mechanisms.
limitations: Attributed broadly to a 'large HDP subset'; no direct membrane disruption assay reported in this paper; cited to prior literature (refs 1-3).

claim_text: The extended hydrophobic surface projected by the phenylalanine zipper motif in the homochiral coiled-coil dimer is proposed to mediate association of the dimer with bacterial membranes.
limitations: Explicitly a proposal/hypothesis; supported only by crystal structure geometry showing exposed nonpolar surface, not by any membrane interaction assay.

claim_text: A coiled-coil-like homochirial dimerization mode, featuring the phenylalanine zipper, plays a functional role in the antibacterial activities of peptides in the magainin 2 family.
limitations: Inferred from convergent structural evidence (three crystal structures, five independent dimer structures); no direct functional assay linking dimerization to antibacterial activity is performed in this paper; NMR support for dimerization under micellar conditions comes from prior literature (refs 13a-e), not new experiments here.

claim_text: Helix dimerization via the phenylalanine zipper leaves considerable nonpolar surface area exposed for interaction with a bacterial membrane, contrary to a prior proposal that dimerization would prevent hydrophobic surface exposure.
limitations: Based solely on structural geometry of crystal structures; no direct assay of membrane association or surface burial performed.

claim_text: SVS-1 kills cancer cells via a membrane-lytic mechanism rather than receptor-mediated binding, as the all-D-enantiomer (D-SVS-1) displays equivalent cytotoxicity against all four cancer cell lines tested.
direct_assay_types: D-enantiomer activity equivalence (MTT cytotoxicity assay)
limitations: D-enantiomer equivalence rules out chiral receptor binding but does not exclude all non-lytic mechanisms.

claim_text: SVS-1 folds into an amphiphilic β-hairpin conformation specifically at negatively charged membrane surfaces, driven by electrostatic interactions between the cationic lysine residues and anionic lipid head groups.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy with model POPC:POPS liposomes
limitations: CD performed with simplified model liposomes (POPC:POPS 1:1), not actual cancer cell membranes; actual membrane composition is more complex.

claim_text: SVS-1 remains unfolded and inactive in aqueous solution and at neutral (zwitterionic POPC) membrane surfaces, requiring a negatively charged surface to adopt its bioactive conformation.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: CD in solution and at neutral vesicles shows random coil; activity against neutral-membrane cells not directly confirmed beyond hRBC and HUVEC data.

claim_text: β-hairpin formation is necessary for SVS-1's membrane-disrupting activity, as the control peptide SVS-2 (identical sequence except L-Pro replacing D-Pro at position 10, preventing hairpin formation) is inactive against all cancer cell lines at concentrations up to 100 µM and induces less than 5% liposome leakage.
direct_assay_types: MTT cytotoxicity assay, Tb/DPA liposome leakage assay, circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: SVS-2 differs from SVS-1 by only one stereochemical change, but this change could affect properties beyond hairpin structure (e.g., aggregation state) that independently influence activity.

claim_text: SVS-1 disrupts membrane integrity by inducing leakage from negatively charged (POPC:POPS 1:1) liposomes but not from neutral (POPC) liposomes, indicating that a negatively charged surface is required to trigger its membrane-disrupting action.
direct_assay_types: Tb/DPA fluorescence liposome leakage assay
limitations: Model lipid membranes are simplified surrogates for cancer cell membranes; actual cell outer leaflet composition differs.

claim_text: SVS-1 and D-SVS-1 induce rapid, non-specific membrane disruption of negatively charged liposomes, reaching approximately 40% leakage at a 1:25 peptide:lipid ratio within minutes at 1 µM peptide concentration.
direct_assay_types: Tb/DPA fluorescence liposome leakage assay, D-enantiomer activity equivalence
limitations: Fast leakage kinetics and D-enantiomer equivalence are consistent with non-specific disruption but do not definitively exclude specific lipid-binding modes.

claim_text: SVS-1 physically disrupts cancer cell (A549) membranes and causes leakage of cytoplasmic and intra-organelle contents, as directly visualized by transmission and scanning electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Imaging performed at IC90 concentration (8 µM) after 4 h endpoint; morphological data does not resolve the temporal sequence of molecular events leading to membrane disruption.

claim_text: Membrane disruption is the primary mode of cell killing by SVS-1, as the concentration inducing 50% LDH release from A549 cells (~4 µM) closely matches the IC50 for cell death (4.9 ± 0.6 µM).
direct_assay_types: LDH release assay, MTT cell viability assay
limitations: LDH release is a secondary marker of membrane permeabilization and cannot distinguish initial membrane damage from secondary necrotic leakage following another primary lethal event.

claim_text: The preferential cytotoxicity of SVS-1 toward cancer cells over normal cells (therapeutic index 10–17) is attributable to the aberrant electronegative lipid composition of cancer cell outer leaflets (phosphatidylserine exposure and sialylated mucins), which selectively triggers membrane-induced folding and disruption.
limitations: PS surface exposure and sialic acid levels on the tested cancer cell lines were not directly measured in this study; other cancer-specific membrane properties could also contribute to selectivity.

claim_text: Once folded at the negatively charged membrane surface, the hydrophobic valine-rich face of the SVS-1 β-hairpin inserts into the lipid portion of the bilayer, destabilizing membrane structural integrity.
limitations: Bilayer insertion of the hydrophobic face was not directly measured; inferred from peptide design logic (unfavorable solvation of valine face by water) and supported indirectly by leakage and EM data.

claim_text: Efrapeptin G (3) is a mitochondrial ATPase inhibitor.
limitations: The paper attributes this mechanism to prior literature; no ATPase inhibition assay is conducted in this study. The compound was re-isolated here and confirmed structurally, but the MOA claim is inherited, not independently demonstrated.

claim_text: The C-terminal blocking group of the efrapeptins may play a role in their biological activity, possibly accounting for the differential cytotoxicity observed between efrapeptin G (3) and the RHMs (1 and 2) against murine cell lines.
limitations: Based solely on structural comparison and differential bioactivity data across compounds; no experiment directly tests the contribution of the C-terminal group. Cited as a suggestion from previous studies.

claim_text: The unusual amino acid composition of efrapeptin G (3) — including isovaline, aminoisobutyric acid, β-alanine, and pipecolic acid — may also contribute to its differential bioactivity relative to RHM1 (1) and RHM2 (2).
limitations: No experimental evidence is provided; inferred by structural comparison between compounds with differing potency. Causal relationship is speculative.

claim_text: Both cyclic and linear antimicrobial peptoids form large pores and deep craters in the S. aureus cellular envelope, indicating bactericidal activity through physical disruption of the cell surface.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
limitations: SEM imaging requires fixation and dehydration, which can introduce artifacts; no quantitative comparison of pore size or frequency between cyclic and linear forms was made; the imaging cannot distinguish between direct membrane rupture and downstream lysis.

claim_text: Peptoid-mediated cell death occurs by compromising membrane integrity (bactericidal rather than bacteriostatic mechanism).
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy (SEM), minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assay
limitations: Bactericidal conclusion is inferred from SEM morphological damage co-observed with MIC results; cell viability was not directly measured (e.g., no CFU time-kill assay); SEM captures endpoint morphology, not the kinetics of killing.

claim_text: Cyclic peptoids intercalate into Langmuir monolayers of anionic lipids (DPPG and kdo2-lipid A) with greater efficacy than their linear analogues, as evidenced by larger relative increases in area per lipid molecule.
direct_assay_types: constant-pressure Langmuir insertion assay, X-ray reflectivity (XR)
limitations: Monolayers consist of saturated lipids only (gel phase), which may not reflect the fluid-phase dynamics of native bacterial membranes; single-leaflet model omits transmembrane asymmetry and bilayer coupling.

claim_text: Cyclic peptoids penetrate into the hydrocarbon chain (hydrophobic core) region of the DPPG monolayer, spanning the full depth of the monolayer, whereas linear peptoids do not significantly permeate this region.
direct_assay_types: X-ray reflectivity (electron density profiling)
limitations: Interpretation relies on slab-model fitting of electron density profiles, which is model-dependent; saturated-lipid gel-phase monolayer may not represent fluid bacterial membranes; penetration depth in a bilayer may differ.

claim_text: Linear peptoid L1 molecules accumulate preferentially on the outer surface of the lipid film rather than inserting into the monolayer interior, reflecting limited membrane penetration.
direct_assay_types: X-ray reflectivity (electron density profiling)
limitations: Excess electron density beneath the lipid monolayer is inferred from model fitting; L2 shows no electron density contribution to either internal region, yet the paper notes this pair shows a less pronounced cyclic-vs-linear difference, suggesting molecule-specific variability.

claim_text: Cyclic peptoids localize within the upper (outer-leaflet) slab of the kdo2-lipid A monolayer, a model of the Gram-negative outer membrane, while linear peptoids remain restricted to the lower (inner) region.
direct_assay_types: X-ray reflectivity (electron density profiling)
limitations: kdo2-lipid A is a truncated LPS mimic lacking the full polysaccharide chain; model is a monolayer, not a bilayer; peptoid behavior in the inner leaflet or across the full outer membrane cannot be inferred.

claim_text: Cyclic peptoids destroy the lateral order of DPPG monolayers (abolish liquid-ordered phase domains) faster than their linear counterparts, indicating more rapid membrane fluidization.
direct_assay_types: epifluorescence microscopy (EFM)
limitations: EFM resolution is ~1 µm and cannot detect sub-micrometer structural changes; the authors note that the mechanisms of cyclic versus linear peptoids are indistinguishable at the micrometer scale; observation is confined to a model monolayer.

claim_text: Both cyclic and linear peptoids fluidize the bacterial membrane by obliterating liquid-ordered lipid domains, though the two forms are mechanistically indistinguishable at the micrometer scale.
direct_assay_types: epifluorescence microscopy (EFM)
limitations: Fluidization is inferred from disappearance of ordered-phase domains in a model monolayer; native bacterial membranes contain proteins, sterols, and lipid heterogeneity absent in the model; authors explicitly state the mechanisms cannot be distinguished at this resolution.

claim_text: Cyclization halves the rotational degrees of freedom of the peptoid backbone, reducing the entropic penalty (by ~4 kcal/mol) for membrane insertion and thereby improving membrane-penetrating activity.
limitations: Entropy reduction is estimated from literature parameters derived for α-helical peptides (not peptoids) and scaled by the number of monomers; no calorimetric or thermodynamic measurement of insertion free energy was performed on these specific compounds; the calculation assumes similar conformational behavior between peptoid hexamers and helical peptides.

claim_text: Cyclization increases the overall membrane activity of antimicrobial peptoids, potentially leading to superior membrane-disruptive behavior compared to linear analogues.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay, constant-pressure Langmuir insertion assay, X-ray reflectivity, epifluorescence microscopy, scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Mechanistic superiority is inferred from the convergence of model-membrane and biological activity data; direct demonstration of deeper in-cell membrane disruption (e.g., inner-membrane permeabilization assays, liposome leakage) was not performed; activity was tested only against S. aureus (Gram-positive) and Gram-negative coverage was only MIC-level without mechanistic follow-up.

claim_text: Syn-BNP 1 does not induce membrane depolarization in E. faecium or A. baumannii, as measured by DiBAC4 fluorescence, ruling out membrane depolarization as its mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiBAC4 fluorescence assay)
limitations: Negative result only; tests one membrane parameter (electrochemical gradient); does not identify the actual target; deoxycholate and polymyxin used as positive controls confirm assay sensitivity but cannot exclude other membrane effects

claim_text: Syn-BNP 1 likely acts through a mechanism analogous to lipid II binding, inferred from its structural similarity to tridecaptin (which kills via lipid II binding), the absence of membrane depolarization, and the inability to raise resistance—a pattern characteristic of lipid II-targeting antibiotics such as teixobactin and vancomycin.
limitations: Lipid II binding not directly tested for syn-BNP 1; structural similarity to tridecaptin is partial (5 of 13 shared residues); spectral activity differs from tridecaptin A1 (Gram-positive vs. Gram-negative), weakening the analogy; failure to raise resistance is consistent with but does not prove lipid II binding

claim_text: Syn-BNP 2 does not function by disruption of ergosterol biology or cell wall integrity, as MIC values were unchanged in the presence of exogenous ergosterol or sorbitol.
direct_assay_types: ergosterol rescue (MIC shift), sorbitol osmotic protection (MIC shift)
limitations: MIC shift assays are indirect proxies that rule out two common antifungal mechanisms but cannot exclude all ergosterol- or cell wall-related targets; actual molecular target explicitly stated as undetermined

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of tachyplesin I is believed to originate from the peptide's ability to permeabilize bacterial cell membranes.
limitations: Stated as a prior-literature belief for TP-I, not directly tested in this paper; cited from references 3 and 5.

claim_text: CDT disrupts the E. coli outer membrane in a dose-dependent manner at sub-micromolar concentrations.
direct_assay_types: outer membrane permeabilization (ANS fluorescence enhancement and blue shift with intact E. coli cells)
limitations: ANS partitioning reports hydrophobic exposure but does not directly measure ion conductance or integrity loss; single bacterial strain (BL21/DE3) tested.

claim_text: CDT permeabilizes model membranes mimicking bacterial inner membranes (7:3 POPC:POPG) in a dose- and time-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: dye leakage (carboxyfluorescein release from SUVs)
limitations: Model membrane only; does not confirm identical mechanism in live bacterial inner membranes.

claim_text: CDT does not permeabilize erythrocyte membranes and lacks hemolytic activity up to 200 μg/mL.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay (hemoglobin release from sheep erythrocytes, absorbance at 414 nm)
limitations: Sheep erythrocytes used as proxy for human red blood cells; single time point (1 h, 37°C).

claim_text: CDT selectively binds and inserts into negatively charged (anionic) membranes but only adheres superficially to zwitterionic/cholesterol-containing membranes.
direct_assay_types: tryptophan intrinsic fluorescence binding assay (emission maximum shift and intensity change with SUVs of varying lipid composition)
limitations: Partition coefficient could not be determined for POPC:cholesterol due to minimal spectral change; SUVs may not fully recapitulate curved bacterial membrane geometry.

claim_text: CDT binding to lipid membranes is an enthalpy-driven process, with highest binding enthalpy for LPS-containing vesicles (−43.7 kJ/mol) and lowest for cholesterol-containing vesicles (−10.4 kJ/mol).
direct_assay_types: isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC; peptide-into-lipid titration)
limitations: Entropic contributions not decomposed; LPS molecular weight (~20 kDa for P. aeruginosa H458) carries uncertainty in lipid:LPS molar ratio calculation.

claim_text: CDT exists as a largely unordered structure in aqueous buffer and adopts a more ordered β-structure upon binding to negatively charged membranes (e.g., POPC:LPS).
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy
limitations: CD spectra in POPC:POPG and POPE:POPG could not be recorded due to peptide-induced turbidity; β-structure vs. extended-strand assignment is approximate from CD alone.

claim_text: CDT binding to negatively charged bilayers induces a conformational change in lipid head groups, moving the phosphate head group away from the bilayer surface toward the aqueous phase.
direct_assay_types: 31P solid-state NMR (oriented bilayers and MLVs: CSA span increase, MAS isotropic chemical shift upfield shift in POPC:POPG bilayers)
limitations: Aligned sample preparation used no bulk water, which may influence results; head group movement direction inferred from chemical shift conventions rather than direct structural measurement.

claim_text: A barrel-stave mechanism of membrane disruption by CDT is unlikely because the peptide is located near the lipid head group region rather than inserting across the hydrophobic core.
limitations: Inference drawn from 31P NMR head group perturbation data and DSC low-enthalpy values; no direct measurement of peptide transmembrane orientation (e.g., 2H or 15N NMR) was performed.

claim_text: CDT does not function by fragmenting lipid bilayers into micelles/SUVs or by promoting non-lamellar (cubic or hexagonal) phase structures.
direct_assay_types: 31P solid-state NMR (lamellar powder pattern lineshape preserved up to 10 mol% CDT in MLVs)
limitations: Only lipid compositions tested were POPC and POPC:POPG; absence of hexagonal/cubic signatures is a negative result dependent on NMR sensitivity.

claim_text: The presence of cholesterol inhibits CDT binding to and disruption of lipid bilayers.
direct_assay_types: 31P solid-state NMR (reduction of CDT-induced disordering upon addition of 20 mol% cholesterol to POPC:POPG bilayers), tryptophan fluorescence (minimal spectral change with POPC:cholesterol SUVs)
limitations: Mechanism of cholesterol-mediated inhibition (e.g., condensation effect, altered membrane fluidity, charge shielding) is not experimentally resolved.

claim_text: CDT does not insert deeply into the hydrophobic core of anionic DMPC:DMPG membranes and is likely located at the membrane–water interface.
limitations: Concluded from low DSC transition enthalpy values compared to expected values for transmembrane-oriented peptides; no direct depth-of-insertion probe (e.g., fluorescence quenching with brominated lipids) was used.

claim_text: The loss of hemolytic activity of CDT relative to TP-I is due to reduced hydrophobicity and amphipathicity resulting from deletion of the four cysteine residues.
limitations: Mechanistic attribution is by structural reasoning (cysteine deletion reduces amphipathic β-hairpin structure); direct measurement of membrane hydrophobic insertion depth in erythrocyte membranes was not performed.

claim_text: Cysteine residues in tachyplesin I do not contribute to its antimicrobial activity, as CDT (with all four cysteines deleted) retains comparable antimicrobial potency against tested Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
limitations: Conclusion drawn from comparative MIC data (CDT vs. TP-I); the structural basis is inferred—CDT is a deletion analog, so side-chain identity and backbone conformation effects are conflated.

claim_text: Cyclotides are believed to act through membrane interactions, a view used to justify hemolytic assays as a proxy marker for biological activity.
limitations: This is stated as a prior belief (citing Kamimori et al. 2005), not demonstrated by a membrane mechanistic assay in this paper; hemolytic activity is used as a surrogate, not a direct membrane-disruption measurement.

claim_text: The anti-HIV activity of cyclotides from V. yedoensis positively correlates with their hydrophobicity and tracks with their ability to disrupt membranes as judged by hemolytic assays on human erythrocytes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (hemolytic assay on human erythrocytes), XTT-based anti-HIV cell-protection assay
limitations: Correlation between hemolysis and anti-HIV activity does not establish a shared causal mechanism; erythrocyte lysis may not recapitulate the relevant membrane in HIV-infected cells; only five cyclotides tested.

claim_text: The mode of action of cyclotides involves membrane interactions, as reinforced by the correlation between hydrophobic surface area and both hemolytic and anti-HIV activities observed in this study.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (hemolytic assay on human erythrocytes)
limitations: No direct mechanistic membrane assay (e.g., lipid-bilayer disruption, membrane leakage) was performed; surface hydrophobicity was calculated from homology models rather than experimentally determined structures; RP-HPLC retention time used as an experimental hydrophobicity proxy.

claim_text: Surface presentation of hydrophobic residues on the cyclotide scaffold, rather than total hydrophobic amino acid composition, is the structural determinant of membrane-disrupting and anti-HIV activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (hemolytic assay), XTT-based anti-HIV assay
limitations: Structural models used for surface area calculation are homology models (not NMR/X-ray structures for most peptides); hydrophobic surface area was a computed value; the inference relies on correlation, not experimental mutagenesis or direct membrane binding data.

claim_text: Gramicidin S kills bacterial cells through destabilization and permeabilization of their cytoplasmic membranes.
limitations: Authors note the mechanism is 'not completely understood' and cite this as 'generally accepted'; no direct permeabilization assay performed in this paper.

claim_text: Cationic antimicrobial peptides kill bacteria via disruption of the pathogen's cytoplasmic membrane, a mechanism that makes induction of resistance rather unlikely.
limitations: Stated as a general class property cited from literature; no direct assay in this paper; resistance-avoidance claim is mechanistically inferred, not tested.

claim_text: An aromatic group at the i+1 position of the GS β-turn is required for full bactericidal potency, as replacement by non-aromatic residues (Gly, D-Ala, D-cyclohexylalanine) yields less active or inactive analogs.
limitations: Activity loss is measured by MIC50; mechanism linking aromatic side chain to membrane disruption is not directly demonstrated; prior-literature data cited, not generated in this paper.

claim_text: The Ac3c analog (8), lacking an aromatic moiety at the β-turn, is practically devoid of antibiotic activity, supporting the essential role of aromaticity at this position for GS bactericidal function.
limitations: Activity assessed by MIC50 only; loss of activity could reflect conformational rather than direct mechanistic requirement for aromaticity.

claim_text: Hydrophobicity above a minimal threshold is required for a peptide to partition into the bacterial or mammalian membrane, and correlates with AMP activity against Gram-positive bacteria and erythrocytes.
limitations: Inferred from RP-HPLC retention times as hydrophobicity proxy correlated with MIC50/HC50; not all analogs follow the trend; no direct membrane partitioning assay performed.

claim_text: Against Gram-negative bacteria, AMPs must traverse the outer membrane before disrupting the plasma membrane, and excessive hydrophobicity can cause AMP sequestration within the outer membrane, preventing access to the plasma membrane target.
limitations: Mechanistic model cited from literature; not directly tested in this paper; proposed to explain differential Gram-negative activity.

claim_text: GS traverses the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria through diffuse binding to LPS and hydrophobic-interaction-driven passage (self-uptake), rather than the high-affinity LPS binding and outer membrane disruption used by most membrane-active AMPs.
limitations: Explicitly attributed to a prior proposal ('it has been proposed'); not directly tested here; the paper's own data on colistin-resistant A. baumannii strains (with modified LPS) partially challenge this model for the current analog series.

claim_text: The bulkiness and rigidity of cyclopropane-containing analogs (6–12) likely impair AMP transit through the Gram-negative outer membrane, preventing them from reaching and disrupting the plasma membrane, regardless of intrinsic membrane-disruption potential.
limitations: Inferred from failure of cyclopropane analogs specifically against Gram-negatives in MIC50 assays; no direct outer-membrane permeability or plasma-membrane assay performed.

claim_text: Cationic character (Orn residues), amphipathic character, β-sheet structure, ring size, and global hydrophobicity are key factors governing GS bioactivity against bacterial membranes.
limitations: Cited as established from prior SAR literature; this paper adds structural data (NMR) and MIC50/HC50 correlations but does not mechanistically deconvolve each factor.

claim_text: For GS analogs active against Gram-negatives, a balanced combination of hydrophobicity, amphipathicity, molecular flexibility, and cationic character is required for productive interaction with outer membrane LPS and subsequent plasma membrane disruption.
limitations: Inferred from structure–activity patterns across the analog series; no direct LPS-binding, outer-membrane permeability, or inner-membrane disruption assays performed.

claim_text: The lethal step for bacteria in vivo is membrane permeabilization, occurring within seconds to minutes of peptide addition and rendering cells incapable of recovery.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye influx), time-course minimum sterilizing concentration assay
limitations: SYTOX Green measures bulk population permeabilization; killing onset inferred from MSC time-course experiments rather than direct single-cell observation

claim_text: These peptides cause rapid cytoplasmic membrane depolarization in E. coli within less than one minute, followed by more extensive membrane disruption (SYTOX Green influx) over 10–40 minutes, suggesting a sequential two-step mechanism beginning with small-ion permeability and progressing to gross membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (diSC3(5) fluorescent dye), membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye influx)
limitations: Sequential causation inferred from timing difference between two independent assays; direct mechanistic linkage between depolarization and subsequent gross permeabilization not established

claim_text: Peptide-induced membrane disruption is independent of the metabolic state of bacterial cells, as membrane permeabilization is equivalent in metabolically dormant cells (PBS), metabolically active cells (LTM), and cells with fully dissipated membrane potential (valinomycin-treated).
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green dye influx) under three metabolic conditions
limitations: Tested only in E. coli; valinomycin also depletes ATP in addition to dissipating membrane potential, so contributions of each cannot be fully separated

claim_text: These peptides permeabilize bacterial membranes independently of the transmembrane electrochemical potential, contradicting the hypothesis that a negative-inside membrane potential is a key driver of AMP selectivity and activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green) in valinomycin-depolarized E. coli cells
limitations: Only tested in E. coli; does not rule out a contributory role of membrane potential in other organisms or at sub-MSC peptide concentrations

claim_text: The antifungal mechanism against Cryptococcus neoformans is different from the antibacterial mechanism, as fungal membrane permeabilization is substantially slower and often incomplete compared to bacteria, and full sterilization requires more than one hour.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Green at 40 min endpoint), time-course minimum sterilizing concentration assay
limitations: Mechanistic basis for slower kinetics not determined; the difference could reflect cell-wall barrier effects, membrane lipid composition differences, or a genuinely distinct mode of action; explicitly noted as under further study

claim_text: Secondary structure is not required for antimicrobial activity, as single D-leucine substitutions that eliminate or substantially reduce β-sheet secondary structure still retain potent activity against at least some microorganisms.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy (secondary structure), minimum sterilizing concentration assay, SYTOX Green membrane permeabilization
limitations: D-amino acid substitution also alters backbone dynamics, membrane-binding geometry, and protease susceptibility in addition to secondary structure; activity retention was organism-dependent and unpredictable, complicating a clean mechanistic interpretation

claim_text: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity is a specific property dependent on interfacial activity rather than secondary structure, because single D-amino acid substitutions always abolish broad-spectrum activity even when species-specific activity is partially retained.
direct_assay_types: minimum sterilizing concentration assay with D-amino acid substituted analogs across four microbial species
