limitations: The conjugate retained some bactericidal activity but at reduced levels compared with free peptide; lower activity could reflect steric hindrance rather than conclusively proving a purely surface-acting mechanism.

claim_text: LPS is a key molecular determinant of susceptibility or resistance in gram-negative bacteria, as coating bacteria with heterologous LPS transfers the donor strain's susceptibility or resistance phenotype to the recipient.
direct_assay_types: bacterial LPS chimera susceptibility assay, transmission electron microscopy
limitations: Efficiency of LPS incorporation was verified by immunostaining and agglutination but partial incorporation cannot be excluded; contributions of other outer-membrane components were not independently controlled.

claim_text: Binding of myotoxin II-(115-129)-peptide to lipid A and the LPS core region of gram-negative bacteria, and to lipoteichoic acids of gram-positive S. aureus, correlates with susceptibility to killing, whereas the O-chain polysaccharide does not bind the peptide and does not confer susceptibility.
direct_assay_types: indirect competitive binding assay (inhibition of bactericidal halo by purified LPS, lipid A, O-chain, and lipoteichoic acid)
limitations: Binding is measured indirectly via competitive inhibition of bactericidal activity rather than direct binding constants; quantitative affinities were not determined.

claim_text: The bactericidal region responsible for membrane-disruptive activity is a short cluster of basic and hydrophobic amino acids near the C-terminal loop of myotoxin II (residues 115-129), which reproduces the full bactericidal effect of the intact protein.
direct_assay_types: colony-forming unit reduction assay with synthetic 13-residue peptide; negative control with non-bactericidal peptide from residues 69-80
limitations: The synthetic peptide may have different conformational properties than the equivalent region in the folded dimer; a disulfide bond (Cys133-Cys50) in the intact protein precludes helix formation in this region in vivo.

claim_text: The proposed mechanism of membrane disruption involves displacement of stabilizing divalent cations (Ca2+ and Mg2+) from negatively charged surface groups (LPS core and lipid A for gram-negative bacteria; phosphate groups of lipoteichoic acids for gram-positive bacteria) by the cationic peptide, followed by insertion of the hydrophobic domain into the lipid bilayer, membrane permeabilization, and cell death.
limitations: Proposed entirely by analogy with other cationic peptides (lactoferricin B, defensins); no direct experimental evidence for cation displacement, hydrophobic insertion, or pore formation was presented in this study.

claim_text: The amphipathic character of the 115-129 peptide—with cationic and hydrophobic residues clustered on opposite faces of a potential helix—is a structural feature enabling membrane disruption, consistent with other antimicrobial peptides of diverse origin.
limitations: Conclusion is based solely on helical-wheel (axial projection) analysis; the three-dimensional structure of the peptide in solution was not determined experimentally, and helical conformation was not confirmed.

claim_text: The bactericidal effect causes cell death rather than bacteriostasis, as transmission electron microscopy shows severe ultrastructural damage in susceptible bacteria including inner-membrane detachment, outer-membrane blistering, electron-dense granule formation, and vacuolization.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological damage is consistent with membrane disruption as the lethal event but does not resolve the molecular mechanism; mesosome-like structures in S. aureus can occasionally be fixation artefacts.

claim_text: Reduced bactericidal potency of myotoxin II and its peptide against gram-positive bacteria relative to gram-negative bacteria may result from the thicker gram-positive cell wall impeding access of the cationic peptide domain to the cytoplasmic membrane.
limitations: This explanation is explicitly tentative ('may be the consequence'); no direct experiment tested cell-wall thickness as the variable.

claim_text: Resistance of Brucella species to myotoxin II-(115-129)-peptide is attributed to low peptide binding affinity to Brucella outer membrane, resulting from reduced divalent-cation stabilization and a comparatively low density of negatively charged groups in Brucella LPS.
direct_assay_types: indirect binding assay (whole cells and purified LPS/lipid A from resistant and susceptible strains compared)
limitations: The cited physicochemical properties of Brucella LPS are from referenced prior literature, not measured in this study; additional resistance mechanisms (e.g., efflux, outer-membrane protein composition) were not investigated.

claim_text: Cationic α-helical AMPs act by inserting into biological membranes, which constitute either their direct target of action or the main barrier to intracellular pathogen targets.
limitations: General field statement attributed to cited literature (refs 5–6); no direct membrane-insertion assay performed in this paper.

claim_text: Incorporating proline residues into AMPs decreases the ability of the peptide to permeabilize the cytoplasmic membrane of Escherichia coli, with a concomitant reduction in antibacterial activity.
limitations: Attributed entirely to prior studies (refs 7–9); this paper does not perform membrane permeabilization assays.

claim_text: Proline-containing peptides resist self-association and interact selectively with anionic lipids present in bacterial target membranes but absent from erythrocyte membranes, conferring antibacterial selectivity and reduced hemolysis.
limitations: Lipid-selectivity mechanism attributed to prior studies (refs 11–12); this paper supports the self-association resistance component via CD, tryptophan fluorescence, SEC, and DOSY NMR, but does not directly measure lipid binding.

claim_text: Peptide self-association in solution, induced by coordinating phosphate anions or increased hydrophobicity, promotes structural ordering and is linked to hemolytic potential rather than antibacterial potency.
limitations: Inferred from parallel CD, tryptophan fluorescence (blue-shift/self-quenching), SEC (earlier elution), and DOSY NMR data correlating ordering/aggregation state with HC50 values; causality is not directly proven.

claim_text: Antimicrobial action and hemolysis proceed via mechanistically distinct pathways, as demonstrated by proline-containing peptides that kill bacteria and cancer cells at concentrations substantially below those required to lyse erythrocytes.
limitations: Concluded from differential MIC50/EC50 vs. HC50 ratios across the peptide series; the molecular basis of each separate mechanism is not directly characterized.

claim_text: Proline-containing peptides kill intraerythrocytic Plasmodium falciparum by penetrating the erythrocyte membrane to reach the intracellular parasite rather than by membrane lysis, as they achieve antiplasmodial activity without causing hemolysis.
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation inferred from EC50 vs. HC50 ratios and light microscopy showing reduced parasitemia without observable erythrocyte damage; no direct membrane-penetration or intracellular-localization assay was performed.

claim_text: Maintaining conformational flexibility (disorder in aqueous solution) improves AMP selectivity for bacterial, plasmodial, and cancerous cell membranes over host erythrocyte membranes, enabling targeting of both extracellular and intracellular pathogens.
limitations: Conclusion drawn from correlation of conformational data (CD, NMR) with multi-target biological activity and HC50 data; the mechanistic link between solution-state flexibility and membrane selectivity is not directly measured.

claim_text: The hydrophobicity and secondary structure of linear cationic amphipathic AMPs govern their ability to self-associate and insert into biological membranes, properties that contribute to both antimicrobial potency and host cell toxicity.
limitations: General mechanistic principle stated and supported by structural characterization (CD, NMR) and correlated activity data in this paper, but without direct membrane-insertion or membrane-disruption assays.

claim_text: Parasin I coats the mucosal surface where it may contribute to the establishment of a local antimicrobial milieu against microbial invasion.
limitations: Localization inferred from immunohistochemistry showing extracellular immunoreactivity at mucosal surface; direct killing mechanism not demonstrated in this paper

claim_text: Parasin I shows antimicrobial activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive fish-specific pathogens (A. salmonicida, C. aquatilis, Y. ruckeri, E. ictaluri, L. garvieae) as measured by MIC.
direct_assay_types: minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assay
limitations: Tested only against fish-specific pathogens; mechanism of killing (membrane disruption, intracellular targeting, etc.) not investigated in this paper

claim_text: Parasin I contributes to the innate host defense of fish against invading microorganisms by functioning as an antimicrobial barrier on the skin mucosal surface.
limitations: Inferred from MIC data and surface localization; no in vivo infection model used; causality not directly demonstrated

claim_text: DvnRV41 reduced viable L. monocytogenes EGDe cell counts in mouse spleens by 5.3 log10 under postchallenge conditions and 3.1 log10 under prechallenge conditions, demonstrating direct antilisterial activity in vivo.
direct_assay_types: CFU enumeration from spleen homogenates (in vivo murine model)
limitations: Small group sizes (n=5 per group); no statistical significance claimed by authors; preliminary study

claim_text: The reduced antilisterial activity of DvnRV41 when administered prechallenge compared to postchallenge is hypothesized to result from a metabolic pathway affecting the peptide before infection, while the peptide remains intact when administered after infection.
limitations: Authors explicitly state the metabolic pathway is 'not clearly understood'; no pharmacokinetic or degradation assays performed

claim_text: Specific amino acids at positions 19 (W19F), 21 (Q21S), 22 (A22G), and 40 (P40V) are important determinants of antilisterial activity, as single amino acid substitutions at these positions reduced activity both in vitro (elevated MICs) and in vivo (reduced CFU log reductions).
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (broth microdilution), CFU enumeration from spleen homogenates (in vivo murine model)
limitations: Mechanism by which these residues contribute to activity is not investigated in this paper; inferred from structure-activity comparison only

claim_text: Class IIa bacteriocins such as DvnRV41 and its structural variants retain antilisterial activity in vivo, supporting their potential use to complement current antibiotics in the treatment of listeriosis.
direct_assay_types: CFU enumeration from spleen homogenates (in vivo murine model), spleen culture conversion
limitations: Preliminary study; no statistical significance; single inbred mouse strain (BALB/c); intravenous challenge model may not reflect natural oral infection route

claim_text: HMPI exerts antimicrobial activity through cell membrane lysis, attacking intracellular targets, and immune modulation, consistent with general AMP mechanisms.
limitations: Stated as a general property of AMPs in the Introduction; not directly demonstrated for HMPI in this study; no membrane permeabilization or intracellular assay performed.

claim_text: As a cationic AMP, HMPI is proposed to bind electrostatically to anionic bacterial membranes, interfere with phospholipid alignment, induce local membrane perturbations, and promote pore formation.
limitations: Presented in the Discussion as the prevailing model for cationic AMPs generally ('Most of them believed...'); not tested for HMPI in this paper; no membrane assay performed.

claim_text: HMPI may translocate across the microbial membrane and inhibit intracellular processes including protein and DNA synthesis.
limitations: Cited as a general AMP mechanism in the Discussion; not tested for HMPI in this paper.

claim_text: HMPI alone induces elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in C. albicans cells.
direct_assay_types: intracellular ROS detection (DCFH-DA fluorescent probe, flow-cytometric microplate reader)
limitations: Tested only in C. albicans ATCC 14053; effect observed at 2–6 h time points at 32 and 64 μM; causal link to fungal killing not established.

claim_text: Cu2+ enhances HMPI-induced ROS production in C. albicans and this elevated ROS may supplement the antifungal activity of HMPI.
direct_assay_types: intracellular ROS detection (DCFH-DA fluorescent probe)
limitations: ROS elevation is measured but its causal contribution to fungicidal activity is not proven; MIC/MFC values of HMPI are unchanged by Cu2+ addition, so ROS is framed as supplementary rather than primary; only one Candida strain tested for ROS.

claim_text: KDEL disrupts the surface membrane integrity of L. tarentolae promastigotes, causing rounding and swelling of cell bodies, release of cytoplasmic contents, and eventual cell death.
direct_assay_types: light microscopy (Giemsa staining), transmission electron microscopy
limitations: Electron microscopy and light microscopy show morphological outcomes but do not reveal the molecular mechanism of membrane disruption; study uses non-pathogenic L. tarentolae only.

claim_text: KDEL causes loss of plasma membrane integrity in L. tarentolae promastigotes, as evidenced by PI uptake (PI+/Annexin V−), consistent with late-stage apoptosis or necrosis.
direct_assay_types: Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry
limitations: PI+/Annexin V− pattern is interpreted as late-stage apoptosis or necrosis but cannot distinguish between the two; dose-dependent effect observed only at 50 and 100 μg/ml vs 25 μg/ml.

claim_text: KDEL induces early-stage apoptosis in L. tarentolae promastigotes, as indicated by phosphatidylserine externalization (Annexin V+/PI−) without loss of membrane permeability.
direct_assay_types: Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry
limitations: Annexin V binding requires Ca2+ and can be artifactual in organisms with divergent membrane biology; apoptosis pathway machinery in Leishmania differs from mammalian cells.

claim_text: KDEL induces depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane potential in L. tarentolae promastigotes, indicating initiation of programmed cell death.
direct_assay_types: JC-1 mitochondrial membrane potential assay, flow cytometry
limitations: JC-1 assay reports membrane potential loss but does not identify downstream effectors; whether this is upstream or downstream of membrane disruption is not established.

claim_text: KDEL-mediated killing involves osmotic instability, vacuolar swelling, and loss of cytosolic contents following membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy
limitations: These are morphological observations interpreted as consequences of membrane disruption; the sequence of events and causal relationships are inferred, not directly tested.

claim_text: Amastigotes are more susceptible to KDEL than promastigotes because the surface metalloprotease gp63 (Ldgp63), which protects against AMP-induced apoptosis, is significantly downregulated in amastigotes.
limitations: The gp63 explanation is cited from prior literature (refs 26, 27) and not experimentally tested in this study; no gp63 expression measurement or knockout experiment was performed here.

claim_text: KDEL acts through at least two mechanisms—apoptotic and non-apoptotic—consistent with known AMP-mediated antimicrobial effects.
limitations: The two-mechanism framework is attributed to a cited reference (ref 28) and is not independently validated for KDEL; the paper's own data primarily demonstrate membrane disruption and apoptotic markers.

claim_text: Cyclotides exert cytotoxic activity by disrupting the lipid bilayer of cell membranes, with membrane permeabilization and disintegration underpinning cyclotide cytotoxicity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH release assay), membrane binding (surface plasmon resonance), live-cell imaging (SYTOX Green influx), flow cytometry
limitations: No cancer-versus-normal cell selectivity was observed, suggesting the mechanism is not tumor-selective; correlation between membrane binding and cytotoxicity does not formally exclude secondary intracellular mechanisms.

claim_text: Hyen D, E, L, M, and cycloviolacin O2 preferentially interact with model lipid membranes containing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) headgroups, with P/Lmax increasing linearly with POPE composition.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) with POPC/POPE model lipid bilayers
limitations: Tested on model membranes, not native cell membranes; hyen C did not bind any tested membrane composition and is an exception to the PE-preference rule.

claim_text: Cyclotides (hyen D, E, L, M, cyO2, and kB1) compromise cell membrane integrity within 2 hours, as evidenced by cytosolic LDH release into the medium.
direct_assay_types: lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assay
limitations: LDH assay measures cumulative leakage over 2 h and does not resolve whether membrane disruption is the primary event or secondary to intracellular damage; LC50 values from LDH were consistent with cytotoxicity assay results.

claim_text: Hyen D induces rapid plasma membrane blebbing followed by membrane rupture and necrotic cell death in HeLa cells.
direct_assay_types: live-cell time-lapse microscopy, SYTOX Green membrane-impermeant nuclear dye
limitations: Demonstrated only in HeLa cells at 1–2 μM; a prior study found cyO2 did not disrupt HeLa membranes at 1 μM using a calcein assay, and the authors attribute the discrepancy to different evaluation methods.

claim_text: The cytotoxic potency of cyclotides from H. enneaspermus correlates with their membrane-binding affinity (P/Lmax in SPR), suggesting the cytotoxicity mechanism is mediated by lipid membrane binding.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR), cytotoxicity assay (CC50)
limitations: Correlation does not establish causation; hyen E displays the lowest P/Lmax yet has the slowest dissociation rate, indicating P/Lmax alone does not fully explain potency differences.

claim_text: The bioactive patch of cyclotides (formed by Glu-6/7 and adjacent residues) mediates specific recognition of phosphatidylethanolamine headgroups on the membrane.
limitations: Directly demonstrated only for the Möbius cyclotide kB1 via prior mutagenesis studies (cited); applied to bracelet hyen cyclotides by structural analogy and homology modeling, not by direct mutagenesis in this study.

claim_text: The hydrophobic patch on the cyclotide surface is responsible for membrane insertion and is essential for cytotoxic activity.
limitations: Not directly tested by mutagenesis in this study; inferred from prior kB1 mutagenesis studies and from the observed lack of cytotoxicity in hyen C, which has a smaller hydrophobic patch.

claim_text: Positively charged residues, particularly two in loop 5 and one in loop 6 of bracelet cyclotides, facilitate peptide–membrane interactions and contribute to cytotoxic potency.
limitations: Not directly tested by mutagenesis in this study; inferred from sequence–activity comparisons across cyclotides with different net charges and from prior literature; net charge is one of several contributing factors.

claim_text: The amphiphilic nature of cyclotides (combination of a hydrophobic patch and positively charged residues) modulates their membrane-binding properties, underpinning cytotoxic potency.
limitations: Amphiphilicity is inferred from structural homology models and electrostatic surface calculations, not directly measured; the relative contribution of the hydrophobic versus electrostatic components was not quantitatively dissected.

claim_text: Anionic phospholipids (POPS) facilitate cyclotide binding to membranes, potentially through electrostatic attraction, as shown by a slight increase in P/Lmax and decrease in KD for cyO2, hyen D, and hyen L on POPC/POPE/POPS membranes.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) with POPC/POPE/POPS (60:20:20) model membranes
limitations: The enhancement effect was described as slight; the electrostatic mechanism is proposed but not directly proved; tested for only three cyclotides.

claim_text: At cytotoxic concentrations (0.5–1 μM), hyen D primarily binds to and compromises cell membranes, while at a sublethal concentration (0.25 μM), most hyen D is internalized into cells through endosomes.
direct_assay_types: flow cytometry with Trypan Blue quenching, confocal microscopy with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled peptide
limitations: Endosomal localization inferred from punctate fluorescence distribution in confocal images, not confirmed by co-localization with endosomal markers; whether internalized hyen D exerts additional intracellular activity is unknown.

claim_text: Hyen C lacks membrane-binding ability and cytotoxic activity because having Gln-6 (instead of Gly-6 as in kB1) disrupts PE-headgroup interaction, and its hydrophobic patch contains two fewer residues than kB1.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR)
limitations: The structural explanation is predicted from homology modeling and analogy to kB1 mutagenesis data ([G6A]kB1 loses PE binding); no mutagenesis of hyen C itself was performed; SPR confirmed absence of binding but did not resolve the molecular basis.

claim_text: Bracelet cyclotide cyO2 inserts into lipid bilayers using loops 2 and 3, whereas the Möbius cyclotide kB1 uses loops 5 and 6 for membrane insertion.
limitations: Based entirely on prior published studies (cited reference 24); not re-tested in this paper; applied here to rationalize the sequence differences between bracelet hyen cyclotides and kB1.

claim_text: Methylation of Glu and acetylation of Lys (loop 5) and Arg (loop 6) in the bracelet cyclotide cyO2 causes significant loss of cytotoxic, anthelmintic, and antibacterial activity, indicating that these bioactive-patch residues are critical for membrane-mediated activity.
limitations: Data originate from prior published studies (cited references 67–69), not generated in this paper; cited to support the importance of the bioactive patch in bracelet cyclotides by analogy to hyen D.

claim_text: KR-12-a5 adopts an α-helical conformation when in a membrane-mimicking (LPC) environment, and its higher antimicrobial activity relative to hBD-3–1CV (which shows a more disordered structure in LPC) suggests that α-helical secondary structure is required for potent antimicrobial activity.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: Relationship between helicity and MIC/MBC is correlational across only three peptides; no direct membrane disruption assay was performed; CD was measured in LPC solution, not actual bacterial membranes.

claim_text: The net positive charge of KR-12-a5 attracts it electrostatically to the anionic bacterial cell surface (which contains acidic phospholipids, LPS, teichoic acids, and lipoteichoic acids), while sparing mammalian cells whose membranes are composed of zwitterionic phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin.
limitations: Inferred from known membrane biochemistry (citing Matsuzaki 2009) and supported circumstantially by differential cytotoxicity data (MTT vs. MIC); no direct membrane-binding or surface-charge interaction assay was performed in this study.

claim_text: The amphipathic α-helical structure of KR-12-a5, combined with its net positive charge, enables penetration through microbial membranes as the basis for its antimicrobial mechanism.
limitations: Mechanism attributed by citing Brogden 2005 and supported indirectly by CD data showing α-helix in LPC; no membrane permeabilization or pore-formation assay was performed in this study.

claim_text: KR-12-a5 has high LPS-binding and neutralizing activity, which enhances its ability to control Gram-negative bacterial infection.
limitations: Cited entirely from Jacob et al. 2013; the LPS-binding assay was not performed in the present study.

claim_text: KR-12-a5 causes membrane compromise (loss of membrane integrity) in E. faecalis and S. mutans within dentin biofilms, as evidenced by propidium iodide uptake in LIVE/DEAD staining, with efficacy increasing with concentration.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LIVE/DEAD BacLight CLSM with propidium iodide)
limitations: Propidium iodide uptake indicates membrane permeability loss but cannot distinguish primary membrane disruption from secondary membrane degradation following killing by another intracellular mechanism; assay performed on preformed 7-day biofilms in dentin, limiting generalizability to planktonic conditions.

claim_text: A delicate balance between net positive charge and hydrophobicity in KR-12-a5 (net charge +5, 42% positive residues, highest hydrophobic angle among KR-12 analogs) underlies its optimal antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Inferred from correlation of RP-HPLC retention time and net charge parameters with MIC/MBC outcomes; no experiments directly manipulating charge or hydrophobicity were performed in this study; citing Jacob et al. 2013 and Rosenfeld et al. 2010 for the mechanistic rationale.

claim_text: The esculentin-2 HYba peptides adopt an amphipathic alpha-helical conformation with segregation of hydrophobic and polar residues to opposite faces of the helix, a structural feature invoked to predict their antimicrobial functional roles.
limitations: Secondary structure determined solely by computational prediction (PSIPRED, JPred4) and helical wheel projection; no experimental structure determination (e.g., CD, NMR) or direct membrane-interaction assay (e.g., lipid vesicle leakage, membrane depolarization) is reported; the inference that amphipathic helix drives mechanism is implicit, not argued in the text.

claim_text: The C-terminally amidated analogs (E2/1-NH2, E2/2-NH2) achieve complete bacterial killing at their MIC within 10–15 minutes, indicating rapid bactericidal activity that is consistent with a membrane-disruptive mechanism.
direct_assay_types: killing kinetics (time-kill assay at MIC and sub-MIC against S. aureus MTCC 9542 and V. cholerae MCV09)
limitations: Speed-of-kill data characterise the rate of activity but do not identify the molecular target; no permeabilization, ion-channel, or intracellular-target assay is included; the mechanistic interpretation (membrane disruption) is not stated in the paper—it is a common inference from rapid kill kinetics in AMP literature.

claim_text: Compound 8 engages BamA (outer membrane beta-barrel assembly protein) as a target, evidenced by the selective emergence of a bamA D703Y resistance mutation in K. pneumoniae during serial passage with compound 8 but not during parallel passages with colistin.
limitations: Evidence is genetic (whole-genome sequencing of resistant mutants); direct physical binding to BamA is not demonstrated in the provided text; other co-occurring mutations (phoQ, arnC, envZ, rne, yiaV, wbgU, pqiB) in the same resistant lineages may also contribute to the resistance phenotype.

claim_text: BamA is functionally required for compound 8 antibacterial activity: complementation of compound 8-resistant K. pneumoniae passage mutants (passages 8, 13, 16) with wild-type bamA significantly restores susceptibility to compound 8 (χ² p<0.01, V≥0.94), whereas introduction of the resistant bamA D703Y allele does not.
limitations: Genetic complementation supports BamA involvement but does not prove direct ligand–protein binding; MICs of colistin and meropenem were unaffected by bamA complementation, providing specificity controls; the passage 8 bamA-complementation result did not reach statistical significance (p>0.01), indicating the relationship is clearest at later, higher-resistance passages.

claim_text: Lipid A modification via the PhoP/Q regulatory pathway (phoQ mutations) and ArnC-mediated 4-amino-arabinose addition to lipid A (arnC mutations) contributes to acquired resistance to compound 8, implicating LPS/lipid A as a component of the compound's interaction with the outer membrane.
limitations: phoQ mutations also arise in colistin-selected K. pneumoniae passages, so this pathway is not unique to compound 8; phoQ/arnC mutations reduce susceptibility to both polymyxins and compound 8, which may reflect the colistin-ring (LPS-binding) chimeric component rather than a distinct MOA; no direct LPS-binding measurements are shown for compound 8 in this text.

claim_text: The chimeric peptides 3 and 4 permeabilize the outer and inner membranes of E. coli, as assessed by membrane-impermeant SYTOX-Green fluorescence dye uptake, release of periplasmic β-lactamase (detected with CENTA substrate), and release of cytoplasmic β-galactosidase (detected with ONPG substrate).
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX-Green fluorescence), outer-membrane disruption (periplasmic β-lactamase/CENTA release assay), inner-membrane disruption (cytoplasmic β-galactosidase/ONPG release assay)
limitations: Quantitative results are presented in Extended Data Figure 3, not reproduced in the provided text; both a PMB-susceptible strain (E. coli ATCC 25922) and a PMB/colistin-resistant strain (E. coli 926415) were included, but the outcome for the resistant strain cannot be assessed from the text excerpt; degree of permeabilization relative to polymyxin B1 comparator is not stated in the text.

claim_text: Compounds 3 and 4 inhibit macromolecular biosynthesis in E. coli, with the profile across DNA, protein, RNA, and cell wall synthesis measured by radiolabeled precursor incorporation to identify the primary biosynthetic target.
direct_assay_types: macromolecular synthesis inhibition ([³H]-thymidine for DNA, L-[³H]-leucine for protein, [³H]-uridine for RNA, N-[³H]-acetyl-glucosamine for cell wall peptidoglycan)
limitations: Quantitative results are in Extended Data Figure 2, not provided in the text; the identity of the predominantly inhibited pathway and whether inhibition is primary (direct) or secondary (consequent to outer-membrane disruption) cannot be determined from the text excerpt alone.

claim_text: Antibacterial activity of chimeric compounds 3 and 4 against E. coli ATCC 25922 is modulated by extracellular Mg²⁺ concentration (2 mM versus 20 µM in BM2 minimal medium), paralleling the Mg²⁺-dependent activity of polymyxin B2, consistent with an LPS-binding mechanism that is sensitive to Mg²⁺-induced lipid A remodeling.
limitations: MIC values at different Mg²⁺ concentrations are tabulated in Table S2e but numerical data are not reproduced in the text excerpt; the mechanistic interpretation (Mg²⁺ induces LPS modification that reduces polymyxin-class binding) is inferred by analogy to the established polymyxin mechanism rather than demonstrated directly for the chimeras.

claim_text: Temporin-GHa–GHd severely disrupt the cell wall and cell membrane of E. coli and S. aureus, leading to final cell lysis, as evidenced by rough, crimpled, and collapsed bacterial morphology observed by scanning electron microscopy after 1 h treatment at 10× MIC.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: SEM reveals morphological damage but does not measure membrane permeabilization, ion leakage, or membrane depolarization at the molecular level; only two bacterial species tested; high peptide concentration (10× MIC) used; no time-course to establish sequence of events.

claim_text: The mechanism of temporin-GHa–GHd against bacteria may involve disruption of the cell wall and cell membrane.
limitations: Authors explicitly use 'may involve' language; inference based solely on SEM morphological data with no mechanistic assays (membrane permeabilization, fluorescent dye leakage, depolarization); SEM cannot distinguish primary target from secondary collapse.

claim_text: Antimicrobial activity of temporin-GHa–GHd is mediated at least partly through electrostatic interactions with the bacterial membrane, as activity is reduced approximately 18% by physiological NaCl (0.15 M) and does not decrease further up to 2 M NaCl.
limitations: Salt effect is modest (~18% reduction); NaCl could alter peptide conformation rather than specifically disrupting electrostatic binding; no direct binding assay performed; activity is never abolished, leaving open alternative mechanisms.

claim_text: Temporin family AMPs react directly with bacterial cell membranes, making it difficult for microorganisms to develop resistance.
limitations: Applied to temporin-GHa–GHd by family association citing external reference [25]; not directly demonstrated for these specific peptides; no resistance-evolution experiments performed in this study.

claim_text: AMPs (as a class, including the peptides studied) attach to anionic bacterial cell walls via electrostatic interaction and insert into phospholipid membranes to disrupt and lyse microorganisms.
limitations: General class mechanism cited from literature (ref [9]); not directly demonstrated experimentally for these specific temporin-GH peptides; applied as contextual background, not a primary finding of this study.

claim_text: AMPs may also exert antimicrobial action by interfering with intracellular processes including DNA duplication, protein translation and folding, cell wall synthesis, and metabolic turnover.
limitations: Cited from general AMP literature (ref [10]) as alternative mechanism class; not tested or assayed for any of the peptides in this study.

claim_text: An α-helical secondary structure is not required for the antimicrobial activity of temporin-GHb, which is predicted to contain zero α-helix content yet retains potent broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity comparable to or stronger than the α-helix-containing temporins.
limitations: Secondary structure is computationally predicted (HNN method), not experimentally determined by CD spectroscopy or NMR; authors acknowledge it is unclear whether the lack of α-helix or the two specific amino acid substitutions (Leu2→Ile, Gln3→His) drives the activity difference; prediction may not reflect structure in membrane-mimetic or bacterial environments.

claim_text: Mycosubtilin induces complete disruption of the transmembrane electrical potential (ΔΨ) in Candida albicans, as demonstrated by significant fluorescence signal release from DiSC3(5)-loaded cells upon addition of 10 µM mycosubtilin, with no additional signal upon subsequent valinomycin addition.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential disruption (DiSC3(5) fluorescence assay)
limitations: Single reference strain tested (C. albicans ATCC 10231); single concentration used (10 µM); mechanism inferred from potential collapse, not directly visualized at molecular level

claim_text: Mycosubtilin causes formation of transmembrane pores in C. albicans, as suggested by extensive cell leakage of UV-absorbing molecules (proteins and nucleic acids).
direct_assay_types: cell leakage assay (UV-absorbing molecule release)
limitations: Pore formation is inferred from leakage data, not directly demonstrated; single strain tested

claim_text: For iturin A, a closely related iturinic lipopeptide to mycosubtilin, a membrane pore-forming mode of action has been suggested for Saccharomyces cerevisiae spheroplasts, and mycosubtilin is assumed to share this mechanism.
limitations: This claim is based on a cited study of iturin A, not mycosubtilin itself; extrapolation across related lipopeptides is stated by analogy only

claim_text: The moderate effectiveness of anteiso-C17 mycosubtilin against sterol-auxotrophic C. glabrata isolates may be explained by free ergosterol in the culture medium acting as a strong iturin antagonist.
limitations: Proposed as an explanation based on known ergosterol-iturin antagonism from literature; not directly tested in this study

claim_text: Antifungal activity of mycosubtilin increases with the number of carbon atoms in the acyl chain, making the C17 homologue more active than shorter-chain isoforms.
limitations: Attributed to a cited PhD thesis (Hhid 1996); not experimentally demonstrated in this paper for the anteiso-C17 isoform specifically

claim_text: Microcin 7 inhibits protein biosynthesis in susceptible E. coli, as measured by reduced incorporation of labeled leucine into TCA-precipitable macromolecules.
direct_assay_types: radiolabeled leucine incorporation (TCA precipitation), pulse-labeling incorporation rate
limitations: Assay performed at MIC in one susceptible strain (E. coli GS7T1); bacteriostatic concentration only; short-term lag before inhibition observed

claim_text: Microcin 7 does not inhibit DNA synthesis, as incorporation of radiolabeled thymine into TCA-precipitable material was unaffected at the MIC.
direct_assay_types: radiolabeled thymine incorporation (TCA precipitation)
limitations: Single strain and concentration tested; assay tracks bulk DNA synthesis, not replication fidelity

claim_text: Microcin 7 does not inhibit RNA synthesis, as incorporation of radiolabeled uridine into TCA-precipitable material and the pulse-labeled uridine incorporation rate were unaffected.
direct_assay_types: radiolabeled uridine incorporation (TCA precipitation), pulse-labeling incorporation rate
limitations: Single strain and concentration; does not distinguish rRNA, mRNA, or tRNA pools

claim_text: Microcin 7 apparently stimulates cell wall synthesis, as incorporation of radiolabeled diaminopimelic acid into SDS-insoluble material increased in treated cells.
direct_assay_types: radiolabeled diaminopimelic acid incorporation (SDS-insoluble fraction)
limitations: Authors note this is 'apparent' stimulation; attributed to indirect secondary effect of protein synthesis inhibition in a relA strain rather than a primary action on cell wall machinery

claim_text: The stimulation of cell wall synthesis by microcin 7 is a secondary consequence of protein synthesis inhibition acting through stringent control in relA strains, not a direct effect on cell wall biosynthesis.
limitations: Inference based on published literature on relA phenotype; not directly tested in this paper; relA status of GS7T1 not explicitly confirmed

claim_text: Microcin 7 does not block leucine transport into the cell, as treated cells transported radiolabeled leucine at the same rate as controls and retained comparable intracellular leucine levels.
direct_assay_types: radiolabeled leucine transport assay (filter-capture)
limitations: Assay performed at twice the MIC concentration used in incorporation experiments; transport tested after 20 min pre-incubation, not kinetically from time zero

claim_text: Microcin 7 likely acts at an intracellular target, as a lag period before protein synthesis inhibition is observed that shortens when cell density is lowered or peptide concentration is raised, consistent with time needed to accumulate sufficient intracellular peptide.
limitations: Intracellular accumulation was not directly measured; the lag could alternatively reflect a multistep extracellular or membrane-associated process

claim_text: Unlike most peptide antibiotics and colicins, microcin 7 does not disrupt the cell membrane permeability barrier, because it selectively inhibits only protein synthesis while leaving DNA, RNA, and cell wall biosynthesis intact.
limitations: No direct membrane permeability assay (e.g., dye leakage, membrane potential) was performed; selectivity of inhibition is used as a proxy; membrane disruption at higher concentrations was not tested

claim_text: Microcin 7 is bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal at its MIC, as treated cells retained viability for at least 8 hours in the presence of the peptide.
direct_assay_types: colony-forming unit viability assay
limitations: Only tested at one concentration (MIC) and up to 8 h; higher concentrations or longer exposures not reported

claim_text: hBD-2 demonstrates broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, with MICs of 62 µg/ml for E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and S. aureus, and 15 µg/ml for E. faecalis.
direct_assay_types: broth microdilution MIC assay, agarose diffusion assay
limitations: Tested only under low-salt, half-strength Mueller-Hinton broth conditions; recombinant baculovirus-derived peptide used, not native purified form

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of hBD-2 against E. coli is salt-sensitive, diminishing eightfold when NaCl concentration is increased from 20 mM to 150 mM.
direct_assay_types: broth microdilution assay with titrated NaCl concentrations
limitations: Tested only against E. coli D31; salt sensitivity of activity against other organisms not directly measured

claim_text: hBD-2 acts synergistically with lysozyme against E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and E. faecalis, with MICs decreased two- to fourfold in the presence of non-bacteriostatic concentrations of lysozyme.
direct_assay_types: broth microdilution MIC assay with combinatorial peptide/protein treatment
limitations: Mechanism of synergy not characterized; non-bacteriostatic concentrations of lysozyme used, so the contribution of lysozyme alone is excluded but the interaction mechanism is unexplained

claim_text: hBD-2 acts synergistically with lactoferrin against E. coli and S. aureus, with MICs decreased two- to fourfold in the presence of non-bacteriostatic concentrations of lactoferrin.
direct_assay_types: broth microdilution MIC assay with combinatorial peptide/protein treatment
limitations: Mechanism of synergy not characterized; non-bacteriostatic concentrations of lactoferrin used

claim_text: hBD-2 may be inactivated in the high-salt environment of cystic fibrosis airway surface fluid, analogous to hBD-1, potentially contributing to impaired innate immunity in CF.
limitations: Described as speculative by the authors; CF-specific salt elevation is itself disputed; no direct measurement of hBD-2 activity in CF airway surface fluid was performed

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides, including hLF1-11, are thought to have a diminished tendency to induce resistance because of the evolutionary difficulty bacteria face in altering their membrane structure.
limitations: Claim is made for the class of antimicrobial peptides generally and attributed to cited references (Hancock 1997); not directly tested for hLF1-11 in this study.

claim_text: At very low systemic dosages, hLF1-11 reduces bacterial load primarily through an immune-inciting (immunomodulatory) effect rather than direct killing.
limitations: This mechanism was presumed by Nibbering et al. (2001) in a mouse thigh infection model and is cited here; not directly demonstrated in the current rabbit osteomyelitis study. The paper uses 'presumed' language.

claim_text: At higher local concentrations, hLF1-11 exerts a direct bacterial killing effect, which is presumed to account for its efficacy in the prophylactic rabbit osteomyelitis model.
limitations: Presumed based on the authors' own prior prophylactic study (Stallmann et al. 2004, ref 21); the direct killing mechanism is not assayed in the current therapeutic study. The paper uses 'presumed' language.

claim_text: In the current therapeutic model, both direct bacterial killing (at high local concentrations in the tibia) and immune-inciting activity (from low systemic concentrations via the bone-serum gradient) may have acted simultaneously to reduce MRSA burden.
limitations: Explicitly speculative; authors state 'more pharmacokinetic studies are required to elucidate the mechanism of action in this model.' No pharmacokinetic or immunological assays were performed in this study to test either mechanism.

claim_text: The antibacterial action of AmBRI-44a is associated with inhibition of bacterial cell wall biosynthesis, as indicated by genetic and phenotypic analysis of selected AmBRI-44a-resistant Bacillus licheniformis B-511.
limitations: No direct biochemical assay of cell wall biosynthesis (e.g., lipid II binding, radiolabeled precursor incorporation) was performed; the conclusion is inferred from resistance-selection genetics (WalK R217S mutation) and cross-resistance profiling, not a direct mechanistic experiment.

claim_text: AmBRI-44a does not act primarily through disruption of the cytoplasmic membrane, as evidenced by the successful selection of stably resistant bacterial strains—an outcome not possible for membrane-disrupting AMPs.
limitations: Membrane non-disruption is inferred from the resistance-selection outcome and narrow spectrum; no direct membrane permeabilization assay (e.g., SYTOX Green uptake, liposome leakage) was performed to formally exclude a membrane component.

claim_text: A mutation (R217S) in the HAMP domain of the WalK histidine kinase—a regulator of cell wall biosynthesis in Gram-positive bacteria—confers stable resistance to AmBRI-44a, implying AmBRI-44a targets a process controlled by the WalK/WalR two-component system.
limitations: The R217S mutation was identified by whole-genome sequencing of the resistant strain; causal sufficiency was not verified by allelic exchange or complementation. A second mutation (V375A in TgpA) was also found but considered unlikely to be the key driver.

claim_text: AmBRI-44a likely targets a cell-surface component of the cell wall (e.g., lipid II or a related structural element) rather than the intracellular domain of WalK directly, because the peptide's mass (>5 kDa) would prevent membrane penetration to reach the cytoplasmic HAMP domain.
limitations: This is explicitly presented as the authors' preferred hypothesis; no direct binding or docking experiments to lipid II or other cell-wall components were conducted in this study.

claim_text: Cross-resistance of the AmBRI-44a-resistant B. licheniformis strain specifically to vancomycin and nisin—but not to membrane-disrupting AMPs (LL-37, tachyplesin-1) or other antibiotics—supports a mechanism involving binding to lipid II or inhibition of a shared cell-wall biosynthesis step.
limitations: Cross-resistance pattern is consistent with shared pathway perturbation but does not prove a shared molecular target; the WalK mutation affects a regulatory kinase upstream of lipid II synthesis, so the cross-resistance could reflect a regulatory adaptation rather than target overlap.

claim_text: The activity of AmBRI-44a against Candida albicans at relatively high MIC (16 µM) likely reflects a nonspecific effect on eukaryotic membranes rather than a specific mechanism.
limitations: Attributed by analogy to observations with other defensin-like peptides of animal origin; no membrane permeabilization or target-identification experiments were performed for the antifungal activity.

claim_text: Enterocins MR10A and MR10B exhibit synergistic antibacterial activity when combined, as demonstrated by increased inhibitory activity in fractions containing both peptides compared to individual fractions.
limitations: Data not shown; synergy inferred from rising AU across purification steps concentrating both peptides together, not from a controlled head-to-head assay of individual vs. combined peptides; no mechanistic basis for synergy determined.

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of enterocin MR10 is mediated by a peptide mechanism rather than a hydrogen-peroxide or small-molecule mechanism, as activity is completely abolished by trypsin and Streptomyces griseus/Aspergillus oryzae proteases but is unaffected by catalase.
direct_assay_types: protease sensitivity assay, catalase sensitivity assay
limitations: Confirms peptide nature and rules out H2O2 as the active agent, but does not identify the downstream cellular target or killing mechanism.

claim_text: MR10A and MR10B are cationic (predicted pI ~10) and highly hydrophobic peptides, properties consistent with membrane-targeting activity typical of class II LAB bacteriocins.
limitations: Inferred solely from deduced amino acid composition and sequence similarity to enterocins L50A/B; no membrane permeabilization, ion-channel, or cytoplasmic membrane potential assay was performed.

claim_text: By analogy to their closest relatives, enterocins L50A and L50B, MR10A and MR10B are proposed to act as two hydrophobic/cationic peptides that function synergistically against target cells.
limitations: Mechanistic attribution derived entirely from sequence homology to L50A/B; no independent MOA experiments conducted on MR10A/B; the analogy is weakened by the fact that MR10A/B differ from L50A/B in host species, genomic location, and activity spectrum (including partial Gram-negative activity).

claim_text: Thrombin-derived C-terminal peptides (GKY25 and related variants) exert bactericidal effects against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria mediated by membrane lysis.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (FITC impermeant probe fluorescence microscopy), scanning electron microscopy, liposome leakage (carboxyfluorescein release)
limitations: Membrane lysis stated as established in prior work; this paper provides corroborating direct assay data for GKY20/GKY25 specifically.

claim_text: GKY25 and GKY20 permeabilize E. coli bacterial membranes, as demonstrated by intracellular uptake of the normally impermeant probe FITC.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (FITC impermeant probe fluorescence microscopy)
limitations: Single bacterial strain (E. coli ATCC 25922); single peptide concentration (30 µM); assay visualizes permeabilization but does not distinguish primary pore-formation from secondary membrane collapse.

claim_text: GKY20 causes local perturbations and breaks in P. aeruginosa and S. aureus plasma membranes with extrusion of intracellular material into the extracellular space.
direct_assay_types: scanning electron microscopy
limitations: Morphological endpoint only; does not resolve kinetics or whether membrane disruption is the primary lethal event versus a secondary consequence.

claim_text: GKY25 and GKY20 disrupt anionic (DOPE/DOPG) liposome membranes, inducing leakage of encapsulated carboxyfluorescein, indicating direct membrane-disruptive activity.
direct_assay_types: liposome leakage (carboxyfluorescein release fluorimetry)
limitations: Synthetic lipid model membranes; lipid composition (DOPE/DOPG 75:25) approximates bacterial but not mammalian membranes; does not recapitulate full membrane complexity.

claim_text: LPS induces a conformational change toward α-helical structure in GKY25, GKY20, and VFR12, suggesting that helical folding upon LPS contact is part of the antimicrobial and LPS-binding mechanism.
direct_assay_types: CD spectroscopy
limitations: CD reports average secondary structure; helical induction by LPS does not establish that helicity is required for activity, only correlated with it.

claim_text: Anionic liposomes induce significant helical conformation in GKY25 but not in GKY20 or VFR12, yet GKY25 and GKY20 show comparable membrane-disruptive activity, indicating that stable helix formation in lipid environments is not strictly required for membrane disruption.
direct_assay_types: CD spectroscopy, liposome leakage (carboxyfluorescein release fluorimetry)
limitations: Dissociation between helical content and leakage activity suggests helix induction may be a correlate rather than a prerequisite; mechanism bridging conformation and disruption is not directly resolved.

claim_text: The lower membrane-disruptive potency of the shorter VFR12 relative to GKY25 and GKY20 likely reflects a higher entropic penalty for membrane insertion of the shorter peptide.
direct_assay_types: liposome leakage (carboxyfluorescein release fluorimetry)
limitations: Entropy penalty is not directly measured; interpretation is by analogy to published data on cardin consensus peptides; other explanations (reduced amphipathicity, charge) are not excluded.

claim_text: Thrombin-derived peptides inhibit LPS-induced nitric oxide production in RAW 264.7 macrophages, indicating suppression of LPS-driven innate immune signaling.
direct_assay_types: macrophage nitric oxide production (Griess reaction)
limitations: Cell-line model (RAW 264.7); NO is a downstream reporter; mechanism of upstream signaling inhibition is not directly characterized in this paper.

claim_text: Thrombin-derived peptides inhibit lipoteichoic acid (LTA)-induced nitric oxide production in RAW 264.7 macrophages, demonstrating activity against Gram-positive cell-wall pattern recognition signaling.
direct_assay_types: macrophage nitric oxide production (Griess reaction)
limitations: Same cell-line limitation; mechanism not resolved beyond downstream NO suppression.

claim_text: Thrombin-derived peptides inhibit zymosan-induced nitric oxide production in RAW 264.7 macrophages, indicating immunomodulatory activity extending to fungal pattern recognition (dectin-1/TLR2 pathways).
direct_assay_types: macrophage nitric oxide production (Griess reaction)
limitations: Pathway not directly verified; zymosan activates multiple receptors and the specific receptor target of peptide action is unresolved.

claim_text: The anti-inflammatory mechanism of GKY20 may involve direct binding to and neutralization of LPS, thereby blocking downstream TLR signaling.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('may involve'); the finding that VFR12 binds LPS and adopts helical conformation in LPS yet lacks anti-inflammatory activity in the macrophage model indicates LPS binding alone is insufficient; mechanism remains unresolved.

claim_text: Additional mechanisms beyond direct LPS binding contribute to the anti-endotoxin effects of GKY20/GKY25, possibly including interactions with host-cell receptors such as CD14, TLRs, or intracellular receptors.
limitations: No direct receptor-binding or receptor-blocking assay performed; proposed by exclusion (LPS-binding peptide VFR12 lacks anti-inflammatory activity, so LPS binding alone is insufficient); all candidate receptors are speculative.

claim_text: GKY20 reduces systemic proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IFN-γ, TNF-α, MCP-1) and increases anti-inflammatory IL-10 in a murine LPS-shock model, indicating modulation of the host cytokine network as part of its protective mechanism.
direct_assay_types: plasma cytokine measurement (cytometric bead array)
limitations: Mouse model only; cytokine changes are downstream readouts and do not establish the molecular mechanism by which GKY20 alters cytokine production; peptide given 30 min post-LPS.

claim_text: A minimum peptide length of approximately 19–20 amino acids is required for full anti-inflammatory (anti-endotoxin) activity, whereas shorter variants retain antimicrobial but not immunomodulatory function, implying that the two activities depend on distinct structural determinants.
direct_assay_types: macrophage nitric oxide production (Griess reaction), MIC assay, radial diffusion assay
limitations: Length cutoff is functional, not mechanistic; the structural basis for the length requirement (e.g., additional contacts with host receptors vs. higher-order LPS aggregate disruption) is not determined.

claim_text: The two central lysine residues (K14 and adjacent K) flanking the evolutionarily conserved WI sequence are particularly important for antimicrobial activity, likely by providing cationic charge for initial electrostatic interaction with anionic bacterial membranes.
direct_assay_types: radial diffusion assay (K→S substitution series)
limitations: Electrostatic mechanism is inferred from the well-established paradigm for AMPs, not directly demonstrated here; K-to-S substitution simultaneously removes charge and alters structure/amphipathicity, confounding mechanistic interpretation.

claim_text: The amphipathic α-helical conformation of antimicrobial peptides may promote interaction with the bacterial membrane.
limitations: Inferred by analogy with other amphipathic helical proteins and antimicrobial peptides described in the literature; no direct membrane interaction assay performed in this paper.

claim_text: Both the α-helical and amphipathic structural motifs are required for antibacterial activity of C13, as amino acid substitutions designed to disrupt either feature abolished activity.
direct_assay_types: serum bactericidal assay with structural analogues (C13A disrupting α-helicity via proline substitutions; C13B disrupting amphipathicity via charge/hydrophobic residue exchange)
limitations: Activity was assessed only in NHS plus sub-MIC cefepime conditions; not tested in broth-based or heat-inactivated serum systems. Edmundson wheel projections were used to predict structural disruption but secondary structure was not directly confirmed by biophysical methods.

claim_text: β-Lactam antibiotic-altered bacteria may be more susceptible to antimicrobial peptides because, analogous to complement, the peptides require access to the bacterial inner membrane for bactericidal activity, and β-lactam modification of the outer membrane facilitates such access.
limitations: Explicitly framed as a hypothesis ('suggested that β-lactam-altered bacteria might be more susceptible to other agents, which in a mechanism similar to complement, need to gain access to the bacterial inner membrane'); no direct assay of inner-membrane access or permeabilization reported in this paper.

claim_text: The late components of the complement pathway (C8-dependent terminal complement complex) are essential for optimal antibacterial activity of peptide C18G in human serum.
direct_assay_types: serum bactericidal assay in C8-depleted sera vs. C8-replenished sera; heat-inactivated serum controls
limitations: Assay measures bacterial killing as endpoint, not a direct mechanistic readout of complement activation or pore formation; the molecular basis of complement potentiation of peptide activity remains stated as unclear.

claim_text: Peptide C18G promotes increased C5b-9 (terminal complement complex) deposition on bacteria.
direct_assay_types: C5b-9 deposition assay
limitations: Described as 'initial studies' and presented without quantitative data in this paper ('data not shown'); the molecular interaction between cefepime-altered bacterial cell, peptide, and complement is stated to remain unclear.

claim_text: Peptide C18G in combination with serum complement disrupts the bacterial outer membrane, resulting in access of the peptide and/or terminal complement components to critical sites in the bacterial cell envelope.
limitations: Explicitly labeled as 'a possible hypothesis'; no direct outer-membrane disruption assay (e.g., membrane permeabilization, electron microscopy) is reported in this paper.

claim_text: β-Lactam antibiotics, which affect the bacterial outer membrane, may augment peptide C18G-plus-complement-mediated killing in some bacterial strains by facilitating outer-membrane disruption.
limitations: Inferred from strain-dependent differences in cefepime enhancement of killing and from prior published work (reference 12) showing β-lactam-dependent C5b-9 deposition; no direct assay of outer-membrane integrity presented here.

claim_text: The mechanism by which peptide C18G acts together with serum complement does not involve stereospecific enzyme recognition or chiral receptors, as the all-D amino acid analogue C18X retains equivalent antibacterial activity both in vitro and in vivo.
direct_assay_types: serum bactericidal assay and neutropenic mouse protection experiment with all-D amino acid analogue C18X
limitations: Absence of stereospecificity rules out chiral receptor/enzyme involvement but does not identify the actual mechanistic target; in vitro data for C18X cited as 'data not shown'.

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of Ib-M peptides against E. coli depends on their net charge and hydrophobicity, as Flórez et al. deliberately altered these properties in the C-terminal domain of Ib-AMP4 to generate the Ib-M analog family with improved antimicrobial activity against non-pathogenic E. coli.
limitations: No mechanistic assay is described; the claim is an inference from a rational-design statement. The dedicated MOA section (1.2.1) and the Results/Discussion sections (5–6) are absent from the provided text, so the paper's full mechanistic account is not available for extraction.

claim_text: Ib-AMP family peptides (parent class of Ib-M) are cationic and highly basic with two disulfide bridges, structural features the paper associates with their antimicrobial function.
limitations: Described as structural properties only; no assay links these features to a specific killing mechanism in the provided text. Causal connection to MOA is implicit, not stated.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides (class including Ib-M) have a low probability of inducing resistance, which the paper attributes to a property of their mechanism of action distinct from that of conventional antibiotics.
limitations: Cited to Pereira 2006 without further mechanistic elaboration in the provided text; no resistance-development assay is reported for Ib-M specifically.

claim_text: Most AMPs exert antimicrobial effects by directly targeting and rupturing pathogen cell membranes.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref [9]); no membrane-disruption assay performed in this study; not tested for cAMP_1 or cAMP_2.

claim_text: A small subset of AMPs enter the cytoplasm to disrupt cellular processes rather than acting on the membrane.
limitations: Cited from prior literature (ref [9]); not investigated experimentally for any peptide in this study.

claim_text: A higher net positive charge enhances electrostatic interactions between AMPs and the negatively charged components of microbial membranes, thereby increasing antibacterial activity.
limitations: Inferred from comparative physicochemical analysis of AMP vs. NAMP datasets (higher isoelectric points in AMPs) and prior literature (ref [25]); not directly tested for cAMP_1 or cAMP_2 via any membrane-interaction assay.

claim_text: Increasing the proportion of hydrophobic amino acids in an AMP can significantly enhance its antibacterial activity, as demonstrated by substituting lysine with isoleucine at positions 20 and 27 in PMAP-37 (K20/27-I), which inhibited bacterial growth and showed therapeutic effects in infected mice.
limitations: Based entirely on cited prior work (ref [58]) on a different peptide (PMAP-37); not tested for cAMP_1 or cAMP_2.

claim_text: AMPs adopt an unordered structure in aqueous solution but, upon entering a membrane environment, form highly stable α-helical secondary structures that interact with phospholipid molecules and facilitate passage through bacterial membranes.
limitations: Inferred from secondary-structure comparative analysis of AMP vs. NAMP datasets and prior literature; no lipid-interaction or membrane-permeability assay was performed in this study; not specifically demonstrated for cAMP_1 or cAMP_2.

claim_text: The three-dimensional conformation of AMPs is essential for their interactions with microbial membranes and intracellular targets.
limitations: Stated as a general principle in the Discussion to motivate future structure-based modelling; no structural or target-binding experiments were conducted in this study.

claim_text: Iturin A rapidly enters HepG2 cells, enabled by its amphiphilic structure (hydrophobic fatty acid chain plus hydrophilic cyclic peptide).
direct_assay_types: fluorescence microscopy with CFNSE-labeled iturin A (cellular uptake within 10 min)
limitations: CFNSE conjugation may alter iturin A physicochemical properties; internalization mechanism (passive diffusion vs. endocytosis) not determined

claim_text: Iturin A causes an intracellular reactive oxygen species burst in HepG2 cells.
direct_assay_types: DCFH-DA ROS fluorescence assay (in vitro); ROS fluorescence staining of frozen tumor sections (in vivo)
limitations: DCFH-DA is not ROS-species-specific; whether ROS burst is causally upstream or downstream of other death signals not established

claim_text: Iturin A disrupts the HepG2 cell cycle, causing G2/M phase arrest and a decrease in the S phase fraction.
direct_assay_types: PI-based flow cytometry cell cycle analysis
limitations: Molecular targets responsible for G2/M arrest (e.g., checkpoint kinases, cyclins) not identified

claim_text: Iturin A induces apoptosis in HepG2 cells, predominantly at the early apoptotic stage.
direct_assay_types: Annexin V-FITC/PI dual-staining flow cytometry
limitations: Late apoptotic and necrotic populations overlap; the apoptotic trigger upstream of phosphatidylserine externalization not directly shown in vitro

claim_text: Iturin A induces apoptosis in HepG2 xenograft tumors via the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway, involving Bax upregulation, Bcl-2 downregulation, cytochrome C release, and activation of caspase-9 and caspase-3.
direct_assay_types: immunoblot/immunohistochemistry for Bax, Bcl-2, cytochrome C; colorimetric caspase-3 and caspase-9 activity assays on tumor lysates
limitations: Measured in excised tumor tissue only (in vivo), not confirmed in vitro in HepG2 cells with equivalent assays; upstream activator of Bax/Bcl-2 axis not identified

claim_text: Iturin A induces paraptosis in HepG2 cells, characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization and swelling of mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum.
direct_assay_types: optical microscopy (vacuole detection); transmission electron microscopy (ultrastructural swelling of mitochondria and ER)
limitations: Paraptosis identified solely on morphological criteria; molecular markers (e.g., AIP1/Alix) not used; paraptosis was not observed in vivo, attributed to indirect drug–cell contact in the tumor microenvironment

claim_text: Iturin A induces autophagy in HepG2 cells and in xenograft tumors, evidenced by autophagosome formation and increased LC3-II with decreased p62.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy (autophagosome detection, in vitro); immunoblot for LC3-II and p62 (in vivo tumor tissue)
limitations: Autophagic flux (i.e., completion to autolysosome) not confirmed with flux inhibitors; whether autophagy is cytoprotective or pro-death in this context not determined

claim_text: The fatty acid chain of iturin A is essential for its anticancer activity; the peptide ring alone has no effect on HepG2 cell proliferation.
direct_assay_types: MTT cell viability assay comparing intact iturin A vs. synthetic peptide fragment (no fatty acid chain) across 5–100 µM
limitations: Synthetic peptide sequence (Asn-Tyr-Asn-Gln-Pro-Asn-Ser) lacks the D-amino acid configuration of native iturin A, potentially confounding the comparison; mechanism by which the fatty acid chain confers activity (membrane partitioning, receptor binding, etc.) not resolved

claim_text: Iturin A downregulates TGF-β1 expression in xenograft tumor tissue, suggesting inhibition of epithelial-mesenchymal transition and suppression of tumor immune escape.
direct_assay_types: fluorescence immunohistochemistry for TGF-β1 in tumor sections
limitations: The downstream immunological consequences (T cell differentiation, dendritic cell function) were not directly measured; immune escape suppression is inferred from the literature, not demonstrated functionally

claim_text: Iturin A downregulates PD-L1 expression in xenograft tumor tissue, potentially reducing T cell suppression and tumor immune escape.
direct_assay_types: fluorescence immunohistochemistry for PD-L1 in tumor sections
limitations: Reduction in PD-L1 did not reach statistical significance (p > 0.05); T cell functional activity and PD-1/PD-L1 axis disruption not directly assayed

claim_text: Iturin A promotes tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte accumulation in xenograft tumors, indicating improvement of the tumor immune microenvironment.
direct_assay_types: H&E histopathology of tumor sections
limitations: Lymphocyte subtypes (CD4+, CD8+, Treg, NK) not characterized; functional cytotoxic activity of infiltrating lymphocytes not measured

claim_text: The amphiphilic character of iturin A is speculated to be the primary mechanism enabling its anticancer activity, by facilitating membrane interaction and intracellular entry.
limitations: Proposed by authors based on analogy to other lipopeptides and the fatty-acid-deletion experiment; membrane interaction, receptor engagement, or endosomal escape not directly characterized for iturin A in cancer cells

claim_text: Cationic antimicrobial peptides with antitumor activity induce lysis of cancer cells through direct interactions with the plasma membrane.
limitations: Stated as established background from cited literature; no direct membrane-disruption assay performed in this study; mechanism inferred from prior work.

claim_text: CAPs selective for cancer cells act via a non-receptor-mediated pathway.
limitations: Asserted as known background; no receptor-blocking or competition experiments performed in this study to demonstrate it.

claim_text: Most CAPs selective for cancer cells interact with the target membrane through the 'carpet model', wherein the peptides align parallel to the outer membrane surface and permeate it after a threshold peptide concentration is reached.
limitations: Cited from external literature; not experimentally tested or verified in this study.

claim_text: Some CAPs trigger apoptosis in cancer cells via disruption of the mitochondrial membrane.
limitations: Attributed generically to 'some CAPs' and cited from external literature; not tested in this study.

claim_text: LfcinB induces cell death in tumor cells by targeting the plasma membrane and, following internalization, disrupting the mitochondria.
limitations: Based on the authors' own prior publications (ref [8]), not demonstrated by any assay conducted in this study.

claim_text: The cationic nature of CAPs facilitates their initial interaction with target cancer cells through electrostatic attraction to negatively charged molecules in the plasma membrane.
limitations: Chemical inference from peptide charge properties; no direct binding or electrostatic assay performed in this study.

claim_text: LfcinB binds to glycosaminoglycans, with higher affinity for heparan sulfate than for chondroitin sulfate.
limitations: Cited from the authors' own prior work (ref [40]); binding affinity measurements not reproduced in this study; relied upon as a premise for the present study's interpretation.

claim_text: Cell surface heparan sulfate sequesters CAPs (LfcinB and KW5) away from the phospholipid bilayer, thereby preventing them from reaching the membrane and impeding their ability to induce cytolysis.
limitations: Sequestration is a proposed model inferred from cytotoxicity outcomes (MTT assay); no direct visualization of peptide localization relative to HS or membrane was performed; heparitinase enzyme-removal experiments were conducted but yielded inconsistent results and are not reported as supporting data; the mechanism is supported indirectly by: enhanced killing of GAG-deficient CHO pgsA-745 cells, sodium chlorate sulfation-reduction enhancing cytotoxicity, exogenous heparin (but not CS) inhibiting cytotoxicity, and greater LfcinB potency against HS-negative vs. HS-positive lymphoma cell lines.

claim_text: Chondroitin sulfate does not substantially inhibit the cytotoxic activity of LfcinB or KW5, in contrast to heparan sulfate, indicating the inhibitory sequestration effect is specific to HS.
direct_assay_types: exogenous GAG competition cytotoxicity assay (MTT), GAG-type profiling via [35S]sulfate radiolabeling with chondroitinase ABC and HNO2 enzymatic degradation
limitations: CS effect was measured only via exogenous addition and cell-line comparison, not by selective CS removal from cell surfaces; heparitinase experiments intended to isolate HS contribution were inconsistent and excluded from the results.

claim_text: Larger cell-surface proteoglycans may hold lytic peptides at a greater distance from the phospholipid bilayer, further reducing peptide access to the membrane and increasing cell resistance to CAPs.
limitations: Speculative extrapolation from Superose-6 gel chromatography data showing HT-29 cells have larger PGs than FEMX cells; no direct test of the distance-resistance relationship was performed; confounded by simultaneous difference in HS vs. CS ratio between the two cell lines.

claim_text: Smaller anionic membrane molecules such as phosphatidylserine and sialic acids, located close to the phospholipid bilayer, facilitate CAP cytotoxic activity, in contrast to the inhibitory effect of the large, extended HS chains.
limitations: Not tested in this study; mechanism proposed by contrast with HS findings and by citing external reports on phosphatidylserine (ref [51]) and sialic acid (ref [50]); no direct comparison experiment was performed.

claim_text: Magainin II kills bacteria primarily by depolarizing and permeabilizing the negatively charged cytoplasmic membrane, making membrane disruption the major killing event.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3(5) fluorescent dye on intact S. aureus), membrane permeabilization (calcein dye leakage from anionic PC/PG 1:1 LUVs)
limitations: membrane-lytic activity and MIC values were not entirely linear; S. aureus used for depolarization assay only; artificial liposomes used for permeabilization

claim_text: Magainin II is localized to the bacterial surface rather than the cytoplasm, consistent with its membrane-lytic mode of action.
limitations: cited from Park et al. 2000 (confocal fluorescence microscopy); not measured in this study

claim_text: Magainin II does not translocate across lipid bilayers.
direct_assay_types: FRET-based translocation assay (Trp donor to dansyl-PE acceptor in PC/PG/dansyl-PE LUVs with encapsulated chymotrypsin; no fluorescence decrease observed over 500 s)
limitations: artificial liposome model only; PC/PG/dansyl-PE composition may not fully replicate bacterial membrane

claim_text: Magainin II dimer disrupts both anionic (PC/PG) and zwitterionic (PC) membranes non-selectively, and its cytotoxicity against mammalian cells is associated with this zwitterionic membrane-lytic activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from PC/PG 1:1 and PC LUVs), hemolysis assay (HC50), cytotoxicity MTT assay on RAW 264.7 cells
limitations: correlation between zwitterionic lysis and cytotoxicity; causation not directly proven; artificial liposomes used

claim_text: Buforin II kills bacteria without disrupting or depolarizing the cytoplasmic membrane, indicating an intracellular rather than membrane-lytic mechanism.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3(5) dye on S. aureus; no depolarization even at MIC), membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from PC/PG LUVs; no leakage detected)
limitations: intracellular molecular targets (DNA, enzymes) not directly assayed in this study; mechanism inferred from absence of membrane effects

claim_text: Buforin II accumulates mainly in the bacterial cytoplasm, consistent with an intracellular mechanism of action.
limitations: cited from Park et al. 2000 (confocal fluorescence microscopy); not measured in this study

claim_text: Buforin II translocates across lipid bilayers to reach intracellular targets, and this translocation is a key component of its antimicrobial mechanism.
direct_assay_types: FRET-based translocation assay (time-dependent decrease in Trp fluorescence via energy transfer to dansyl-PE in PC/PG/dansyl-PE LUVs with encapsulated chymotrypsin)
limitations: demonstrated in artificial liposomes; specific intracellular targets not identified in this study; translocation efficiency in live bacteria not directly measured

claim_text: The buforin II dimer exerts antimicrobial activity through a dual mechanism: it both depolarizes and selectively permeabilizes anionic bacterial membranes, and also translocates across the membrane to target intracellular components.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3(5) assay on S. aureus; >50% dissipation), membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage ~60% from PC/PG LUVs; no leakage from PC LUVs), FRET-based translocation assay (faster and more effective than magainin II dimer)
limitations: intracellular targets not directly identified; exact mode of action not fully elucidated per authors; membrane-lytic activity and MIC not entirely linear; all membrane assays use artificial liposomes

claim_text: Buforin II dimer selectively disrupts anionic membranes but not zwitterionic membranes, and this selectivity correlates with its lack of cytotoxicity against mammalian cells.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from anionic PC/PG 1:1 and zwitterionic PC LUVs), hemolysis assay (HC50 > 200 μM), cytotoxicity MTT assay on RAW 264.7 cells (LC50 > 200 μM)
limitations: correlation between anionic-membrane selectivity and mammalian cell sparing; direct causation not proven; artificial liposome selectivity may not fully recapitulate in vivo selectivity

claim_text: The K6A-derived 19-mer KDAMP binds directly to bacterial cells, as demonstrated by colocalization of TAMRA-tagged peptide with P. aeruginosa under fluorescence microscopy.
direct_assay_types: bacterial binding (fluorescence microscopy with TAMRA-tagged peptide, colocalization with SYTOX Blue)
limitations: Demonstrated only for P. aeruginosa strain 6206; TAMRA tag altered 19-mer activity against S. marcescens, E. coli, and S. pyogenes, so tag may affect binding in those organisms

claim_text: KDAMPs cause bacterial cell wall/membrane permeabilization, as shown by uptake of the cell-impermeant dye SYTOX Blue in 19-mer-treated P. aeruginosa but not in untreated or scrambled-peptide-treated controls.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX Blue cell-impermeant dye staining, fluorescence microscopy)
limitations: Demonstrated for P. aeruginosa only; the paper explicitly acknowledges that permeabilization may be secondary to cell death via another mechanism rather than the primary lethal event

claim_text: The rapid bactericidal kinetics of the 19-mer (71.7% killing at 5 min, >90% at 15 min) indicate that direct membrane disruption, rather than inhibition of macromolecular synthesis, is the primary killing mechanism.
direct_assay_types: time-kill kinetics assay
limitations: Inference rests on a kinetic threshold comparison (>30 min required for macromolecular synthesis inhibitors); no direct assay excluding DNA/RNA/protein synthesis inhibition was performed

claim_text: KDAMPs inhibit bacterial swimming motility, as 19-mer-treated P. aeruginosa lost motility and some cells aggregated within 15 minutes, while untreated or scrambled-peptide-treated bacteria remained motile.
direct_assay_types: motility assay (real-time video phase-contrast microscopy)
limitations: Qualitative observation only; the mechanistic basis of motility loss (membrane damage, energy depletion, etc.) was not investigated

claim_text: Glycine residues at positions 2 and 8 are required for KDAMP bactericidal activity, as G2A/G8A substitutions in the 10-mer significantly reduced killing of P. aeruginosa (~86% vs >98%, P < 0.0001).
direct_assay_types: site-directed mutagenesis, bactericidal viability assay
limitations: Only two glycine positions tested in one variant (10-mer); alanine substitutions maintained similar amphipathicity and physicochemical properties but activity reduction was partial, not complete
