claim_text: KDAMP bactericidal activity does not require α-helical secondary structure; circular dichroism confirmed that all active KDAMPs (19-mer, 17-mer, 10-mer) maintained random coil conformation even in helix-promoting 100% TFE solvent.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy, K2D2 spectral analysis
limitations: CD performed in solution; secondary structure in the presence of intact bacterial membranes was not measured; the one longer variant (36-mer) did adopt helical structure in 100% TFE yet retained activity, complicating interpretation

claim_text: KDAMP bactericidal activity is independent of net cationic charge, as peptides with neutral net charge at pH 7.0 (13-mer, 10-mer) showed bactericidal activity comparable to positively charged variants.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal viability assay across multiple charge variants
limitations: Charge independence inferred from structure-activity comparison across variants; direct charge manipulation (e.g., by chemical modification) without altering sequence was not performed; charge and sequence are confounded across variants

claim_text: KDAMP bactericidal activity is retained at physiological salt concentration (150 mM NaCl), unlike classical cationic antimicrobial peptides (β-defensins, LL-37) whose activity is markedly reduced by salt.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal viability assay in 150 mM NaCl vs. water
limitations: Salt tolerance tested systematically only for the 19-mer against P. aeruginosa; other KDAMP variants and other pathogens not evaluated under salt conditions

claim_text: A specific amino acid sequence is required for KDAMP bactericidal activity, as a scrambled 19-mer with similar predicted net charge and coil structure showed little or no killing of all five P. aeruginosa isolates tested.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal viability assay with sequence-scrambled control peptide
limitations: The scrambled 19-mer also had a lower hydrophobic moment (0.138 μH vs 0.279 μH) and lacked predicted transmembrane helix formation, so loss of activity cannot be attributed to sequence alone

claim_text: P. aeruginosa LPS is not a primary determinant of KDAMP susceptibility, as mutations abolishing LPS O-antigen or core oligosaccharide had only minor impact on 19-mer bactericidal activity.
direct_assay_types: bactericidal viability assay with isogenic LPS mutant strains
limitations: Residual minor effects of LPS mutations were observed; experiment rules out LPS as a dominant target but does not identify the actual target; only tested for P. aeruginosa PAC1R and the 19-mer

claim_text: Glycine repeats in KDAMPs may confer high structural flexibility that enables their antimicrobial mechanism of action.
limitations: Purely speculative; proposed by analogy with known glycine-rich proteins; no direct experimental evidence for this role was provided in the paper

claim_text: The specific mechanism by which K6A-derived peptides disrupt the bacterial cell wall/membrane may be novel, given that their structural features (low charge, no required α-helix, salt tolerance) differ from those of all previously characterized antimicrobial peptide classes.
limitations: Based on comparison of predicted structural features with literature; no direct mechanistic experiments (e.g., pore formation assays, lipid bilayer studies, target identification) were performed to characterize or confirm novelty

claim_text: The mechanism of antibacterial action of stylisin 1 (8) may be interference with the cell membrane functions by penetrating the outer membrane of bacteria through porin channels.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('may be'); no mechanistic assay performed; proposed by analogy to other cyclic peptides, not tested for this compound.

claim_text: Salusin-β depolarizes the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane of Staphylococcus aureus NBRC 12732 in a concentration-dependent manner, as demonstrated by slow, concentration-dependent leakage of DiSC3(5) fluorescence dye.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiSC3(5) fluorescent dye assay)
limitations: Tested on a single bacterial strain (S. aureus NBRC 12732) only; described as 'slow' compared to gramicidin S; causal link to antibacterial activity is suggested but not proven

claim_text: Membrane depolarization may be linked to the antibacterial activity of salusin-β.
limitations: Authors use cautious language ('may be linked'); no direct causal experiment (e.g., rescued viability) was performed to confirm the membrane disruption is the killing mechanism

claim_text: The N-terminal region of salusin-β is more important than the C-terminal region for expression of antimicrobial activity, based on the progressive loss of activity in N-terminal deletion analogs.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (microplate dilution method)
limitations: Structural basis not established; deletions alter both sequence and potentially conformation simultaneously

claim_text: The α-helical conformation of salusin-β, observed by CD spectroscopy, does not clearly contribute to its antimicrobial activity, because analogs with similar activity (e.g., [1]) lack a salusin-β-like CD profile.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy
limitations: CD performed in methanol, not in a membrane-mimetic environment; authors explicitly state the contribution is 'not clear'

claim_text: The principal modes of antibiotic action of gramicidin S, tyrocidine A, and gratisin result from interaction with the cell membrane of target microorganisms.
limitations: Attributed to prior literature (refs 2–15), not demonstrated by new experiments in this paper; no membrane assay performed here.

claim_text: No resistance has been found for gramicidin S, tyrocidine A, and gratisin because resistance would require significant alteration of the lipid composition of the cell membrane.
limitations: Mechanistic rationale cited from ref 16, not experimentally tested in this paper.

claim_text: The GS-like amphiphilic β-sheet conformation is very important for exhibiting both high antibiotic activity and high hemolytic activity.
limitations: Inferred from correlation between CD spectra (conformation maintenance) and MIC/hemolysis data across analogues 1–3; no direct membrane assay performed.

claim_text: The dissociation of high antimicrobial activity and low hemolytic activity in analogues 4 and 5 is caused by differential ionic interaction against the prokaryotic membrane versus the eukaryotic membrane, attributable to their additional positive charges.
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation is proposed by the authors based on MIC and hemolysis data; no direct membrane interaction or binding assay was performed to confirm differential ionic interactions.

claim_text: The Pro5,5′ residues with pyrrolidine ring at the β-turn part are important for maintaining the GS-like β-sheet conformation, and replacement of Pro5,5′ may be partially effective through a structural change in the biological activity of analogue 5.
limitations: Based on CD spectral differences between analogue 5 and GS in methanol; solution conformation may not reflect membrane-bound active conformation.

claim_text: Amino acid residues with neutral amide (Asn) and acidic (Asp) side chains at position 5,5′ are almost ineffective for interaction with both bacterial membrane and sheep cell membrane.
limitations: Conclusion drawn from MIC and hemolysis data for analogues 6 and 7; no direct membrane interaction assay performed.

claim_text: Piscidins exert their fungicidal effects by disrupting the fungal plasma membrane through pore formation.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from LUVs), membrane depolarization (DiBAC4(3) flow cytometry), protoplast regeneration, membrane fluidity (DPH fluorescence anisotropy)
limitations: Pore formation inferred from DPH anisotropy decrease by analogy with melittin; discrete pore structures not directly visualized; in vivo experiments limited to C. albicans only

claim_text: The biological action of piscidins is carried out through the lipid membrane, as membrane-permeabilizing ability in model phospholipid vesicles correlates with fungicidal and hemolytic activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from LUVs)
limitations: Model LUV membranes do not fully recapitulate fungal or erythrocyte membrane composition; correlation does not establish causation

claim_text: Piscidin 1 exerts its fungicidal activity by interacting with the plasma membrane of C. albicans rather than the cell wall.
direct_assay_types: protoplast regeneration
limitations: Reduced protoplast regeneration frequency is an indirect readout and could reflect intracellular effects not related to membrane disruption

claim_text: Piscidin 1 dissipates the plasma membrane potential of C. albicans by injuring the membrane, causing depolarization.
direct_assay_types: membrane depolarization (DiBAC4(3) flow cytometry)
limitations: Depolarization could be a secondary consequence of membrane permeabilization rather than a mechanistically distinct event

claim_text: Piscidin 1 forms pores in the fungal plasma membrane of C. albicans, triggering release of intracellular ions and larger molecules.
direct_assay_types: membrane fluidity (DPH fluorescence anisotropy)
limitations: Pore formation is inferred from decreased DPH anisotropy by analogy with melittin positive control; DPH anisotropy decrease reflects membrane perturbation but does not distinguish pores from general membrane disruption

claim_text: Against bacteria, piscidin permeabilizes the membrane by toroidal pore formation rather than the barrel-stave mechanism.
limitations: This claim is cited from a prior study (Campagna et al. 2007, ref 15) and not experimentally tested in the present paper; mechanism was characterized in a bacterial system, not fungi

claim_text: The higher cationicity and hydrophobicity of piscidin 1 compared to piscidin 3 contribute to its greater antifungal activity and hemolytic activity.
limitations: Stated as a hypothesis based on structural comparison of P1 and P3; not directly tested by mutagenesis or charge/hydrophobicity manipulation

claim_text: The biological activity of piscidins is less dependent on alpha-helical content, because the less helical peptide (P1) exhibits greater membrane-permeabilizing ability than the more helical P3.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from LUVs)
limitations: CD spectroscopy data establishing helicity values are from a prior publication (ref 27), not measured in this study; helicity and membrane-permeabilizing ability co-vary with other structural differences between P1 and P3

claim_text: Cationic amphipathic α-helical antimicrobial peptides kill bacteria presumably by disrupting their membranes, operating in a receptor-independent mode as demonstrated by enantiomeric all-D analogs exhibiting the same activities as all-L wild-type peptides.
limitations: Membrane disruption is stated as presumed; receptor-independence inference from D-analog activity is cited from prior literature, not measured in this paper.

claim_text: PGLa-NH2 lies flat on the membrane surface at low peptide concentration with charged residues pointing toward the water phase, then adopts a tilted state (~35° from membrane plane) at higher concentration, consistent with dimer formation rather than a stable transmembrane pore.
direct_assay_types: solid-state 19F NMR, solid-state 2H NMR
limitations: NMR data are from cited prior studies by the same group, not new experiments in this paper; pore formation is explicitly described as short-lived and not stable on the NMR timescale.

claim_text: When PGLa-NH2 is mixed with magainin 2 in a 1:1 ratio it adopts an almost upright transmembrane orientation compatible with pore formation.
direct_assay_types: solid-state NMR
limitations: Cited from prior work; upright orientation is described as 'compatible with' pore formation but not directly proven by a pore-function assay.

claim_text: At high concentrations PGLa-NH2 forms extended immobile aggregates in membranes, suggesting aggregation as a secondary membrane-disruption mechanism.
direct_assay_types: solid-state NMR
limitations: Cited from prior studies; mechanistic role of aggregation in killing is speculative.

claim_text: MSI-103-NH2 adopts a flat surface-bound state at low concentration and a tilted state at high concentration similar to PGLa-NH2, suggesting it forms dimers and may share the same membrane-disruption mechanism.
direct_assay_types: solid-state NMR
limitations: NMR data cited from a diploma thesis; mechanism inference is explicitly speculative ('is expected to form dimers', 'may thus have a similar mechanism').

claim_text: MSI-103 induces dimerization and aggregation in membranes at lower peptide concentrations than PGLa-NH2, which may contribute to its higher antimicrobial potency.
limitations: Structural basis from NMR cited from prior/concurrent work; link to potency is speculative inference by the authors.

claim_text: MAP-NH2 forms large membrane aggregates at very low concentration and may have a different mode of action from PGLa and MSI-103.
direct_assay_types: solid-state NMR
limitations: Cited as unpublished results; mechanism described as speculative ('may have a rather different mode of action').

claim_text: Dimerization of amphipathic helices in the membrane is speculatively linked to antimicrobial activity, while aggregation may be responsible for hemolytic activity.
limitations: Explicitly flagged by the authors as speculation ('If we may speculate here'); no direct experimental support provided in this paper.

claim_text: Higher positive charge of amidated peptides compared to their free-acid analogs partly explains greater antimicrobial activity, as antimicrobial activity is generally correlated with positive charge.
limitations: Charge correlation is based on literature precedent; the authors note charge alone is insufficient to explain all activity differences observed.

claim_text: Greater hydrophobicity of amidated peptides relative to their free-acid analogs explains their higher hemolytic activity, since hemolytic activity is correlated with peptide hydrophobicity.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Hemolysis assay measures bulk lysis, not a direct membrane-interaction mechanism; hydrophobicity–hemolysis correlation is from literature; authors note other factors are likely also involved for MAP.

claim_text: NYAD-36, NYAD-66, and NYAD-67 bind the C-terminal domain (CTD) of HIV-1 capsid (CA) protein, producing significant NMR spectral perturbations consistent with tight binding predominantly at CTD residues, with dissociation constants of 10.12 μM, 3.60 μM, and 2.63 μM, respectively.
direct_assay_types: 1H-15N HSQC NMR titration, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC)
limitations: NMR and ITC used a monomeric W184A/M185A double-mutant CA construct to prevent CA dimerization, not wild-type CA; binding constants may differ for the native protein

claim_text: NYAD-36, NYAD-66, and NYAD-67 disrupt formation of mature-like HIV-1 CA assemblies in vitro in a dose-dependent manner by targeting CA-CA interactions.
direct_assay_types: negative-stain electron microscopy of in vitro CA assembly, turbidity-based in vitro CA assembly assay
limitations: NYAD-67 showed tight CA binding by NMR yet did not reduce assembly rate or extent in the turbidity assay, indicating binding does not always translate to assembly disruption; in vitro assembly conditions (NaCl-driven tube formation) may not fully replicate intracellular assembly

claim_text: i,i+7 stapled peptides impair Gag precursor (Pr55Gag) processing in virus-producing cells, causing accumulation of unprocessed Gag, without inhibiting virus release from the cell.
direct_assay_types: metabolic labeling ([35S]Met/Cys), immunoprecipitation with HIV-Ig, SDS-PAGE with phosphorimager quantification of cell- and virion-associated Gag species
limitations: Gag accumulation was described as modest; the mechanistic basis for impaired processing (e.g., direct protease inhibition vs. structural interference with the Gag lattice) was not established

claim_text: HIV-1 virions produced in the presence of i,i+7 stapled peptides display markedly impaired infectivity, consistent with a CA-level defect imposed during virus assembly.
direct_assay_types: single-cycle infectivity assay (luciferase reporter in TZM-bl cells) with RT-normalized virus stocks
limitations: Peptide was diluted ~20-fold from producer-cell concentration before infection assay, reducing potential carry-over entry effects; infectivity defect attributed to CA but not mechanistically separated from Gag processing impairment

claim_text: i,i+7 stapled peptides inhibit HIV-1 entry in an Env-dependent manner by binding the gp120 V3 loop, as demonstrated by specific binding to gp120 that is abrogated >5-fold upon V3 loop deletion.
direct_assay_types: surface plasmon resonance (SPR) with immobilized full-length Yu2 gp120 and V3-deleted gp120ΔV3, ITC with cyclic V3 loop peptide
limitations: NYAD-66 showed no detectable binding to the cyclic V3 loop peptide in ITC despite showing antiviral activity; SPR used immobilized recombinant gp120, which may not fully represent the native trimeric Env spike; the precise V3 contact residues were not mapped

claim_text: Viral resistance to NYAD-36 emerged via two mutations in gp120 (V120Q in the C1 region and A327P at the base of the V3 loop), but not in Gag/CA, implicating Env-mediated entry as a primary antiviral target of the i,i+7 peptides in spreading infection.
direct_assay_types: viral resistance selection in Jurkat cells, PCR amplification and sequencing of gag and env coding regions, single-cycle and spreading-infection assays with engineered V120Q/A327P mutant virus
limitations: Resistance selection was performed only with NYAD-36; mutations severely attenuated viral fitness in PBMC, confounding interpretation; no CA mutations were identified despite CA binding, suggesting CA binding alone is insufficient to drive resistance in cell culture

claim_text: i,i+7 stapled peptides exert a dual mechanism: Env mutations (V120Q/A327P) confer resistance to the entry-blocking component but do not rescue the infectivity defect when mutant virions are produced in the presence of peptide, demonstrating a CA-dependent inhibitory activity independent of Env targeting.
direct_assay_types: single-cycle infectivity assay comparing WT vs. V120Q/A327P virions produced in peptide-treated 293T producer cells
limitations: Separation of CA and Env effects is indirect and based on differential rescue by Env mutations; the contribution of impaired Gag processing versus direct CA assembly disruption to the CA-based infectivity defect is not resolved

claim_text: VSV-G pseudotyping of HIV-1 abolishes the entry-inhibitory activity of i,i+7 stapled peptides when peptide is present during infection, confirming that the entry component of inhibition is specifically Env-dependent.
direct_assay_types: single-cycle infectivity assay with VSV-G-pseudotyped HIV-1 particles in the presence of peptide during the infection step
limitations: VSV-G-pseudotyped virions produced in the presence of peptide still show infectivity defects, attributed to the CA mechanism, making entry-specific quantification indirect

claim_text: Cell penetration efficiency is required for the intracellular CA-targeting and assembly-inhibitory activity of i,i+7 stapled peptides, and the net charge of −4 renders them less cell-permeable than the i,i+4 peptide NYAD-1 (net charge 0).
direct_assay_types: FACS analysis of cellular uptake of FAM-conjugated peptides in 293T cells, confocal microscopy
limitations: Cell penetration was measured separately from assembly inhibition; causality is inferred by correlation between penetration efficiency, net charge, and antiviral potency across the peptide series rather than by direct ablation of penetration

claim_text: Hydrocarbon stapling confers α-helical structure on the linear CAI-derived peptide, and this α-helicity is essential for cell penetration and subsequent intracellular targeting of HIV-1 CA.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy comparing stapled (NYAD-36, -66, -67) vs. linear control (NYAD-41) peptides
limitations: CD confirms α-helicity of stapled peptides; essentiality for cell penetration is inferred from prior i,i+4 studies cited as background and from the failure of the unstapled linear peptide to penetrate or inhibit—direct mutagenic or structural uncoupling of helicity from penetration was not performed in this paper

claim_text: NYAD-1 (i,i+4 stapled peptide) reduces infectivity of both wild-type and V120Q/A327P Env mutant HIV-1 to a similar extent (~10-fold), indicating that NYAD-1 acts primarily through CA and lacks the Env/entry-targeting component seen with i,i+7 peptides.
direct_assay_types: single-cycle infectivity assay comparing WT and V120Q/A327P mutant virus in the presence of NYAD-1
limitations: Only a single concentration of NYAD-1 was tested in this comparison; mechanism of CA-based infectivity reduction by NYAD-1 is characterized in prior work cited, not re-established here

claim_text: Cecropins (and by homology peptide 8.4.1) interact with negatively charged bacterial membranes, and peptide charge is a key determinant of this interaction.
limitations: The paper cites this as general knowledge about cecropins, not a direct finding from experiments on 8.4.1; no membrane assay was performed in this study.

claim_text: Peptide 8.4.1 likely adopts a two-amphipathic-alpha-helix structure with a sharp bend at proline-23, consistent with the cecropin structural scaffold.
limitations: Inferred entirely from 90% sequence identity to Bombyx mori cecropin D and presence of proline at position 23; no structural determination (CD, NMR, X-ray) was performed.

claim_text: The neutral net charge of peptide 8.4.1 (six positive and six negative residues at physiological pH) likely explains its poor MIC (53 µM) relative to canonical cecropins (0.2–20 µM), because reduced cationic character diminishes electrostatic attraction to anionic bacterial membranes.
limitations: Post-hoc rationalisation of MIC data; no membrane-binding, zeta-potential, or electrostatic-perturbation assay was conducted; other structural differences from canonical cecropins are not ruled out.

claim_text: The slightly greater antibacterial potency of peptide 5.11.1 (MIC 43 µM) compared to 8.4.1 (MIC 53 µM) may be related to its higher net positive charge (+5), which would enhance interaction with negatively charged bacterial membranes.
limitations: Speculative; the MIC difference is small; no charge-titration or membrane-interaction experiment was performed; 5.11.1 has a unique sequence with unknown fold, making charge the only feature the authors can comment on.

claim_text: The positive charge of P4 (+4) is important for the initial electrostatic attraction of the peptide to the negatively charged phospholipid membranes of bacteria and other microorganisms.
limitations: Claim is based on predicted chemicophysical properties (ProtParam) and general AMP literature; no direct binding assay performed on P4.

claim_text: The electrostatic potential on the molecular surface of P4 plays an important role in electrostatic bonding between P4 and the negatively charged bacterial cell membrane, consistent with the molecular electroporation theory.
limitations: Electrostatic potential computed in silico (Arguslab/CCP4MG); the molecular electroporation theory is cited as the explanatory framework but no direct membrane-interaction experiment was performed.

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of P4 is attributable to its well-developed β-sheet secondary/tertiary structure.
limitations: Based on computational secondary-structure prediction (HNN) and homology-based tertiary-structure modeling (Swiss-Model on 1fjn.pdb template); no mutational or direct structural confirmation.

claim_text: Both the β-sheet and the α-helix conformation are involved in the antimicrobial mechanism of P4, because P4 transitions from a largely unstructured/β-sheet state in aqueous solution to a significant α-helical conformation upon contact with membrane-mimicking environments.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy (CD) in water, 50% TFE, and 25 mM SDS
limitations: CD was performed with membrane-mimicking solvents (TFE, SDS), not with actual bacterial membranes; α-helix content observed in SDS (39.7%) and TFE (26.6%) is used as a proxy for membrane interaction, but the link to killing activity is inferred, not demonstrated with a paired functional assay.

claim_text: Disulfide bond(s) in P4 (predicted between Cys9–Cys17) are likely involved in stabilizing the peptide structure and may contribute to its antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Disulfide bond predicted computationally (DIpro) only; no biochemical confirmation of bond formation, and the contribution to activity is explicitly stated as speculative ('may play a role').

claim_text: The hydrophobicity of P4 (GRAVY index higher than other longicin analogs, but at a moderate level) is an essential feature enabling its interaction with bacterial membranes.
limitations: GRAVY index is a computed property; the paper notes that increased hydrophobicity correlates with mammalian cell toxicity and loss of antimicrobial specificity, so P4's moderate level is presented as optimal, but no direct membrane-interaction experiment was conducted.

claim_text: The amphipathic character of P4 (high mean amphipathicity as an α-helix) is a key determinant of its antimicrobial activity, as amphipathicity is more important than hydrophobicity and α-helical content alone in governing AMP activity.
limitations: Amphipathicity calculated computationally (WHAT software); the primacy-of-amphipathicity claim is attributed to Pathak et al. [24] and applied by analogy to P4, not directly tested here.

claim_text: P4 shows low cytolytic activity against mammalian cells (less than 15% hemolysis at up to 500 µM against bovine erythrocytes; less than 50% growth inhibition of Vero cells, with significant inhibition beginning at 16 µM), suggesting a degree of selectivity for microbial over host cells.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay (erythrocytes of cattle, dog, rabbit at 540 nm); cytotoxicity assay (Vero cells, CellTiter 96 MTS assay at 550 nm)
limitations: Hemolytic safety threshold is relative; Vero cell inhibition becomes significant at 16 µM, which overlaps with the reported antibacterial MIC range (2–10 µM from Tsuji et al. [33]), so the therapeutic window is narrow and warrants further evaluation.

claim_text: The antimicrobial peptides studied (Stripe and derivatives) act by disrupting the integrity of bacterial plasma membranes, which are essential for bacteria to sustain cellular functions.
limitations: No membrane disruption assay was performed in this study; the claim is attributed to cited prior literature (refs 3–8) and applied by analogy to the peptides designed here.

claim_text: The positively charged AMPs interact electrostatically with the negatively charged bacterial cell wall/membrane to form channel-forming agents and ionophores in the bacterial membrane.
limitations: Channel formation or ionophore activity was not directly measured; this is a background mechanistic framework from cited literature applied generally to the peptide class.

claim_text: Targeting bacterial cell membranes confers a low probability of inducing bacterial resistance, an advantage attributed to the membrane-disruption mechanism of the AMPs studied.
limitations: No resistance-evolution experiments were performed; the claim is taken from cited literature (refs 9, 10).

claim_text: Amphipathicity is the structural property crucial for the antimicrobial activity of the peptides, as loss of amphipathic character (StripeLD, AltStripe) correlates with reduced MICs across all strains tested.
limitations: Mechanistic link between amphipathicity and membrane disruption is inferred from MIC comparisons and CD-derived secondary structure data; no direct membrane-permeabilization or leakage assay was performed.

claim_text: StripeLD shows reduced antimicrobial activity compared to Stripe because simple L-to-D alternation disrupts the amphipathic secondary structure without conferring a new productive conformation.
limitations: Inference based on CD spectra (weak signal ~200 nm, not characteristic of a well-defined helix) and MIC data; the actual conformation of StripeLD in a membrane environment was not determined.

claim_text: AltStripe displays very weak antimicrobial activity because, although it forms an α-helix, the rearranged sequence yields a non-amphipathic helical face that cannot effectively interact with bacterial membranes.
limitations: Conclusion is based on helical-wheel analysis, CD confirmation of α-helical structure, and MIC values; no direct membrane interaction or amphipathicity quantification assay was performed.

claim_text: AltStripeLD achieves higher antimicrobial activity than AltStripe because the LD-alternating sequence allows the peptide to adopt an amphipathic β6.3-helix (analogous to Gramicidin A) that presents cationic and hydrophobic faces on opposite sides, enabling effective membrane interaction.
limitations: β6.3-helix formation for AltStripeLD could not be confirmed by CD (weak signal); conclusion relies on molecular modeling (MOE, constrained backbone based on GA PDB 1MAG) and MIC improvement over AltStripe; no direct membrane assay performed.

claim_text: RT53 rapidly permeabilizes the plasma membranes of cancer cells, inducing necrotic cell death characterized by membrane disruption and release of intracellular contents.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH release), transmission electron microscopy
limitations: LDH kinetics measured at single concentration (20 µM); TEM performed on U2OS only

claim_text: RT53-induced plasma membrane permeabilization is selective for cancer cells and does not affect non-malignant cells (HaCat, MRC-5) or erythrocytes.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH release), hemolysis assay
limitations: Only two non-malignant cell lines tested; erythrocyte assay at a single concentration (20 µM) and single timepoint (1 h)

claim_text: RT53 acts through a non-regulated, membranolytic mode of necrosis that is independent of caspase activation, necroptosis (RIPK1-mediated), and mitochondrial permeability transition pore (MPTP)-mediated regulated necrosis.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH release) with pharmacological inhibitors (zVAD-fmk, necrostatin-1, cyclosporin A)
limitations: Inhibitor experiments performed in U2OS only; inhibitor concentrations and on-target efficacy not independently validated in this study

claim_text: The membranolytic activity of RT53 requires intact leucine residues at positions 384 and 391 of the AAC-11 heptad repeat region, as substitution to alanine (RT53M mutant) abolishes plasma membrane permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (LDH release), mutant peptide comparison
limitations: Mechanism by which leucine substitutions abolish activity (loss of helix amphipathicity vs. loss of partner binding) is not distinguished

claim_text: RT53 acts via a non-specific, detergent-like membrane disruption mechanism is ruled out because it does not lyse erythrocytes, unlike typical amphiphilic detergent peptides.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: Absence of hemolysis at 20 µM does not fully exclude unspecific activity at higher concentrations or other membrane compositions

claim_text: RT53 inserts into cancer cell membranes through interaction with a yet-unknown cancer cell-specific membrane-bound AAC-11 protein partner, and this binding likely increases the local concentration of RT53, resulting in membrane lysis via its membrane-active alpha-helical structure.
limitations: The putative partner protein has not been identified; selectivity for cancer cell membranes could also reflect differences in membrane lipid composition; alpha-helical pore-forming mechanism is inferred from structural properties, not directly measured here

claim_text: RT53 triggers aggregation and plasma membrane surface exposure of calreticulin (CRT) through a caspase-independent and eIF2α phosphorylation-independent pathway, distinct from the canonical chemotherapy-induced CRT exposure pathway.
direct_assay_types: CRT-GFP biosensor fluorescence microscopy, Western blot (eIF2α phosphorylation), pharmacological inhibition (zVAD-fmk)
limitations: CRT aggregation (fluorescence redistribution) used as a proxy for surface exposure; actual surface CRT quantification (e.g., flow cytometry) not shown in this study; U2OS stable line may not represent all cancer types

claim_text: RT53 induces dose-dependent extracellular release of HMGB1 from cancer cells, consistent with passive release secondary to plasma membrane destruction.
direct_assay_types: HMGB1 ELISA (culture supernatant)
limitations: Active vs. passive release not formally distinguished; experiments performed in U2OS only

claim_text: RT53 treatment causes a dramatic increase in extracellular ATP release from cancer cells.
direct_assay_types: ATP bioluminescence assay (culture supernatant)
limitations: Active secretion vs. passive leakage through disrupted membrane not distinguished; single cell line (U2OS)

claim_text: HMGB1 and ATP released by RT53-treated dying cells are likely passively liberated as a consequence of plasma membrane destruction rather than through regulated secretion pathways.
limitations: Passive vs. active release not experimentally tested; inference is based on the non-regulated necrotic mode of cell death established by inhibitor studies

claim_text: The immunogenic cell death induced by RT53 is not a mere consequence of non-specific spillage of intracellular components, as freeze-thaw necrosis producing similar spillage is non-immunogenic, indicating RT53-triggered necrosis has additional immunogenic qualities.
limitations: Comparison to freeze-thaw necrosis is based on published literature, not a direct within-study comparison; the molecular basis for immunogenic versus non-immunogenic necrosis remains uncharacterized for RT53

claim_text: BCR1, BCR3, BCR5, and BCR8 kill bacteria by increasing cell membrane permeability, evidenced by propidium iodide uptake and a large reduction in colony-forming units in E. coli.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (PI staining, DAPI staining, flow cytometry), colony-forming unit reduction
limitations: Tested in E. coli as a model γ-proteobacterium; direct activity against the native target Buchnera aphidicola was not tested; assayed at a single concentration (5 µM) for morphology/permeability experiments

claim_text: BCR2 permeabilizes the E. coli cell membrane without exhibiting significant bactericidal activity, indicating membrane disruption can be decoupled from killing.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (PI staining, DAPI staining, flow cytometry), colony-forming unit assay
limitations: Tested at 5 µM only; activity spectrum at other concentrations not assessed; mechanism distinguishing sub-lethal permeabilization from lethal permeabilization not elucidated

claim_text: BCR1 and BCR3 cause morphological cell elongation in E. coli, an effect shared with NCR peptides acting on rhizobia.
direct_assay_types: cell morphology by fluorescence microscopy, forward scatter (FSC) by flow cytometry
limitations: Molecular basis of elongation not investigated; elongation could be a secondary consequence of membrane stress rather than a primary mechanistic action

claim_text: BCR3 and BCR8 promote cell aggregation in E. coli, as observed by flow cytometry side-scatter and fluorescence microscopy.
direct_assay_types: cell morphology by flow cytometry (SSC), fluorescence microscopy
limitations: Mechanism of aggregation not investigated; could reflect surface charge changes, membrane destabilization, or other physicochemical effects

claim_text: BCR1 and BCR8 permeabilize the S. meliloti cell membrane, increasing PI and DAPI fluorescence and cell size, indicating the membrane-disrupting mechanism extends to α-proteobacteria.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (PI staining, DAPI staining), cell size by flow cytometry (FSC, SSC)
limitations: Bactericidal endpoint (CFU) for S. meliloti at these concentrations not shown in the main figure; phylogenetic extrapolation to Buchnera remains untested

claim_text: The antimicrobial activity of BCR peptides involves the bacterial inner-membrane protein SbmA/BacA, because E. coli sbmA deletion mutants and S. meliloti bacA deletion mutants are significantly more sensitive to BCR1, BCR3, and BCR8 than their isogenic wild-type parents.
direct_assay_types: colony-forming unit assay comparing isogenic wild-type and deletion mutant strains
limitations: SbmA/BacA are peptide importers; increased sensitivity in the mutant likely reflects loss of peptide internalization/sequestration rather than a characterised protective mechanism; the molecular basis by which SbmA/BacA modulates sensitivity is not established in this study; effect size differences between wild type and mutant were described as small

claim_text: BCR peptides likely act via a BacA/SbmA-independent mechanism to affect Buchnera membrane permeability and survival, because no bacA/sbmA homolog is present in the Buchnera genome.
limitations: Inferred entirely from genomic absence of bacA/sbmA in Buchnera; no direct experiments on Buchnera were performed; alternative uptake or resistance pathways were not excluded

claim_text: BCR peptides may control Buchnera population size within bacteriocytes through their antimicrobial activity, analogous to coleoptericin-A in weevil–Sodalis symbiosis and NCR peptides in legume–rhizobia symbiosis.
limitations: No in vivo aphid experiments performed; function in intact aphid bacteriocytes entirely uncharacterised; analogy to other systems is speculative

claim_text: BCR peptides that permeabilize the bacterial membrane may facilitate metabolic exchange of amino acids and other compounds between Buchnera and host bacteriocyte cells, analogous to Alnus defensin-like peptide Ag5 inducing amino acid release from Frankia.
limitations: Purely analogical; no metabolite release experiments performed on BCR-treated bacteria; the loss of transporter genes in the aphid genome is cited as circumstantial support but does not confirm this mechanism

claim_text: The higher susceptibility of Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli and P. aeruginosa) compared to Gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus and S. pyogenes) to SSAP indicates the possibility of SSAP being target-specific against lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in its antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Explicitly framed only as a 'possibility'; no LPS-binding, LPS-neutralization, or competitive-inhibition assay was performed; differential MIC values reflect multiple structural differences between Gram-negative and Gram-positive cell envelopes beyond LPS alone; a broader panel of organisms (fungi, yeast) was acknowledged as untested.

claim_text: The ovalbumin-derived antimicrobial peptide (GLEIPNFN) disrupts bacterial cell membrane permeability in both E. coli and Salmonella, as demonstrated by increased conductivity of bacterial culture media caused by leakage of intracellular ions (K⁺, Ca²⁺, Na⁺).
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (conductivity measurement of ion leakage)
limitations: Conductivity measures bulk ion leakage as a proxy for membrane disruption; not a direct structural visualization; only a single peptide concentration (10 mg/mL) tested; only gram-negative bacteria tested—gram-positive activity not studied.

claim_text: The ovalbumin-derived antimicrobial peptide (GLEIPNFN) inhibits bacterial protein synthesis in E. coli and Salmonella, as indicated by decreased soluble protein content in treated bacterial cultures.
limitations: Inhibition of synthesis is inferred from reduced soluble protein content, which conflates synthesis inhibition with protein leakage through a disrupted membrane; no radiolabeling or direct translation assay was performed.

claim_text: The ovalbumin-derived antimicrobial peptide (GLEIPNFN) causes leakage of intracellular reducing sugars across the bacterial cell membrane in E. coli and Salmonella.
direct_assay_types: reducing sugar leakage assay (direct titration method)
limitations: Leakage of reducing sugars is a downstream consequence of membrane damage rather than a primary mechanism; only gram-negative bacteria tested; single concentration used.

claim_text: General antimicrobial peptide mechanisms include destroying cell membrane proteins, blocking cell membrane synthesis, cytoplasmic coagulation, penetrating damaged cell walls to specifically bind intracellular targets and inhibit protein and RNA synthesis, leakage of intracellular components, disruption of normal cellular reproduction and metabolism, and inhibition of molecular active transport.
limitations: Presented as a literature-derived taxonomy of general AMP mechanisms (citing refs [11][12][13]); not experimentally demonstrated for the ovalbumin-derived peptide in this study; it is unclear which of these mechanisms the specific peptide GLEIPNFN employs beyond membrane permeabilization.

claim_text: MCh-AMP1 caused permeabilization of the fungal cell membrane in Candida albicans.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization
limitations: Data cited from a prior publication by the same group (Seyedjavadi et al., 2020); assay details not reported in this paper.

claim_text: MCh-AMP1 induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in Candida albicans.
direct_assay_types: ROS production assay
limitations: Data cited from a prior publication by the same group (Seyedjavadi et al., 2020); assay details not reported in this paper.

claim_text: DiMCh-AMP1 may act via the same antifungal mechanism as the parent peptide MCh-AMP1 (membrane permeabilization and ROS induction), because the linker caused minimal conformational change to the native peptide structure.
limitations: No direct mechanistic assay performed on DiMCh-AMP1 in this study; inference rests entirely on in silico structural similarity (RMSD 1.76 Å) and the assumption that function follows structure.

claim_text: The reduced hemolytic activity of DiMCh-AMP1 relative to MCh-AMP1 is attributed to its lower total hydrophobic ratio (36% vs. 47%), because highly hydrophobic peptides penetrate more deeply into the hydrophobic core of red blood cell membranes, causing stronger hemolysis through pore or channel formation.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay
limitations: The mechanistic explanation (pore/channel formation via hydrophobic core penetration) is borrowed from Chen et al. (2007) and not directly tested here; only haemoglobin-release outcome was measured, not membrane pore formation.

claim_text: LL-37 binds LPS and neutralizes its bioactivity by inhibiting LPS-induced nitric oxide production from isolated rat aortic tissue.
direct_assay_types: LPS-induced nitric oxide inhibition (Griess reagent nitrate/nitrite assay, rat aorta ex vivo)
limitations: LPS binding is not measured directly; nitrate/nitrite accumulation is a downstream proxy for NO; ex vivo rat model; single LPS concentration (1 ng/ml) tested

claim_text: N-terminally truncated LL-37 analogs (fragments 106 and 110), the 18-mer LLKKK, and BMAP-27 retain LPS-neutralizing activity at potencies similar to LL-37, as shown by inhibition of LPS-induced nitric oxide production in rat aorta.
direct_assay_types: LPS-induced nitric oxide inhibition (Griess reagent nitrate/nitrite assay, rat aorta ex vivo)
limitations: Fragment 106 was significantly less potent than LL-37 at 2 µM; LPS binding is not directly measured; ex vivo rat model

claim_text: LL-37 causes concentration-dependent hemolysis of human erythrocytes, with cytotoxicity attributed to hydrophobic interactions between the peptide and the eukaryotic cell membrane.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis (hemoglobin release, absorbance at 540 nm)
limitations: Hydrophobic membrane interaction as the molecular mechanism is cited from prior literature (Oren et al., ref 18) and not directly demonstrated here; this study contributes supporting evidence (more hydrophobic peptides cause more hemolysis)

claim_text: LL-37 induces internucleosomal DNA fragmentation consistent with apoptosis in human vascular smooth muscle cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: internucleosomal DNA fragmentation (cell death detection ELISA)
limitations: Experiments conducted under serum-free conditions only; DNA fragmentation confirms apoptosis but the upstream induction mechanism is not characterized in this study

claim_text: LL-37 and its N-terminally truncated analogs (fragments 106 and 110) attract human neutrophil granulocytes through a chemotactic mechanism mediated by the formyl peptide receptor FPRL1.
direct_assay_types: neutrophil chemotaxis (transmembrane migration assay, polycarbonate membrane, 5-µm pores)
limitations: FPRL1 receptor involvement is cited from prior literature (refs 1, 21, 29) and not confirmed by receptor blockade or competitive binding experiments here; biphasic concentration-response is not mechanistically explained

claim_text: The antibacterial activity of LL-37 depends on its alpha-helical conformation, which is disrupted by anions such as Cl-, explaining the reduced potency observed at physiological salt concentrations.
limitations: Mechanism is based entirely on prior literature (ref 8, Johansson et al.); no structural or conformational assays performed here; invoked to interpret observed salt-dependent activity changes

claim_text: The loss of antifungal activity of LL-37 and its analogs against Candida albicans at physiological NaCl concentrations is attributed to salt-induced conformational changes in the peptide molecules.
limitations: The paper explicitly states the results do not provide an explanation; the conformational-change hypothesis is speculative, untested, and applied by analogy from antibacterial salt-sensitivity data

claim_text: LL-37's antimicrobial activity in serum is reduced because it binds plasma proteins, particularly apolipoprotein A-I, which sequesters and inactivates the peptide.
direct_assay_types: radial diffusion assay with human serum (0%, 40%, 99%)
limitations: Direct binding to apolipoprotein A-I is cited from prior literature (refs 24, 28); this study measures only functional serum inhibition of antibacterial activity, not protein-peptide binding affinity

claim_text: The N-terminal hydrophobic amino acids of LL-37 mediate its interaction with plasma proteins such as apolipoprotein A-I through hydrophobic forces, since their removal substantially reduces serum-mediated inactivation of antibacterial activity.
direct_assay_types: radial diffusion assay with human serum
limitations: Direct protein-peptide binding was not measured; hydrophobic nature of the interaction is inferred from structural differences between peptides and supported by prior literature (refs 24, 28) but not proven here

claim_text: At 10 µM, the 18-mer LLKKK exhibits markedly greater chemotactic activity than LL-37, probably due to loss of receptor selectivity and nonspecific agonism at chemoattractant receptors beyond FPRL1.
limitations: Mechanism is speculative (paper states 'probably due to a loss of selectivity'); no receptor binding, displacement, or selectivity assays were performed

claim_text: The designed cathelicidin-like peptides (TN1 and TN3) integrated into membrane lipids by pulling negatively charged phosphate groups of lipids via positively charged arginine residues, shrinking the membrane and decreasing its original thickness.
limitations: Evidence is from molecular dynamics (MD) simulation only, not wet-lab direct measurement of membrane thickness or lipid interaction.

claim_text: A single peptide molecule is capable of creating a hydrophilic channel in the bacterial membrane, allowing free passage of water molecules and hydrophilic molecules such as SYBR Green.
limitations: Channel formation is inferred from MD simulation; the SYBR Green fluorescence assay supports membrane disruption but does not directly confirm channel formation by a single molecule.

claim_text: TN1 disrupts the S. aureus cell membrane, causing bacteria to split into halves, as observed by transmission electron microscopy.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy (TEM)
limitations: Only TN1 was tested by TEM; single concentration (64 µg/ml) and single time point (15 min); one organism tested.

claim_text: Treatment of S. aureus with TN1 results in membrane disruption sufficient for the nucleic acid dye SYBR Green to penetrate bacterial cells and bind to intracellular DNA.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYBR Green fluorescence assay)
limitations: SYBR Green entry indicates membrane compromise but does not distinguish specific mechanisms (pore formation vs. generalized membrane disruption); only S. aureus and TN1 tested.

claim_text: TN3 strongly binds to the active site of glycosyltransferase, the major S. aureus enzyme responsible for building the peptidoglycan cell wall.
limitations: Evidence is entirely from computational molecular docking (GRAMM-X) and MD simulation; no biochemical binding or enzyme inhibition assay was performed to confirm this interaction in vitro.

claim_text: Elongating the hydrophobic tail of peptides (as in TN4) causes self-aggregation between peptide molecules, which eliminates antibacterial activity by inhibiting peptide-membrane interaction.
limitations: Self-aggregation is inferred from MD simulation showing TN4 requires 4 molecules to self-cluster versus 2 for TN3; the mechanistic link to loss of activity is inferred, not directly demonstrated by a binding assay.

claim_text: Positively charged arginine residues in the peptides electrostatically interact with the negatively charged phosphate groups of bacterial membrane phospholipids, driving membrane association.
limitations: Primarily inferred from peptide design rationale and supported by MD simulation; no direct biophysical measurement (e.g., zeta potential, isothermal titration calorimetry) reported.

claim_text: HTP2 killed P. aeruginosa cells in a concentration-dependent manner, with ~1-log and ~3-log reductions at 25 μg/mL and 50 μg/mL respectively within 15 minutes.
direct_assay_types: time-killing kinetics
limitations: Single strain tested (PAO1); only 0, 15, and 30 min time points assessed

claim_text: HTP2 primarily binds to the surface of P. aeruginosa cells, with weak fluorescence also detectable inside the cell, indicating both surface and intracellular action sites.
direct_assay_types: FITC-labeled peptide confocal laser-scanning microscopy
limitations: Fluorescence localization does not distinguish active binding from passive diffusion of permeabilized cells; single concentration tested (10 μg/mL)

claim_text: Electrostatic interactions mediate HTP2 binding to P. aeruginosa, as exogenous cations (especially divalent) and exogenous LPS competitively reduce HTP2 antibacterial activity.
direct_assay_types: LPS competition binding assay, salt stability/cation sensitivity assay
limitations: MIC shift is a functional readout, not a direct binding measurement; does not quantify binding affinity

claim_text: HTP2 disrupts the integrity of the P. aeruginosa cell membrane in a concentration-dependent manner, causing rapid membrane permeabilization.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green fluorescence)
limitations: Assay measures outer membrane permeability to the dye, not direct pore formation; single strain (PAO1)

claim_text: HTP2 disrupts the membrane potential of P. aeruginosa cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
direct_assay_types: membrane potential assay (DiBAC4(3) fluorescence)
limitations: DiBAC4(3) signal decrease can reflect depolarization or dye displacement; single strain (PAO1)

claim_text: HTP2 induces accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in P. aeruginosa cells.
direct_assay_types: ROS measurement (DCFH-DA fluorescence)
limitations: DCFH-DA is a general oxidative stress probe; source of ROS (bacterial vs. peptide-generated) not distinguished; single strain

claim_text: ROS induced by HTP2 may damage DNA, RNA, proteins, and membrane lipids of P. aeruginosa.
limitations: No direct measurement of ROS-mediated macromolecular damage; extrapolated from citation to general ROS biology

claim_text: HTP2 interacts with both RNA and plasmid DNA, retarding their migration in gel electrophoresis.
direct_assay_types: nucleic acid gel retardation (binding) assay
limitations: Gel retardation shows binding but not the functional consequence; intracellular access not directly demonstrated

claim_text: HTP2's interaction with nucleic acids may inhibit DNA replication, transcription, and translation in P. aeruginosa.
limitations: No functional replication, transcription, or translation assays performed; inferred from nucleic acid binding result

claim_text: HTP2 inhibits biofilm formation of P. aeruginosa in a concentration-dependent manner, reducing biomass by ~24%, ~41%, and ~72% at 6.25, 12.5, and 25 μg/mL respectively.
direct_assay_types: biofilm formation assay (crystal violet staining)
limitations: Anti-biofilm mechanism (membrane disruption vs. signaling inhibition vs. growth inhibition) not distinguished; single strain (PAO1); sub-inhibitory concentrations not confirmed to be non-bactericidal

claim_text: HTP2 significantly inhibits swimming and swarming motility of P. aeruginosa at sub-MIC concentrations.
direct_assay_types: swimming motility assay, swarming motility assay (agar plate)
limitations: Mechanism of motility inhibition (flagella, flagellar gene expression, energy, etc.) not determined; single strain

claim_text: HTP2 inhibits pyocyanin production of P. aeruginosa, reducing output by ~9.6% and ~19.6% at 6.25 and 12.5 μg/mL respectively.
direct_assay_types: pyocyanin extraction and colorimetric quantification
limitations: Effect size is modest at tested concentrations; whether inhibition is direct (biosynthesis pathway) or indirect (growth rate reduction) not determined

claim_text: HTP2 inhibits elastase production/activity of P. aeruginosa, reducing it by ~7.7% (non-significant) and ~18.1% (significant) at 6.25 and 12.5 μg/mL respectively.
direct_assay_types: elastase activity assay (ECR substrate colorimetric)
limitations: Assay measures combined production and activity; lower dose effect not statistically significant (p > 0.05); mechanism of inhibition not determined

claim_text: HTP2 significantly reduced P. aeruginosa bacterial load and inhibited inflammatory infiltration in a mouse subcutaneous infection model, demonstrating in vivo antibacterial activity.
direct_assay_types: in vivo mouse subcutaneous infection model (CFU counting, H&E histology)
limitations: In vivo mechanism of action not dissected (host immune contribution not controlled); small group size (n=6); single dose and route tested

claim_text: The mechanism of action of cationic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) primarily involves disruption or displacement of the bacterial membrane, giving rise to a lower likelihood of resistance development compared to traditional antibiotics.
limitations: General background claim about AMPs cited from prior literature (Zasloff 2002, Hancock & Sahl 2006), not experimentally demonstrated for the peptoids studied here.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptoids display membrane permeability or interact with intracellular targets such as bacterial DNA.
limitations: Stated as prior literature knowledge in the introduction; not directly demonstrated for the specific peptoids synthesized in this study.

claim_text: Multiple cationic charges in cell-penetrating peptoids favour endosomal accumulation, while lipophilicity promotes mitochondrial localization.
limitations: Cited from prior work (Kölmel et al. 2012, 2014); serves as design rationale rather than being re-demonstrated experimentally in this paper.

claim_text: Peptoids 1 and 11 permeabilize the bacterial membrane of more than half the S. aureus ATCC 29737 population (54.6% and 54.4% SYTOX green-positive cells, respectively) at 1× MIC.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green uptake measured by flow cytometry)
limitations: Assessed at a single concentration (1× MIC) and single time point (2 h); only one S. aureus strain tested; SYTOX green detects compromised membranes but does not distinguish the mode of disruption.

claim_text: Peptoids 10 and 11 kill S. aureus through membrane disruption that precedes bactericidal activity, ultimately resulting in cell lysis and death.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green uptake, flow cytometry), time-concentration kill kinetics (CFU counts)
limitations: Temporal relationship between membrane damage and killing is inferred by combining two separate assays rather than measured in a single real-time experiment; causal direction is interpretive.

claim_text: Peptoid 1 kills S. aureus (and is cytotoxic to mammalian cells) by extensively lysing cell membranes, as evidenced by high SYTOX green uptake and rapid bactericidal activity at 1× MIC.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green uptake, flow cytometry), time-concentration kill kinetics (CFU counts)
limitations: Mammalian membrane lysis is inferred from the low selectivity ratio (SR = 2) and cytotoxicity data rather than directly visualised; non-selective lysis of both bacterial and mammalian membranes is a mechanistic interpretation, not independently verified.

claim_text: Peptoids 2, 5, and 6 kill S. aureus through a mechanism that does not primarily involve membrane permeabilization, implying at least one additional intracellular or non-membrane mechanism of action.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (SYTOX green uptake, flow cytometry), time-concentration kill kinetics (CFU counts)
limitations: The alternative mechanism is not identified or characterised; conclusion is based solely on the discordance between low SYTOX green uptake (<10% permeabilised cells) and confirmed bactericidal activity, not on a positive intracellular-target assay.

claim_text: The active peptoids selectively kill Gram-positive bacteria and mycobacteria but not Gram-negative E. coli because hydrophobicity enables insertion into Gram-positive membranes while charged lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane presents an additional electrostatic barrier that prevents peptoid entry.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (lack of activity against E. coli)
limitations: The mechanistic explanation (hydrophobicity-driven Gram-positive selectivity and LPS electrostatic barrier) is cited from prior AMP literature (references 24–26) and not directly tested; outer membrane penetration was not measured.

claim_text: Higher MICs against mycobacteria compared to S. aureus are attributable to the mycolic acid outer layer of mycobacteria, which renders them relatively more impermeable to antimicrobial agents.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (comparative MIC values across species in Table 1)
limitations: Mechanistic attribution to mycolic acid is cited from prior literature (reference 23), not experimentally demonstrated; alternative explanations (e.g., efflux pumps, altered target affinity) were not ruled out.

claim_text: The tetrameric peptoids (except peptoid 6) localize in the mitochondria of HeLa cells, indicating that their cell-penetrating mechanism targets the mitochondrial compartment rather than lysing the plasma membrane.
direct_assay_types: confocal microscopy with MitoTracker Green co-staining (Pearson correlation coefficients 0.75–0.957 for peptoids 1–5, 7–11)
limitations: Demonstrated in mammalian cells only; mitochondrial localisation within bacteria was not assessed; all peptoids carry a Rhodamine B label which itself has mitochondriotropic properties and may contribute to the observed localisation.

claim_text: The peptoids penetrate RAW 264.7 macrophages and accumulate in their mitochondria, suggesting a potential mechanism for reaching intracellular pathogens (e.g., M. tuberculosis) residing within macrophage granulomata.
direct_assay_types: confocal microscopy with MitoTracker Green co-staining in RAW 264.7 macrophages
limitations: Only localisation is demonstrated; antimicrobial efficacy against intracellular bacteria within macrophages was not tested; extrapolation from localisation to functional killing of intracellular pathogens is speculative.

claim_text: Malformin A1 induces cytotoxicity in HeLa cancer cells through epigenetic changes by modifying lysine residues of histone H3 and H4 via acetylation or methylation.
direct_assay_types: immunofluorescence staining for histone modifications (H3K9me2, H3K9me3, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, H4K5ac, H4K16ac)
limitations: Immunofluorescence measures correlation between histone mark changes and cytotoxicity; no direct causal mechanistic experiment (e.g., rescue assay, enzyme inhibition assay) was performed; histone changes are downstream readouts, not proven causal drivers

claim_text: Malformin A1 upregulates H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 in HeLa cells, which may suppress transcription of oncogenes linked to carcinogenesis.
direct_assay_types: immunofluorescence staining
limitations: Suppression of oncogene transcription is inferred from published literature on H3K9me2/me3 biology; no gene expression or transcriptomics data presented; causal link not directly demonstrated

claim_text: Malformin A1 upregulates H4K16ac in HeLa cells, consistent with reduced genomic instability and DNA damage response restoration, supporting its cytotoxic chemotherapeutic activity.
direct_assay_types: immunofluorescence staining
limitations: DNA damage response improvement is inferred from published H4K16ac biology; no DNA damage or genomic stability assays performed in this study

claim_text: Malformin A1 downregulates H3K27me3 (at 10 ng/mL), which may inhibit proliferation of cancerous cells by reducing PcG-complex-mediated gene repression associated with cancer metastasis.
direct_assay_types: immunofluorescence staining
limitations: Anti-proliferative interpretation is inferred from published PcG/H3K27me3 biology; no proliferation, metastasis, or PcG protein level assays conducted; effect seen only at 10 ng/mL, not 100 ng/mL

claim_text: Malformin A1 downregulates H3K27ac (at 100 ng/mL) and H4K5ac (at 100 ng/mL) in HeLa cells, supporting its chemotherapeutic activity by reducing marks associated with cancer severity and faulty DNA replication.
direct_assay_types: immunofluorescence staining
limitations: Mechanistic interpretation relies on published literature; no direct DNA replication, chromatin compaction, or transcriptional assays performed; concentration-dependent effects differ for H3K27me3 vs H3K27ac/H4K5ac

claim_text: The high anti-HIV potency of GLRC-2 is likely due to its high hydrophobicity, as the three most active GLRC peptides showed HIV inhibitory activities proportional to hydrophobicity measured by HPLC retention time.
limitations: Correlation holds only for the three most potent GLRC peptides; authors explicitly note it 'could not be extended to all the peptides'; hydrophobicity-potency correlation does not establish causality or identify a molecular target.

claim_text: GLRC-2 may act on viral membranes, by analogy to the HIV-inhibitory cyclotide cycloviolacin Y5, which was proposed to act on viral membranes and is also the most hydrophobic member of its family.
limitations: Authors explicitly state 'whether GLRC-2 acts by the same mechanism remains to be established'; no membrane disruption or fusion assays were performed; the analogy is to a structurally unrelated peptide class.

claim_text: Positively charged residues (Arg/Lys) are important for anti-Gram-negative (E. coli) activity of GLRC peptides, as GLRC-7 with the fewest positive charges was the least active against E. coli.
limitations: Inference drawn from a single outlier peptide (GLRC-7) that also differs from others in length and loop size; multiple co-varying structural parameters prevent clean attribution to charge alone; no direct membrane or electrostatic interaction assay performed.

claim_text: High hydrophobic content contributes to activity against Gram-positive bacteria (B. subtilis), as GLRC-6, with the highest hydrophobic residue percentage (50%) among the GLRC peptides, was the only member with moderate activity against B. subtilis.
limitations: Single-peptide observation; GLRC-6 also differs from other peptides in sequence and terminal truncation; no mechanistic assay (e.g., membrane depolarization, dye leakage) performed to confirm membrane-targeting mechanism.

claim_text: The peptides kill Candida cells within minutes, consistent with the rapid membrane-disrupting action of short cationic amphipathic α-helical antimicrobial peptides.
direct_assay_types: colony forming unit determination, rhodamine 6G efflux time course
limitations: Time course demonstrated only for LL-III, LL-III/12, and HAL-1/10; >95% cell death at 1 min confirmed by CFU plating but not for all analogs.

claim_text: AMP treatment causes rapid efflux of rhodamine 6G from loaded Candida cells, with >80% of the dye released within 1 minute, indicating disruption of membrane barriers.
direct_assay_types: rhodamine 6G efflux (spectrofluorometric and fluorescent microscopy)
limitations: Only tested with LL-III, LL-III/12, and HAL-1/10; rhodamine 6G efflux reflects membrane disruption but does not distinguish which specific membrane is disrupted first.

claim_text: AMP treatment permeabilizes the Candida plasma membrane sufficiently to allow entry of propidium iodide (a normally membrane-impermeant DNA-binding dye) into >90% of cells within 10 minutes.
direct_assay_types: propidium iodide staining, fluorescent microscopy
limitations: Explicitly demonstrated only for HAL-1/10 at 40 µM; 10-minute incubation used.

claim_text: AMP treatment permeabilizes the Candida plasma membrane sufficiently to allow nuclear DAPI staining in >90% of cells within 10 minutes, an event that requires membrane permeabilization in Candida (unlike mammalian cells).
direct_assay_types: DAPI staining, fluorescent microscopy
limitations: Explicitly demonstrated only for HAL-1/10 at 50 µM; authors note this Candida-specific impermeability is distinct from mammalian cells.

claim_text: The peptides disrupt not only the plasma membrane but also intracellular membrane barriers, as shown by redistribution of mitochondria-localized rhodamine 6G from uneven to uniform intracellular distribution before its release from cells at MIC concentrations.
direct_assay_types: rhodamine 6G efflux, fluorescent microscopy
limitations: Inference from fluorescence redistribution pattern; intracellular membrane identity not confirmed with organelle-specific markers; redistribution could reflect passive diffusion after initial plasma membrane breach.

claim_text: At sub-MIC concentrations the peptides do not easily enter intact Candida cells; multiple peptide molecules must cooperate to overcome membrane barriers, consistent with pore-forming models.
direct_assay_types: fluorescein-labeled peptide uptake (Fluo-LL-III, fluorescent microscopy)
limitations: Only Fluo-LL-III tested; pore-forming model invoked from cited literature, not directly demonstrated (e.g., by electrophysiology or lipid-vesicle leakage assays); Fluo-LL-III has ~4-fold lower antifungal activity than native LL-III.

claim_text: At MIC and above, co-addition of unlabeled AMP causes all Candida cells to become immediately and uniformly fluorescent when treated with Fluo-LL-III, demonstrating that the labeled peptide enters cells once membrane barriers are overcome.
direct_assay_types: fluorescein-labeled peptide uptake, fluorescent microscopy
limitations: Entry of Fluo-LL-III required co-addition of unlabeled LL-III or HAL-1/10 at MIC; whether labeled peptide itself contributes to killing or is a passive tracer not resolved.

claim_text: The killing mechanism is necrotic rather than apoptotic, based on rapid total membrane disruption and outflow of cell contents without evidence of regulated programmed cell death.
direct_assay_types: rhodamine 6G efflux, propidium iodide staining, DAPI staining, colony forming unit determination
limitations: Authors explicitly state they did not measure any apoptotic markers (caspases, AIF, metacaspase, annexin V, etc.); necrosis conclusion is by exclusion; short detection interval (10 min) used.

claim_text: The antifungal killing mechanism is not energy-dependent, as pretreatment with metabolic inhibitors NaN3 or NaCN does not affect peptide effectiveness.
direct_assay_types: metabolic inhibitor assay (NaN3, NaCN)
limitations: Data not shown in the paper; result only briefly mentioned; specific peptides and concentrations tested are not described.

claim_text: Programmed (apoptotic) cell death may occur at low AMP concentrations in a small fraction of cells, but this mechanism is considered unlikely for the peptides studied because they do not enter cells readily at sub-MIC concentrations.
limitations: Authors explicitly did not measure apoptotic markers; hypothesis is based on comparison with other AMPs in cited literature (melittin, lactoferrin, dermaseptins, plant defensins) and on negative fluorescent-peptide entry data at low concentrations.

claim_text: Fowlicidin-2, as a cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide, exerts nonspecific membrane-lytic antibacterial activity, making resistance development by bacteria extremely difficult.
limitations: Membrane-lytic activity is asserted for AMPs as a class and applied to fowlicidin-2 by category membership; no membrane permeabilization or membrane integrity assay was performed on fowlicidin-2 in this study.

claim_text: Fowlicidin-2 exerts potent lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-neutralizing activity, supporting its potential as an antisepsis agent.
limitations: LPS-neutralizing activity is cited from prior studies (Xiao et al, 2006 and 2009; references 8 and 9) and not experimentally demonstrated in the present study.

claim_text: The α-helical amphipathic structure of fowlicidin-2—with an N-terminal amphipathic helix and a more hydrophobic C-terminal helix—is proposed to underlie its cytotoxic activity against cancer cells, consistent with the general principle that increased α-helicity and mean hydrophobicity enhance AMP cytotoxicity toward cancer cells.
limitations: Authors explicitly state that 'the mechanism of action of the peptide on cancer cells requires further investigation'; structural features are invoked by analogy to other AMPs (references 9, 33, 34), not by direct mechanistic assay on fowlicidin-2.

claim_text: The hemolytic activity of recombinant fowlicidin-2 against human erythrocytes is dose-dependent, and differences in spatial (three-dimensional) structure between the recombinant and chemically synthesized forms may account for the higher EC50 observed in this study compared with prior reports.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (hemolysis via hemoglobin release assay)
limitations: Structural differences between recombinant and synthetic fowlicidin-2 are proposed but not confirmed; the authors state 'the underlying mechanism is unclear.'

claim_text: The target of surface-active antimicrobial peptides, including pleurocidin, appears to be the cellular lipid bilayer membrane.
limitations: Stated as 'appears to be'; no direct mechanistic assay performed in this paper; general inference from literature

claim_text: Pleurocidin's antibacterial activity correlates with its membrane-disrupting activity.
limitations: Attributed to cited prior work (Saint et al., 2002); not independently demonstrated in this paper

claim_text: L-pleurocidin causes membrane permeabilization (pore formation), as shown by strong calcein leakage from PC:cholesterol large unilamellar vesicles.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from liposomes)
limitations: Liposomes composed of PC:cholesterol (10:1 w/w) are a mammalian membrane model, not a bacterial membrane; mechanism against bacterial targets is not directly tested

claim_text: L-pleurocidin disrupts mammalian erythrocyte membranes, as evidenced by hemoglobin release from human red blood cells.
direct_assay_types: hemolysis assay (human RBCs)
limitations: Hemolysis assay measures disruption of mammalian cells; does not directly address mechanism against bacterial membranes

claim_text: D-pleurocidin does not effectively form pores in membranes, consistent with its dramatically reduced hemolytic activity relative to L-pleurocidin.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (calcein leakage from liposomes), hemolysis assay
limitations: Pore formation tested only in PC:cholesterol mammalian-model liposomes; reduced pore activity against mammalian-like membranes may not fully explain reduced antibacterial potency against bacterial membranes

claim_text: The degree of α-helicity is a major determinant of the difference in antibacterial activity between L-pleurocidin and D-pleurocidin, as D-Ple adopts a more helical structure than L-Ple yet shows lower antibacterial potency.
direct_assay_types: circular dichroism spectroscopy
limitations: Association between helicity and activity is correlational; causal mechanism is not established; greater helicity in D-Ple paradoxically associates with lower activity, so the direction of the relationship is not resolved

claim_text: Hydrophobicity is not responsible for the differential antibacterial activity between L-pleurocidin and D-pleurocidin, as both peptides show identical HPLC retention times.
direct_assay_types: reverse-phase HPLC
limitations: Eliminates hydrophobicity as explanatory variable but does not itself identify the operative mechanism; HPLC retention time is an indirect measure of hydrophobicity

claim_text: Most antimicrobial peptides are cationic, and this cationic character plays a key role in their antimicrobial activity.
limitations: Attributed to cited literature (Hancock 1998, Zasloff 2002, Brogden 2005, Maróti 2011); no mechanistic assay performed in this study.

claim_text: Some antimicrobial peptides bind to bacterial lipopolysaccharide, thereby preventing the effects of septic shock.
limitations: Cited from Giacometti et al. 2003; not tested in this study.

claim_text: Muramyl dipeptide acts as a NOD2 agonist that induces NF-κB and MAPK signaling, leading to production of antimicrobial and proinflammatory substances as part of its antibacterial mechanism.
limitations: Background immunomodulatory mechanism from prior literature; MDP derivatives in this study showed predominantly low direct antibacterial activity (MIC >512 µg/mL), so relevance of this pathway to the observed in vitro MIC results is unclear; MIC assays used were cell-free and cannot capture immunomodulatory effects.

claim_text: MDP stimulates macrophages to produce microbicidal oxygen radicals and secrete inflammatory cytokines (IL-1 and TNF-α), thereby increasing nonspecific host resistance to bacterial infection.
limitations: Cited mechanism from background literature; in vitro cell-free MIC assay system used in this study cannot reflect this host-mediated mechanism.

claim_text: Retro-tuftsin and tuftsin derivatives exert antibacterial effects in part by stimulating monocytes, macrophages, and neutrophils through immunomodulation.
limitations: Immunomodulatory basis cited from Wardowska et al. studies; cell-free MIC assays used here cannot capture immune-cell-dependent activity.

claim_text: Tuftsin supports site-specific delivery of antibiotics into macrophages, thereby enhancing the therapeutic effect against macrophage-based bacterial infections.
limitations: Cited from Gupta & Haq 2005 and animal model studies; not tested in this study; mechanism is indirect (carrier) rather than direct bactericidal activity.

claim_text: Anthraquinone analogs linked to retro-tuftsin residues (compounds 3a–3d) are proposed to act as topoisomerase inhibitors.
limitations: Design rationale from a prior publication (Dzierzbicka et al. 2006); no topoisomerase inhibition assay was performed in this study.

claim_text: The isopeptide bonds in the retro-tuftsin portion of compounds 3c and 3d reduce susceptibility to enzymatic hydrolysis, limiting activity-reducing degradation and likely contributing to their observed antimicrobial activity against S. aureus.
limitations: Structural reasoning only; no protease stability assay, degradation study, or control without isopeptide bonds was performed to test this explanation.

claim_text: Combining compounds with different mechanisms of action (e.g., immunomodulatory peptides with anthraquinones) may improve the clinical antibacterial efficacy of both components.
limitations: Explicitly stated as a hypothesis by the authors; no synergy or combination experiments were performed in this study.

claim_text: Duramycins B and C, duramycin, and cinnamycin all inhibit human phospholipase A2 (from PMN leukocytes and synovial fluid) with IC50 values in the micromolar range (~0.6–1.5 µM).
direct_assay_types: radiometric phospholipase A2 enzyme inhibition assay using [1-14C]oleate-labeled E. coli as substrate, IC50 determination from dose-response plots
limitations: Assay used only two human enzyme sources (PMN leukocytes and synovial fluid); selectivity against other phospholipase subtypes not reported here; mechanism of enzyme inhibition (competitive, allosteric, substrate sequestration) not determined

claim_text: At least one thioether (lanthionine/methyllanthionine) bridge is essential for phospholipase A2 inhibitory activity, because oxidation of all three thioether groups to sulfoxides (trisulfoxide 5) completely abolishes activity at concentrations up to 30 µM.
direct_assay_types: phospholipase A2 inhibition assay of chemically modified analog (trisulfoxide 5); identity confirmed by FAB-MS
limitations: Oxidation produces a mixture of diastereoisomers (confirmed by 1H NMR), so the loss of activity could reflect conformational disruption rather than direct thioether involvement; individual mono- or di-sulfoxide intermediates were not tested; does not distinguish which specific thioether bridge is required

claim_text: Thanatin and its analogues disrupt bacterial membranes, as shown by carboxyfluorocalcein leakage from negatively charged PC/PS liposomes, and this liposome disruption activity correlates with anti-Gram-positive antibacterial activity.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (liposome carboxyfluorocalcein leakage)
limitations: Maximum disruption was ≤40% even after >100 min incubation; PC/PS liposomes are an imperfect bacterial membrane mimic; correlation holds only for Gram-positive activity, not Gram-negative activity

claim_text: Thanatin and its analogues are considered to act by directly interacting with the Gram-positive bacterial cytoplasmic membrane, because Gram-positive bacteria lack an outer membrane barrier.
limitations: Inferred from bacterial cell-envelope architecture combined with liposome disruption correlation; no direct assay of cytoplasmic membrane interaction in intact bacteria was performed

claim_text: An additional mechanism beyond membrane disruption is likely responsible for the strong anti-Gram-negative activity of thanatin, because liposome disruption activity does not correlate with anti-Gram-negative antibacterial activity.
