limitations: No experimental evidence for the additional mechanism is presented; the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria may simply restrict liposome-model relevance rather than implicating a separate killing mechanism

claim_text: The disulfide bond of thanatin is essential for antibacterial activity, as shown by the Th6 analogue in which both cysteines were replaced by alanines, which exhibited no or negligible antibacterial activity against all bacterial strains tested.
limitations: Activity loss inferred solely from MIC data; alanine substitution removes the loop constraint and alters overall structure (Th6 showed random coil in SDS by CD), so the effect cannot be attributed solely to absence of the disulfide bond; no redox-control experiment (e.g., reduced native peptide) was reported

claim_text: Adoption of an α-helical conformation in the membrane-mimicking SDS environment is associated with higher membrane-disrupting activity and higher anti-Gram-positive antibacterial activity, as the analogue Th1 showed the greatest α-helical propensity in SDS and the highest liposome disruption and anti-Gram-positive potency among all peptides tested.
direct_assay_types: membrane permeabilization (liposome carboxyfluorocalcein leakage), CD spectroscopy in SDS
limitations: Evidence is correlative only; SDS micelles imperfectly mimic bacterial lipid bilayers; 3D structure of thanatin or Th1 in an actual membrane environment was not determined; the paper notes NMR in membrane-mimicking conditions would be needed to confirm the structural basis of activity

claim_text: Temporin-La and palustrin-Ca treatment of HeLa cells causes breached membrane integrity, cytoplasmic leakage, mitochondria vacuolization, cristae loss, and blurred boundaries.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy
limitations: Observed only at 10×MIC in a single cell line (HeLa) after 24 h; morphological readout only, no biochemical confirmation of downstream events.

claim_text: Antimicrobial peptides rely on amphiphilic α-helix structures to associate with prokaryotic lipid bilayers, forming transmembrane ion channels that cause cell leakage, mitochondrial failure, or activation of apoptotic signaling cascades.
limitations: General background claim attributed to the AMP class; no ion-channel or structural assay performed in this paper for temporin-La or palustrin-Ca.

claim_text: The selective cytotoxicity of antimicrobial peptides against tumor cells may be due to higher acidic phospholipid content in tumor cell membranes and reduced integrity of the cytoskeleton system.
limitations: Explicitly speculative ('may be due to'); no lipid-composition or cytoskeletal assay performed in this paper.

claim_text: Membrane insertion of antimicrobial peptides causes bilayer melting and membrane puncture, leading to leakage of intracellular contents, mitochondria vacuolization, cristae loss, chromosomal DNA breakage, and inhibition of chromosomal DNA synthesis.
direct_assay_types: transmission electron microscopy (partial support for membrane breach, cytoplasmic leakage, mitochondrial changes)
limitations: TEM supports morphological membrane and mitochondrial damage; chromosomal DNA breakage and DNA synthesis inhibition are asserted without direct measurement (no comet assay, BrdU, or equivalent).

claim_text: Another possible mechanism by which antimicrobial peptides kill tumor cells is induction of apoptosis.
limitations: Supported only by citation of a different peptide (DP1) in a different study; no apoptosis assay (annexin V, caspase activation, TUNEL) performed for temporin-La or palustrin-Ca.

claim_text: Temporin-La inhibits Gram-positive bacteria and cancer cells without damaging the membranes of healthy mammalian cells, as evidenced by the large separation between antitumor IC50 values and the hemolytic concentration.
direct_assay_types: MIC assay, MTT antitumor assay, hemolysis assay
limitations: Selectivity is inferred by comparing IC50/MIC vs HC50 across separate assays; mechanism for differential selectivity is not directly demonstrated.

claim_text: Pumilacidins A and B inhibit hog gastric H+, K+-ATPase in a concentration-dependent manner, with IC50 values of 2.7 and 3.2 µg/ml respectively, and are approximately 4-fold more potent than omeprazole or SCH 28080 in this assay.
direct_assay_types: enzyme inhibition assay (pNPP hydrolysis as ATP surrogate substrate)
limitations: Hog gastric enzyme used, not human; pNPP is a surrogate substrate, not the native ATP substrate; assay performed at fixed pH 7.4 and KCl conditions that may not reflect the gastric luminal environment; only IC50 reported, no kinetic mode-of-inhibition (competitive/non-competitive) determined

claim_text: H+, K+-ATPase inhibition is implicated as the mechanistic basis for pumilacidin B's antiulcer activity, as the compound both inhibits the proton pump in vitro and significantly reduces Shay ulcer formation in rats at 100 mg/kg subcutaneously.
limitations: The paper juxtaposes the two findings but does not explicitly assert causation; the in vivo antiulcer effect could involve additional or alternative mechanisms (e.g., cytoprotection, mucus secretion); only pumilacidin B was tested in vivo; pharmacokinetic data and gastric tissue drug levels are absent

claim_text: The cyclic lactone (depsipeptide) structure is required for biological activity, as linear peptides generated by alkaline hydrolysis of the lactone linkage are biologically inactive.
limitations: Which specific biological activity (antiviral, ATPase inhibition, or antiulcer) was tested on the linear derivatives is not stated; the conformational or chemical basis for loss of activity is not investigated; only alkaline hydrolysis products were tested, not other ring-opened analogs

claim_text: RP 71955 inhibited the HIV-1 aspartyl protease with an IC50 of 1 to 3 µg/ml.
direct_assay_types: fluorometric protease inhibition assay
limitations: IC50 range spans 3-fold; assay details are cited to a companion reference (Hirel et al., 1990) rather than described here; no selectivity data against host aspartic proteases reported.

claim_text: RP 71955 inhibited the production of reverse transcriptase with an IC50 of 4 µg/ml.
limitations: The paper does not describe the assay format or distinguish between inhibition of RT enzymatic activity versus inhibition of RT production as a downstream consequence of protease inhibition; the latter interpretation is consistent with the paper's stated mechanism (protease blockade → immature virions lacking processed RT).

claim_text: RP 71955 was active in a T-lymphocyte HIV-1 infection assay, as measured by inhibition of the cytopathogenic effect of the virus, with an IC50 of 35 µg/ml.
direct_assay_types: cytopathogenic effect inhibition (cell-based)
limitations: Data attributed to a personal communication (A. Bousseau) and not published; cell-based CPE assay measures a downstream composite endpoint and does not distinguish the molecular target responsible for antiviral effect; IC50 is ~10–35× higher than the cell-free protease IC50, suggesting poor cell penetration, off-target activity, or a different primary mechanism in the cellular context.

claim_text: Tylopeptins A and B, as peptaibols, exert their antibiotic activity via the formation of amphipathic helices that interact with phospholipid bilayers, perturbing membrane permeability by forming voltage-gated ion channels.
limitations: No direct mechanistic assays were performed on tylopeptins A or B in this study; the mechanism is attributed by class membership—the paper identifies tylopeptins as peptaibols and cites established peptaibol literature (refs 1–4) for the ion-channel mechanism. The claim is not validated here for these specific compounds.

claim_text: The increase in net positive charge (from −1 to +1) and hydrophobicity ratio of M-Brucin (from 36% to 40%) caused its specific antibacterial activity against the gram-positive bacteria, S. epidermidis and S. pyogenes.
limitations: Causal attribution inferred from comparison of physicochemical properties across variants; no direct mechanistic assay performed; correlation between charge/hydrophobicity changes and activity does not establish mechanism.

claim_text: The enhanced inhibitory activity against S. epidermidis of M-Brucin may be due to the increase in its hydrophobicity, since there is evidence that antimicrobial activity increases linearly with increases in peptide hydrophobicity in similar peptides.
limitations: Authors explicitly state this is speculative ('may due to'); supporting evidence is from external studies on different peptides, not direct assay on M-Brucin.

claim_text: Electrostatic interaction promotes the adsorption of AMPs onto the microbial membrane, and the positive charge of M-Brucin is relevant to its antibacterial activity.
limitations: General AMP principle cited from literature (Nikken et al., 2013), not demonstrated for M-Brucin specifically; no membrane-binding or adsorption assay performed.

claim_text: The interaction with the bacterial cell wall should be further investigated to understand the mechanism of its antibacterial action.
limitations: This is an explicit statement by the authors that the mechanism is unknown and untested; no mechanistic assay was conducted.

claim_text: Siamycins I and II inhibit HIV-induced syncytia formation, as they were identified and monitored throughout isolation using a syncytia inhibition assay (SIA).
direct_assay_types: syncytia inhibition assay (SIA)
limitations: SIA measures a cell-fusion outcome; the paper does not identify the molecular step targeted (e.g., receptor binding, membrane fusion, viral entry). The assay result is used as a bioactivity readout, not a mechanistic probe.

claim_text: Siamycins I and II exhibit selective antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Micrococcus luteus, Bacillus subtilis) with no activity against Gram-negative species tested.
direct_assay_types: MIC determination (nutrient agar, 32°C, 18h)
limitations: The Gram-positive selectivity pattern is documented but no mechanism is proposed or tested in this paper; the basis of selectivity (e.g., outer membrane exclusion, specific target) is not addressed.

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 induces apoptosis in MCF-7 human breast adenocarcinoma cells via the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, as evidenced by activation of caspase-9.
direct_assay_types: caspase luminescence assay (Caspase-Glo 9), annexin V-FITC/PI apoptosis assay
limitations: Intrinsic pathway assignment rests solely on caspase-9 activation; upstream mitochondrial events (cytochrome c release, Bcl-2 family changes, mitochondrial membrane potential) were not measured in this study.

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 activates caspase-3/7 (executioner caspases) in MCF-7 cells in a time-dependent manner at 12, 24, and 48 hours.
direct_assay_types: caspase luminescence assay (Caspase-Glo 3/7)
limitations: Caspase-3 and -7 activities are measured together and cannot be distinguished by the assay used; no protein-level confirmation (e.g., Western blot for cleaved caspase-3).

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 does not meaningfully activate caspase-8 in MCF-7 cells, indicating the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway is not the primary apoptotic route.
direct_assay_types: caspase luminescence assay (Caspase-Glo 8)
limitations: Absence of significant caspase-8 activation at the tested time points does not fully exclude extrinsic pathway involvement at other concentrations or later time points.

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 causes concentration-dependent inhibition of MCF-7 cell proliferation, with an IC50 of 20 µg/mL at 72 hours.
direct_assay_types: MTT cell viability assay
limitations: MTT measures metabolic activity as a proxy for viability; does not distinguish cytostatic from cytotoxic effects.

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 induces predominantly early apoptosis (73.67% at 24 h) that transitions toward late apoptosis over time in MCF-7 cells, with apoptotic death peaking between 48 and 72 hours.
direct_assay_types: annexin V-FITC/PI apoptosis assay (fluorescence microscopy)
limitations: Fluorescence microscopy-based cell counting (200 cells per sample) is lower throughput and more operator-dependent than flow cytometry; no flow cytometric confirmation presented.

claim_text: Hepcidin TH1-5 may induce both apoptosis and inflammation in cancer cells, based on prior reports of caspase-7 downregulation at the gene-expression level in HeLa cells.
limitations: This claim is extrapolated from a cited external study (Chang et al., 2011) on a different cell line (HeLa); no inflammation or gene-expression assays were performed in the present study.

claim_text: The molecular target of goadsporin is apparently specific to streptomycetes and not common to other organisms such as DNA, protein kinases, or ribosomes.
limitations: Absence of activity against non-streptomycetes and absence of protein kinase C inhibition or apoptosis induction in mammalian cells are used as negative evidence; actual target identity is not established.

claim_text: Goadsporin acts on a common regulation pathway for sporulation and secondary metabolism shared across streptomycetes.
limitations: Inferred solely from the breadth of phenotypic response (36/42 strains); no molecular pathway component was identified or tested.

claim_text: Goadsporin growth inhibition at high concentrations is caused by premature induction of aerial hyphae formation before sufficient substrate mycelium development.
limitations: Presented as a proposed explanation for the ring-shaped inhibition zone; no direct developmental time-course or genetic evidence is provided.

claim_text: Goadsporin may not permeate the cell membrane of its producing strain, explaining why the producer does not respond to exogenously added goadsporin.
limitations: Speculative; intracellular accumulation in the producer is observed but membrane impermeability is not directly measured; non-response could also reflect target-level resistance or desensitization.

claim_text: Feglymycin shares the rare 3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine and 4-hydroxyphenylglycine residues with known HIV replication inhibitors RPI-856 (an HIV-1 protease inhibitor) and chloropeptin (a gp120–CD4 binding inhibitor), implying feglymycin may act via HIV-1 protease inhibition or blockade of gp120–CD4 binding.
limitations: The paper explicitly states 'The molecular mechanism of the antiviral activity has not yet been investigated.' The implied mechanistic analogy rests solely on shared rare amino acid residues with structurally related natural products; feglymycin was not tested in any protease inhibition or gp120-CD4 binding assay.

claim_text: The phenolic hydroxyl group of the tyrosine residue is essential for the antifungal activity of iturin A, mycosubtilin, and bacillomycin L, as substitution of this residue by methyl or acetyl groups abolishes activity across all concentrations tested.
limitations: Structure-activity relationship inference only; direct functional role of the phenolic group (e.g., receptor binding, membrane insertion) is not mechanistically demonstrated; same conclusion drawn by analogy to prior antibacterial SAR data

claim_text: Iturin A, mycosubtilin, and bacillomycin L exert their antifungal activity by interacting with the yeast cytoplasmic membrane, as reversal of activity by membrane lipids implies the antibiotic must bind membrane lipid components to act.
direct_assay_types: lipid antagonism/reversal-of-inhibition assay
limitations: Lipid antagonism in liquid culture is consistent with membrane interaction but does not directly demonstrate it; protoplast lysis and membrane permeabilization data cited are from prior bacterial (M. luteus) studies not replicated in the yeast system tested here

claim_text: A polar interaction between the antibiotics and cholesterol accounts for cholesterol being the strongest lipid antagonist, as cholesterol methyl ether, cholesterol acetate, and cholesterol stearate (which block or replace the free hydroxyl) show little or no inhibitory effect.
limitations: Inferred purely from comparative antagonism data with cholesterol derivatives; no direct binding measurements; solubility and partitioning differences among derivatives are not controlled for

claim_text: The cis-configuration of unsaturated fatty acids allows them to wrap around the antibiotic molecule into a compact complex, thereby preventing the antibiotic from reaching its membrane target and explaining why cis- but not trans-unsaturated fatty acids are inhibitory.
limitations: Purely speculative structural model; no direct evidence (e.g., NMR, calorimetry, binding assays) is presented; supported only by the differential inhibitory effect of cis- vs. trans-isomers in the antagonism assay

claim_text: The position of the double bond in the hydrocarbon chain of cis-unsaturated fatty acids determines the degree of inhibition of antifungal activity, as oleic acid, cis-vaccenic acid, and petroselinic acid (different positional isomers) show different inhibitory profiles across the three antibiotics.
limitations: Comparative inhibition data only; chain length differences co-vary with double-bond position, so the specific contribution of bond position versus chain length is not isolated

claim_text: The carboxyl group of fatty acids participates in the interaction specifically with bacillomycin L but not with iturin A or mycosubtilin, as esterification of fatty acids reduces their inhibitory effect against bacillomycin L but not against the other two antibiotics.
limitations: Inferred from differential SAR of lipid inhibitors; esterification also alters hydrophilicity and solubility, which are not separately controlled; mechanistic basis for the antibiotic-selectivity of this effect is unexplained

claim_text: The inhibitory effect of phospholipids on antifungal activity depends on both the nature of the polar headgroup and the fatty acid moiety, with phosphatidyl choline inhibiting iturin A and bacillomycin L while diphosphatidyl glycerol inhibits bacillomycin L and mycosubtilin.
direct_assay_types: lipid antagonism/reversal-of-inhibition assay
limitations: Structural correlations are descriptive; the molecular basis for antibiotic-selectivity of individual phospholipids is not explained; only a limited panel of phospholipids was tested

claim_text: The lipid-antibiotic complex formed in solution cannot interact with the yeast membrane, which is why exogenous lipids reverse antifungal activity.
limitations: Mechanistic model proposed by the authors with no direct structural or biochemical evidence; the existence of a discrete complex is assumed, not demonstrated
